    return c, np.array([10 * np.log10(X[(f >= fc / 2 ** .5) & (f < fc * 2 ** .5)].sum() + 1e-12) for fc in c])

def main():
    cut = float(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else -3; fq = float(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 3000
    bt, (v, sing) = beat(), vocal()
    v *= 10 ** ((lufs(bt) - 4 - lufs(v[sing])) / 20)       # vocal sits 4 LU under the beat while singing (a dense mix)
    bt2 = peq(bt, fq, cut, 1.0)
    c, B = bands(bt, sing); _, V = bands(v, sing); _, B2 = bands(bt2, sing)
    print(f"Vocal minus beat, per octave band, while the vocal sings. Cut on the beat: {cut:g} dB at {fq:g} Hz, Q 1")
    print(f"{'band':>8}{'before':>9}{'after':>9}")
    for fc, b1, vv, b2 in zip(c, B, V, B2):
        print(f"{fc:>6.0f} Hz{vv - b1:>8.1f}{vv - b2:>9.1f}" + ("   <- beat louder here" if vv - b1 < -0.5 else ""))
    print(f"\nBeat loudness: {lufs(bt):.2f} LUFS before, {lufs(bt2):.2f} after ({lufs(bt2) - lufs(bt):+.2f} LU)")
    print(f"Full mix:      {lufs(bt + v):.2f} LUFS before, {lufs(bt2 + v):.2f} after ({lufs(bt2 + v) - lufs(bt + v):+.2f} LU)")
    dyn = np.where(sing, bt2, bt); gap = ~sing
    print(f"Cut only while the vocal sings (sidechained dynamic EQ): beat between phrases {lufs(dyn[gap]) - lufs(bt[gap]):+.2f} LU")
    print(f"Turning the whole vocal up 3 dB instead: full mix {lufs(bt + v * 10 ** (3/20)) - lufs(bt + v):+.2f} LU, and the vocal gains 3.0 dB in every band, mud included")

if __name__ == "__main__": main()
$ python3 mask_check.py
Vocal minus beat, per octave band, while the vocal sings. Cut on the beat: -3 dB at 3000 Hz, Q 1
    band   before    after
   250 Hz    -2.0     -2.0   <- beat louder here
   500 Hz    -0.0      0.1
  1000 Hz    -0.6     -0.2   <- beat louder here
  2000 Hz    -3.3     -1.5   <- beat louder here
  4000 Hz    -2.7     -0.6   <- beat louder here
  8000 Hz   -10.9    -10.5   <- beat louder here

Beat loudness: -11.35 LUFS before, -11.72 after (-0.38 LU)
Full mix:      -10.59 LUFS before, -10.91 after (-0.31 LU)
Cut only while the vocal sings (sidechained dynamic EQ): beat between phrases +0.00 LU
Turning the whole vocal up 3 dB instead: full mix +0.66 LU, and the vocal gains 3.0 dB in every band, mud included

### What the numbers say
Before the cut, the beat is 3.3 dB louder than the vocal at 2 kHz and 2.7 dB louder at 4 kHz. That’s the range the words need. After a 3 dB cut on the beat, the vocal is only 1.5 and 0.6 dB under it there. It got back 1.8 and 2.1 dB right where it matters, and nothing changed at 250 Hz.
Look at what the cut cost the beat. Its loudness dropped from −11.35 to −11.72 LUFS, just 0.38 LU, and the full mix only moved 0.31 LU. Most of a beat’s loudness sits in the low end, so a cut up at 3 kHz barely shows on a loudness meter. It does show in how clearly you can follow the words.
Now the other way. Turning the whole vocal up 3 dB makes the full mix 0.66 LU louder. Every band of the vocal goes up 3 dB, including the low mids where vocals and beats tend to build up mud. That’s more level on the master and more for the limiter to work with, and the words still aren’t much easier to follow than with the cut.
These are synthetic signals, so treat the exact numbers as a model. On a real song the busiest range might sit at 2.5 kHz or 4 kHz. The idea is the same.

### Only cut while the vocal sings
The last line of the output is the trick that makes this almost free. Put the cut on a dynamic EQ and key it from the vocal, so the band only dips while someone is singing. Between phrases the beat is back to full level, +0.00 LU in our test. The drop and the instrumental breaks keep all their sparkle, and the vocal still gets its space when it needs it.

### How to do it in your session
1. Find the clash. Put an analyzer on the beat bus and one on the vocal, or one that overlays both. Look at 1 to 5 kHz while the vocal sings. Where the beat sits above the voice is where to cut.
2. Cut on the beat bus, not on every track. Start with 2 to 3 dB, Q around 1, at the center of the clash. Wider and gentler usually sounds more natural than a narrow notch.
3. Make it dynamic if you can. Sidechain the band from the vocal, aiming for 2 to 3 dB of reduction on sung parts and none between them.
4. Compare at matched loudness. The cut makes the beat a hair quieter, and quieter often sounds worse at first. Match levels before you decide, the same trap as in your mix sounding better loud.
5. Then set the vocal level. Once the words come through, you may find the vocal can come down a dB. How loud the vocal should sit has a way to measure it.
If the vocal still sounds lost after this, check the vocal’s own effects. A wide, dark reverb return is often what’s smearing it, which filtering the reverb return deals with. And if your fix ends up being a brighter vocal, keep an ear on the esses, since harsh S’s get louder after mastering.
For the A/B, one easy way is to bounce the mix both ways and drop them into CoProducer’s A/B, which plays them at matched loudness so the quieter version doesn’t lose just for being quieter. You can also run each one through the analyzer to check the integrated LUFS before and after.
Q: Why can I hear my vocal but not understand the words?
A: Usually the beat is louder than the voice around 2 to 4 kHz, where consonants and vowel detail live. In our test the beat was 3.3 dB over the vocal at 2 kHz and 2.7 dB over it at 4 kHz.
Q: Should I boost the vocal or cut the beat?
A: Cut the beat first. In our test a 3 dB cut on the beat at 3 kHz got the vocal back about 2 dB where the words live and only dropped the beat 0.38 LU. Turning the vocal up 3 dB made the whole mix 0.66 LU louder and raised the mud too.
Q: What frequency should I cut to make room for vocals?
A: Look for where the beat sits above the vocal between about 1 and 5 kHz while the vocal sings. 2 to 4 kHz is a common range. Start with a 2 to 3 dB cut with a Q of about 1.
Q: What is a sidechained dynamic EQ for vocals?
A: An EQ band on the beat that only cuts when the vocal is playing, triggered by the vocal track. The beat keeps its full brightness between phrases.

---

## Sidechain pumping out of time? Set the release from the tempo
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/sidechain-pumping-out-of-time-set-release-to-tempo.html
Section: Low end · 29 October 2026 · 7 min
Summary: Why a sidechain duck feels late or makes the bass vanish: the release doesn’t fit the tempo, so the bass is still ducked when the next kick hits. Measured at 140 and 90 BPM, with a script that shows how much each release time leaves behind.

If a sidechain pump sounds late rather than just long, check latency first: lookahead, plug-in delay compensation and a key signal that arrives behind the kick will all shift the duck, whatever the release is. Once the timing lines up, work the release from the tempo: one beat is 60,000 ÷ BPM milliseconds (428.6 ms at 140 BPM), the bass should be fully back before the next kick, and in our test that took a release of roughly a quarter to a third of a beat.
You key the bass off the kick, set a few dB of gain reduction, and the groove should start breathing. Instead it does something strange. The bass seems smaller overall, the pump feels smeared, and on some beats it feels like the duck is happening a little behind the kick instead of with it.
Nine times out of ten that’s the release. Attack decides how fast the bass gets out of the way. Release decides when it comes back. If it comes back too slowly, the next kick shows up while the bass is still on its way up, and the compressor ducks it again from wherever it was.

### The beat sets the deadline
A beat lasts 60,000 divided by the BPM, in milliseconds. At 140 BPM that’s 428.6 ms. At 90 BPM it’s 666.7 ms. On a four-on-the-floor kick, that’s the whole window the bass has to duck and come all the way back. Same math as setting a delay from the tempo in your delay sounds off the beat, just pointed at a compressor. There is a table of starting release times from 80 to 160 BPM further down.
To see what different release times leave behind, we wrote duck_check.py. It keys a plain compressor from a kick on every beat, ducks 6 dB at the hit with a 1 ms attack, and tries a range of release times. For each one it prints how much the bass is still ducked right before the next kick, and how much of each beat the bass spends back within 1 dB of full level:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""How much is the bass still ducked when the next kick lands? Sidechain release vs tempo.
  python3 duck_check.py [bpm] [depth_db]
Keys a simple log-domain compressor (1 ms attack) from a four-on-the-floor kick and reports, for each
release time: gain reduction left at the next hit, and how much of each beat the bass spends within 1 dB
of full level. Release here is the one-pole time constant (to ~63% recovered); plugins label it differently."""
import sys, numpy as np

SR = 48000
def kick_pattern(bpm, beats=16):
    beat = int(SR * 60 / bpm); n = beat * beats; t = np.arange(int(0.12 * SR)) / SR
    hit = np.exp(-t / 0.03)                                # key signal: a 120 ms kick envelope
    x = np.zeros(n)
    for b in range(beats): x[b * beat:b * beat + len(hit)] += hit
    return x, beat

def duck(key, depth_db, att_ms, rel_ms):
    target = -depth_db * key / key.max()                   # full depth at the kick's peak
    a, r = np.exp(-1 / (SR * att_ms / 1000)), np.exp(-1 / (SR * rel_ms / 1000))
    g, out = 0.0, np.empty_like(target)
    for i, tg in enumerate(target):
        c = a if tg < g else r                             # falling = attack, rising = release
        g = c * g + (1 - c) * tg; out[i] = g
    return out

def main():
    bpm = float(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 140
    depth = float(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 6
    key, beat = kick_pattern(bpm)
    print(f"{bpm:g} BPM, one beat = {beat / SR * 1000:.1f} ms, duck depth {depth:g} dB, attack 1 ms")
    print(f"{'release':>9}  {'still ducked at next kick':>25}  {'beat back within 1 dB':>21}")
    for rel in (25, 50, 100, 150, 250, 400, 800):
        g = duck(key, depth, 1, rel)
        last = g[-2 * beat:-beat]                          # a settled beat, late in the loop
        left = g[-beat - 1]                                # just before the next kick
        free = (last > -1).mean() * 100
        print(f"{rel:>6} ms  {left:>22.2f} dB  {free:>20.0f} %")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
$ python3 duck_check.py 140
140 BPM, one beat = 428.6 ms, duck depth 6 dB, attack 1 ms
  release  still ducked at next kick  beat back within 1 dB
    25 ms                   -0.00 dB                    79 %
    50 ms                   -0.00 dB                    71 %
   100 ms                   -0.11 dB                    52 %
   150 ms                   -0.39 dB                    33 %
   250 ms                   -1.11 dB                     0 %
   400 ms                   -2.02 dB                     0 %
   800 ms                   -3.34 dB                     0 %
Read the middle column first. With a 100 ms release, the bass is 0.11 dB down when the next kick hits. That’s fully back for any ear. At 150 ms it’s 0.39 dB down, still fine. At 250 ms it’s 1.11 dB down, and the right-hand column drops to zero: the bass never gets back within 1 dB of its real level during the whole beat. At 800 ms it sits 3.34 dB down permanently.
That last case is the one that fools people. With a release that long, there’s barely any pump at all. The compressor just holds the bass a few dB lower all the time, so it sounds like the bass got quieter, and the natural move is to turn it up. Then the master gets louder and the groove still doesn’t breathe.

### Same settings, slower song
Here’s the same check at 90 BPM:
$ python3 duck_check.py 90
90 BPM, one beat = 666.7 ms, duck depth 6 dB, attack 1 ms
  release  still ducked at next kick  beat back within 1 dB
    25 ms                   -0.00 dB                    87 %
    50 ms                   -0.00 dB                    81 %
   100 ms                   -0.01 dB                    69 %
   150 ms                   -0.08 dB                    57 %
   250 ms                   -0.43 dB                    32 %
   400 ms                   -1.10 dB                     0 %
   800 ms                   -2.46 dB                     0 %
At 90 BPM, a 250 ms release leaves 0.43 dB and gives the bass about a third of each beat at full level. That’s usable. Take the same preset to a 140 BPM track and it’s the 1.11 dB row with no recovery at all. A sidechain preset doesn’t know your tempo. If it sounded right on the last beat and wrong on this one, that’s probably why.

### Too fast is a problem too
At 25 to 50 ms, the bass is back for 71 to 79% of the beat at 140 BPM. That sounds like the answer, but the duck is so short it feels more like a gap than a pump. On low notes it can also get grainy. A 55 Hz bass cycle takes about 18 ms, so a release that short moves the gain within a cycle or two, and that bends the waveform. If the bass gets a little fuzzy when the sidechain is on, try a longer release before you blame the bass sound.

### Release time by BPM: a starting table
One beat is 60,000 ÷ BPM in milliseconds, and an eighth note is half of that. The last two columns are where we would start: a quarter to a third of the gap between kicks, which is where the bass came back in time in the 140 and 90 BPM runs above. They are starting points to check against the gain reduction meter, not rules.
BPM | Quarter note (kick every beat) | Eighth note (kick every half beat) | Start release, kick every beat | Start release, kick on eighths
80 | 750.0 ms | 375.0 ms | 188 to 250 ms | 94 to 125 ms
90 | 666.7 ms | 333.3 ms | 167 to 222 ms | 83 to 111 ms
100 | 600.0 ms | 300.0 ms | 150 to 200 ms | 75 to 100 ms
110 | 545.5 ms | 272.7 ms | 136 to 182 ms | 68 to 91 ms
120 | 500.0 ms | 250.0 ms | 125 to 167 ms | 62 to 83 ms
128 | 468.8 ms | 234.4 ms | 117 to 156 ms | 59 to 78 ms
130 | 461.5 ms | 230.8 ms | 115 to 154 ms | 58 to 77 ms
140 | 428.6 ms | 214.3 ms | 107 to 143 ms | 54 to 71 ms
150 | 400.0 ms | 200.0 ms | 100 to 133 ms | 50 to 67 ms
160 | 375.0 ms | 187.5 ms | 94 to 125 ms | 47 to 62 ms
Plugins label release differently, so the same number can behave differently in two compressors. Loop a bar and watch the meter reach zero just before each kick, then adjust by ear.

### How to set it in your session
1. Work out the beat. 60,000 ÷ BPM. If the kick plays every half beat, halve it. That’s the deadline.
2. Start around a quarter to a third of the beat. In our model that was the range where the bass came back right before the next hit: about 100 to 150 ms at 140 BPM, 150 to 250 ms at 90.
3. Watch the gain reduction meter, not the number. Plugins measure release differently, so the same 150 ms can behave differently in two compressors. Loop a bar and check that the meter touches zero just before each kick. If it never gets there, shorten the release.
4. Listen in context, then shape. Lengthen it until you hear the bass swell back in time with the groove, and stop before it misses the next hit. If your compressor has a hold control, a few ms of hold can keep the duck clean on long kicks.
5. Check the irregular parts. In trap and drill the kick pattern isn’t even. Set the release for the shortest gap between kicks that matter, then check the busy bars.
If the compressor is ducking more than it should on the 808 because the key signal is full of low end, that’s a related problem with its own fix in your bus compressor is pumping on the 808. And if you’re still deciding whether to sidechain at all, your kick and 808 are arguing in the same chair lays out the other options.

### When the kick is baked into a sample
Sometimes the kick you want to duck from is inside a loop or a flipped record, not on its own track. Keying from the whole loop doesn’t work well, because the snare and hats trigger the compressor too. One way around it is to split the drums out first, with something like NoDAW StemSplit, and key the sidechain from the drum stem. Low-pass the key around 150 Hz so mostly the kick drives it. The original drummer wasn’t on your grid, so the duck follows the record’s real kicks instead of where the grid thinks they are. There’s more on working with split drums in sampling from separated stems.
Tempo-synced volume shapers do the same job with a drawn curve instead of a compressor. The same rule holds there: the curve should be back at full level before the next hit.
Q: What release time should I use for sidechain compression?
A: Long enough that the bass swells back in time with the groove, short enough that it’s fully back before the next kick. In our 140 BPM test that was about 100 to 150 ms. At 250 ms the bass was still 1.11 dB ducked when the next kick hit.
Q: Why does my sidechain make the bass quieter instead of pumping?
A: The release is too long for the tempo. The bass never fully recovers between kicks, so the compressor keeps it a few dB down the whole time. In our test an 800 ms release at 140 BPM held it 3.34 dB down permanently.
Q: How do I calculate the beat length from BPM?
A: Divide 60,000 by the BPM to get one beat in milliseconds. 140 BPM is 428.6 ms and 90 BPM is 666.7 ms. Halve it if the kick plays on every eighth note.
Q: Can a sidechain release be too fast?
A: Yes. A very short release makes the duck feel like a gap instead of a pump, and on low notes it can add distortion because the gain moves within a cycle or two of the bass.
Q: What sidechain release time should I use at 120 BPM?
A: One beat at 120 BPM is 500 ms, so start with a release of about 125 to 167 ms if the kick plays on every beat, and about 62 to 83 ms if it plays on every eighth note. Then watch the gain reduction meter and shorten the release if it does not reach zero before the next kick.
Q: Why does my sidechain feel late even with a short release?
A: Check latency first. Lookahead, plug-in delay compensation and the way the key signal is routed can all shift the duck behind the kick, and a release time cannot fix that. Once the duck lands on the kick, set the release from the tempo: 60,000 ÷ BPM is the length of one beat in milliseconds.

---

## Fade-out drops off a cliff? Curve it, and fade after the limiter
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/fade-out-sounds-abrupt-curve-it-and-fade-after-the-limiter.html
Section: Mastering · 29 October 2026 · 7 min
Summary: Why a song fade-out seems to hang and then vanish: a straight-line fade loses only 6 dB in its first half, and a limiter after the fade eats the first few dB of it. Measured fade shapes and a limited master, with the script.

A fade-out that seems to hang and then suddenly disappear is usually a straight-line fade, often with a limiter after it. A linear fade only drops 6 dB in its first half, then falls from −20 dB to silence in the last tenth. A limiter that comes after the fade cancels out the first few dB of it. Use a curved fade that falls more evenly in decibels, and put the fade after the limiter so it moves from the first second.
The outro is the vibe. You draw a long fade so the song can float away. On playback it doesn’t float. For the first several seconds nothing seems to happen, then near the end it suddenly drops out like someone pulled the cable.
Two things usually cause that, and they often show up together: the shape of the fade, and where it sits in the chain.

### A straight line isn’t straight to your ears
Most DAWs draw a linear fade by default. It turns the volume down in equal steps of amplitude. Our ears don’t hear amplitude in equal steps. We hear something much closer to decibels, and in decibels a linear fade is lopsided. Here’s what fade_check.py measured for a 10-second fade in a few common shapes:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Fade-out shapes, and what a limiter does to a fade drawn in front of it.
  python3 fade_check.py
Part 1: level (dB) at each tenth of a 10-second fade for three common shapes.
Part 2: a dense synthetic 'master' driven 8 dB into a simple peak limiter, faded linearly over 10 s
either before the limiter or after it; short-term level per second, relative to the unfaded master."""
import numpy as np

SR = 48000
def db(x): return 20 * np.log10(np.maximum(x, 1e-12))
SHAPES = {"linear":        lambda p: 1 - p,
          "equal-power":   lambda p: np.cos(p * np.pi / 2),
          "dB to -40":     lambda p: np.where(p < 1, 10 ** (-40 * p / 20), 0.0),   # even steps in dB, then cut
          "dB to -60":     lambda p: np.where(p < 1, 10 ** (-60 * p / 20), 0.0)}

def limiter(x, ceiling_db=-1.0, rel_ms=100):
    c = 10 ** (ceiling_db / 20); need = np.minimum(1, c / np.maximum(np.abs(x), 1e-12))
    r, g, out = np.exp(-1 / (SR * rel_ms / 1000)), 1.0, np.empty_like(x)
    for i, n in enumerate(need):
        g = n if n < g else r * g + (1 - r) * n            # instant attack (clips nothing), smooth release
        out[i] = g
    return x * out

def master(seconds):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(7); n = int(SR * seconds); t = np.arange(n) / SR
    x = rng.standard_normal(n) * 0.25
    beat = (np.sin(2 * np.pi * 2.333 * t) > 0.6).astype(float)      # 140 BPM thumps on top
    x += 0.9 * beat * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 55 * t)
    return x / np.abs(x).max() * 10 ** (7 / 20)                      # peaks 8 dB over a −1 dBFS ceiling

def rms_db(x): return 10 * np.log10((x ** 2).mean() + 1e-20)

def main():
    print("Part 1: level at each point of a 10 s fade (dB)")
    print("  time  " + "".join(f"{k:>13}" for k in SHAPES))
    for p in np.linspace(0, 1, 11):
        print(f"  {p * 10:4.0f} s" + "".join((f"{v:>13.1f}" if v > -200 else f"{'silent':>13}") for v in (db(np.atleast_1d(f(p)))[0] for f in SHAPES.values())))
    print("  share of the fade below -20 dB" + "".join(f"{(db(f(np.linspace(0, 1, 10001))) < -20).mean() * 100:>12.0f}%" for f in SHAPES.values()))

    x = master(10); ramp = 1 - np.arange(len(x)) / len(x)
    ref = limiter(x)
    before, after = limiter(x * ramp), ref * ramp
    print("\nPart 2: linear 10 s fade on a master limited ~8 dB (dB vs the unfaded master)")
    print("  second   fade after limiter   fade before limiter")
    for s in range(10):
        sl = slice(s * SR, (s + 1) * SR)
        print(f"  {s:>4}-{s + 1:<2} {rms_db(after[sl]) - rms_db(ref[sl]):>14.1f} {rms_db(before[sl]) - rms_db(ref[sl]):>20.1f}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
$ python3 fade_check.py
Part 1: level at each point of a 10 s fade (dB)
  time         linear  equal-power    dB to -40    dB to -60
     0 s          0.0          0.0          0.0          0.0
     1 s         -0.9         -0.1         -4.0         -6.0
     2 s         -1.9         -0.4         -8.0        -12.0
     3 s         -3.1         -1.0        -12.0        -18.0
     4 s         -4.4         -1.8        -16.0        -24.0
     5 s         -6.0         -3.0        -20.0        -30.0
     6 s         -8.0         -4.6        -24.0        -36.0
     7 s        -10.5         -6.9        -28.0        -42.0
     8 s        -14.0        -10.2        -32.0        -48.0
     9 s        -20.0        -16.1        -36.0        -54.0
    10 s       silent       silent       silent       silent
  share of the fade below -20 dB          10%           6%          50%          67%
The linear fade is only 6 dB down at the halfway point. That’s about the difference between a verse and a chorus. Then it’s −14 dB at 8 seconds, −20 dB at 9, and silent at 10. In the last tenth of the fade it loses more than it lost in the first nine. That’s the cliff.
Equal-power is even more top-heavy. It’s built for crossfades, where two sounds need to keep the total level steady, not for ending a song. At 7 seconds it has only dropped 6.9 dB.
The curves that fall evenly in decibels sound like a steady walk away. But look at the bottom row. A fade that goes evenly to −60 dB spends 67% of its length below −20 dB. On a phone in a car, that part is basically silent, so a 10-second fade ends after about three. Going evenly to −40 spends half its length down there. A good fade-out usually lives between the straight line and those curves. Most DAWs offer exponential, logarithmic or adjustable curve shapes for exactly this.

### The limiter that eats your fade
The second problem is sneakier. If the fade is drawn on the mix bus, or on the tracks, and there’s a limiter after it on the master, the limiter fights the fade. While the music is hitting the ceiling, turning it down just means the limiter does less work. The level coming out barely changes.
We built a dense synthetic master, drove it about 8 dB into a simple peak limiter with a −1 dBFS ceiling, and applied the same 10-second linear fade in both places. This is the level of each second compared with the unfaded master:
Part 2: linear 10 s fade on a master limited ~8 dB (dB vs the unfaded master)
  second   fade after limiter   fade before limiter
     0-1            -0.4                 -0.1
     1-2            -1.4                 -0.4
     2-3            -2.5                 -0.8
     3-4            -3.7                 -1.2
     4-5            -5.2                 -1.8
     5-6            -6.9                 -3.0
     6-7            -9.1                 -4.5
     7-8           -12.0                 -7.7
     8-9           -16.2                -12.0
     9-10          -24.7                -19.8
With the fade after the limiter, the first three seconds drop 0.4, 1.4 and 2.5 dB. With the fade before it, they drop 0.1, 0.4 and 0.8 dB. Halfway through, the faded-before version is only 3.0 dB down instead of 6.9. The limiter quietly cancelled the first few dB of the fade, then had nothing left to cancel, and the rest of the fade happened all at once.
There’s a sound to it too. As the limiter lets go, the drums get some of their punch back, so the start of the fade can sound like the song opens up a bit before it gets quieter. That’s rarely what anyone wants in an outro.
Note: Our limiter is a simple model, and a real one will give different numbers. The direction is the point: any compressor or limiter after the fade fights the first part of it, and the harder it’s working, the more it eats.

### How to fade a song so it sounds like a fade
1. Put the fade last. Automate a gain plugin after the limiter on the master, or the master fader if your DAW puts it after the inserts. Then the fade starts moving the moment it starts.
2. Pick a curved shape. Start with an exponential or logarithmic fade and adjust it until the level seems to fall at the same speed the whole way. Trust your ears at a normal listening level, not the shape on screen.
3. Make the end land in silence. If your curve stops at −40 or −50 dB, add a short final fade to zero so there’s no click at the end. The same reason is covered in clicks at your edit points.
4. Let the effects fade with the music. Draw the fade in the session, so reverb and delay tails fade with everything else instead of ringing on after the music stops.
5. Sending it to mastering? Many engineers would rather get the song without the fade and do it themselves after their limiter. Send the unfaded version and note where the fade should start and how long it should be.

### Check that the body didn’t change
Moving the fade to the end of the chain shouldn’t change anything before the fade starts. To be sure, bounce the old and new versions and drop both into the CoProducer analyzer. It reads integrated LUFS and true peak on your own computer, so you can confirm the song itself still measures the same and only the outro changed. On an album, how long the fade takes also sets up the gap before the next song, which album consistency is a batch problem gets into.
Length is taste. Some fades take four bars, some take thirty seconds. Whatever length you pick, the shape and the order decide whether people hear a fade or a cutoff.
Q: Why does my fade-out sound abrupt at the end?
A: A linear fade drops only 6 dB in its first half, then falls from −20 dB to silence in the last tenth. A limiter after the fade makes it worse by cancelling the first few dB. Use a curved fade and put it after the limiter.
Q: Should I fade out before or after the limiter?
A: After. In our test, a fade placed before a limiter working about 8 dB moved only 0.8 dB in its first three seconds, against 2.5 dB when the fade came after the limiter.
Q: What fade curve is best for a song fade-out?
A: One that sounds like the level falls at a steady speed, usually somewhere between linear and an even-in-decibels curve. Exponential or logarithmic presets are a good starting point. Equal-power curves are made for crossfades, not fade-outs.
Q: Should I fade out the song before sending it to mastering?
A: Ask your engineer. Many prefer the unfaded version with a note on where the fade starts and how long it lasts, so they can fade after their own limiter.

---

## Why −18 dBFS? Gain staging into analog-style plugins
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/plugin-input-level-gain-staging-minus-18-dbfs.html
Section: Mixing · 28 October 2026 · 7 min
Summary: Why the level you hit an analog-modelled plugin with changes its sound, and why −18 dBFS keeps coming up. Measured on a simple saturation model: harmonics, THD and what five plugins in a row add up to. Script inside.

Gain staging still matters in a 32-bit float DAW because analog-modelled plugins react to how hard you hit them. Most are built so a signal around −18 dBFS RMS sits at their nominal level, 0 VU. Hit them 6 or 12 dB hotter and they add more distortion, mostly odd harmonics, and the effect stacks up across every plugin in the chain. Keep the average level near −18 dBFS going into each one, and use the plugin’s own drive control when you want the colour.
You load the same compressor emulation everyone raves about. On their videos it sounds thick and expensive. On your vocal it sounds a little fuzzy, a little crowded, and the meter barely moves no matter where you set the threshold. You start doubting your ears, then the plugin, then the whole mix.
Before you blame either, look at the level going in. If the vocal track is peaking near 0 dBFS and averaging around −8, you’re feeding that plugin about ten dB more than it was built to expect.

### Float doesn’t clip. The plugins still care
Inside a modern DAW the mix runs in floating point, so a track can go over 0 dBFS and come back down with nothing lost. That part is true, and we measured it in how much headroom to leave for mastering. It’s why people say gain staging doesn’t matter anymore.
But a plugin that models a console, a tape machine or an old compressor isn’t just passing numbers along. It’s copying a circuit that behaves differently when it’s pushed. To do that, it has to decide what level counts as normal. Many of them treat a sine somewhere between −20 and −14 dBFS RMS as 0 VU, and −18 dBFS is the most common choice. The manual usually says which. Anything above that, the model starts leaning into its curve.
So the question isn’t whether the file will clip. It’s whether you meant to drive the circuit.

### What one stage does at each level
To see it without any brand in the way, we wrote a plain saturation stage in drive_check.py: a slightly lopsided soft clipper, calibrated so −18 dBFS RMS is its nominal level. It’s a model, not a copy of any real plugin, but it bends the way analog-style stages tend to. Then we fed it a 55 Hz sine, roughly a low bass note, at six levels:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""How input level changes what an analog-style stage does to the sound.
The 'stage' is a slightly asymmetric tanh saturator, calibrated the way many analog-modelled
plugins are: a sine at -18 dBFS RMS is its nominal level (0 VU). It's a model, not any real plugin.
  python3 drive_check.py     run a 55 Hz sine from -30 to -6 dBFS RMS through the stage"""
import numpy as np
SR, F, NOMINAL, BIAS = 48000, 55.0, -18, 0.1

def stage(x):
    g = 10 ** (-NOMINAL / 20) / 8.0               # dBFS -> internal level; nominal sits low on the curve
    return (np.tanh(x * g + BIAS) - np.tanh(BIAS)) / g

def harmonics(y):
    Y = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(y * np.hanning(len(y)))); k = int(round(F * len(y) / SR))
    h = np.array([Y[n * k - 2:n * k + 3].max() for n in range(1, 10)])
    return np.sqrt((h[1:] ** 2).sum()) / h[0], 20 * np.log10(h[1:5] / h[0])

t = np.arange(SR * 2) / SR
print(f"{'input':>10s} {'vs 0 VU':>8s} {'THD':>8s} {'2nd':>7s} {'3rd':>7s} {'4th':>7s} {'5th':>7s} {'level change':>13s}")
for lvl in (-30, -24, -18, -12, -9, -6):
    x = np.sqrt(2) * 10 ** (lvl / 20) * np.sin(2 * np.pi * F * t)
    y = stage(x); thd, h = harmonics(y)
    change = 10 * np.log10((y ** 2).mean() / (x ** 2).mean())
    print(f"{lvl:+5d} dBFS {lvl - NOMINAL:+6d} dB {100 * thd:7.2f}% " + " ".join(f"{v:7.1f}" for v in h) + f" {change:+10.2f} dB")
print("harmonics in dB below the 55 Hz fundamental; input is sine RMS")


# Five of those stages in a row, the way a channel strip, a bus and a tape plugin stack up.
print(f"\nfive stages in series:  {'input':>10s} {'THD':>8s}")
for lvl in (-18, -12, -6):
    y = np.sqrt(2) * 10 ** (lvl / 20) * np.sin(2 * np.pi * F * t)
    for _ in range(5): y = stage(y)
    print(f"{'':23s} {lvl:+5d} dBFS {100 * harmonics(y)[0]:7.2f}%")
$ python3 drive_check.py
     input  vs 0 VU      THD     2nd     3rd     4th     5th  level change
  -30 dBFS    -12 dB    0.22%   -53.1   -76.0  -122.9  -150.5      -0.09 dB
  -24 dBFS     -6 dB    0.44%   -47.1   -64.0  -104.9  -126.5      -0.10 dB
  -18 dBFS     +0 dB    0.91%   -41.2   -52.0   -87.1  -102.6      -0.15 dB
  -12 dBFS     +6 dB    1.94%   -35.5   -40.2   -69.5   -78.9      -0.34 dB
   -9 dBFS     +9 dB    2.94%   -33.0   -34.4   -61.1   -67.3      -0.58 dB
   -6 dBFS    +12 dB    4.62%   -30.7   -28.9   -53.2   -56.2      -1.02 dB
harmonics in dB below the 55 Hz fundamental; input is sine RMS
At its nominal level the stage adds 0.91% total harmonic distortion. Mostly it’s the second harmonic, 41.2 dB under the note, an octave up. That’s the warmth people are paying for. It’s quiet and it’s musical.
Push 6 dB harder and the distortion doubles, to 1.94%. At −6 dBFS, 12 dB over nominal, it’s 4.62%. The more telling number is the third harmonic. It climbs from −52.0 dB to −28.9 dB, 23 dB louder for 12 dB more input, and by −6 dBFS it’s louder than the second. Second harmonics tend to sound full. Third and higher sound edgier and fuzzier, and on a bass they pile up in the low mids right where the vocal lives.
Look at the last column too. At nominal the stage takes 0.15 dB off the level. At −6 dBFS it takes 1.02 dB. That’s the stage squashing the top of the wave, a bit of compression you never asked for.

### It adds up down the chain
One plugin running hot is rarely the problem. A track usually goes through a channel strip emulation, then an EQ, then a compressor, then a bus with a console and a tape plugin. If each stage is modelled, each one adds its own harmonics to the last one’s. Here’s the same stage five times in a row:
five stages in series:       input      THD
                          -18 dBFS    4.13%
                          -12 dBFS    7.55%
                           -6 dBFS   13.48%
At −18 dBFS, five stages land at 4.13%. That’s about where one stage was when you drove it 12 dB too hard. Start 6 dB hot and it’s 7.55%. Start 12 dB hot and it’s 13.48%. That fuzz on the vocal wasn’t one bad plugin. It was a whole chain that never got a break.
Note: A real plugin’s numbers will be different from this model. The shape is the point: more level in means more distortion out, the odd harmonics climb fastest, and it compounds stage after stage.

### How to set it up so plugins behave
1. Trim at the start of the chain. Use the clip gain or a trim plugin first in the insert list so the track averages around −18 dBFS. A quick way to check: peaks on most sources land somewhere near −10 to −6 dBFS when the average is there.
2. Look at the plugin’s own meter. If it has a VU meter, aim for the needle around 0 on the loud parts, not pinned to the right.
3. Use the output knob too. If a plugin adds gain, take it back off at its output so the next one sees the same level the first one did.
4. Drive on purpose. When you want grit, turn up the plugin’s drive or input and pull its output down by the same amount. Then the extra harmonics are a choice, and you can hear them without the level fooling you.
5. Leave the master fader alone. If the mix bus is too hot, lower the tracks or the bus input, not just the last fader. Pulling the master after a console plugin doesn’t un-drive it.

### Level-match before you decide
Here’s the trap. A hotter stage comes out louder, and louder almost always sounds better for the first few seconds. So when you A/B “clean” against “driven,” the driven one wins even when it’s worse. It’s the same thing covered in your mix sounds better loud and thinner quiet.
Bounce both versions, then drop each one into the CoProducer analyzer. It reads the integrated LUFS of each file, so you know exactly how much to turn the louder one down before you compare. Then listen again at the same loudness. If the driven one still sounds better, keep it. That’s taste, not volume.

### When hot is right
None of this means hitting plugins hard is wrong. Lo-fi drums, distorted 808s, a vocal that’s supposed to sound like it’s coming through a broken radio: those want the curve. Some engineers push a tape emulation on the drum bus on purpose because the softened transients are exactly the sound. The difference is that they chose it, they know which stage is doing it, and they matched levels before deciding.
Set every stage near its nominal level by default. Then break the rule on one plugin, on purpose, where you can hear it.
Q: Why do people say to gain stage at −18 dBFS?
A: Because many analog-modelled plugins treat a signal around −18 dBFS RMS as their nominal level, 0 VU. Feed them that and they behave like the hardware at its normal operating level. Feed them much more and they add extra distortion and compression.
Q: Does gain staging matter in a 32-bit float DAW?
A: For clipping, mostly not: float keeps overs and turning down recovers them. For plugins that model analog gear, yes, because their sound depends on input level. In our model, going from −18 to −6 dBFS took distortion from 0.91% to 4.62%.
Q: Is −18 dBFS peak or average?
A: Average. The usual meaning is a sine or an RMS level of −18 dBFS reading 0 VU. On real music, peaks will sit well above that, often somewhere around −10 to −6 dBFS.
Q: My plugin sounds distorted even at low settings. Why?
A: Check the level going into it. If the track averages far above the plugin’s nominal level, the model is already being driven before you touch a knob. Trim the input first, then adjust.

---

## Layered kick sounds thinner? Check polarity and timing
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/layered-kick-sounds-thinner-check-polarity-and-timing.html
Section: Low end · 28 October 2026 · 7 min
Summary: Why adding a sub or a second kick sample can make the low end weaker: the layers are out of polarity or a millisecond or two apart, so they cancel. Measured on a synthetic kick and sub layer, with a script that finds the right offset and flip.

When adding a second kick or a sub layer makes the kick sound thinner, the two layers are cancelling in the low end. One is usually flipped in polarity, starts a millisecond or two late, or both. Zoom in, line up the first low cycle of each layer, flip the polarity of one if their waves move in opposite directions, and check that the low end gets bigger when you add the layer, not smaller.
The top kick has the click. The sub layer has the weight. Solo either one and it sounds great. Play them together and the kick gets… smaller. The snap is still there, but the chest-thump you were adding the layer for is gone. So you turn the sub up, and somehow that barely helps.
That’s not your ears. It’s two waves pushing in opposite directions at the same moment, and in the low end that moment lasts long enough to hear.

### Why low layers cancel
A kick’s low end is basically a sine that starts high and drops fast. At 60 Hz one cycle takes about 16.7 ms. If your sub layer is a copy of that motion but upside down, every push from one layer meets a pull from the other, and they subtract. If it’s the right way up but a millisecond or two late, part of each cycle still lines up against the opposite half of the other one.
Both happen all the time. Pack samples aren’t made to match each other. A resampled sub might come out inverted depending on the chain. A sample might have a couple of milliseconds of silence before the hit, or a fade-in. None of that shows at a normal zoom level.
The click on top barely cares. High frequencies have short cycles, and they’re mostly in one layer anyway. That’s why the layered kick still sounds sharp while the body disappears.

### We made a layer that fights the kick
In make_kicks.py we built two samples at 48 kHz: a top kick with a click and a pitch drop from 170 to 55 Hz, and a sine sub that follows the same pitch drop with a longer tail. That’s the standard sub-under-the-kick move. Then we wrote the sub the way plenty of samples arrive: polarity flipped, with 1.5 ms of silence in front. Both peak at −6 dBFS.
This script checks a pair of layers. It tries every offset up to 5 ms either way, with and without a polarity flip, and keeps the one that gives the most low end in the first 100 ms, which is the hit you actually feel:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Check two layered samples (kick + kick, kick + 808) for polarity and timing before you blend them.
  python3 layer_check.py top.wav sub.wav [--max-ms 10]
Low end (below 150 Hz) is where layers cancel, so it tries every offset up to --max-ms either way,
with and without a polarity flip, and keeps the one with the most low end in the first 100 ms
(the hit you feel, not the tail)."""
import sys, numpy as np, soundfile as sf
from scipy.signal import butter, sosfilt

def low(x, sr): return sosfilt(butter(4, 150, "low", fs=sr, output="sos"), x)
def lowband_db(x, sr): return 10 * np.log10((low(x, sr)[:int(0.1 * sr)] ** 2).sum() + 1e-20)
def shift(x, k): return np.concatenate([np.zeros(k), x])[:len(x)] if k >= 0 else np.concatenate([x[-k:], np.zeros(-k)])

def main():
    a, sr = sf.read(sys.argv[1]); b, _ = sf.read(sys.argv[2])
    a, b = (v.mean(axis=1) if v.ndim > 1 else v for v in (a, b))
    m = max(len(a), len(b)); a, b = np.pad(a, (0, m - len(a))), np.pad(b, (0, m - len(b)))
    max_ms = float(sys.argv[sys.argv.index("--max-ms") + 1]) if "--max-ms" in sys.argv else 5.0
    L, head = int(sr * max_ms / 1000), int(0.1 * sr)
    la, lb = low(a, sr), low(b, sr)
    hit = lambda x: (x[:head] ** 2).sum()
    e = {(k, p): hit(la + p * shift(lb, k)) for k in range(-L, L + 1) for p in (1, -1)}
    top = max(e.values())                                  # within 0.01 dB of the best, prefer the smallest move
    k, pol = min((kp for kp, v in e.items() if v >= top * 10 ** -0.001), key=lambda kp: abs(kp[0]))
    ref = max(lowband_db(a, sr), lowband_db(b, sr))
    opts = {"as loaded": a + b, "polarity flipped": a - b,
            f"moved {k / sr * 1000:+.2f} ms": a + shift(b, k), "moved + flipped": a - shift(b, k)}
    print(f"{sys.argv[1]} + {sys.argv[2]}  (low end below 150 Hz in the first 100 ms, vs the louder layer alone)")
    for name, s in opts.items():
        print(f"  {name:18s} {lowband_db(s, sr) - ref:+6.2f} dB   peak {20 * np.log10(np.abs(s).max() + 1e-12):+6.2f} dBFS")
    print(f"best: move layer 2 by {k} samples ({k / sr * 1000:+.2f} ms)" + (" and flip its polarity" if pol < 0 else ", keep polarity"))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
$ python3 layer_check.py kick_top.wav kick_sub.wav
kick_top.wav + kick_sub.wav  (low end below 150 Hz in the first 100 ms, vs the louder layer alone)
  as loaded           -2.19 dB   peak  -3.85 dBFS
  polarity flipped    +3.94 dB   peak  -2.53 dBFS
  moved -1.40 ms     -10.76 dB   peak -10.09 dBFS
  moved + flipped     +4.80 dB   peak  -0.14 dBFS
best: move layer 2 by -67 samples (-1.40 ms) and flip its polarity
As loaded, adding the sub made the low end 2.19 dB weaker than the top kick on its own. You added a layer and lost weight. Flipping the polarity alone got it to +3.94 dB. Moving the sub 1.40 ms earlier without flipping made it far worse, −10.76 dB, because that lines the waves up perfectly opposite. Both together gave +4.80 dB.
That’s a 7 dB swing in the low end of the hit from two clicks, with no EQ, no compression and no new samples.
The script settled on 1.40 ms rather than the 1.5 ms we put in. The two layers drop pitch at slightly different rates, so the best fit isn’t exactly the delay we added. Within 0.01 dB it prefers the smallest move, and your ears won’t hear the difference.

### Doing it by ear and eye in the DAW
1. Zoom in on the start. Put both layers on the same grid line and zoom until you can see single cycles. Line up where each layer’s first low cycle starts, not where the click starts.
2. Look at the direction. If one wave goes up while the other goes down, flip the polarity of one. Most DAWs have a polarity or phase button on the channel or in a utility plugin. It might be labelled Ø.
3. Flip and listen in mono. Toggle the flip with both layers playing. The right setting is the one where the low end gets bigger. If you can’t tell, check in mono at a low volume, where the difference is easiest to hear.
4. Nudge in small steps. Move the sub by a fraction of a millisecond at a time. Some DAWs let you nudge by samples. A delay plugin with a negative or small positive time works too.
5. Then turn it down. Once the layers add instead of cancel, the peak goes up. In our test it went from −3.85 dBFS as loaded to −0.14 dBFS fixed. Trim the layer or the kick bus before it hits the next plugin.
If the two layers have very different pitches, you won’t get them to agree everywhere. In that case, a common move is to let one layer own the lows and high-pass the other one so they overlap less. That’s the same idea as giving the kick and 808 their own space in your kick and 808 are arguing in the same chair.

### Layering over a sampled break
This gets sneakier when the kick you’re reinforcing lives inside a loop or a record. If you split a drum stem out of a sample, say with NoDAW StemSplit, and stack your own kick on top, line it up against the kick in the stem, not the grid. The original drummer wasn’t on your grid, and a few milliseconds of drift between hits is normal. Check the polarity on a couple of hits through the loop, not just the first one. There’s more on working with split drums in sampling from separated stems.

### Same problem, other places
Anything doubled in the low end can do this: a DI bass with an amp track, two mics on a kick, a dry track against a parallel compressor that adds latency. That last one has its own essay, parallel compression sounds thin? Check the latency first. The fix is the same every time. Line them up, check the polarity, and make sure adding the second one makes the low end bigger.
Q: Why does my kick sound thinner when I layer it?
A: The layers are cancelling in the low end. Usually one is flipped in polarity, starts a millisecond or two late, or both. In our test that made the low end 2.19 dB weaker than the top kick alone.
Q: Should I flip the polarity of my sub layer?
A: Try it with both layers playing and keep whichever setting makes the low end bigger. There’s no rule which way is right. It depends on how each sample was made.
Q: How do I line up two kick samples?
A: Zoom in until you can see single cycles and line up where each one’s first low cycle starts. Then nudge the layer in small steps, a fraction of a millisecond at a time, while you listen to the low end.
Q: Is polarity the same as phase?
A: Not quite. Flipping polarity turns the whole wave upside down. A phase or timing difference shifts it in time, which affects different frequencies by different amounts. Layered kicks often need both fixes.

---

## Should you normalize on export? Turn it off before mastering
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/normalize-on-export-turn-it-off-for-mastering.html
Section: Delivery · 27 October 2026 · 8 min
Summary: Why the normalize option in your DAW’s export window works against a mix headed for mastering: it fills the headroom, can push true peak over 0 dBFS and gives every version its own gain. Measured on a synthetic main mix and instrumental. Script inside.

Turn normalize off when you export a mix for mastering. The normalize option rescales the finished bounce, usually so the loudest sample hits 0 dBFS or the file lands on a loudness target. That throws away the headroom you left, can push the true peak over full scale, and gives every version of the song its own gain, so the main mix, the instrumental and the stems stop matching.
You did everything right. Mix bus clean, no limiter, peaks sitting around −6 dBFS because that’s what the mastering engineer asked for. You bounce, open the file, and the waveform is slammed against the top of the window. Peak: 0.0.
Nothing in the mix changed. Somewhere in the export window there’s a checkbox that says normalize, and it’s ticked. Maybe you ticked it once for a demo, and the DAW remembered. Maybe it was on in a preset. Either way, it quietly undid the one thing you were asked to do.

### What the normalize box actually does
Normalize waits until the render is finished, measures it, and applies one gain change to the whole file. Peak normalize moves the loudest sample to a target, usually 0 dBFS or a hair under. Some DAWs also offer a loudness version that moves the whole file to a LUFS target. It isn’t compression and it doesn’t change the shape of anything. It’s a fader move you didn’t make, decided by whichever moment of the song happened to be loudest.
That sounds harmless, and on one file sometimes it is. The trouble comes from three places: the headroom is gone, the peaks between the samples can end up over full scale, and every file you bounce gets a different fader move.
It’s also not the same thing as streaming normalization. Platforms turn songs up or down at playback and leave your file alone, which is covered in why streaming platforms turn loud masters down. Export normalize changes the file itself.

### We bounced one song three ways
To see it in numbers, we built a four-bar song at 120 BPM in make_versions.py: kick, snare, hats, a bass and chords, plus a vocal that comes in on bar 2. It renders a main mix, an instrumental with the vocal muted, and an a cappella, all through the same mix-bus gain, with the main mix peaking at −6 dBFS. Then it runs the main mix and the instrumental through both kinds of normalize:
$ python3 make_versions.py
main         peak-normalize gain  +6.00 dB   -14 LUFS gain  +6.42 dB (1 sample past full scale, clipped in 24-bit)
instrumental peak-normalize gain  +6.71 dB   -14 LUFS gain  +9.03 dB (82 samples past full scale, clipped in 24-bit)
Here’s the script that measures them: sample peak, true peak by 4x oversampling, and integrated loudness with a BS.1770 meter. It also does a null test, which we’ll get to:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Peak, true peak and loudness for one or more bounces, plus an optional null test.
  python3 export_check.py a.wav b.wav ...           sample peak, 4x true peak, integrated LUFS
  python3 export_check.py --null a.wav b.wav 0 2    residual of a - b between 0 and 2 seconds
True peak is estimated by 4x oversampling (polyphase FIR), as in ITU-R BS.1770; LUFS is BS.1770
K-weighting with the -70 LUFS absolute and -10 LU relative gates."""
import sys, numpy as np, soundfile as sf
from scipy.signal import lfilter, resample_poly

db = lambda v: 20 * np.log10(max(v, 1e-12))

def k_weight(x, sr):                                     # BS.1770 pre-filter + RLB high-pass at any rate
    K = np.tan(np.pi * 1681.974450955532 / sr); Vh = 10 ** (3.99984385397 / 20); Vb = Vh ** 0.4996667741545416
    Q = 0.7071752369554196; a0 = 1 + K / Q + K * K
    x = lfilter([(Vh + Vb * K / Q + K * K) / a0, 2 * (K * K - Vh) / a0, (Vh - Vb * K / Q + K * K) / a0],
                [1, 2 * (K * K - 1) / a0, (1 - K / Q + K * K) / a0], x, axis=0)
    K = np.tan(np.pi * 38.13547087602444 / sr); Q = 0.5003270373238773; a0 = 1 + K / Q + K * K
    return lfilter([1, -2, 1], [1, 2 * (K * K - 1) / a0, (1 - K / Q + K * K) / a0], x, axis=0)

def lufs(x, sr):
    y = k_weight(x.reshape(len(x), -1), sr); blk, hop = int(0.4 * sr), int(0.1 * sr)
    z = np.array([(y[i:i + blk] ** 2).mean(axis=0).sum() for i in range(0, len(y) - blk + 1, hop)])
    lk = -0.691 + 10 * np.log10(z + 1e-20)
    z = z[lk > -70]; rel = -0.691 + 10 * np.log10(z.mean()) - 10
    return -0.691 + 10 * np.log10(z[-0.691 + 10 * np.log10(z) > rel].mean())

def true_peak(x):
    return np.abs(resample_poly(x.reshape(len(x), -1), 4, 1, axis=0)).max()

def main():
    if sys.argv[1] == "--null":
        (a, sr), (b, _) = sf.read(sys.argv[2]), sf.read(sys.argv[3])
        i, j = int(float(sys.argv[4]) * sr), int(float(sys.argv[5]) * sr)
        r = a[i:j] - b[i:j]; rms = np.sqrt((r ** 2).mean())
        print(f"null {sys.argv[2]} - {sys.argv[3]}, {sys.argv[4]}-{sys.argv[5]} s: " +
              ("digital silence - identical" if rms == 0 else f"residual RMS {db(rms):.1f} dBFS, peak {db(np.abs(r).max()):.1f} dBFS"))
    else:
        print(f"{'file':24s} {'peak':>9s} {'true peak':>10s} {'LUFS-I':>7s}  full-scale samples")
        for f in sys.argv[1:]:
            x, sr = sf.read(f)
            print(f"{f:24s} {db(np.abs(x).max()):+6.2f} dB {db(true_peak(x)):+7.2f} dB {lufs(x, sr):7.2f}  "
                  f"{int((np.abs(x) >= 1 - 2 ** -22).sum())}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
$ python3 export_check.py main.wav instrumental.wav main_norm0.wav instrumental_norm0.wav main_norm14.wav instrumental_norm14.wav
file                          peak  true peak  LUFS-I  full-scale samples
main.wav                  -6.00 dB   -5.99 dB  -20.42  0
instrumental.wav          -6.71 dB   -6.33 dB  -23.03  0
main_norm0.wav            -0.00 dB   +0.01 dB  -14.42  1
instrumental_norm0.wav    -0.00 dB   +0.38 dB  -16.32  1
main_norm14.wav           -0.00 dB   +0.25 dB  -14.00  1
instrumental_norm14.wav   +0.00 dB   +1.38 dB  -14.01  82
Look at the gains first. To reach 0 dBFS, the main mix needed +6.00 dB and the instrumental +6.71 dB. Without the vocal on top, the instrumental’s loudest moment is quieter, so normalize pushes it harder. To reach −14 LUFS the gap is bigger: +6.42 dB against +9.03 dB, 2.61 dB apart.
Now the true-peak column. Peak normalize put both files’ loudest sample at 0 dBFS, but the waveform between samples kept going: the instrumental reads +0.38 dB true peak, and the main mix sits right at full scale. The loudness version is worse, because −14 LUFS needed more gain than the headroom allowed. Those samples got clipped flat when the 24-bit file was written: one in the main mix, 82 in the instrumental, which still reads +1.38 dB true peak. A float export can carry overs without clipping, but whatever opens the file next might not, and lossy encoders are where they hurt, as in true peak is what codecs clip.

### Versions that don’t line up anymore
Bar 1 has no vocal, so the main mix and the instrumental should be identical there. A null test subtracts one file from the other. If they match, what’s left is digital silence:
$ python3 export_check.py --null main.wav instrumental.wav 0 2
null main.wav - instrumental.wav, 0-2 s: digital silence - identical
$ python3 export_check.py --null main_norm0.wav instrumental_norm0.wav 0 2
null main_norm0.wav - instrumental_norm0.wav, 0-2 s: residual RMS -39.2 dBFS, peak -22.1 dBFS
$ python3 export_check.py --null main_norm14.wav instrumental_norm14.wav 0 2
null main_norm14.wav - instrumental_norm14.wav, 0-2 s: residual RMS -26.5 dBFS, peak -11.7 dBFS
Before normalizing, the intro nulls perfectly. After peak normalize, the leftover is −39.2 dBFS RMS. After loudness normalize it’s −26.5 dBFS, with peaks at −11.7. That’s the beat at two different levels, all the way through the song.
This matters more than it looks. A mastering engineer usually runs the main, the instrumental, the clean and the TV mix through the same chain at the same settings, so they come back matching. Feed that chain files at different levels and the limiter works harder on some than others. The instrumental comes back louder and flatter than the beat under the vocal, and nobody can tell why. The same goes for stems that are supposed to add back up to the mix, covered in exporting stems for a mixer, and for a clean version that’s meant to match the explicit one, as in making a clean version.

### The headroom was the point
Mastering engineers ask for room below 0 dBFS so the first thing in their chain, often an EQ that adds a few dB somewhere, isn’t starting already at the ceiling. Peak normalize fills that room on purpose. How much to leave, and why the exact number matters less than you’d think, is in how much headroom to leave for mastering. The same reasoning is behind turning the mix down before you limit: gain staging is a decision, not something a checkbox does after the fact.

### Export settings that keep versions honest
1. Turn normalize off everywhere. Check the main export dialog, every saved preset, the stem or multitrack export, and bounce-in-place. Some DAWs keep a separate setting for each.
2. One mix-bus gain for every version. Main, instrumental, a cappella, clean and stems all come from the same session with the same master fader. Mute parts. Don’t rebalance.
3. Export 24-bit or 32-bit float at the session’s sample rate. No limiter on the bus unless the engineer asked for your print through it.
4. Null the intro. Pull the main and the instrumental into a session, flip one’s polarity and play a section where the vocal is silent. It should disappear. If it doesn’t, something changed the gain.
5. Read the numbers. Peak and true peak should be where you left them, not at zero.
For that last step you don’t need a script. Bounce the same mix once with normalize on and once with it off and drop both into CoProducer. It reads LUFS, true peak and clips for each file, so the normalized bounce gives itself away: true peak at or over zero, and several dB more loudness than the mix you actually left. In our test that was 6.00 dB, the whole of the headroom.

### When normalize is fine
A rough mix for your phone, a reference for the car, a quick bounce for a friend: if nobody will process the file further, normalizing it is just a volume knob. The rule is narrower than “never.” Don’t normalize anything that’s headed into mastering, anything that has to match another file, or anything that’s already been through a limiter, where it will raise the ceiling and the true peak with it.

### Genre notes
- Hip-hop and trap. Instrumentals and performance tracks get used on stage and for features. If yours was normalized, the beat jumps in level the moment the vocal comes out.
- Beat sellers. Tagged and untagged versions, MP3 and WAV, should come from one bus gain. Our instrumental took 0.71 dB more than the main at peak and 2.61 dB more at loudness.
- Film, TV and sync. Alternate mixes and stems get swapped mid-scene. They have to cut together without a level jump, so nothing in the set can be normalized on its own.
- Pop and R&B. Clean, explicit and a cappella versions get mastered as a set. Send them at the same gain and let the engineer decide the loudness once.
Note: Leave the gain where you mixed it. Normalize nothing that’s headed for mastering.
Q: Should I normalize my mix before sending it to mastering?
A: No. Normalize moves the loudest peak to 0 dBFS or the file to a loudness target, which removes the headroom the engineer asked for and changes the gain of each version differently. Turn it off and export at the level you mixed.
Q: Does normalizing reduce audio quality?
A: A gain change on its own is clean in a 24-bit or float file. The trouble is where it puts the peaks: in our test, peak-normalized files read up to +0.38 dB true peak, and loudness-normalized ones clipped in 24-bit.
Q: Why is my instrumental louder than my main mix?
A: Usually because each file was normalized on its own. Without the vocal, the instrumental’s peaks are lower, so normalize turns it up more. In our test that was 0.71 dB more at peak and 2.61 dB more to reach −14 LUFS.
Q: Is export normalize the same as Spotify normalization?
A: No. Streaming platforms adjust the volume at playback and leave your file untouched. Export normalize rewrites the file before anyone else hears it.

---

## Sample playing at the wrong speed or pitch? It’s a sample-rate mismatch
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/sample-plays-at-wrong-pitch-sample-rate-mismatch.html
Section: Pitch · 27 October 2026 · 8 min
Summary: Why a sample or loop plays slower and flat, or faster and sharp: it was made at one sample rate and played at another without conversion. The exact speed, semitone and BPM error for 44.1, 48, 88.2 and 96 kHz, and a script that reads the WAV header and catches mislabeled files.

When a sample plays a little too slow and flat, or too fast and sharp, it’s almost always a sample-rate mismatch: audio made at one rate is being played back at another without being converted. A 48 kHz file played at 44.1 kHz runs at 0.91875x speed and about 1.47 semitones flat. The other way round it runs 1.088x fast and 1.47 semitones sharp. Set the project rate, let the DAW convert the file instead of just playing it, and check the rate in the file’s header.
The loop sounded perfect in the pack preview. You drop it in, and something’s off. A little dark, a little lazy, not quite on the grid however you line it up. Or it’s the other way: brighter and pushier than you remember, with the vocal chop a touch chipmunky. The person who sent it swears it’s 140.
Or the beat is fine in the session, and then you put it under a video and by the second chorus the drums and the picture have drifted apart.
Same cause, most of the time. Nothing’s wrong with the audio. It’s being played on the wrong clock.

### Why the rate changes the pitch
A WAV file is a long list of numbers plus a header that says how many of them make a second. Take one second of 48 kHz audio, 48,000 numbers, and play it at 44,100 per second, and that second takes longer to get through. Every wave is stretched, so every note is lower. Speed and pitch move together, exactly like a turntable at the wrong speed. That’s resampling-style varispeed, one of the three different jobs in resampling, pitch shifting and tempo change.
The arithmetic is just the ratio of the two rates. Here it is for the four common ones:
$ python3 rate_math.py
file rate -> played at   speed      pitch        140 BPM ->   3:00 song ->
   44.1 k ->  48.0 k   x1.08844   +1.467 st    152.38 BPM   2:45.37 (-14.63 s)
   44.1 k ->  88.2 k   x2.00000  +12.000 st    280.00 BPM   1:30.00 (-90.00 s)
   44.1 k ->  96.0 k   x2.17687  +13.467 st    304.76 BPM   1:22.69 (-97.31 s)
   48.0 k ->  44.1 k   x0.91875   -1.467 st    128.62 BPM   3:15.92 (+15.92 s)
   48.0 k ->  88.2 k   x1.83750  +10.533 st    257.25 BPM   1:37.96 (-82.04 s)
   48.0 k ->  96.0 k   x2.00000  +12.000 st    280.00 BPM   1:30.00 (-90.00 s)
   88.2 k ->  44.1 k   x0.50000  -12.000 st     70.00 BPM   6:00.00 (+180.00 s)
   88.2 k ->  48.0 k   x0.54422  -10.533 st     76.19 BPM   5:30.75 (+150.75 s)
   88.2 k ->  96.0 k   x1.08844   +1.467 st    152.38 BPM   2:45.37 (-14.63 s)
   96.0 k ->  44.1 k   x0.45937  -13.467 st     64.31 BPM   6:31.84 (+211.84 s)
   96.0 k ->  48.0 k   x0.50000  -12.000 st     70.00 BPM   6:00.00 (+180.00 s)
   96.0 k ->  88.2 k   x0.91875   -1.467 st    128.62 BPM   3:15.92 (+15.92 s)

48 k file at 44.1 k vs a video: audio is 5.31 s behind after 1 minute, 21.22 s after 4
semitone ratio 2^(1/12) = 1.05946; 48/44.1 = 1.08844 = 146.7 cents
The one that bites is 44.1 against 48. The ratio is 1.08844, which is 146.7 cents, about a semitone and a half. That’s not a clean wrong key. It sits between notes, which is why it sounds “off” rather than obviously in the wrong key, and why your ear keeps trying to fix it with EQ. A 140 BPM loop turns into 128.62 or 152.38 BPM. A three-minute song gains 15.92 seconds or loses 14.63. Doubling a rate is a full octave, which nobody misses.
Against video the drift is easy to spot once you know to look: at 0.91875x the audio is 5.31 seconds behind after one minute and 21.22 seconds behind after four. If the sync looks right at the start and worse by the chorus, check the sample rate before you start nudging clips.

### Where the mismatch sneaks in
- Importing into a session at another rate. Some DAWs convert on import automatically, some ask, and some play the file as-is unless you tell them otherwise.
- Samplers and older tools. Some load the raw sample data and play it at the engine’s rate, whatever the file says.
- Mixed-rate sample packs. One folder, loops from three sources, two rates. The odd one out plays wrong next to the others.
- The interface and the project disagree. On some setups the audio device can be set to one rate while the software expects another.
- The header itself is wrong. A broken export or a bad edit writes the wrong number into the file. Now even a careful DAW plays it wrong, because it’s trusting the file.

### Check what the file says
This script reads the rate straight out of the WAV header and tells you what happens if it plays in your session unconverted. Give it a note you know should be in the file, like a tuning tone, a held note or an 808 you know the key of, and it also checks whether the header is telling the truth:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Read the sample rate a WAV file *says* it is (straight from the RIFF fmt chunk), and what happens
if it plays in your session without conversion. Optional: --expect-hz checks the strongest tone
against the pitch it should be, which catches files whose header itself is wrong.
  python3 rate_check.py --session 48000 [--bpm 140] [--expect-hz 440] *.wav"""
import argparse, math, struct, sys, numpy as np

def read_wav(path):
    with open(path, "rb") as fh:
        riff, _, wave_id = struct.unpack("<4sI4s", fh.read(12))
        if riff not in (b"RIFF", b"RF64") or wave_id != b"WAVE": sys.exit(f"{path}: not a WAV file")
        fmt = data = None
        while (hdr := fh.read(8)) and len(hdr) == 8:
            cid, size = struct.unpack("<4sI", hdr)
            if cid == b"fmt ": fmt = fh.read(size)
            elif cid == b"data": data = fh.read(size); break
            else: fh.seek(size, 1)
            if size % 2: fh.seek(1, 1)                   # chunks are word-aligned
    tag, ch, sr, _, _, bits = struct.unpack("<HHIIHH", fmt[:16])
    if tag == 0xFFFE: tag = struct.unpack("<H", fmt[24:26])[0]   # WAVE_FORMAT_EXTENSIBLE
    if tag == 3: x = np.frombuffer(data, f"<f{bits // 8}").astype(float)
    elif bits == 24:
        b = np.frombuffer(data[: len(data) // 3 * 3], np.uint8).reshape(-1, 3)
        x = (np.c_[np.zeros(len(b), np.uint8), b].copy().view("<i4").ravel() >> 8) / 2 ** 23
    else: x = np.frombuffer(data, {16: "<i2", 32: "<i4"}[bits]) / 2 ** (bits - 1)
    return sr, ch, bits, ("float" if tag == 3 else "PCM"), x.reshape(-1, ch).mean(axis=1)

def strongest_hz(x, sr):                                 # FFT peak, parabolic interpolation
    n = min(len(x), sr * 4); w = x[:n] * np.hanning(n)
    m = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(w, 4 * n)); k = int(np.argmax(m[1:])) + 1
    a, b, c = np.log(m[k - 1:k + 2] + 1e-20); k += 0.5 * (a - c) / (a - 2 * b + c)
    return k * sr / (4 * n)

ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(); ap.add_argument("files", nargs="+")
ap.add_argument("--session", type=int, required=True); ap.add_argument("--bpm", type=float)
ap.add_argument("--expect-hz", type=float); a = ap.parse_args()
def effect(r):                                           # speed ratio -> readable consequences
    return (f"x{r:.5f} speed, {12 * math.log2(r):+.3f} semitones" +
            (f", {a.bpm:g} BPM plays at {a.bpm * r:.2f}" if a.bpm else ""))

for f in a.files:
    sr, ch, bits, kind, x = read_wav(f)
    print(f"{f}: header says {sr} Hz, {ch} ch, {bits}-bit {kind}, {len(x)/sr:.3f} s")
    if a.expect_hz:
        hz = strongest_hz(x, sr); off = 1200 * math.log2(hz / a.expect_hz)
        print(f"  strongest tone at the header rate: {hz:.1f} Hz ({off:+.0f} cents vs {a.expect_hz:g})")
        if abs(off) > 50:                                # more than half a semitone: the header is lying
            true = round(sr * a.expect_hz / hz)
            print(f"  header looks wrong: the audio was made at about {true} Hz. Played by its header: "
                  f"{effect(sr / true)}\n  fix: re-stamp the header to {true} Hz (no resampling)")
            continue
    if sr == a.session: print("  matches the session: plays at the right speed")
    else:
        print(f"  unconverted in a {a.session} Hz session: {effect(a.session / sr)}, "
              f"lasts {len(x) / a.session:.3f} s\n  fix: convert it to {a.session} Hz (sample-rate conversion)")
The test files come from make_loops.py: two bars at 140 BPM, an A at 440 Hz with a click on every beat. One is a proper 48 kHz file, one a proper 44.1 kHz file, and one is the 48 kHz audio with a header that says 44.1:
$ python3 rate_check.py --session 48000 --bpm 140 --expect-hz 440 loop_48k.wav loop_44k1.wav mislabeled.wav
loop_48k.wav: header says 48000 Hz, 2 ch, 24-bit PCM, 3.429 s
  strongest tone at the header rate: 440.0 Hz (+0 cents vs 440)
  matches the session: plays at the right speed
loop_44k1.wav: header says 44100 Hz, 2 ch, 24-bit PCM, 3.429 s
  strongest tone at the header rate: 440.0 Hz (+0 cents vs 440)
  unconverted in a 48000 Hz session: x1.08844 speed, +1.467 semitones, 140 BPM plays at 152.38, lasts 3.150 s
  fix: convert it to 48000 Hz (sample-rate conversion)
mislabeled.wav: header says 44100 Hz, 2 ch, 24-bit PCM, 3.732 s
  strongest tone at the header rate: 404.3 Hz (-147 cents vs 440)
  header looks wrong: the audio was made at about 48000 Hz. Played by its header: x0.91875 speed, -1.467 semitones, 140 BPM plays at 128.62
  fix: re-stamp the header to 48000 Hz (no resampling)
The 44.1 kHz loop is fine as a file. Its tone measures 440.0 Hz at its own rate. Unconverted in a 48 kHz session it plays at 152.38 BPM and 1.467 semitones sharp, and the fix is to convert it. The mislabeled one is different. Its header says 44.1, but the tone measures 404.3 Hz at that rate, 147 cents flat of where it should be. The header is the liar. Honoring it plays the loop at 128.62 BPM. The fix there is to re-stamp the header to 48 kHz without touching the audio. Convert it instead and you bake the wrong speed in for good.

### Fixing it in the session
1. Choose the project rate first. Pick it from where the song is going, 48 kHz for most video work, and set it before you import anything. Delivery rates are covered in sample rate and bit depth are delivery hygiene.
2. Let the DAW convert on import. Look for an import option that converts the sample rate or matches the project, and turn it on.
3. Convert folders before you use them. A mixed-rate pack is easier to batch-convert once with a good converter than to catch loop by loop.
4. Match the interface. Make sure the audio device is running at the project rate.
5. Mislabeled file? Re-stamp, don’t convert. If a known note measures about 1.47 semitones off, the header is wrong. Change the rate in the header and leave the samples alone.
6. Check with your ears and a tuner. Put a tuner on a held note or the 808 tail. A whole loop that’s about 147 cents off is a rate problem. A few cents off is just tuning, as in tuning an 808 to the key of your song.

### The accident is a real effect
Here’s the funny part. Playing audio slower so the pitch drops with it is the whole sound of a chopped-and-screwed slowdown. A mismatch is that effect without anyone choosing it: 0.91875x and 1.47 semitones down. If you want the drop, make it on purpose, at the amount you like, then do it properly to a fresh file. You can hear what that sounds like in the ScrewAI demo, and when to slow the bounce covers where it belongs in the workflow. Keep the session itself on one clock.

### Genre notes
- Hip-hop and sampling. Rips, crate digs and old loops come at every rate. Convert to the session rate before you chop, or every chop is 1.47 semitones off the key you set.
- Content and video. Video timelines are commonly 48 kHz. Bounce the beat at the rate of the video project so it doesn’t drift.
- Collaborations. Agree on one rate before anyone sends stems, and say it in the file names, as in exporting stems for a mixer.
- High-rate sessions. 88.2 or 96 kHz files in a 44.1 or 48 kHz player come out around an octave low and half speed, so you’ll hear it at once. The near misses are the ones that hide.
Note: Wrong clock, not wrong audio. Convert when the session doesn’t match the file. Re-stamp when the header is lying.
Q: Why does my sample sound slower and lower in my DAW?
A: It was made at a higher sample rate than it’s being played at, and it isn’t being converted. A 48 kHz file at 44.1 kHz plays at 0.91875x speed and 1.47 semitones flat. Convert it to the project rate on import.
Q: How many semitones is the difference between 44.1 and 48 kHz?
A: 1.467 semitones, or 146.7 cents. The speed ratio is 1.08844 one way and 0.91875 the other, so a 140 BPM loop plays at 152.38 or 128.62 BPM.
Q: Should I resample the file or change the sample rate in the header?
A: Resample (convert) when the header is right and your session runs at a different rate. Change the header when the header itself is wrong. Measure a note you know: if the whole file is about 147 cents off at its own rate, the header is wrong.
Q: Why is my audio drifting out of sync with my video?
A: Often a sample-rate mismatch. Audio made at 48 kHz played as 44.1 kHz falls 5.31 seconds behind after one minute. Export at the video project’s rate and make sure the editor isn’t reinterpreting the file.

---

## Song ending cut off when you export? Let the tail ring past the last bar
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/song-ending-cut-off-on-export-let-the-tail-ring.html
Section: Delivery · 26 October 2026 · 7 min
Summary: Why the end of your song gets cut off on export and how to fix it: run the export range past the last bar until the reverb and delay tails die, check the file ends in silence, then trim the silence, not the tail. Tail math and a script inside.

If the end of your song gets cut off when you export, the export range is stopping at the last bar line while the reverb and delay are still ringing. Run the range at least two bars past the last note, longer for big reverbs, high-feedback delays and slow tempos, then check that the file ends in silence and not mid-sound. Trim the extra silence afterwards. Never trim the tail.
You play the bounce back and the last chord just stops. Not a fade, not a decay. A door slamming. In the session it rang out beautifully. Or the last word of the vocal had a delay throw that echoed off into the dark, and in the bounce the echoes get chopped off mid-repeat.
Nothing is wrong with the mix. The export did exactly what it was told: render from here to here. The “here” at the end is usually the last bar line or the end of the last region, and the effects don’t know the song is over.

### Why the bounce stops early
Reverb and delay keep making sound after the notes feeding them stop. Some DAWs have a tail or “remainder” option in the export window. Others render exactly the selection you give them, and not a sample more. Loop-brace exports, region bounces and bounce-in-place are the usual suspects, along with an end marker someone set months ago, before the outro got its big reverb.
A cut ending also clicks. A sound that stops at full swing is a hard edge, the same thing we measured in clicks at your edit points. At the very end of a file it’s the worst place for one, because nothing comes after it to cover it up.

### How far past the last bar?
Far enough for the slowest thing in the session to die away. Here’s the arithmetic for bar lengths, reverb decays and delay feedback:
$ python3 tail_math.py
bar length (4/4):
   70 BPM  1 bar 3.429 s   2 bars 6.857 s
   90 BPM  1 bar 2.667 s   2 bars 5.333 s
  120 BPM  1 bar 2.000 s   2 bars 4.000 s
  140 BPM  1 bar 1.714 s   2 bars 3.429 s
  160 BPM  1 bar 1.500 s   2 bars 3.000 s

reverb: a 60 dB decay of N seconds is how many bars?
  1.2 s decay  = 0.45 bars at 90 BPM, 0.70 bars at 140 BPM
  2.4 s decay  = 0.90 bars at 90 BPM, 1.40 bars at 140 BPM
  4.0 s decay  = 1.50 bars at 90 BPM, 2.33 bars at 140 BPM

delay throw: repeats until the echo is 60 dB down (quarter note at 90 BPM = 0.667 s)
  feedback 0.30: 10.5 dB quieter per repeat,  6 repeats,  4.00 s
  feedback 0.45:  6.9 dB quieter per repeat,  9 repeats,  6.00 s
  feedback 0.60:  4.4 dB quieter per repeat, 14 repeats,  9.33 s
  feedback 0.75:  2.5 dB quieter per repeat, 25 repeats, 16.67 s

this demo: tail runs 3.683 s past the last bar line = 1.38 bars -> export 2 extra bars
  slowed to 0.8x the same tail lasts 4.604 s
  slowed to 0.75x the same tail lasts 4.911 s
A few things jump out. A 2.4-second reverb is under a bar at 90 BPM but 1.4 bars at 140. Delay feedback is the sneaky one. At 0.45 feedback each repeat is only 6.9 dB quieter than the last, so a quarter-note throw at 90 BPM takes 9 repeats and 6 seconds to fall 60 dB. Push the feedback to 0.75 for a dub-style throw and it’s 25 repeats and 16.67 seconds. Those are 60 dB below where each effect starts. Tails that start quieter reach silence sooner, but you can’t know that until you check.
Two extra bars is a good default. For ambient outros, dub throws and slow ballads, give it four or more and trim later. If you sync your throws to the tempo, setting delay time from the tempo has the note lengths.

### Check that the file actually ends
You can hear a hard stop on good speakers. It’s easy to miss on a laptop, and nobody listens to the last second of every alternate bounce. This script reads a WAV and reports how loud the last 50 ms are, when the tail drops below −60 and −80 dBFS for good, and how much silence trails it:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Does a bounce end, or does it get cut off? Reads a 16/24/32-bit WAV and reports how loud the last
50 ms are, where the tail drops below -60 and -80 dBFS for good, and how much silence trails it.
Usage: python3 tail_check.py song.wav"""
import sys, wave, numpy as np

with wave.open(sys.argv[1]) as w:
    sr, ch, sw, nf = w.getframerate(), w.getnchannels(), w.getsampwidth(), w.getnframes()
    raw = w.readframes(nf)
if sw == 3:                                             # 24-bit: pad each sample to 4 bytes
    b = np.frombuffer(raw, np.uint8).reshape(-1, 3)
    x = (np.c_[np.zeros(len(b), np.uint8), b].copy().view("<i4").ravel() >> 8).astype(float) / 2 ** 23
else:
    x = np.frombuffer(raw, {2: "<i2", 4: "<i4"}[sw]).astype(float) / 2 ** (8 * sw - 1)
x = x.reshape(-1, ch)
db = lambda v: 20 * np.log10(v + 1e-12)
hop = int(0.05 * sr)                                    # 50 ms RMS windows
lv = db(np.sqrt((x[: len(x) // hop * hop].reshape(-1, hop, ch) ** 2).mean(axis=(1, 2))))
print(f"{sys.argv[1]}: {len(x)/sr:.3f} s, {sr} Hz, {ch} ch, {8*sw}-bit")
fmt = lambda v: "digital silence" if v < -200 else f"{v:.1f} dBFS"
print(f"  last 50 ms RMS: {fmt(lv[-1])}; last sample: {fmt(db(np.abs(x[-1]).max()))}")
for thr in (-60, -80):
    above = np.nonzero(lv > thr)[0]
    end = (above[-1] + 1) * hop / sr if len(above) else 0.0
    left = len(x) / sr - end
