    print(f"  below {thr} dBFS for good at {end:.3f} s" if left > 0.05 else
          f"  below {thr} dBFS: never - still above it when the file ends")
nz = np.nonzero(np.abs(x).max(axis=1) > 0)[0]
print(f"  trailing digital silence {(len(x) - 1 - nz[-1]) / sr if len(nz) else len(x)/sr:.3f} s")
print("  verdict: " + ("CUT OFF - the tail is still ringing when the file stops" if lv[-1] > -60 else
                       "ends cleanly - the tail has died away before the file stops"))
We built a 90 BPM ending with make_ending.py: a C minor 7 chord on the downbeat of the last bar into a reverb with a 2.4-second decay, a kick that stops a bar earlier, and a quarter-note delay throw at 0.45 feedback on the last vocal word. One export stops at the last bar line, 10.667 s. The other runs 8 seconds past it:
$ python3 tail_check.py ending_cut.wav
ending_cut.wav: 10.667 s, 44100 Hz, 2 ch, 16-bit
  last 50 ms RMS: -31.8 dBFS; last sample: -25.8 dBFS
  below -60 dBFS: never - still above it when the file ends
  below -80 dBFS: never - still above it when the file ends
  trailing digital silence 0.000 s
  verdict: CUT OFF - the tail is still ringing when the file stops

$ python3 tail_check.py ending_full.wav
ending_full.wav: 18.667 s, 44100 Hz, 2 ch, 16-bit
  last 50 ms RMS: digital silence; last sample: digital silence
  below -60 dBFS for good at 14.350 s
  below -80 dBFS for good at 15.050 s
  trailing digital silence 2.554 s
  verdict: ends cleanly - the tail has died away before the file stops
The cut version’s last 50 ms sit at −31.8 dBFS and its very last sample at −25.8 dBFS. That isn’t a tail fading out. That’s the song still playing when the file stops. The long version drops below −60 dBFS for good at 14.350 s, which is 3.68 seconds or 1.38 bars past the bar line. Two extra bars would have covered it.

### Export long, then trim the silence
1. Export long. Two bars past the last note by default, more for the long reverbs, heavy feedback and slow tempos above.
2. Check the end. Run the script, or zoom in on the last second of the waveform with the vertical zoom up. The tail should taper into nothing, not stop at a wall.
3. Trim the extra. Cut a little after the tail falls below about −60 dBFS, or −80 if the ending is quiet and exposed, and put a short fade on the last part so the cut itself lands in silence. Our long bounce still had 2.554 seconds of digital silence after the tail was gone. You don’t need all of that.
4. Don’t fade the tail to save time. If the reverb is too long for the song, shorten the reverb in the mix. The ending should be a decision, not an export accident.
5. Do the start too. Silence before the first note has its own cost, covered in the silence at the top of your bounce.
Sending it to a mastering engineer? Send the full tail with the extra silence and let them trim. It’s easy to cut silence and impossible to get back a tail that was never rendered. Stems follow the same rule: every stem runs the same length, past the last tail, as covered in exporting stems for a mixer.

### Fade-outs, albums and slowed versions
If the song fades out, draw the fade in the session so the reverb and delay fade with the music. A fade drawn on the bounced file after a hard cut still has the cut in it, just quieter.
On an album where songs run into each other, the end of one track and the start of the next are a single sequencing decision, and the gap between them has its own traps once the files are encoded. That’s in why gapless albums get gaps after MP3 or AAC.
Slowing a song down stretches everything, tail included. From the bottom of the arithmetic above, our 3.68-second tail lasts 4.60 seconds at 0.8x and 4.91 seconds at 0.75x. If you trimmed the master tight and then slow it down, there’s no extra silence for that longer tail to ring into. So if you’re slowing a song in the ScrewAI demo, start from the long export and trim after. More on when to slow in when to slow the bounce.

### Genre notes
- Ballads, gospel and cinematic. The hall or plate tail is part of the ending. Give slow songs four bars or more: a 4.0-second decay is 1.5 bars at 90 BPM.
- Hip-hop and trap. Endings often stop dead on purpose, and that’s fine. Make the stop happen in the session by muting the reverb and delay returns on the last hit, so the stop is clean, not a render cut.
- Dub, reggae and lo-fi. High-feedback throws are the outro. At 0.75 feedback a quarter-note delay at 90 BPM runs 16.67 seconds, so export very long and decide by ear where it ends.
- Club edits. The outro is built for DJs to mix out of, so keep the drums on the grid to the last bar and let any final effects tail run past it. Even if nobody hears the last second, the file still shouldn’t click.
Note: Export long, check the end, trim the silence and never the tail.
Q: Why does my song cut off at the end when I export?
A: The export range stops at the last bar or region while reverb and delay are still ringing. Some DAWs render only the selection you give them. Extend the range two bars or more past the last note and export again.
Q: How much silence should be at the end of a song?
A: Enough for the tail to die away, plus a short fade. Trim a little after the tail falls below about −60 dBFS. On an album, the gap before the next song is a sequencing choice, so set it there.
Q: Should I fade out the end of the bounce?
A: Fade the silence after the tail, not the tail itself. If you want the song to fade out, draw the fade in the session so the effects fade with the music.
Q: Do stems need the reverb tail too?
A: Yes. Export every stem the same length, from the same start to a point past the last tail, so they line up and nothing gets cut short in the mix.

---

## Compressor killing your drums’ punch? Slow the attack down
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/compressor-kills-the-punch-slow-the-attack.html
Section: Dynamics · 26 October 2026 · 8 min
Summary: Why compression makes drums lose their punch and how to set attack and release so the crack gets through: measured on a synthetic snare at 0.1, 1, 10 and 30 ms attack, plus what a long release does to a 16th-note roll. Script inside.

When a compressor kills the punch of your drums, the attack is usually too fast. It clamps down on the first few milliseconds of the hit, the crack you hear as punch, and turns it down along with everything else. Slow the attack until the front of the hit gets through and the compressor works on the body behind it, then set the release so it lets go before the next hit.
The snare sounds great soloed. Then you put a compressor on it because that’s what you do, pull the threshold down until the meter moves, and it gets smaller. Thicker maybe, rounder, but the smack is gone. Turn the makeup gain up to match and it’s just a louder, duller snare.
The compressor did exactly what you asked. It was just faster than the part you wanted to keep.

### Where the punch actually is
A drum hit is two things in a row. First a crack that lasts a few milliseconds: the stick, the beater, the click at the front of the sample. Then the body that rings after it: shell, wires, room. Punch is mostly the gap in level between the two, how far the crack sticks up out of the body.
A compressor slow enough to miss the crack turns down only the body, so the gap grows and the drum hits harder. One fast enough to catch the crack turns both down, and the gap shrinks or disappears. That’s the whole trick, and the attack knob decides which one you get.
In the simple compressor we used for the tests below, attack is a time constant: the time it takes to get about 63% of the way to the gain reduction the threshold and ratio ask for. Here’s what that means in milliseconds, plus how much time you have between hits at a few tempos:
$ python3 attack_math.py
gain reduction applied after:   1 ms    3 ms   10 ms
  attack  0.1 ms                100%    100%    100% 
  attack    1 ms                 63%     95%    100% 
  attack   10 ms                 10%     26%     63% 
  attack   30 ms                  3%     10%     28% 

time between hits:  quarter    eighth      16th
   85 BPM            706 ms     353 ms     176 ms 
  100 BPM            600 ms     300 ms     150 ms 
  140 BPM            429 ms     214 ms     107 ms 
  170 BPM            353 ms     176 ms      88 ms 
A 10 ms attack has applied only 10% of its gain reduction one millisecond in, and 26% at three. A 0.1 ms attack is fully clamped before the first millisecond is over. Plugins don’t all define attack the same way. Some measure to a different point, and some change it with the material on purpose. So read the number on the knob as “faster or slower,” and let your ears decide the rest.

### We measured it on a snare
This script runs a basic compressor over a drum file and measures every hit: the crack (the peak of the first 5 ms), the body (the RMS level from 20 to 150 ms), and the punch, the gap between them:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""What does a compressor's attack do to the punch of a drum? Runs a simple feed-forward compressor
(peak detector, hard knee, one-pole attack/release on the gain) over a drum file and measures, per hit:
the crack (peak of the first 5 ms) and the body (RMS from 20 to 150 ms), before and after.
'Punch' here = crack level minus body level, in dB. Usage:
python3 punch_check.py snare.wav [threshold dBFS] [ratio] [release ms] [hit spacing s] [attacks ms, comma-separated]"""
import sys, wave, numpy as np
with wave.open(sys.argv[1]) as w:
    sr = w.getframerate(); x = np.frombuffer(w.readframes(w.getnframes()), "<i2") / 32768.0
thr = float(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else -24
ratio = float(sys.argv[3]) if len(sys.argv) > 3 else 4
rel = float(sys.argv[4]) if len(sys.argv) > 4 else 60
gap = float(sys.argv[5]) if len(sys.argv) > 5 else 0.6
db = lambda v: 20 * np.log10(v + 1e-12)

def compress(x, att_ms, rel_ms):
    want = np.maximum(db(np.abs(x)) - thr, 0) * (1 - 1 / ratio)       # gain reduction the knee asks for
    a, r = np.exp(-1 / (att_ms * 1e-3 * sr)), np.exp(-1 / (rel_ms * 1e-3 * sr))
    gr = np.empty_like(want); g = 0.0
    for i, v in enumerate(want):
        c = a if v > g else r
        g = c * g + (1 - c) * v; gr[i] = g
    return x * 10 ** (-gr / 20), gr

def measure(y):
    starts = np.arange(0, len(y) - int(0.15 * sr), int(gap * sr))
    crack = np.mean([db(np.abs(y[s:s + int(0.005 * sr)]).max()) for s in starts])
    body = np.mean([db(np.sqrt(np.mean(y[s + int(0.02 * sr):s + int(0.15 * sr)] ** 2))) for s in starts])
    return crack, body, starts

c0, b0, starts = measure(x)
print(f"threshold {thr:g} dBFS, ratio {ratio:g}:1, release {rel:g} ms, hits {gap*1000:.0f} ms apart")
print(f"dry:            crack {c0:6.1f} dBFS  body {b0:6.1f} dBFS  punch {c0-b0:5.1f} dB")
atts = [float(a) for a in sys.argv[6].split(",")] if len(sys.argv) > 6 else (0.1, 1, 10, 30)
for att in atts:
    y, gr = compress(x, att, rel)
    c, b, _ = measure(y)
    at_crack = np.mean([gr[s:s + int(0.005 * sr)].max() for s in starts])
    left = np.mean([gr[s - 1] for s in starts[1:]])
    print(f"attack {att:4g} ms:  crack {c:6.1f} ({c-c0:+5.1f})  body {b:6.1f} ({b-b0:+5.1f})  "
          f"punch {c-b:5.1f} dB ({(c-b)-(c0-b0):+5.1f})  GR in first 5 ms {at_crack:4.1f} dB, "
          f"still on at next hit {left:4.1f} dB")
The test file is a synthetic snare from make_snare.py: eight hits at 100 BPM, each a short noise crack over a 190 Hz shell tone and a noisy body, peaking at −3 dBFS. Threshold −20 dBFS, ratio 4:1, release 60 ms:
$ python3 punch_check.py snare.wav -20 4 60
threshold -20 dBFS, ratio 4:1, release 60 ms, hits 600 ms apart
dry:            crack   -3.0 dBFS  body  -21.9 dBFS  punch  18.9 dB
attack  0.1 ms:  crack   -8.7 ( -5.7)  body  -26.7 ( -4.8)  punch  18.0 dB ( -0.9)  GR in first 5 ms  7.8 dB, still on at next hit  0.0 dB
attack    1 ms:  crack   -3.9 ( -0.9)  body  -25.9 ( -4.0)  punch  21.9 dB ( +3.0)  GR in first 5 ms  5.1 dB, still on at next hit  0.0 dB
attack   10 ms:  crack   -3.1 ( -0.1)  body  -24.2 ( -2.3)  punch  21.1 dB ( +2.2)  GR in first 5 ms  1.3 dB, still on at next hit  0.0 dB
attack   30 ms:  crack   -3.0 ( -0.0)  body  -23.1 ( -1.2)  punch  20.1 dB ( +1.2)  GR in first 5 ms  0.5 dB, still on at next hit  0.0 dB
At 0.1 ms the compressor caught the crack and took 5.7 dB off it, more than the 4.8 dB it took off the body, so the punch went down 0.9 dB. That’s the flattened snare. At 1 ms the crack lost only 0.9 dB while the body lost 4.0, and the punch went up 3.0 dB, the most of the four. 10 ms still added 2.2 dB. At 30 ms the compressor was late for almost everything: the crack untouched and only 1.2 dB off the body.
So slower isn’t automatically better. Too slow and you’re barely compressing the hit at all. On this snare the sweet spot was 1 to 10 ms. On a real kit it moves: a kick with a long beater click, a snare sample with a fat front, a room mic with no crack at all. Start in that range, slow it down if the hit sounds pushed back, and speed it up if the front pokes out too much.

### Release: let go before the next hit
Release is how fast the compressor stops compressing. If it’s still holding down when the next hit arrives, that hit’s crack gets turned down before the attack even matters. The room you have is the gap between hits, from the second half of the table above: 16th notes at 100 BPM are 150 ms apart, and at 140 BPM only 107 ms.
We rendered a 16th-note roll at 100 BPM, hits 150 ms apart, and ran it at 10 ms attack with a 60 ms and a 400 ms release:
$ python3 punch_check.py roll.wav -20 4 60 0.15 10
threshold -20 dBFS, ratio 4:1, release 60 ms, hits 150 ms apart
dry:            crack   -3.0 dBFS  body  -22.3 dBFS  punch  19.3 dB
attack   10 ms:  crack   -3.6 ( -0.6)  body  -24.5 ( -2.2)  punch  20.9 dB ( +1.6)  GR in first 5 ms  1.5 dB, still on at next hit  0.6 dB

$ python3 punch_check.py roll.wav -20 4 400 0.15 10
threshold -20 dBFS, ratio 4:1, release 400 ms, hits 150 ms apart
dry:            crack   -3.0 dBFS  body  -22.3 dBFS  punch  19.3 dB
attack   10 ms:  crack   -5.7 ( -2.7)  body  -26.1 ( -3.8)  punch  20.4 dB ( +1.1)  GR in first 5 ms  3.2 dB, still on at next hit  3.1 dB
With the 60 ms release, 0.6 dB of gain reduction was still on when each next hit landed, and the crack lost 0.6 dB. With 400 ms, 3.1 dB was still on and the crack lost 2.7 dB. Same attack, same threshold. The long release took the punch because the compressor never let go. On busy parts like hats, rolls and fast trap hi-hat patterns, a release longer than the gap between hits turns the compressor into a fader that’s always half down.

### Setting it in the session
1. Start in the middle. Attack around 10 ms, a release that finishes before the next hit, and the threshold down until the meter moves on every hit, not just the loudest.
2. Sweep the attack and listen to the front. Go from slow to fast. The moment the crack goes soft, back off a little.
3. Set the release by the meter. The gain reduction should get back to zero, or close, before the next hit. Watch it at the busiest part of the song, not the intro.
4. Compare at the same level. Match the output with makeup gain and toggle bypass. Louder always sounds better, which is the trap in pick one monitoring level.
5. Want weight and crack? Blend a slammed, fast copy under the untouched drums. Check the latency first, or the blend comes out thin, as in parallel compression sounds thin.
If you’d rather see it than trust your ears at 3 a.m., bounce the drum bus once with the compressor bypassed and once engaged, and put both through CoProducer. Its dynamic-range readouts sit next to LUFS and true peak in the report, so a bus that got flattened shows up as a smaller number, not just a feeling. Why that number isn’t loudness is in crest factor is not loudness.

### Genre notes
- Hip-hop and trap. If the drum bus ducks every time the 808 hits, that isn’t the attack. It’s the detector hearing the low end, covered in your bus compressor is pumping on the 808.
- Rock and live drums. Room mics have little crack to lose, so fast attack on the rooms is fine and often the sound. The close mics are where a slower attack keeps the stick.
- Pop and R&B. Programmed drums are often compressed or limited inside the sample already. If there’s no crack left, a slower attack can’t bring it back. Pick a different sample or reach for a transient shaper.
- EDM and house. A clipper or limiter at the end of the chain shaves the very top of the crack anyway. Keep the punch from the drum compressor in the mix and decide how much the master takes, as in clipper vs limiter.
Note: Slow enough to let the crack through, fast enough to catch the body, and let go before the next hit.
Q: Why does compression make my drums lose punch?
A: The attack is catching the first few milliseconds of the hit, the crack, and turning it down along with the body. Slow the attack so the crack gets through and the compressor works on the body instead.
Q: What attack time should I use on drums?
A: There’s no single number, because plugins define attack differently. On our test snare, 1 to 10 ms added the most punch, 0.1 ms flattened it and 30 ms barely compressed it. Start around 10 ms and adjust by ear.
Q: What release should I use on a drum compressor?
A: Short enough that the gain reduction gets back to zero before the next hit. At 100 BPM, 16th notes are 150 ms apart. A 400 ms release on a 16th-note roll left 3.1 dB of gain reduction on every hit.
Q: Does a slow attack make drums louder?
A: It makes the peaks stick out further above the body, so drums hit harder at the same loudness. It also leaves taller peaks for the limiter to deal with, so check the master afterwards.

---

## 808 sounds off-key? Find its real note, then tune it to the song
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/tune-808-to-the-key-of-your-song.html
Section: Low end · 23 October 2026 · 7 min
Summary: How to tune an 808 to the key of your song: measure the note of the sustained tail, not the punch or the filename, then set coarse and fine tune so it lands on the root. Note table and script inside.

To tune an 808 to your song, find the note its sustained tail actually plays, not the note in the filename or the pitch of the punch, then use the sampler’s coarse and fine tune to put that tail on the song’s root before you write the bassline. Down in the 808’s range a semitone is only 2 to 4 Hz, so an 808 that’s 25 or 30 cents off doesn’t sound like a wrong note. It sounds like mud: a low end that never locks with the chords, no matter how much you EQ it.
The beat’s nearly done. Chords are right, the 808 pattern hits, the kick punches. But the low end feels cloudy, like it’s sitting next to the song instead of under it. So you EQ it, compress it, sidechain it, swap the kick. It gets a bit cleaner and never quite right.
A lot of the time that’s tuning, and no amount of EQ fixes a note that’s between two notes.

### Why an off-key 808 doesn’t sound wrong
Ears are good at pitch in the middle of the keyboard and bad at it in the bottom octave. Here’s how small the steps are down there, with A4 at 440 Hz:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Bass-register note frequencies (equal temperament, A4 = 440 Hz), how many Hz one semitone and
25 cents are at each note, and how far varispeed (tape-style slowing) moves the pitch of a whole beat."""
import math
NAMES = ["C", "C#", "D", "D#", "E", "F", "F#", "G", "G#", "A", "A#", "B"]
def freq(name, octave): return 440 * 2 ** ((NAMES.index(name) - 9) / 12 + (octave - 4))

print("note   Hz     1 semitone up   25 cents")
for octave in (1,):
    for n in NAMES:
        f = freq(n, octave)
        print(f"{n+str(octave):<5} {f:6.2f}   +{f*(2**(1/12)-1):4.2f} Hz        {f*(2**(25/1200)-1):4.2f} Hz")
print("\nvarispeed  pitch shift")
for s in (0.95, 0.9, 0.85, 0.8, 0.75):
    st = 12 * math.log2(s); whole = round(st); cents = (st - whole) * 100
    print(f"  x{s:<5}   {st:+6.2f} st  = {whole:+d} st {cents:+4.0f} cents")
$ python3 note_math.py
note   Hz     1 semitone up   25 cents
C1     32.70   +1.94 Hz        0.48 Hz
C#1    34.65   +2.06 Hz        0.50 Hz
D1     36.71   +2.18 Hz        0.53 Hz
D#1    38.89   +2.31 Hz        0.57 Hz
E1     41.20   +2.45 Hz        0.60 Hz
F1     43.65   +2.60 Hz        0.63 Hz
F#1    46.25   +2.75 Hz        0.67 Hz
G1     49.00   +2.91 Hz        0.71 Hz
G#1    51.91   +3.09 Hz        0.76 Hz
A1     55.00   +3.27 Hz        0.80 Hz
A#1    58.27   +3.46 Hz        0.85 Hz
B1     61.74   +3.67 Hz        0.90 Hz

varispeed  pitch shift
  x0.95     -0.89 st  = -1 st  +11 cents
  x0.9      -1.82 st  = -2 st  +18 cents
  x0.85     -2.81 st  = -3 st  +19 cents
  x0.8      -3.86 st  = -4 st  +14 cents
  x0.75     -4.98 st  = -5 st   +2 cents
At G1, a whole semitone is 2.9 Hz and a quarter of one is 0.7 Hz. Nobody hears “that 808 is 25 cents sharp” on its own. What you hear is the 808 rubbing against the bass notes in the chords, and its harmonics (the 2nd, 3rd and up, which is most of what a phone plays back) fighting the keys and pads that live in the same range. That rub reads as mud, not as a wrong note. It’s also why a saturated 808 shows bad tuning more than a clean sine one does: you’ve turned up exactly the part that clashes. More on what phones play in why your 808 disappears on phone speakers.

### The filename is a guess, and the punch is sharp
Sample packs label 808s by note, and the label is usually where the designer aimed, often before they saturated, pitched or trimmed it. Then there’s the hit itself: most 808s start high and drop fast into the tail. That pitch drop is the punch. A tuner that reads the first 50 milliseconds reports something sharp, and a tuner that reads the whole thing averages the two.
So measure the tail. This script finds the lowest strong peak between 150 ms and 1 s and, if you give it a key, tells you the coarse and fine tune that put it on the nearest root:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Find the real note of an 808 (or any bass one-shot) from its tail, and the sampler tuning that puts it
on a target note. Usage: python3 find_808_note.py 808.wav [target note, e.g. F or A#]"""
import sys, wave, math, numpy as np
NAMES = ["C", "C#", "D", "D#", "E", "F", "F#", "G", "G#", "A", "A#", "B"]

def load(path):
    with wave.open(path) as w:
        sr, ch, sw = w.getframerate(), w.getnchannels(), w.getsampwidth()
        x = np.frombuffer(w.readframes(w.getnframes()), {2: "<i2", 4: "<i4"}[sw]).astype(float)
    return x.reshape(-1, ch).mean(axis=1) / (2 ** (8 * sw - 1)), sr

def lowest_peak(seg, sr, lo=25, hi=250):
    n = 1 << 20                                             # heavy zero-padding for fine bins
    spec = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(seg * np.hanning(len(seg)), n)); fr = np.fft.rfftfreq(n, 1 / sr)
    band = (fr >= lo) & (fr <= hi); s, f = spec[band], fr[band]
    pk = [i for i in range(1, len(s) - 1) if s[i] > s[i-1] and s[i] >= s[i+1] and s[i] > s.max() / 4]
    i = pk[0]                                               # lowest peak within 12 dB of the strongest
    a, b, c = np.log(s[i-1:i+2]); d = 0.5 * (a - c) / (a - 2 * b + c)
    return f[i] + d * (f[1] - f[0])

def note_of(hz):
    m = 69 + 12 * math.log2(hz / 440); k = round(m)
    return f"{NAMES[k % 12]}{k // 12 - 1}", (m - k) * 100, k

x, sr = load(sys.argv[1])
print("pitch over the first 300 ms (the punch glides down):")
for ms in range(0, 300, 60):
    a = int(sr * ms / 1000); hz = lowest_peak(x[a:a + int(sr * 0.06)], sr)
    print(f"  {ms:3d}-{ms+60:3d} ms  ≈ {hz:5.1f} Hz")
tail = x[int(sr * 0.15):int(sr * 1.0)]
hz = lowest_peak(tail, sr); name, cents, k = note_of(hz)
print(f"tail (150-1000 ms): {hz:.2f} Hz = {name} {cents:+.0f} cents")
if len(sys.argv) > 2:
    t = NAMES.index(sys.argv[2].upper())
    best = min((12 * o + t + 12 for o in range(0, 4)), key=lambda m: abs(m - (69 + 12 * math.log2(hz / 440))))
    shift = best - (69 + 12 * math.log2(hz / 440)); coarse = round(shift); fine = (shift - coarse) * 100
    print(f"to land on {NAMES[t]}{best // 12 - 1} ({440 * 2 ** ((best - 69) / 12):.2f} Hz): "
          f"coarse {coarse:+d} st, fine {fine:+.0f} cents")
We ran it on a synthetic 808 named the way a pack would name it, 808_Fsharp.wav, built so its tail sits at 47.0 Hz, for a song in F:
$ python3 find_808_note.py 808_Fsharp.wav F
pitch over the first 300 ms (the punch glides down):
    0- 60 ms  ≈  66.5 Hz
   60-120 ms  ≈  47.8 Hz
  120-180 ms  ≈  47.0 Hz
  180-240 ms  ≈  47.0 Hz
  240-300 ms  ≈  47.0 Hz
tail (150-1000 ms): 47.00 Hz = F#1 +28 cents
to land on F1 (43.65 Hz): coarse -1 st, fine -28 cents
The punch reads around 66 Hz and the pitch settles by about 120 ms. The tail is F#1 plus 28 cents, so the “F#” sample really sits about a quarter of the way to G. Drop it a semitone for F and it’s still 28 cents sharp on every note of the bassline. Put −28 cents in fine tune as well, and it lands on F1 at 43.65 Hz.
Treat the result as a starting point. A heavily distorted 808 can have a 2nd harmonic louder than its fundamental, and the script takes the lowest strong peak to stay clear of that, but your ears get the final word.

### Tuning it in the sampler
1. Fix the cents first. Put the fine-tune number on the sample so it plays a true note. Here that’s −28 cents, so the F# sample is really F#.
2. Tell the sampler the root. Set the root key to the note the sample now plays (F#1). Then pressing F plays F, and every note you program after that is in tune.
3. Check it against something you trust. Hold the song’s root on a piano or a sine an octave or two up and play a long 808 under it. A slow wobble or beating means you’re close but not there. Nudge fine tune until it goes still.
4. Measure with glide off. Portamento and pitch envelopes move the note on purpose. Tune the dry one-shot, then add the slides back.
5. Then the kick. A kick with a strong low note can clash with the 808 too. We go through that in your kick and 808 are arguing in the same chair.

### Which octave, and when the chords move
The roots in the table run from 32.70 Hz (C1) to 61.74 Hz (B1). Small speakers and many earbuds give back very little near the bottom of that range, so songs in C, C# or D often put the 808 an octave up (C2 is 65.41 Hz, double C1) or lean on saturation so the harmonics carry it. Keys from E to B keep the root between 41 and 62 Hz, which hits hard on a big system and still has harmonics small speakers can play.
Then follow the chords. If the progression moves from F minor to D-flat and the 808 keeps holding F across the change, the low end turns sour, and it isn’t tuning at all. Move the 808 to the new root, or shorten it so it’s gone before the chord changes.

### Slowed and screwed beats change key too
Slowing a beat tape-style drops everything together, so the beat stays in tune with itself. It just doesn’t land neatly on a new key. From the bottom of the script output above: 0.8x is 3.86 semitones down, four semitones plus 14 cents. A beat in A minor slowed to 0.8 sits 14 cents sharp of F minor. Only 0.75x comes out close to a whole step (five semitones, plus 2 cents).
That matters the moment you add something new on top. A fresh 808, a vocal or a keys part should be tuned to the slowed beat, not to the original key. If you’re slowing things down in the ScrewAI demo, run the slowed bounce through the script with the new key and take its cents number. Why slowing a beat is a different job from shifting its pitch is covered in resampling, pitch shifting and tempo change.

### Genre notes
- Trap and drill. The 808 is the bassline, so tuning is the bassline. Slides should start and land on notes in key, with the landing held long enough to be heard as a note.
- R&B and pop. The 808 sits under bigger chords. Follow the chord roots and keep notes short enough to clear each change.
- Boom bap and sample-based beats. Records aren’t always at A440, so a sample can sit between keys. Measure the bass note in the sample, then tune the 808 to the sample, not to a chart.
- House and techno. The sub and the kick both carry pitch. Tune the kick’s low note to the root or the fifth, and the sub to the root.
Note: Measure the tail, fix the cents, then write the bassline. Your EQ will have a lot less to do.
Q: How do I find what key my 808 is in?
A: Measure the sustained tail, not the attack. Read it with a tuner or a spectrum analyzer from about 150 ms in, or run a short script that finds the lowest strong peak. The note in the filename is often off by a quarter semitone or more.
Q: Why does my 808 sound muddy even on the right note?
A: It’s probably a few cents off. In the bottom octave a semitone is only 2 to 4 Hz, so 25 cents off is under a hertz. You won’t hear a wrong note, but its harmonics clash with the chords and the low end sounds cloudy.
Q: Should the 808 follow the root or just stay in key?
A: Usually the root of each chord. A long 808 held across a chord change clashes even when it’s perfectly tuned, so move it or shorten it.
Q: Does slowing a beat change its key?
A: Yes. Tape-style slowing lowers the pitch by 12 × log2(speed) semitones. At 0.8x that’s 3.86 semitones, so the beat lands 14 cents sharp of a key four semitones down. Tune anything new to the slowed beat.

---

## Making a clean version? Edit the vocals, keep the length, then check it against the explicit
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/clean-version-of-a-song-mute-reverse-or-replace.html
Section: Delivery · 23 October 2026 · 8 min
Summary: How to make a clean version of a song: mute, reverse or replace the words on the vocal tracks, chase the reverb and delay tails, bounce through the same master at the same length, then compare it to the explicit. Script inside.

A clean version is the explicit song with only the flagged words changed on the vocal tracks: muted, reversed or replaced, then bounced through the same master chain at exactly the same length. Edit the vocals, not the stereo mix, so the beat never drops out, and chase every copy of the word, including doubles, ad-libs and the reverb and delay tails. Then compare the two bounces. They should match everywhere except your edits.
Someone wants the clean. A radio show, a playlist, a sync brief, a school event, your distributor. The fast way is to drop the whole mix out on every curse, and it sounds exactly like that: the beat cuts out mid-bar, the energy dies, and the edit is louder than the word ever was.
A good clean edit is one where people only notice the word is gone, not that you were there.

### Mute, reverse or replace
Method | How it sounds | Good for
Mute (short fades) | A gap in the vocal while the beat keeps going | Fast verses, where a small gap reads like a breath
Reverse | The word plays backwards, so rhythm and energy stay | Hip-hop radio edits. Reverse the word, not the phrase
Replace | A re-sung or alternate word, or an ad-lib over it | Radio, sync and anything that should sound unedited
Effect drop | A filter, tape stop or sound effect swallows the word | Once or twice a song, or it starts to draw attention
Whatever you choose, cut from just before the first consonant to just after the last one. The front of a hard consonant is how a listener recognises a word, and a reversed word with the original first letter still in it isn’t clean. Some stations and platforms have their own rules on reversals, so if the edit is for someone specific, ask what they accept.

### Where the word is hiding
The lead vocal is the easy part. A word you muted can still be in the song in half a dozen places:
- Doubles, stacks and harmonies. Every track that sings the line sings the word.
- Ad-libs and hype tracks. They often carry more of it than the lead does.
- Reverb and delay. Mute the word on the dry vocal after the send and the delay throw repeats it a beat later. Edit before the sends, or automate the send down for that word. If the effect returns were printed, edit those too. Throws are covered in setting your delay from the tempo.
- The beat. Vocal chops and samples in the instrumental, or the hook teased in the intro.
- Bleed. On a live-tracked record the vocal is in the drum overheads and room mics too. Muting the vocal track leaves the word under the cymbals.
Fade every edit by a few milliseconds so nothing clicks. We measured why in clicks at your edit points.

### Same chain, same length
Bounce the clean from the same session, through the same master chain, with the same settings and the same start point. Don’t master it separately. A different chain changes the tone and loudness, and the two versions stop lining up. When they match sample for sample, a DJ can switch between them mid-song, a video editor can drop one in for the other, and any cue points or sync timings work on both.
When you upload, the clean is its own track with its own ISRC, and most distributors ask you to mark it as the clean version of the explicit one. A song that never had explicit lyrics isn’t a clean version, it’s just not explicit.

### Check the clean against the explicit
Ears are good at finding the words you missed. They’re bad at noticing that the clean is 40 milliseconds shorter or half a dB louder. A file comparison catches those in a second. This script checks the format and length, then lists every stretch where the two files differ by more than −60 dBFS:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Check a clean (or radio) edit against the explicit bounce: same format, same length, and a list of
every place the two files differ. Outside your edits they should match. Usage:
python3 compare_versions.py explicit.wav clean.wav [threshold dB, default -60]"""
import sys, wave, numpy as np

def load(path):
    with wave.open(path) as w:
        p = (w.getframerate(), w.getnchannels(), w.getsampwidth()); nf = w.getnframes()
        x = np.frombuffer(w.readframes(nf), {2: "<i2", 3: None, 4: "<i4"}[p[2]]).astype(float)
    return x.reshape(-1, p[1]) / (2 ** (8 * p[2] - 1)), p

(a, pa), (b, pb) = load(sys.argv[1]), load(sys.argv[2])
thr = float(sys.argv[3]) if len(sys.argv) > 3 else -60
sr = pa[0]
print(f"format: {pa[0]} Hz / {pa[1]} ch / {8*pa[2]}-bit vs {pb[0]} Hz / {pb[1]} ch / {8*pb[2]}-bit"
      + ("  OK" if pa == pb else "  MISMATCH"))
print(f"length: {len(a)} vs {len(b)} samples ({len(a)/sr:.3f} s vs {len(b)/sr:.3f} s)"
      + ("  OK" if len(a) == len(b) else f"  OFF BY {abs(len(a)-len(b))} samples"))
m = min(len(a), len(b)); hop = sr // 100
d = (a[:m] - b[:m])[: m // hop * hop].reshape(-1, hop, a.shape[1])
lvl = 20 * np.log10(np.sqrt((d ** 2).mean(axis=(1, 2))) + 1e-12)        # 10 ms RMS of the difference
diff = lvl > thr
regions, i = [], 0
while i < len(diff):
    if diff[i]:
        j = i
        while j < len(diff) and (diff[j] or (j + 5 < len(diff) and diff[j:j + 5].any())): j += 1  # bridge <50 ms gaps
        regions.append((i, j)); i = j
    else: i += 1
same = 100 * (1 - diff.mean())
print(f"identical (difference under {thr:.0f} dBFS) for {same:.1f}% of the song; {len(regions)} edit region(s):")
for k, (i, j) in enumerate(regions[:12], 1):
    print(f"  {k}: {i/100:6.2f}-{j/100:6.2f} s  ({(j-i)*10:4d} ms)  peak difference {lvl[i:j].max():6.1f} dBFS")
if len(regions) > 12 or same < 50:
    print("  -> differs almost everywhere: not the same mix/master chain, or the files are offset")
We built a 12-second test: a beat and a vocal of 13 short sung words, mastered with gain and a simple peak limiter with a 100 ms release. In the clean, the words at 3.10 s and 7.60 s are muted with 5 ms fades and the word at 9.85 s is reversed:
$ python3 compare_versions.py explicit.wav clean.wav
format: 44100 Hz / 2 ch / 16-bit vs 44100 Hz / 2 ch / 16-bit  OK
length: 529200 vs 529200 samples (12.000 s vs 12.000 s)  OK
identical (difference under -60 dBFS) for 90.7% of the song; 3 edit region(s):
  1:   3.10-  3.51 s  ( 410 ms)  peak difference   -6.9 dBFS
  2:   7.60-  8.01 s  ( 410 ms)  peak difference   -7.5 dBFS
  3:   9.85- 10.15 s  ( 300 ms)  peak difference   -2.1 dBFS
Same format, same length, identical for 90.7% of the song, and three edits for the three words we changed. That count is the point: if your list says four words and the script finds three, one slipped through. The two mutes show up as 410 ms for a 300 ms word, because the limiter on the master eased off for its 100 ms release once the word was gone, so the beat under the gap came up slightly. That’s normal with a limiter on the bus. The reversed word changes only its own 300 ms.
Here’s the same check after bouncing the clean through the master 0.5 dB hotter, as if it had been mastered separately:
$ python3 compare_versions.py explicit.wav clean_hot.wav
format: 44100 Hz / 2 ch / 16-bit vs 44100 Hz / 2 ch / 16-bit  OK
length: 529200 vs 529200 samples (12.000 s vs 12.000 s)  OK
identical (difference under -60 dBFS) for 0.2% of the song; 1 edit region(s):
  1:   0.00- 12.00 s  (12000 ms)  peak difference   -2.1 dBFS
  -> differs almost everywhere: not the same mix/master chain, or the files are offset
Half a dB is easy to miss by ear and impossible to miss here. The script can only tell you what changed, not what didn’t, so a word you forgot to edit won’t show up. Listen to every edit plus a second after it for tails, then play the whole clean once from top to bottom. If a plugin in the chain adds noise or random modulation, the files won’t match exactly even where nothing changed. Raise the threshold to around −50 dBFS, or print those tracks first.

### When you only have the master
Old song, dead hard drive, a beat from a producer who stopped answering. If all you have is the stereo master, separating it lets you edit the words on the vocal alone and play it back over the instrumental, so the beat keeps running under every edit. Pull the vocal with StemSplit, edit and fade the words on that stem, then sum the two back together. Separated stems rarely add back to the exact master, so run the compare script at a looser threshold, around −40 dBFS, and trust your ears over the numbers around each edit. The bleed caveats are the same as in sampling from separated stems.

### Genre notes
- Hip-hop. Reverses and mutes are both familiar to radio ears. Mute short words in fast verses and reverse longer ones, and check the ad-lib track first.
- Pop and R&B. Replace where you can. Re-singing a word while the session is still open takes minutes and sounds like nothing happened.
- Rock and metal. Gang vocals and room mics carry words. On live-tracked songs, plan to edit several tracks or replace the line.
- Live recordings. The crowd and every open mic can carry the word. A replacement or an effect drop is often the only clean option.
Note: Edit the vocals, chase the tails, bounce through the same chain, then let the two files tell you what changed.
Q: How do you make a clean version of a song?
A: Edit the explicit words on every vocal track (mute, reverse or replace them, with short fades), deal with the reverb and delay tails, then bounce from the same session through the same master chain so the clean is the same length as the explicit.
Q: Should I mute or reverse curse words?
A: Both are common. Muting leaves a gap that works in fast verses; reversing keeps the rhythm and energy. Cut from just before the first consonant, and ask the station or platform what they accept if the edit is for them.
Q: Why can I still hear the word after I muted it?
A: It’s usually somewhere else: a double, an ad-lib, a delay or reverb tail fed before your edit, or vocal bleed in other mics. Edit before the sends and check every track that sings the line.
Q: Does a clean version need its own ISRC?
A: Yes. The clean is a separate recording version, so it gets its own ISRC, and most distributors ask you to mark it as the clean version of the explicit track.

---

## Panned parts get quieter in mono? That’s your pan law, not your ears
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/pan-law-why-panned-parts-change-level.html
Section: Mix · 22 October 2026 · 7 min
Summary: What pan law is and why it matters: a centered sound is turned down on both sides so panning doesn’t change its loudness. Fold to mono and the center jumps up to 3 dB. Table and script inside.

Pan law is how much a mono sound is turned down on each side when it sits in the center, so it doesn’t sound louder there than panned hard. With the common −3 dB law the stereo loudness stays even across the pan, but fold the mix to mono and anything in the center comes out 3 dB louder than the same sound panned hard. That’s why hard-panned guitars and hats seem to fall back on a phone or a club’s mono system.
You balance the mix on headphones and it feels right: guitars wide, hats off to one side, vocal and 808 dead center. Then you hit the mono button, or play it on a phone, and the vocal and bass jump forward while the panned parts sink. Nothing is out of phase. The correlation meter looks fine. It’s still a different mix.
Most of that shift comes from a setting you probably never chose: the pan law.

### What the pan knob is actually doing
A mono track panned to the center plays out of both speakers. Two speakers playing the same thing add up, so if the panner left both sides at full level, the sound would get louder every time you moved it toward the middle. A pan law turns both sides down at center to stop that. The question is by how much, and there are four common answers. This little script prints all four for a sound in the center, halfway left (L50) and hard left (L100):
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Pan law table: per-side gain and level change for a mono source, in stereo and folded to mono.
Levels are relative to the same source panned hard to one side (which every law leaves at unity)."""
import math, sys

def gains(law_db, pos):
    """pos -1 (hard L) .. 0 (center) .. +1 (hard R). Returns (L, R) linear gains."""
    t = (pos + 1) / 2                      # 0..1
    if law_db == 0:                        # balance-style: center is unity on both sides
        return min(1, 2 * (1 - t)), min(1, 2 * t)
    p = math.cos(t * math.pi / 2), math.sin(t * math.pi / 2)   # constant power, -3 dB at center
    lin = 1 - t, t                                              # linear, -6 dB at center
    if law_db == -3: return p
    if law_db == -6: return lin
    if law_db == -4.5: return tuple(math.sqrt(a * b) for a, b in zip(p, lin))
    raise SystemExit("laws: 0, -3, -4.5, -6")

db = lambda x: 20 * math.log10(x) if x > 0 else float("-inf")
laws = [float(a) if "." in a else int(a) for a in sys.argv[1:]] or [0, -3, -4.5, -6]
print(f"{'law':>6} {'pan':>6} {'L gain':>8} {'R gain':>8} {'stereo':>8} {'mono':>8}")
for law in laws:
    for pos, name in ((0, "C"), (-0.5, "L50"), (-1, "L100")):
        l, r = gains(law, pos)
        stereo = 10 * math.log10(l * l + r * r)    # acoustic power from two speakers
        mono = db(l + r)                           # both sides summed to one speaker
        print(f"{law:>5}dB {name:>6} {db(l):>7.1f}  {db(r):>7.1f}  {stereo:>+7.1f}  {mono:>+7.1f}")
$ python3 pan_law.py
   law    pan   L gain   R gain   stereo     mono
    0dB      C     0.0      0.0     +3.0     +6.0
    0dB    L50     0.0     -6.0     +1.0     +3.5
    0dB   L100     0.0     -inf     +0.0     +0.0
   -3dB      C    -3.0     -3.0     +0.0     +3.0
   -3dB    L50    -0.7     -8.3     +0.0     +2.3
   -3dB   L100     0.0     -inf     +0.0     +0.0
 -4.5dB      C    -4.5     -4.5     -1.5     +1.5
 -4.5dB    L50    -1.6    -10.2     -1.0     +1.2
 -4.5dB   L100     0.0     -inf     +0.0     +0.0
   -6dB      C    -6.0     -6.0     -3.0     +0.0
   -6dB    L50    -2.5    -12.0     -2.0     +0.0
   -6dB   L100     0.0     -inf     +0.0     +0.0
Read the table against a sound panned hard left, which every law leaves alone. The stereo column is what you hear from two speakers in a room, and the mono column is what happens when both sides are added together into one speaker.
- 0 dB (no compensation). Center is 3 dB louder in stereo and 6 dB louder in mono. You’ll mostly meet this on balance knobs, not true panners.
- −3 dB (constant power). Loudness stays even as you pan in stereo. Fold to mono and the center is 3 dB hotter than anything hard-panned.
- −6 dB. Perfect in mono, but in stereo the center dips 3 dB, so centered parts feel a bit too quiet on speakers.
- −4.5 dB. The compromise. Center is 1.5 dB down in stereo and 1.5 dB up in mono.
No law is right in both places at once. That’s the whole point: pick one, know which way it leans, and check the other way before you bounce.

### Why your mix changes in mono
With a −3 dB law, mixing on speakers or headphones gives you a fair picture of the stereo balance. But a lot of playback is effectively mono: phone speakers, many Bluetooth speakers, club systems and some broadcast chains. In mono everything you put in the middle gets a 3 dB lift relative to anything panned hard, and parts at half-pan get about 2.3 dB. So the vocal, kick, snare and 808 move forward together, and the double-tracked guitars, wide pads and panned percussion step back.
Three decibels doesn’t sound like a lot until it’s the hats in a drill beat or the rhythm guitars in a rock mix. That’s the difference between a part that drives the song and one you have to look for. If your low end also lives in the center, mono makes the bass feel bigger too, which is one more reason a mix that’s balanced on headphones can sound heavy and narrow on a phone. We go into the phone side in why the 808 disappears on phone speakers.

### The pan knob on a stereo track is usually a balance knob
In many DAWs, the single pan knob on a stereo track doesn’t move the sound anywhere. It turns the opposite side down. Push a stereo synth halfway left and you haven’t moved it, you’ve made its right channel quieter, and whatever was only on the right side is fading away. Hard left and the right channel is gone. If you want to move or narrow a stereo source, use a stereo panner or width control (many DAWs offer one on the track), or split it into two mono tracks and pan each one.

### When pan law bites you in practice
1. Moving a session between DAWs. Open the same mix in an app with a different default law and every panned part shifts against the centered ones by a dB or more. If a collaborator says your session sounds different, check the pan law in both projects before you touch a fader.
2. Changing the law mid-mix. Most DAWs let you set it per project. Change it halfway through and your balance moves. Pick one at the start and leave it.
3. Summing stems somewhere else. Panning is printed into the stems, so they come back correctly. But if you send mono stems and let the mix engineer pan them, their law decides the balance, not yours. Our note on exporting stems for a mix engineer covers what to print.
4. Automating pans. A sweep from hard left to center with a −3 dB law is level in stereo but rises 3 dB in mono. If the move needs to be level everywhere, ride the volume a touch with it.

### A quick routine that works
1. Find the pan law in your project settings, write it down, and keep it the same for the whole record.
2. Balance in stereo first. That’s how most people judge a mix.
3. Fold to mono at a low monitor level for ten seconds per section. Listen for which parts drop out, not for the whole mix getting smaller.
4. If a hard-panned part disappears, bring it a little toward center (70 to 80% often keeps the width and loses less in mono) or lift it 1 to 2 dB, then recheck stereo.
5. Bounce and measure the file, not the session. A low correlation reading is a separate problem from pan law, covered in phase correlation and mono.

### Genre notes
- Hip-hop and trap. Vocal, kick and 808 in the middle get the mono lift, so hats and percussion panned hard are the first things to vanish on a phone. Keep the main hat closer to center and spread the extras.
- Rock and metal. Double-tracked guitars hard left and right are the sound of the genre, and they’re exactly what drops 3 dB in mono. Check that the riff still carries before you pull the vocal up.
- EDM and house. Club systems are often mono or close to it. Leads and stabs you widened with a balance knob can lose half their content. Use a real width tool and check it summed.
- Jazz and acoustic. Panning often mirrors where players stood. A gentler spread, around half-pan, keeps that picture in mono with only about a 2 dB shift.
Note: Stereo balance, mono check, then the file. When the bounce is done, run it through CoProducer to catch phase problems a pan law won’t explain.
Q: What is pan law?
A: Pan law is the amount a mono sound is turned down on each side when it’s panned to the center, so it doesn’t get louder than when it’s panned hard. Common values are 0, −3, −4.5 and −6 dB.
Q: Which pan law should I use?
A: −3 dB keeps stereo loudness even as you pan and is a common default. −6 dB keeps mono even instead, and −4.5 dB splits the difference. The best choice is the one you pick at the start and keep, then check the other way before you bounce.
Q: Why do my panned instruments get quieter in mono?
A: With a −3 dB pan law, a centered sound adds up to 3 dB louder in mono than the same sound panned hard. So centered parts like the vocal and 808 come forward and hard-panned parts like guitars and hats fall back.
Q: Is the pan knob on a stereo track a panner?
A: In many DAWs it’s a balance control. Turning it left lowers the right channel instead of moving the sound, so anything only on the right side fades out. Use a stereo panner or width control to move or narrow a stereo source.

---

## Loud breaths in your vocal? Turn them down before the compressor, don’t cut them
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/vocal-breaths-turn-them-down-dont-cut-them.html
Section: Vocals · 22 October 2026 · 7 min
Summary: How to handle breaths in a vocal: lower them with clip gain before compression instead of deleting them. A compressor with make-up gain can shrink the gap between singing and breath from 12 dB to 3 dB.

Breaths get loud because compression and limiting turn down the singing but not the quieter breath, then make-up gain lifts everything. Lower each breath with clip gain before the compressor, usually by 4 to 10 dB, instead of deleting it. A vocal with no breaths sounds chopped and robotic; a vocal with breaths sitting well under the words sounds human and still clean.
The raw vocal sounded fine. Then you put a compressor on it, pushed it into the beat, and now every line starts with a gasp that’s almost as loud as the first word. After mastering it’s worse. The obvious fix is to cut every breath out, and that’s usually where the vocal stops sounding like a person.
Breaths aren’t the problem. The gap between the breath and the singing is, and your chain is what’s closing it.

### Why compression brings breaths up
A compressor only turns down what goes over its threshold. The singing is loud, so it gets pulled down. The breath is quieter, often under the threshold, so it doesn’t. Then you add make-up gain to bring the singing back to where it was, and that gain lifts the breath too. Here’s the arithmetic for a simple 4:1 compressor:
$ python3 comp_math.py -12 -24 -24 4
in : sung -12.0  breath -24.0  gap 12.0 dB
out: sung -12.0  breath -15.0  gap 3.0 dB  (threshold -24.0, 4.0:1, make-up +9.0 dB)
Going in, the breath sat 12 dB under the singing. Coming out, it’s 3 dB under. Same take, same breath, it just lost most of the space around it. Breaths that start further down still lose half their gap:
$ python3 comp_math.py -12 -30 -24 4
in : sung -12.0  breath -30.0  gap 18.0 dB
out: sung -12.0  breath -21.0  gap 9.0 dB  (threshold -24.0, 4.0:1, make-up +9.0 dB)
A mastering limiter does the same thing again on the whole mix. That’s why breaths you never noticed in the session show up on the master, the same way esses get louder after mastering.

### Turn them down first, with clip gain
The fix is to set the breath level before the compressor sees it. Clip gain (also called region or item gain) changes the audio before any plugin, so the compressor works on a vocal where the breaths are already in their place.
1. Split around each breath. Cut just before it starts and just after it ends, leaving the first consonant of the word alone.
2. Lower it, don’t mute it. Start with 6 dB down and adjust by ear. Some breaths are part of the phrasing and only need 3 or 4. A big gasp before a loud chorus might want 10 or more.
3. Fade the edges. A few milliseconds of fade on each split keeps the gain change from clicking. We measured why in clicks at edit points.
4. Then compress. Now the compressor and make-up gain bring everything up together and the breath stays where you put it.
On a long session you can let a script find the breaths first. This one looks for stretches that are quieter than the singing, well above silence, and mostly high-frequency noise, and tells you how much clip gain puts each one 18 dB under the sung level:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""List likely breaths in a mono or stereo vocal WAV and how much clip gain brings each to a target level.
A breath here = a stretch of 10 ms frames that is quieter than the singing but well above silence, with
most of its energy above 1.5 kHz. Usage: python3 find_breaths.py vocal.wav [target_dB_below_vocal]"""
import sys, wave, numpy as np

def load(path):
    with wave.open(path) as w:
        sr, ch, sw = w.getframerate(), w.getnchannels(), w.getsampwidth()
        x = np.frombuffer(w.readframes(w.getnframes()), {2: "<i2", 4: "<i4"}[sw]).astype(float)
    return x.reshape(-1, ch).mean(axis=1) / (2 ** (8 * sw - 1)), sr

x, sr = load(sys.argv[1]); below = float(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 18
hop = sr // 100; frames = x[: len(x) // hop * hop].reshape(-1, hop)
rms = 20 * np.log10(np.sqrt((frames ** 2).mean(axis=1)) + 1e-12)
spec = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(frames * np.hanning(hop), axis=1)) ** 2
hi = spec[:, np.fft.rfftfreq(hop, 1 / sr) >= 1500].sum(axis=1) / (spec.sum(axis=1) + 1e-20)
voice = np.percentile(rms[rms > -60], 90)                 # loud sung level
is_breath = (rms < voice - 6) & (rms > voice - 45) & (hi > 0.7)
print(f"sung level ≈ {voice:.1f} dBFS (10 ms RMS); target for breaths: {voice - below:.1f} dBFS")
i, n = 0, 0
while i < len(is_breath):
    if is_breath[i]:
        j = i
        while j < len(is_breath) and is_breath[j]: j += 1
        if j - i >= 8:                                      # at least 80 ms
            lvl = 10 * np.log10(np.mean(10 ** (rms[i:j] / 10)))
            n += 1
            print(f"breath {n}: {i/100:6.2f}-{j/100:6.2f} s  {lvl:6.1f} dBFS  clip gain {min(0, voice - below - lvl):+5.1f} dB")
        i = j
    else: i += 1
Run on a test vocal with three sung phrases and a breath before each one:
$ python3 find_breaths.py vocal.wav
sung level ≈ -11.5 dBFS (10 ms RMS); target for breaths: -29.5 dBFS
breath 1:   0.30-  0.65 s   -24.0 dBFS  clip gain  -5.5 dB
breath 2:   2.73-  3.08 s   -24.0 dBFS  clip gain  -5.5 dB
breath 3:   5.16-  5.51 s   -24.0 dBFS  clip gain  -5.5 dB
Treat the list as a map, not a verdict. Thresholds that fit one singer and mic won’t fit every take, and a soft sung word or a breathy note can look like a breath. You still listen to every one.

### Why not just cut them, or gate them?
- Cutting leaves holes. Room tone and headphone bleed disappear and come back on every line. Hard silence between phrases sounds edited, especially on a quiet song.
- Breaths carry the timing. The inhale tells the listener the next line is coming. Remove it and phrases start out of nowhere, which is a big part of the robotic, over-tuned feel.
- Gates chatter. A gate set to catch breaths also chops soft word endings and the start of quiet consonants, and it opens and closes on reverb tails.
- De-breath plugins help, carefully. They’re quick on long takes, but they tend to work by reducing, not removing. Set them to turn breaths down a few dB and check the soft passages.

### Genre notes
- Pop and R&B. Heavy compression and stacked vocals make breaths add up fast. Lower them on the lead, and on doubles and harmonies cut them or bring them way down, since five breaths at once sounds like wind.
- Rap. Breaths before a fast verse are part of the energy. Keep them, just under the words. Ad-lib tracks usually don’t need their own breaths at all.
- Acoustic, folk and jazz. Lighter compression means breaths stay lower on their own. Touch only the ones that jump out, and leave the rest of the performance alone.
- Podcasts and voiceover. The same rule applies. Cut-out breaths are the first thing listeners notice as over-edited speech.
The same goes for an acapella you pulled from a finished song. Separation keeps the breaths along with the voice, so if you’re pulling a vocal with StemSplit for a remix, set the breaths on the stem first, then build your chain on top. More on that workflow in sampling from separated stems.
Note: Breaths down, not out, then compress. When the vocal’s in the mix, measure the bounce before it ships.
Q: Should you remove breaths from vocals?
A: Usually no. Deleting every breath makes a vocal sound chopped and robotic. Lower them with clip gain, often 4 to 10 dB, so they sit well under the words.
Q: Why are breaths so loud after compression?
A: A compressor turns down the loud singing but not the quieter breath, then make-up gain lifts both. In a 4:1 example with a −24 dB threshold, a breath 12 dB under the singing ends up only 3 dB under.
Q: Should I edit breaths before or after compression?
A: Before. Clip gain works before any plugin, so the compressor reacts to a vocal where the breaths are already at the right level.
Q: How much should I turn down a breath?
A: Start around 6 dB and adjust by ear. Breaths that are part of the phrasing may only need 3 or 4 dB; a large gasp before a loud section can take 10 dB or more.

---

## Your delay sounds off the beat? Set it from the tempo, not by ear
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/delay-time-from-bpm-sync-your-throws.html
Section: Mix · 21 October 2026 · 7 min
Summary: How to calculate delay time from BPM: 60,000 ÷ BPM is a quarter note in ms. Straight, dotted and triplet times, grid-locked pre-delay, and why 'close enough' drifts.

A quarter note lasts 60,000 ÷ BPM milliseconds, so at 140 BPM it’s 428.6 ms and an eighth is 214.3 ms. Halve it for shorter notes, multiply by 1.5 for dotted and by 2/3 for triplets. A delay set by ear a little off that number drifts further off the grid with every repeat, and that’s what makes a throw feel sloppy.
You throw a delay on the last word of the hook and it sounds great on the first repeat. By the third one it’s smearing into the snare and the pocket feels a little drunk. You nudge the time knob, it gets better in one spot and worse in another, and twenty minutes later you’ve automated it off entirely.
Most of the time the delay isn’t too loud or too dark. It’s just a few milliseconds off the tempo, and every repeat doubles down on the mistake.

### The one formula
There are 60,000 milliseconds in a minute. Divide by the tempo and you have one beat, which in 4/4 is a quarter note. Everything else comes from that:
- Straight notes. Halve for an eighth, halve again for a sixteenth. Double for a half note.
- Dotted notes. Multiply by 1.5. The dotted eighth is the classic bouncing guitar and vocal delay.
- Triplets. Multiply by 2/3. Triplet delays roll against a straight beat, which is why they sound so good on trap hats and swung vocals.
Here it is as a small script, so you never have to look up a chart again:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Delay and pre-delay times from tempo, in milliseconds.
usage: python3 delay_times.py 140 [0.8]     (optional second number: a playback-speed factor, e.g. a slowed bounce)"""
import sys
bpm = float(sys.argv[1])
if len(sys.argv) > 2:
    bpm *= float(sys.argv[2])                    # slowing the whole bounce slows the tempo by the same factor
beat = 60_000 / bpm                              # one quarter note in ms
notes = [("1/2", 2), ("1/4", 1), ("1/8", 0.5), ("1/16", 0.25)]
print(f"{bpm:g} BPM  (quarter note = {beat:.1f} ms)")
print(f"{'note':>6} {'straight':>10} {'dotted':>10} {'triplet':>10}")
for name, q in notes:
    ms = beat * q
    print(f"{name:>6} {ms:10.1f} {ms*1.5:10.1f} {ms*2/3:10.1f}")
print(f"reverb pre-delay that lands on the grid: 1/64 = {beat/16:.1f} ms, 1/32 = {beat/8:.1f} ms")
$ python3 delay_times.py 140
140 BPM  (quarter note = 428.6 ms)
  note   straight     dotted    triplet
   1/2      857.1     1285.7      571.4
   1/4      428.6      642.9      285.7
   1/8      214.3      321.4      142.9
  1/16      107.1      160.7       71.4
reverb pre-delay that lands on the grid: 1/64 = 26.8 ms, 1/32 = 53.6 ms
If your delay plugin has a sync button, use it, and you’re done. This matters when it doesn’t: hardware units, older plugins, a tape-style delay where you dial milliseconds, or a reverb whose pre-delay only takes a number.

### Why “close enough” falls apart
Say you dialed 250 ms by ear in a 140 BPM session. That’s the eighth note at 120 BPM, and on the first repeat it sounds almost right, because 35.7 ms is easy to miss on one hit. But each repeat is a copy of the last one, so the error stacks:
$ python3 drift.py 140 250 0.5
grid 214.3 ms, delay set to 250.0 ms (+35.7 ms per repeat)
repeat 1:   +35.7 ms off the grid  (+16.7% of a step)
repeat 2:   +71.4 ms off the grid  (+33.3% of a step)
repeat 3:  +107.1 ms off the grid  (+50.0% of a step)
repeat 4:  +142.9 ms off the grid  (+66.7% of a step)
repeat 5:  +178.6 ms off the grid  (+83.3% of a step)
By the third repeat the echo lands exactly a sixteenth late, which is a different rhythm, not a slightly loose one. By the fifth it’s most of the way to the next eighth. This is why a long feedback tail set by ear can make a tight beat feel rushed or dragging even when the first slap sounds fine.
The fix is boring: type the number. If you want the delay a hair behind for feel, push it a few milliseconds late on purpose, and keep the feedback low so the drift can’t pile up.

### Pre-delay can sit on the grid too
Reverb pre-delay is the gap before the reverb starts. It keeps the dry vocal clear of its own wash, which is half of what we covered in filtering the reverb return. Any value from about 10 to 60 ms can work, but picking one that’s a clean division of the beat makes the tail feel attached to the groove. At 140 BPM a 1/64 note is 26.8 ms and a 1/32 is 53.6 ms. Start at the 1/64 for a vocal that needs to stay up front, and try the 1/32 on a slow ballad or a snare plate where you want the space to open up.

### Slowed and sped-up versions
When you slow the whole bounce, everything printed in it slows together, delays included, so the repeats stay locked to the beat. That goes for a screw in ScrewAI, a tape-style varispeed, or a nightcore speed-up. What doesn’t follow along is any new delay you add after the fact. At 0.8× speed a 140 BPM record becomes 112 BPM, so a fresh throw needs the new tempo:
$ python3 delay_times.py 140 0.8
112 BPM  (quarter note = 535.7 ms)
  note   straight     dotted    triplet
   1/2     1071.4     1607.1      714.3
   1/4      535.7      803.6      357.1
   1/8      267.9      401.8      178.6
  1/16      133.9      200.9       89.3
reverb pre-delay that lands on the grid: 1/64 = 33.5 ms, 1/32 = 67.0 ms
The eighth goes from 214.3 ms to 267.9 ms. Re-use the old number on the slowed version and you’re back to drifting. If you’re making a slowed cut for a release, our note on why screw tempo still needs a legal peak covers the delivery side.

### Making throws sit
1. Put the delay on a send, not the insert. Then you can automate the send level on the exact word you want thrown, and leave the rest of the vocal dry.
2. Filter the return. A high-pass around 300 to 500 Hz and a low-pass somewhere in the 4 to 8 kHz range keeps repeats behind the lead instead of competing with it.
3. Keep feedback low on busy beats. Two or three audible repeats is plenty under a full arrangement. Long tails belong in the gaps.
4. Duck it. A compressor on the delay return keyed from the dry vocal pushes the repeats down while the singer is singing and lets them bloom in the space after.
5. Check it in mono. Ping-pong delays are wide by design. Fold to mono and make sure the throw doesn’t vanish or flam. More in why wide mixes fail in mono.

### Genre notes
- Trap and drill. Eighth-triplet throws on the last word of a bar sit right with triplet hat rolls. Keep them short and ducked so they don’t mask the 808.
- R&B. A quarter or dotted eighth with gentle feedback on a send, filtered dark, gives the vocal a trail without pushing it back.
- Rock and indie. A slapback around 80 to 140 ms is usually set for feel rather than the grid, and that’s fine because it has no feedback to drift.
- House and techno. Dotted eighths on a stab or vocal chop are the default for a reason. Sync it, and automate the feedback for builds.
- Reggae and dub. Long, high-feedback tails are the instrument. That’s exactly when the number has to be right, because you’re going to hear every repeat.
Note: Tempo in, milliseconds out, and the throw stays in the pocket. The same maths sets a compressor’s release: see starting release times by BPM for a sidechain. If you’re making a slowed version, hear the ScrewAI demo, then measure the bounce before it ships.
Q: How do I calculate delay time from BPM?
A: Divide 60,000 by the tempo to get a quarter note in milliseconds. At 140 BPM that’s 428.6 ms. Halve it for an eighth (214.3 ms), multiply by 1.5 for a dotted note and by 2/3 for a triplet.
Q: What is a dotted eighth delay in milliseconds?
A: Three-quarters of a beat: 60,000 ÷ BPM × 0.75. At 140 BPM it’s 321.4 ms, at 120 BPM it’s 375 ms.
Q: Why does my delay sound off beat even though it’s close?
A: Each repeat copies the one before, so a small error adds up. A 250 ms delay in a 140 BPM song is 35.7 ms late on the first repeat and a full sixteenth note late by the third.
Q: Should reverb pre-delay be synced to tempo?
A: It doesn’t have to be, but a value that’s a clean division of the beat tends to feel attached to the groove. At 140 BPM, 1/64 is 26.8 ms and 1/32 is 53.6 ms, both inside the common 10 to 60 ms range.

---

## Clicks at your edit points come from cutting mid-wave. Fade every cut
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/clicks-at-edit-points-fade-every-cut.html
Section: Editing · 21 October 2026 · 7 min
Summary: Why audio edits click and pop: a cut or splice that lands mid-waveform makes an instant jump. A 5 ms fade or crossfade removes it. Includes a click-finder script.

An edit clicks when the waveform jumps instantly from one value to another, which happens whenever you cut or splice in the middle of a cycle instead of at silence. That jump is a burst of high-frequency energy. A short fade on every cut, or a crossfade on every splice, around 5 ms, smooths the jump out and the click disappears.
You comp the best vocal take out of six, chop a sample into a new pattern, or trim the tail off an 808, and it all looks fine on the screen. Then on headphones there’s a tiny tick right where the edit is. Sometimes you only hear it after mastering, when the limiter and a brighter top end pull it forward.
It isn’t the plugin and it isn’t your interface. It’s the edit.

### Why a cut clicks
Audio is a wave moving up and down around zero. If you stop it when it’s at zero, nothing happens. If you stop it at the top of a cycle, the next sample is zero and the speaker cone has to snap back instantly. That instant jump isn’t a low note anymore, it’s a broadband spike, and your ears hear it as a click.
Splices do the same thing. Two takes of the same note are almost never at the same point in their cycle at the edit, so the waveform jumps from where take one was to where take two is. Low, sustained sounds give it away first: 808s, bass, pads, held vowels. Drums usually hide it, because a hit is already a jump.

### We made four edits and measured them
A synthetic 48 kHz file: one long 55 Hz note at −6 dBFS, about where a sustained 808 or bass would sit. We stopped it mid-wave once with no fade and once with a 5 ms fade-out, and spliced it to a second take a quarter-cycle off once with no fade and once with a 5 ms crossfade. A clean 55 Hz note has almost nothing above 2 kHz, so anything up there near an edit is the click:
Edit | Loudest content above 2 kHz near the edit
Stop mid-wave, no fade | −13.3 dBFS
Same stop, 5 ms fade-out | −82.9 dBFS
Splice to the other take, no fade | −8.9 dBFS
Same splice, 5 ms crossfade | −78.4 dBFS
The unfaded edits throw a burst only a few dB under the note itself, in a range where the note has nothing. Five milliseconds of fade drops that by about 70 dB, which puts it well below anything you’ll hear. Five milliseconds is also short enough that nobody notices the fade.

### Fade lengths that work
- Most cuts: 2 to 10 ms. Enough to smooth the jump, short enough to be invisible. Five is a good default.
- Drum hits and chops: 1 to 2 ms fade-in. A long fade-in softens the transient you wanted. Start the slice on the hit, as in our sampling from separated stems workflow, and keep the fade-in tiny.
- Low notes: a little longer. A 40 Hz cycle is 25 ms long. A fade of 10 ms or so keeps the bottom from thumping at the cut.
- Comps inside a sustained vowel: 10 to 30 ms crossfade. Longer crossfades hide the change in tone between takes, not just the click.
- Crossfade shape. Use equal-power for two different takes and equal-gain when the material on both sides is nearly identical, such as a loop to itself.
Snapping to zero crossings helps, and most DAWs can do it, but it isn’t enough on its own. A zero crossing on one side of a splice can still meet the other take going in the opposite direction, and in stereo the left and right channels rarely cross zero at the same moment. A fade fixes both.

### Find the ones you missed
After a long comp it’s easy to lose track of an edit. This scans a bounce for sudden changes in the waveform’s slope that stand far above the audio around them, which is what an unfaded edit looks like:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Flag edit clicks: sudden jumps in the waveform's slope that a fade would have smoothed.
usage: python3 find_clicks.py file.wav [threshold_dB]      (pip install numpy soundfile)"""
import sys
import numpy as np, soundfile as sf
x, sr = sf.read(sys.argv[1], always_2d=True)
x = x.mean(axis=1)
thr = float(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 20.0
d2 = np.abs(np.diff(x, 2))                                  # second difference: ~0 on smooth audio, a spike at a discontinuity
win = int(0.05 * sr)
local = np.sqrt(np.convolve(d2**2, np.ones(win) / win, mode="same")) + 1e-12
ratio = 20 * np.log10(d2 / local + 1e-12)
hits, last = [], -sr
for i in np.flatnonzero(ratio > thr):
    if i - last > int(0.02 * sr):                           # one report per 20 ms
        hits.append(i); last = i
print(f"{sys.argv[1]}: {len(hits)} likely click(s) above {thr:g} dB")
for i in hits:
    print(f"  {i / sr:8.3f} s   spike {ratio[i]:4.1f} dB above the surrounding audio")
$ python3 find_clicks.py comp.wav
comp.wav: 2 likely click(s) above 20 dB
     1.512 s   spike 30.8 dB above the surrounding audio
     3.507 s   spike 30.8 dB above the surrounding audio
It found the two raw edits and ignored both faded ones. It’s a rough tool, not a mastering-grade declicker: sharp drum hits and some synths can trip it too, so treat every hit as a place to listen, and raise the threshold if a busy track flags too much. On a vocal, bass or pad stem it’s quick and honest.

### Where edit clicks hide
1. Vocal comps. Every take boundary is a splice. Crossfade all of them, then solo the vocal and listen at the edits.
2. Trimmed tails. Cutting the end of an 808 or a reverb tail without a fade-out leaves a click on the last sample.
3. Loops and chops. A loop that doesn’t start and end at the same point in the cycle clicks every time it repeats.
4. Bounce starts and ends. A file that starts mid-note or gets cut before the tail finishes clicks at the very edge. Leave a short fade on both ends of the master.
5. Stems you split yourself. When you chop a vocal or a bass line out of a separated stem, the chops need the same fades as anything else. If you pull stems with StemSplit, cut on the stem, fade, then sample.

### Why mastering makes them louder
A click is mostly high-frequency energy, and mastering usually adds some top end and brings everything up toward the limiter. Both pull a tick that was barely there in the mix right to the front. Clicks also sit in the same band as harsh esses after mastering, for the same reason. Fix them in the edit, before the bounce, where it takes two seconds.
Note: Fade every cut, crossfade every splice, scan the stem before you bounce. If the edit started as a separated stem, hear how StemSplit handles the split, then measure the final bounce.
Q: Why do my audio edits click?
A: The cut or splice lands in the middle of a waveform cycle, so the signal jumps instantly between two values. That jump is a burst of high-frequency energy you hear as a click or pop.
Q: How long should a crossfade be to remove clicks?
A: Around 5 ms works for most cuts. Use 1 to 2 ms on drum hits so the transient survives, around 10 ms on low notes, and 10 to 30 ms inside a sustained vowel when comping vocals.
Q: Is cutting at zero crossings enough?
A: Not always. A splice can meet the other take moving in the opposite direction, and stereo channels rarely cross zero together. A short fade fixes both cases.
Q: How much does a 5 ms fade help?
A: In our test on a −6 dBFS 55 Hz note, the content above 2 kHz at an unfaded stop peaked at −13.3 dBFS. With a 5 ms fade-out it dropped to −82.9 dBFS, roughly 70 dB lower.

---

## Sending stems to a mixer? Export them so they line up and add back up
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/export-stems-for-a-mix-engineer.html
Section: Delivery · 20 October 2026 · 8 min
Summary: How to export stems for a mixing engineer: same start, same length, one sample rate, no mix-bus chain, and a null test against your rough before you send the link.

Stems a mixer can use all start at the same point, run the same length, share the session’s sample rate, and add back up to your rough mix when every fader sits at zero. Export every track from the same start to the same end, keep send effects on their own stems, switch off the mix-bus chain, and null the stems against your bounce before you send the link.
You send the link, feel good about it, and the first reply isn’t about the mix. The vocal comes in two bars early. The 808 sounds a little sharp. Where are the adlibs? And the rough you sent has a glue the mixer can’t find on any of the stems. Day one of a paid mix gets spent on email.
Every one of those is an export setting, and you can catch all of them in about thirty seconds before the files leave your machine.

### What “lined up” actually means
- Same start. Every stem begins at the same moment: bar 1, or one shared point before it if there’s a count-in or a pickup. Not at the first note on that track.
- Same length. Every stem runs to the same end, past the last reverb tail. Drop them all at zero in any DAW and they play in time with no nudging.
- Same format. One sample rate (the session’s), one bit depth, WAV or AIFF. Nothing lossy.
- They add back up. With every fader at zero, the stems summed together should be your rough mix. That’s the one people skip.
The last check is a null test. Flip the polarity of your rough bounce and play it against all the stems at once. If what’s left is silence, the stems are the mix, and the mixer starts exactly where you left off. If what’s left is loud, something on the rough never made it into the stems.

### We broke a session on purpose
To put numbers on it we built a small synthetic session: eight bars at 140 BPM, 48 kHz, five stems (drums, 808, vocal, keys, adlibs). The vocal doesn’t start until bar 3 and the adlibs until bar 5. We exported it cleanly once. Then we exported it the way a rushed export goes: the vocal as region-only, the 808 at 44.1 kHz with its fader pushed 12 dB, the adlib track still muted, and a soft-clip glue on the mix bus that only the rough went through.
What went wrong | What the mixer gets | The fix
Vocal exported from its first note | A 10.256 s file instead of 13.714 s. Dropped at zero, it plays 3.459 s early: two bars plus the 30 ms pickup | Export every stem from the same start bar, even when the track is silent there
808 bounced at 44.1 kHz in a 48 kHz session | Either the DAW converts it on import, or it plays about 8.8% fast and 1.47 semitones sharp (48,000 ÷ 44,100) | Export everything at the session rate. Let the mixer decide on any conversion
808 fader pushed 12 dB, 24-bit fixed | The peak went from −11.4 dBFS to over full scale, so 18,488 samples were flattened at 0 dBFS. That clipping is printed, and the mixer can’t undo it | Leave headroom on the stem, or export 32-bit float, which keeps overs intact
Adlib track muted | A file of digital silence with the right name | Unmute and unsolo everything, and check no file is empty
Glue on the mix bus, rough only | The stems summed back up miss the rough by a residual only 9.9 dB under the mix. That’s a different record | Bypass the bus chain for the stems and the rough, or send a second rough with it on and tell them what the chain is
The clean export, by contrast, nulled to −120.4 dB under the mix, which is just rounding, with zero samples of lag. That’s what a stem folder should look like.

### Check the folder before you send it
This reads a folder of stems and, optionally, your rough bounce. It prints each stem’s rate, format, length, peak and where its first audio starts, then lists anything a mixer would email you about. With a rough it lines every stem up at zero, adds them together and runs the null test:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Check a folder of exported stems before they go to a mixer.
usage: python3 stem_check.py STEMS_DIR [MIX.wav]      (pip install numpy soundfile)"""
import sys, pathlib
import numpy as np, soundfile as sf

def db(v): return 20 * np.log10(max(float(v), 1e-12))
folder = pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1]); mix_path = sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else None
files = sorted(p for p in folder.iterdir() if p.suffix.lower() in (".wav", ".aif", ".aiff", ".flac"))
problems, stems = [], {}
print(f"{'stem':<11}{'rate':>7}{'format':>8}{'length s':>10}{'peak dBFS':>11}{'first audio':>13}")
for p in files:
    i = sf.info(p); x, sr = sf.read(p, dtype="float64", always_2d=True); stems[p.name] = (x, sr)
    peak = np.abs(x).max(); loud = np.flatnonzero(np.abs(x).max(axis=1) > 1e-4)   # above -80 dBFS
    first = f"{loud[0] / sr:.2f} s" if loud.size else "silent"
    print(f"{p.stem:<11}{sr:>7}{i.subtype:>8}{i.frames / sr:>10.3f}{(f"{db(peak):.1f}" if peak else "-inf"):>11}{first:>13}")
    if not loud.size: problems.append(f"{p.name}: silent (muted when you exported?)")
    clipped = int((np.abs(x) >= 0.99999).sum())
    if clipped and i.subtype != "FLOAT": problems.append(f"{p.name}: {clipped} samples at full scale, clipped on export")
rates = {sr for _, sr in stems.values()}; lengths = {len(x) for x, _ in stems.values()}
if len(rates) > 1: problems.append(f"mixed sample rates {sorted(rates)}: re-export everything at the session rate")
if len(lengths) > 1:
    longest = max(len(x) / sr for x, sr in stems.values())
    for name, (x, sr) in stems.items():
        if longest - len(x) / sr > 0.001:
            problems.append(f"{name}: {longest - len(x) / sr:.3f} s shorter than the longest stem")
if mix_path and len(rates) == 1:
    mix, _ = sf.read(mix_path, dtype="float64", always_2d=True)
    total = np.zeros_like(mix)
