    for x, sr in stems.values():                     # line every stem up at zero, the way a mixer imports them
        n = min(len(x), len(total)); total[:n, :x.shape[1]] += x[:n]
    a, b = mix.mean(axis=1), total.mean(axis=1)      # lag between the mix and the stems added back up
    n = 1 << int(np.ceil(np.log2(len(a) * 2)))
    xc = np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(a, n) * np.conj(np.fft.rfft(b, n)), n)
    lag = int(np.argmax(xc)); lag = lag - n if lag > n // 2 else lag
    resid = db(np.sqrt(np.mean((mix - total) ** 2)) / np.sqrt(np.mean(mix ** 2)))
    print(f"\nnull vs {pathlib.Path(mix_path).name}: residual {resid:.1f} dB under the mix, best lag {lag} samples")
    if resid > -40: problems.append("stems don't add back up to the mix (bus processing, missing FX return, moved stem?)")
print("\n" + ("\n".join("- " + s for s in problems) if problems else "ok: same rate, same length, nulls against the mix"))
On the clean export:
$ python3 stem_check.py clean mix_clean.wav
stem          rate  format  length s  peak dBFS  first audio
01_drums     48000  PCM_24    13.714       -1.6       0.00 s
02_808       48000  PCM_24    13.714      -11.4       0.00 s
03_vocal     48000  PCM_24    13.714      -16.5       3.46 s
04_keys      48000  PCM_24    13.714      -18.7       0.00 s
05_adlibs    48000  PCM_24    13.714      -20.5       8.15 s

null vs mix_clean.wav: residual -120.4 dB under the mix, best lag 0 samples

ok: same rate, same length, nulls against the mix
On the rushed one. The null test is skipped because the sample rates don’t match, and that alone is a reason to re-export:
$ python3 stem_check.py messy mix_glue.wav
stem          rate  format  length s  peak dBFS  first audio
01_drums     48000  PCM_24    13.714       -1.6       0.00 s
02_808       44100  PCM_24    13.714        0.0       0.00 s
03_vocal     48000  PCM_24    10.256      -16.5       0.00 s
04_keys      48000  PCM_24    13.714      -18.7       0.00 s
05_adlibs    48000  PCM_24    13.714       -inf       silent

- 02_808.wav: 18488 samples at full scale, clipped on export
- 05_adlibs.wav: silent (muted when you exported?)
- mixed sample rates [44100, 48000]: re-export everything at the session rate
- 03_vocal.wav: 3.459 s shorter than the longest stem
And on correct stems sent with a rough that went through the bus glue. Everything looks fine file by file. Only the null test catches it:
$ python3 stem_check.py busonly mix_glue.wav
stem          rate  format  length s  peak dBFS  first audio
01_drums     48000  PCM_24    13.714       -1.6       0.00 s
02_808       48000  PCM_24    13.714      -11.4       0.00 s
03_vocal     48000  PCM_24    13.714      -16.5       3.46 s
04_keys      48000  PCM_24    13.714      -18.7       0.00 s
05_adlibs    48000  PCM_24    13.714      -20.5       8.15 s

null vs mix_glue.wav: residual -9.9 dB under the mix, best lag 0 samples

- stems don't add back up to the mix (bus processing, missing FX return, moved stem?)
Note the vocal’s “first audio” of 3.46 s on the clean export. That’s correct. A stem should carry its silence. A first-audio time of 0.00 on a part you know comes in late is the tell that it was trimmed.

### Export settings that save a day
- Format. WAV at the session sample rate, 24-bit or 32-bit float. Float if any stem peaks over 0 dBFS on its own fader. Turn normalise off. No MP3s, ever, not even “just to listen”.
- Start and end. Same start for every stem. Run the export at least a bar past the last note so reverb and delay tails aren’t cut, two bars for long halls.
- Mix bus off. Bypass the bus compressor, clipper, limiter and anything “mastering” on the main out. If that chain is the sound, say so in a note and send a second rough with it on.
- Send effects get their own stems. A reverb or delay on a send becomes its own file: “Vocal FX”, “Keys verb”. Insert effects that are part of the part (the distortion on the 808, the tuning on the lead) get printed on that stem. For the lead vocal, send the printed version and the raw one if you can.
- Sidechain. If the 808 ducks off the kick and you like it, print it ducked and include the kick as its own stem, so the mixer can keep it or rebuild it.
- Names. Number them in a sensible order (01_Kick, 02_808, 08_Lead_Vox) and put the BPM and key in the folder name. A short text file with the BPM, key, sample rate and which stems have printed effects answers the first three questions before they’re asked.
- Send the rough from the same start. It’s what the mixer listens to first and what the null test runs against.
Mono or stereo files is mostly preference. Mono sources can go as mono files; stereo is never wrong. If you don’t know what your mixer likes, ask once and save the answer.
Lost the session and only have the two-track? StemSplit can pull vocals, drums and bass out of the bounce on your own machine, so a mixer can at least hear what they’re working with. Just tell them which stems came from a separator. Separated stems won’t null against the bounce, and they’re a rescue, not a delivery: stems diagnose mixes, they don’t replace them.

### Genre notes
- Trap and drill. Kick and 808 always on separate stems, with the 808’s saturation printed. Split the vocal by role (lead, doubles, adlibs, tags), because those get very different treatment. Tags with long throws need their delay stem too.
- R&B and soul. Group stacks and harmonies into a few stems (low BGVs, high BGVs) rather than one “background vocals” file. Lead dry plus lead FX. Long tails, so give the export two bars after the last note.
- Rock and live bands. If the mixer is actually mixing the drums, send the multitracks (kick in, snare top, overheads and so on), not a stereo drum stem, and keep the count-in on every file so everything shares a start.
- House and techno. Long arrangements, so the null test earns its keep: one moved clip in a six-minute track is easy to miss by ear. Print the pumping if the sidechain is the groove, and send the kick separately.
Note: Same start, same length, one rate, bus off, null it. Do that and the mixer’s first email is about the music. Before you bounce anything, sample rate and bit depth are delivery hygiene and how much headroom to leave cover the format side. Only have the bounce? Hear what a split sounds like with StemSplit.
Q: How do I export stems for a mixing engineer?
A: Export every track or group from the same start point to the same end, past the last tail, as WAV at the session sample rate in 24-bit or 32-bit float. Bypass the mix-bus chain, give send effects their own stems, then sum the stems against your rough bounce. If they null, the mixer can rebuild your rough exactly.
Q: Should stems have effects on them?
A: Print insert effects that are part of the sound, like 808 distortion or vocal tuning, on the stem. Put send effects such as reverb and delay on their own stems so the mixer can rebalance them. Leave the mix-bus chain off, and send a second rough with it on if it’s part of the vibe.
Q: What sample rate and bit depth should stems be?
A: The session’s own sample rate and 24-bit or 32-bit float WAV. Don’t mix rates in one folder: in our test a 44.1 kHz 808 in a 48 kHz session would play about 8.8% fast and 1.47 semitones sharp if the DAW didn’t convert it. Use float if any stem peaks over 0 dBFS.
Q: How do I check that my stems line up?
A: Drop them all at zero with your rough bounce, flip the bounce’s polarity and play. Silence means they line up and add back up. In our synthetic session a clean export nulled to −120 dB, while correct stems against a rough with mix-bus glue left a residual only 9.9 dB under the mix.

---

## Your mix sounds better loud and thinner quiet. Pick one monitoring level
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/mix-sounds-better-louder-pick-one-monitor-level.html
Section: Monitoring · 20 October 2026 · 7 min
Summary: Why your mix changes with the volume knob: equal-loudness, and louder always winning the A/B. Calibrate one listening level, level-match, then check loud and quiet.

Your ears change with the volume knob: as playback gets quieter, the bass and the very top fade faster than the mids, and whatever is a little louder tends to sound better. Pick one listening level for most of the mix, mark the knob, level-match every comparison, and check loud and quiet on purpose, briefly, at the end.
Two in the morning, everyone’s asleep, so you mix quietly and push the 808 until it feels right. Next afternoon you play it at a normal volume and the low end is a mess. Or the other way round: you crank it to feel the record, pull the bass down because it’s shaking the desk, and the next morning on earbuds the whole thing is thin.
Neither mix was wrong for the volume you made it at. That’s the problem. The knob changed what you heard, and you mixed to the knob.

### Your ears have a volume-dependent EQ
Human hearing isn’t flat, and how unflat it is depends on level. Researchers have mapped this since Fletcher and Munson in the 1930s, and the modern version is the equal-loudness contours in the ISO 226 standard. The short version: we’re most sensitive in the low few kilohertz, where speech lives. As the level drops, low frequencies (and the extreme top) need more and more energy to sound as loud as the mids.
In a session that means:
- Mix quiet and you over-feed the ends. The 808 and the air sound weak, so you push them. Played louder, the bottom booms and the top hisses.
- Mix loud and you starve them. Everything sounds full already, so the bass goes down and harshness in the upper mids hides inside the excitement. Played quieter, it’s thin.
- The song didn’t change. Your ears’ balance did. Nothing on the meter moves when you turn the monitor knob.

### Louder wins every A/B
The second trap is the same effect in a comparison. When two versions differ in level, the louder one usually comes across as fuller and clearer, even when the gap is only a decibel or so and nothing else changed. It’s why good plugins have an output trim or auto-gain, and why “this EQ sounds amazing” so often means “this EQ is louder”.
So level-match before you judge. This measures integrated loudness (the same ITU-R BS.1770 measure streaming services use) and tells you how much to pull the louder one down:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Level-match two bounces before you decide which one is better.
usage: python3 level_match.py A.wav B.wav      (pip install numpy soundfile pyloudnorm)"""
import sys
import numpy as np, soundfile as sf, pyloudnorm as pyln

def measure(path):
    x, sr = sf.read(path, always_2d=True)
    lufs = pyln.Meter(sr).integrated_loudness(x)          # ITU-R BS.1770 integrated loudness
    return lufs, 20 * np.log10(np.abs(x).max())
(la, pa), (lb, pb) = measure(sys.argv[1]), measure(sys.argv[2])
print(f"A {sys.argv[1]}: {la:6.2f} LUFS integrated, sample peak {pa:5.1f} dBFS")
print(f"B {sys.argv[2]}: {lb:6.2f} LUFS integrated, sample peak {pb:5.1f} dBFS")
d = lb - la
if abs(d) < 0.1: print("within 0.1 LU: compare as they are")
else:
    loud = "B" if d > 0 else "A"
    print(f"{loud} is {abs(d):.1f} LU louder: turn {loud} down {abs(d):.1f} dB (don't turn the other up) before you judge")
We made a version B of a synthetic loop with a 3 dB high shelf and 1.5 dB more gain, then compared it with the original:
$ python3 level_match.py ab_A.wav ab_B.wav
A ab_A.wav: -19.38 LUFS integrated, sample peak  -4.2 dBFS
B ab_B.wav: -17.49 LUFS integrated, sample peak  -1.4 dBFS
B is 1.9 LU louder: turn B down 1.9 dB (don't turn the other up) before you judge
B came out 1.9 LU louder, not 1.5, because the brighter top adds measured loudness too. Unmatched, B wins on volume alone. Matched, you finally hear whether the shelf is actually better. Turn the louder one down rather than the quieter one up; it keeps your headroom and your ears.

### Set one level you can come back to
The usual way to calibrate is pink noise at a known digital level, played through one speaker at a time, with an SPL meter at your listening position set to C-weighting and slow response. Turn the monitor level until each speaker reads your target, then mark that spot on the knob. This writes the noise file:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Pink noise at -20 dBFS RMS for setting a monitoring level with an SPL meter.
usage: python3 calibration_noise.py [seconds]      (pip install numpy soundfile)"""
import sys
import numpy as np, soundfile as sf

sr, secs = 48000, float(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 60
n = int(sr * secs); rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
spec = np.fft.rfft(rng.standard_normal(n)); f = np.fft.rfftfreq(n, 1 / sr)
band = (f >= 20) & (f <= 20000)
spec[band] /= np.sqrt(f[band]); spec[~band] = 0         # -3 dB per octave from 20 Hz to 20 kHz
x = np.fft.irfft(spec, n)
x *= 10 ** (-20 / 20) / np.sqrt(np.mean(x ** 2))        # exactly -20 dBFS RMS
fade = int(0.05 * sr); x[:fade] *= np.linspace(0, 1, fade); x[-fade:] *= np.linspace(1, 0, fade)
sf.write("pink_-20dBFS_rms.wav", x, sr, subtype="PCM_24")
rms, peak = np.sqrt(np.mean(x ** 2)), np.abs(x).max()
print(f"wrote pink_-20dBFS_rms.wav: {secs:.0f} s mono, {sr} Hz, 24-bit")
print(f"RMS {20*np.log10(rms):.2f} dBFS, peak {20*np.log10(peak):.2f} dBFS, crest {20*np.log10(peak/rms):.1f} dB")
X = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x)) ** 2; octave = lambda c: X[(f >= c / np.sqrt(2)) & (f < c * np.sqrt(2))].sum()
for c in (31.5, 125, 500, 2000, 8000):                  # pink noise: equal energy in every octave
    print(f"  octave at {c:>6g} Hz: {10*np.log10(octave(c) / octave(500)):+5.1f} dB vs 500 Hz")
$ python3 calibration_noise.py 60
wrote pink_-20dBFS_rms.wav: 60 s mono, 48000 Hz, 24-bit
RMS -20.00 dBFS, peak -5.93 dBFS, crest 14.1 dB
  octave at   31.5 Hz:  +0.0 dB vs 500 Hz
  octave at    125 Hz:  +0.0 dB vs 500 Hz
  octave at    500 Hz:  +0.0 dB vs 500 Hz
  octave at   2000 Hz:  +0.0 dB vs 500 Hz
  octave at   8000 Hz:  +0.0 dB vs 500 Hz
Pink noise has equal energy in every octave, which is why it’s used for this: the meter sees the whole range at once instead of one frequency your room happens to like. The 14.1 dB crest factor is also about what you’d expect from real music.
What target? Big film stages have traditionally calibrated around 85 dB SPL per speaker, but that’s a large room with the speakers far away. In a bedroom or a small studio most people land lower, somewhere in the 70s. The exact number matters less than coming back to the same one. A phone SPL app can be a few dB off, but it’ll be off the same way every time, and consistency is the whole point.
No meter at all? Use the conversation test: at your mix level you should be able to talk to someone next to you in a normal voice without raising it. It’s rough, but it’s repeatable, which a level you pick by feel each night isn’t.

### How long you can listen
There’s a second reason to mix at a moderate level. In the US, NIOSH recommends limiting noise exposure to 85 dBA averaged over eight hours, and halving the time for every 3 dB above that:
Level (dBA) | NIOSH recommended limit per day
85 | 8 hours
88 | 4 hours
91 | 2 hours
94 | 1 hour
97 | 30 minutes
100 | 15 minutes
A ten-hour session at a level that feels exciting can be several days’ worth of exposure. Mixing in the 70s isn’t only better for balance. It’s how you’re still hearing the top end in twenty years. Take breaks, too: after a few hours your sense of the top end gets less trustworthy, which is a good time to stop making EQ decisions.

### Then check loud and quiet, on purpose
1. Do most of the mix at your marked level. Balance, EQ and compression decisions happen here.
2. Quiet check. Drop it to just above a whisper. The lead vocal should still be clear and the kick and 808 should still read as a groove. If the vocal disappears when it’s quiet, it’s too low in the mix, not just quiet.
3. Loud check, briefly. Thirty seconds at a loud level shows you what jumps out: sibilance, a harsh synth, a boomy note. Not a chorus on loop for an hour.
4. Level-match every comparison. References, your last version, the plugin on and off. Run the script or use a matched A/B.
5. Read the file, not the room. A meter doesn’t have a volume knob. Run the bounce through CoProducer and the report reads integrated LUFS and true peak straight off the file, the same at 2 a.m. as at noon.

### Genre notes
- Trap and drill. The 808 is the first casualty of quiet late-night mixing. Set its level at your marked volume, confirm on headphones, and if it changes when you lean back, that’s the room, not the mix.
- R&B and soul. The quiet check is your friend. A lead vocal that still carries at whisper volume is a lead vocal that’s sitting right, and it tells you when the ad-libs are fighting it.
- House and techno. It’ll be played loud, which is exactly why you shouldn’t mix it loud. Get the balance at your level, then use the short loud check to catch harshness that only shows up when it’s pushed.
- Rock and metal. Walls of guitars sound huge loud and hide everything. If the vocal drops behind them in the quiet check, ride it up or carve the guitars, because that’s how most people will hear it.
- Lo-fi and ambient. A lot of it gets played quietly in the background. Spend more time at low volume than usual, and make sure the bass doesn’t vanish.
Note: One marked level, matched comparisons, a short loud and quiet check, and a meter that can’t hear your knob. Analyze a bounce, or compare it against a reference in the desktop app. Pro is $29 one-time. When the comparison is a released track, read why not to match a streamed reference and reference matching without guesswork.
Q: What volume should I mix at?
A: Pick one moderate level and come back to it every time. Calibrate with pink noise at −20 dBFS RMS and an SPL meter (C-weighted, slow) at your seat. Large film rooms use about 85 dB SPL per speaker. In small rooms most people go lower, into the 70s. Consistency matters more than the exact number.
Q: Why does my mix sound different at different volumes?
A: Because hearing sensitivity changes with level. The equal-loudness contours (Fletcher and Munson, now ISO 226) show that at lower volumes bass and extreme treble need more energy to sound as loud as the mids. Mix quiet and you tend to over-boost the lows; mix loud and you tend to under-do them.
Q: Why does the louder version always sound better?
A: A small level difference, around a decibel, is often heard as fuller or clearer rather than simply louder. Level-match before comparing. In our test a version with a 3 dB high shelf and 1.5 dB more gain measured 1.9 LU louder, so it would win an unmatched A/B on volume alone.
Q: How do I calibrate my monitors without an SPL meter?
A: A phone SPL app is fine for consistency even if it’s a few dB off. With nothing at all, use the conversation test: at your mix level you should be able to talk to someone beside you without raising your voice. Then mark the knob so you can return to it.

## Reverb making the mix muddy? Filter the return, not the vocal
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/reverb-makes-the-mix-muddy-filter-the-return.html
Section: Mix craft · 19 October 2026 · 8 min
Summary: Reverb muddying the mix? Most of a return’s energy sits in low-mids you don’t hear as space. High-pass the return, add pre-delay, duck it and time the decay.

When reverb makes a mix muddy, the fix is usually on the return, not the vocal: a dark hall puts most of its energy below 1 kHz and keeps ringing there in the gaps between notes. High-pass the return around 250–400 Hz, give it enough pre-delay that the dry attack lands first, and time the decay to the song so the tail clears before the next line.
Here’s how it usually goes. The vocal sounds great soloed with its reverb. Then the beat comes in and the whole middle of the mix turns to fog. So you start cutting the vocal at 300 Hz, then the keys, then you try a different reverb, and somehow the vocal ends up thin and the mix is still cloudy.
The vocal was never the problem. Mute the reverb return and the fog goes with it. What you’re hearing is the reverb’s low-mids, smeared across time and parked in exactly the spaces the dry parts used to leave open. So fix it where it lives: on the return.

### Why the mud lives in the return
A reverb return is a copy of everything you send it, stretched over a second or three. Two things make that copy heavier in the low-mids than the source.
- Your sends are bottom-heavy. A sung vocal carries a lot of its energy in the fundamentals and first few harmonics, roughly 150–500 Hz for most voices. Keys, guitars and snare body live there too. Send three things to one hall and you get all three, blended.
- Lows ring longer. Most halls and plates (real or simulated) decay more slowly at the bottom. Plugins often expose this as a bass multiplier or low decay control. So the low-mid part of the tail is the part still hanging around when the next word starts.
Average it over a whole chorus and the extra low-mid looks tiny, which is why neither a meter nor an EQ on the mix bus flags it. The damage happens in the gaps: between syllables, between chord hits, in the half-beat before a downbeat. Those little dips are what make a mix sound open. Reverb fills them in.

### We measured it on a synthetic ballad
To put numbers on it we built a test session at 48 kHz and 75 BPM: a vocal-like line (harmonics, formants, vibrato and short consonant bursts), piano-ish keys on every beat and a bass. The vocal and the keys (6 dB lower) both feed one synthetic stereo hall with a 2.8 s low decay, 2.0 s mids and 1.0 s highs. The return is set once, unfiltered, 8 dB under the dry vocal, and stays at that gain for every row unless it says level-matched. Synthetic test signals, so trust the shape more than the decimals.
On its own, that unfiltered return put 86% of its energy below 1 kHz and 13% in the 1–6 kHz range where you actually hear space and distance.
Return version | Gap fill, 150–500 Hz | Low-mid contrast | Return 1–6 kHz | Return level | Low-mid tail
No reverb | — | 18.0 dB | — | — | —
Unfiltered | +4.3 dB | 15.9 dB | 0.0 | 0.0 | −31.5 dB
HPF 150 Hz | +4.1 dB | 16.0 dB | 0.0 | −0.2 | −32.6 dB
HPF 250 Hz | +3.1 dB | 16.3 dB | 0.0 | −0.9 | −36.5 dB
HPF 350 Hz | +2.1 dB | 16.6 dB | 0.0 | −1.7 | −40.5 dB
HPF 350 Hz, 24 dB/oct | +2.0 dB | 16.5 dB | 0.0 | −1.5 | −44.0 dB
HPF 350 + LPF 7 kHz, level-matched | +2.9 dB | 16.2 dB | +1.6 | 0.0 | −38.8 dB
Low decay halved (2.8 → 1.4 s) | +2.2 dB | 17.1 dB | 0.0 | −1.4 | −49.8 dB
HPF 350 + LPF 7 kHz + low decay halved | +1.0 dB | 17.2 dB | −0.1 | −2.7 | −56.9 dB
Gap fill is how much the return raises the mix’s 150–500 Hz energy in the short gaps between sung notes. Low-mid contrast is how much that band still rises and falls from moment to moment (the spread between loud and quiet 25 ms frames); lower means more filled in. Return 1–6 kHz and Return level are relative to the unfiltered return. Low-mid tail is the return’s 150–500 Hz energy half a beat to a beat and a half after the last note, relative to the dry vocal’s. Filters are 12 dB per octave unless marked.
Three things to take from that table into a session:
- The mud is in the gaps, not the average. Across the whole phrase, the unfiltered return lifted the mix’s 150–500 Hz band by only 0.6 dB. In the gaps between notes it lifted it by 4.3 dB, and the band lost about 2 dB of its movement. That’s the cloudiness, and it’s why EQ on the mix bus never quite fixes it.
- Filtering costs you almost none of the space. A 350 Hz high-pass halved the gap fill, dropped the leftover low-mid tail by 9 dB and left the 1–6 kHz part of the reverb exactly where it was. The return as a whole got 1.7 dB quieter, nearly all of it mud. Push the fader back up by that much and the gaps are still cleaner than before (+2.9 dB against +4.3), with the audible space 1.6 dB louder.
- The default low cut is aimed at rumble, not mud. A 150 Hz cut barely moved anything (+4.1 dB). Below about 250 Hz you’re cleaning sub rumble, which matters too, just not for this.
The bottom two rows are the other lever. Halving the low decay alone took the leftover tail from −31.5 to −49.8 dB, and with the filter it fell to −56.9: 25 dB less low-mid hanging over the next line, while the 1–6 kHz part moved by 0.1 dB. If your reverb has a bass multiplier or a low-frequency damping control, it is a mud control.

### Pre-delay keeps the front of the word dry
Pre-delay doesn’t clean the low-mids (in this test the mix’s 150–500 Hz rise stayed between 0.0 and 0.3 dB whatever the pre-delay). What it buys is articulation. With the reverb arriving a beat-fraction late, the consonant and the attack of each note reach your ear dry, and the wash follows.
Pre-delay | Dry over wet, first 30 ms of each note | Same, 2.5–9 kHz (consonants)
0 ms | +14.8 dB | +16.8 dB
10 ms | +15.5 dB | +18.1 dB
25 ms (1/128 note at 75 BPM) | +18.3 dB | +20.8 dB
50 ms (1/64 note at 75 BPM) | +34.9 dB | +41.7 dB
100 ms (1/32 note at 75 BPM) | +33.4 dB | +39.4 dB
Once the pre-delay is longer than the attack you care about, the front of the note is effectively dry. Past that point more pre-delay stops helping the consonant and starts sounding like a slap. Somewhere between 20 and 60 ms is where most sung vocals land. Syncing it to a small note value keeps it from feeling rhythmically off.

### Duck the return off the dry vocal
Put a compressor (or a ducker) on the reverb return and key its sidechain from the dry vocal. The reverb sinks while the singer sings and blooms in the spaces. We used a gentle setting: 6 dB at most, 5 ms attack, 250 ms release, on the filtered return with 25 ms of pre-delay.
- Gain reduction averaged 5.4 dB while singing and 1.8 dB in the gaps and tail.
- While the vocal was sounding, the return went from 10.4 dB under the dry vocal to 15.9 dB under it. That’s the clarity.
- The tail in the gaps came out 3.6 dB lower than without ducking, because a 250 ms release is still recovering when the line ends. Shorten the release if you want the bloom back sooner.
Ducking doesn’t change the low-mid average much (+0.3 to +0.1 dB in this test). It’s a front-to-back tool: the vocal stays in front, the reverb still reads as big, it just stops talking over the singer.

### Time the decay to the song
A tail that’s still ringing when the next phrase starts is mud you added on purpose. A quick way to get a starting point is to let the tempo pick the numbers:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""reverb_times.py: tempo-synced pre-delay and decay starting points.
    python3 reverb_times.py 72            # one tempo
    python3 reverb_times.py 72 140 120 85 # several
Decay is the note length minus the pre-delay, so the tail is done by the time
that note value has passed. These are starting points: set them, then listen."""
import sys

def note_ms(bpm, frac):                  # frac of a whole note, e.g. 1/16
    return 60000 / bpm * 4 * frac

for bpm in map(float, sys.argv[1:] or ["72"]):
    print(f"{bpm:g} BPM  (quarter = {note_ms(bpm, 1/4):.0f} ms)")
    pre = {n: note_ms(bpm, f) for n, f in (("1/128", 1/128), ("1/64", 1/64), ("1/32", 1/32))}
    print("  pre-delay  " + "   ".join(f"{n} = {v:.0f} ms" for n, v in pre.items()))
    for name, frac in (("1/4 note", 1/4), ("1/2 note", 1/2), ("1 bar", 1), ("2 bars", 2)):
        total = note_ms(bpm, frac)
        print(f"  decay to clear in {name:8s} {total/1000:5.2f} s total -> "
              f"{(total - pre['1/64'])/1000:4.2f} s decay with 1/64 pre-delay")
Run for four tempos we’ll use in the genre notes below:
$ python3 reverb_times.py 68 140 120 85
68 BPM  (quarter = 882 ms)
  pre-delay  1/128 = 28 ms   1/64 = 55 ms   1/32 = 110 ms
  decay to clear in 1/4 note  0.88 s total -> 0.83 s decay with 1/64 pre-delay
  decay to clear in 1/2 note  1.76 s total -> 1.71 s decay with 1/64 pre-delay
  decay to clear in 1 bar     3.53 s total -> 3.47 s decay with 1/64 pre-delay
  decay to clear in 2 bars    7.06 s total -> 7.00 s decay with 1/64 pre-delay
140 BPM  (quarter = 429 ms)
  pre-delay  1/128 = 13 ms   1/64 = 27 ms   1/32 = 54 ms
  decay to clear in 1/4 note  0.43 s total -> 0.40 s decay with 1/64 pre-delay
  decay to clear in 1/2 note  0.86 s total -> 0.83 s decay with 1/64 pre-delay
  decay to clear in 1 bar     1.71 s total -> 1.69 s decay with 1/64 pre-delay
  decay to clear in 2 bars    3.43 s total -> 3.40 s decay with 1/64 pre-delay
120 BPM  (quarter = 500 ms)
  pre-delay  1/128 = 16 ms   1/64 = 31 ms   1/32 = 62 ms
  decay to clear in 1/4 note  0.50 s total -> 0.47 s decay with 1/64 pre-delay
  decay to clear in 1/2 note  1.00 s total -> 0.97 s decay with 1/64 pre-delay
  decay to clear in 1 bar     2.00 s total -> 1.97 s decay with 1/64 pre-delay
  decay to clear in 2 bars    4.00 s total -> 3.97 s decay with 1/64 pre-delay
85 BPM  (quarter = 706 ms)
  pre-delay  1/128 = 22 ms   1/64 = 44 ms   1/32 = 88 ms
  decay to clear in 1/4 note  0.71 s total -> 0.66 s decay with 1/64 pre-delay
  decay to clear in 1/2 note  1.41 s total -> 1.37 s decay with 1/64 pre-delay
  decay to clear in 1 bar     2.82 s total -> 2.78 s decay with 1/64 pre-delay
  decay to clear in 2 bars    5.65 s total -> 5.60 s decay with 1/64 pre-delay
The decay knob on most reverbs is a 60 dB decay time (RT60). In a busy mix the last 30 dB or so of that tail is masked anyway, so a decay set to one bar sounds like it clears well before the bar ends. Set it from the table, then adjust by ear with the whole mix playing, not soloed.

### Check what your return is actually doing
Solo and bounce the dry vocal and the reverb return (100% wet, same start). This shows where the return puts its energy next to the dry part:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""wet_dry_bands.py: where does your reverb return put its energy, next to the dry vocal?
Solo and bounce the dry vocal and the reverb return (return only, 100% wet), same start, then:
    python3 wet_dry_bands.py vocal_dry.wav reverb_return.wav"""
import sys, subprocess, numpy as np

def load(path):  # any format ffmpeg reads -> stereo float at 48 kHz (mono files are copied to both sides)
    raw = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", path, "-ac", "2", "-ar", "48000", "-f", "f32le", "-"],
                         capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
    return np.frombuffer(raw, np.float32).reshape(-1, 2).astype(np.float64)

def power(x, n):  # power spectrum summed over both channels (a stereo return is not folded to mono)
    return (np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x[:n], axis=0)) ** 2).sum(axis=1)

dry, wet = load(sys.argv[1]), load(sys.argv[2])
n = min(len(dry), len(wet)); f = np.fft.rfftfreq(n, 1 / 48000)
D, W = power(dry, n), power(wet, n)
bands = [("sub 20-150", 20, 150), ("low-mid 150-500", 150, 500), ("mid 500-1k", 500, 1000),
         ("presence 1-6k", 1000, 6000), ("air 6-16k", 6000, 16000)]
print(f"{'band':16s} {'return vs dry':>13s} {'share of return':>16s}")
for name, lo, hi in bands:
    m = (f >= lo) & (f < hi)
    ratio = f"{10*np.log10(W[m].sum() / D[m].sum()):+11.1f} dB" if D[m].sum() > 1e-4 * D.sum() else "   (dry ~none)"
    print(f"{name:16s} {ratio} {100 * W[m].sum() / W.sum():14.0f} %")
print(f"{'broadband':16s} {10*np.log10(W.sum() / D.sum()):+11.1f} dB")
On our session, first unfiltered, then with the 350 Hz high-pass and 7 kHz low-pass:
$ python3 wet_dry_bands.py vocal_dry.wav reverb_return.wav
band             return vs dry  share of return
sub 20-150          (dry ~none)              0 %
low-mid 150-500         -7.9 dB             43 %
mid 500-1k              -8.1 dB             43 %
presence 1-6k           -8.8 dB             14 %
air 6-16k              -11.0 dB              0 %
broadband               -8.1 dB

$ python3 wet_dry_bands.py vocal_dry.wav reverb_return_hpf350.wav
band             return vs dry  share of return
sub 20-150          (dry ~none)              0 %
low-mid 150-500        -12.1 dB             24 %
mid 500-1k              -8.6 dB             56 %
presence 1-6k           -8.8 dB             20 %
air 6-16k              -14.2 dB              0 %
broadband               -9.8 dB
The low-mid share of the return fell from 43% to 24%, and the presence band (−8.8 dB against the dry vocal) didn’t change at all. If your own return shows 150–500 Hz as its biggest band, that’s where to start.
No session, just a bounce? Splitting the vocal out with StemSplit and listening to it on its own gives you a decent feel for how much wash got printed. Separators don’t always agree on where a tail belongs, so use it as a listening aid, not a measurement.

### Fold it to mono once
A plain stereo reverb is mostly decorrelated left to right (our return measured −0.09). Fold the mix to mono and it gets quieter relative to the centred vocal: 3.4 dB quieter here. So mono doesn’t make a normal reverb muddier. It makes it drier, which is worth knowing if most people will hear the song on a phone. If your return gets louder or hollower in mono, something on it, a widener or a polarity trick, is fighting itself. Wide mixes fail in mono covers that check.

### Genre notes
- R&B ballad vocal (around 68 BPM). Big halls and plates are part of the sound, so keep the length and take the mud out: high-pass at 300–400 Hz, pre-delay near 1/64 (55 ms), decay around a bar (3.5 s) and a few dB of ducking. Stacks and harmonies can share the lead’s return; don’t give every layer its own hall.
- Trap vocal (140 BPM, half-time feel). Dense 808s leave no room for a long tail. Short plate or room, decay around a half note (0.8 s), high-pass at 400 Hz or higher and duck it hard. Let delay throws on the last word carry the space.
- Rock snare (around 120 BPM). A plate or room on the snare is where a lot of the body comes from, so be gentler: high-pass around 200–250 Hz and time the decay to land by the next kick, about a quarter note (0.47 s). A gate on the return instead of a long natural decay is a classic move for a reason.
- Lo-fi (around 85 BPM). Dark reverb is the aesthetic, so low-pass lower (4–5 kHz) but still high-pass it. The warmth should come from the dry keys, not from a 300 Hz tail sitting on them. A decay of about a half note (1.4 s) keeps the loop breathing.
Note: Filter the return, pre-delay it, duck it, time it, in that order, and the reverb goes back to sounding like space instead of fog. If the vocal itself still feels buried, read how loud the vocal should sit. If the reverb is spreading sibilance around the room, de-ess before the send. Got a bounce but no session? Pull the vocal with StemSplit and listen.
Q: Why does reverb make my mix muddy?
A: Because a reverb return is mostly low-mid energy that keeps ringing after the dry note stops. On our synthetic ballad, an unfiltered hall raised the mix’s 150–500 Hz band by only 0.6 dB on average but by 4.3 dB in the gaps between notes, which is where clarity lives.
Q: What frequency should I high-pass a vocal reverb at?
A: Start around 250–400 Hz on the return, not the vocal. In our test a 350 Hz high-pass halved the low-mid fill in the gaps and cut the leftover tail by 9 dB, while the 1–6 kHz part of the reverb didn’t change. A 150 Hz cut barely helped.
Q: How much pre-delay should vocal reverb have?
A: Enough that the start of each word lands dry, typically 20–60 ms. In our test 25 ms raised the dry-over-wet ratio in the first 30 ms of each note from 14.8 to 18.3 dB, and 50 ms made it effectively dry. Sync it to a 1/128 or 1/64 note to keep it in time.
Q: Does reverb get muddier in mono?
A: A plain stereo reverb gets quieter in mono, not muddier. Our return was almost fully decorrelated, and folding to mono dropped it 3.4 dB relative to the centred vocal. If your return gets louder or hollower in mono, something on it is out of polarity between the two sides.

---

## Your low end changes when you move your chair. That’s the room, not the mix
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/low-end-changes-when-you-move-your-chair.html
Section: Monitoring · 19 October 2026 · 8 min
Summary: Bass booms in one spot and vanishes a foot away? That’s room modes. Work out your room’s modes, find a better seat and check low end without treatment.

If your 808 or bass gets louder or disappears when you lean back or roll the chair a foot, you’re hearing room modes: low frequencies that resonate between parallel walls (f = c ÷ 2L for each dimension) and pile up in some spots while cancelling in others. In an untreated room, don’t EQ the mix to your chair. Find a better seat, then check the low end on headphones, against references and on a meter.
Every bedroom producer has had this night. The 808 sounds perfect at the desk. You lean back to listen like a fan and it’s twice as big. You walk to the door and one note of the line just vanishes. Then the bounce goes to the car and it’s either boomy or gone, and you can’t tell which version of your room lied to you.
All of them, a little. Below a couple of hundred hertz a small room isn’t a neutral box. It’s a set of resonances, and where you sit decides which ones you hear.

### What a room mode is
Bass wavelengths are long: about 8 m at 41 Hz, the low E of a lot of 808 lines. When half a wavelength fits exactly between two parallel walls, sound bouncing back and forth reinforces itself and the room resonates. That happens at f = c ÷ (2 × L), where c is the speed of sound (about 343 m/s) and L the distance between the walls, and again at every whole multiple of that frequency.
Each of those resonances has a fixed pattern in the room. Pressure is highest at the walls. For the first mode it drops to almost nothing halfway between them, so a seat in the middle of the room sits in a hole at that frequency. The second mode has two holes, at a quarter and three quarters of the way. And so on up.
These wall-to-wall ones are called axial modes, and they’re the strongest. There are weaker ones that bounce off four walls (tangential) or all six (oblique). In a bedroom-sized room they’re spread far enough apart that the low end behaves like a handful of separate peaks and holes rather than a smooth curve, until they get dense somewhere in the low hundreds of hertz.

### Work out your own room’s modes
You need a tape measure and this. It lists the axial modes for each dimension, flags the ones that land on top of each other and the big gaps between them, and shows where the length-mode holes are:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""room_modes.py: axial room modes for a rectangular room, plus where they bunch up.
    python3 room_modes.py 3.6 3.0 2.4          # length width height in metres
    python3 room_modes.py 12 10 8 --ft         # or in feet
Axial modes (between two parallel walls) are the strongest: f = n * c / (2 * L).
Rigid-wall rectangle maths: a real room with doors, windows and stud walls will differ."""
import sys

C = 343.0                                    # speed of sound in m/s at about 20 °C
args = [a for a in sys.argv[1:] if not a.startswith("--")]
dims = [float(a) * (0.3048 if "--ft" in sys.argv else 1) for a in args] or [3.6, 3.0, 2.4]
names, top = ("length", "width", "height"), 300

modes = []
for name, L in zip(names, dims):
    n = 1
    while n * C / (2 * L) <= top:
        modes.append((n * C / (2 * L), name, n)); n += 1
modes.sort()

L, W, H = dims
print(f"room {L:.2f} x {W:.2f} x {H:.2f} m, axial modes up to {top} Hz")
for name, d in zip(names, dims):
    print(f"  {name:6s} {d:4.2f} m: " + ", ".join(f"{f:.1f}" for f, nm, _ in modes if nm == name) + " Hz")

print("\nall axial modes, low to high (gap = distance to the previous one)")
prev = None
for f, name, n in modes:
    gap = f - prev if prev else 0
    flag = ""
    if prev and gap < 0.05 * f: flag = "  <- within 5% of the last one: expect a pile-up"
    elif prev and gap > 20 and f < 200: flag = "  <- big gap below it: expect a hole"
    print(f"  {f:6.1f} Hz  {name} {n}  gap {gap:5.1f}{flag}")
    prev = f

print(f"\nlength-mode nulls sit at these distances from the front wall (m):")
for n in (1, 2, 3):
    print(f"  {n * C / (2 * L):5.1f} Hz: " + ", ".join(f"{(2 * k + 1) * L / (2 * n):.2f}" for k in range(n)))
print(f"38% of the length: {0.38 * L:.2f} m from the front wall (a starting point, not a cure)")
print(f"dead centre {L / 2:.2f} m sits in the null of every odd length mode")
For a common bedroom, 3.6 × 3.0 × 2.4 m (about 12 × 10 × 8 ft):
$ python3 room_modes.py 3.6 3.0 2.4
room 3.60 x 3.00 x 2.40 m, axial modes up to 300 Hz
  length 3.60 m: 47.6, 95.3, 142.9, 190.6, 238.2, 285.8 Hz
  width  3.00 m: 57.2, 114.3, 171.5, 228.7, 285.8 Hz
  height 2.40 m: 71.5, 142.9, 214.4, 285.8 Hz

all axial modes, low to high (gap = distance to the previous one)
    47.6 Hz  length 1  gap   0.0
    57.2 Hz  width 1  gap   9.5
    71.5 Hz  height 1  gap  14.3
    95.3 Hz  length 2  gap  23.8  <- big gap below it: expect a hole
   114.3 Hz  width 2  gap  19.1
   142.9 Hz  length 3  gap  28.6  <- big gap below it: expect a hole
   142.9 Hz  height 2  gap   0.0  <- within 5% of the last one: expect a pile-up
   171.5 Hz  width 3  gap  28.6  <- big gap below it: expect a hole
   190.6 Hz  length 4  gap  19.1
   214.4 Hz  height 3  gap  23.8
   228.7 Hz  width 4  gap  14.3
   238.2 Hz  length 5  gap   9.5  <- within 5% of the last one: expect a pile-up
   285.8 Hz  length 6  gap  47.6
   285.8 Hz  width 5  gap   0.0  <- within 5% of the last one: expect a pile-up
   285.8 Hz  height 4  gap   0.0  <- within 5% of the last one: expect a pile-up

length-mode nulls sit at these distances from the front wall (m):
   47.6 Hz: 1.80
   95.3 Hz: 0.90, 2.70
  142.9 Hz: 0.60, 1.80, 3.00
38% of the length: 1.37 m from the front wall (a starting point, not a cure)
dead centre 1.80 m sits in the null of every odd length mode
A few things jump out. Nothing at all below 47.6 Hz, so an E1 at 41 Hz gets no help from the length of the room. Three modes in the first 72 Hz, then a 24 Hz hole before 95 Hz. And 142.9 Hz is shared by the length and the height, because 3.6 m is exactly one and a half times 2.4 m. Builders love neat ratios. Rooms with neat ratios stack their modes, and a stacked mode is a note that rings.

### Same 808, seven chairs
Mode frequencies tell you where the trouble is. They don’t tell you what your seat hears. For that we ran a textbook modal model of the same room. It’s computed, not measured: rigid walls, a low-frequency decay of 0.6 s (a typical untreated small room), two speakers 0.6 m from the front wall and 0.9 m from the side walls playing mono bass, and a listener centred left to right with ears at 1.1 m. Each number is the level at that seat compared with the room’s average at that frequency (averaged over 1,100 points), so 0 dB means the seat hears what the room does on average.
Seat (from front wall) | E1 41 Hz | G1 49 Hz | A1 55 Hz | C2 65 Hz | D2 73 Hz | 100 Hz | 808 line, loudest − quietest note
25% (0.90 m) | −1.3 | +0.6 | +0.4 | −3.1 | −7.3 | −5.2 | 7.8 dB
32% (1.15 m) | −5.7 | −1.5 | −0.3 | −0.9 | −2.3 | −1.8 | 5.4 dB
38% (1.37 m) | −11.7 | −4.4 | −2.3 | −1.5 | −1.6 | +1.4 | 10.2 dB
45% (1.62 m) | −18.2 | −10.5 | −6.2 | −3.5 | −2.1 | +3.3 | 16.0 dB
50%, dead centre (1.80 m) | −9.8 | −20.0 | −10.6 | −5.3 | −2.6 | +3.5 | 17.4 dB
62% (2.23 m) | −1.9 | −6.2 | −10.9 | −30.4 | −9.9 | +1.6 | 28.6 dB
Near the back wall (3.30 m) | +3.9 | +2.9 | +2.2 | +1.4 | −2.4 | +0.1 | 6.3 dB
The 808 line is E1, G1, A1, C2, D2. Real rooms leak bass through doors, windows and stud walls, so they’re usually less extreme than a rigid-wall model. The pattern is what to take away, and it’s not subtle:
- Dead centre is the worst seat in the room. G1 at 49 Hz sits right on the first length mode (47.6 Hz), and the middle of the room is that mode’s hole: −20 dB. Mix there and you’ll push that note until it’s huge everywhere else.
- Thirty centimetres is a different mix. Rolling back 30 cm from the 38% seat took G1 from −4.4 to −12.4 dB and A1 from −2.3 to −7.2. Sliding 30 cm sideways changed every 808 note by 0.3 dB or less, because a symmetric pair of speakers playing mono bass barely excites the first side-to-side mode. In this room, front to back is what matters.
- 38% is a starting point, not a cure. The old rule of sitting about 38% of the way into the room keeps you out of the worst length-mode holes, and it was fine from C2 up here. But E1 still sank 11.7 dB. The most even 808 line in this room was at 32%.
- The back wall lies the other way. Against it, most of the 808 line gets louder (+1.4 to +3.9 dB). It’s fairly even, but it’s even and too loud, so mixes made there tend to come out thin.
And no seat is flat. Scanning 35–120 Hz in quarter-hertz steps, every seat had at least 16 dB between its loudest and quietest point, and the 62% seat had 37 dB. That’s why you don’t trust any single chair with the low end. You use the room for what it’s good at and check the bass somewhere else.

### Checks that work without treatment
1. Find the least-bad seat. Start around 38% of the room length, away from the exact centre, speakers symmetric. Play the tones below and move your head forward and back in 15–30 cm steps. Pick the spot where the notes sound most even, then mark the floor so you sit there every time.
2. Listen to steps, not songs. A song hides the room because the notes keep moving. Stepped sine tones let you name the note that booms and the one that vanishes. A slow sine sweep works too, but steps are easier to write down.
3. Measure if you can. An inexpensive measurement mic and free room-analysis software (REW is the one most people use) will draw the curve your ears are guessing at. Measure a few points around your head and average them; one point is as misleading as one chair.
4. Check the bass on headphones, in mono. Headphones skip the room entirely. They’re not perfect in the sub, but they don’t have nulls that move with your head. Play the 808 line in mono and listen for notes that jump out or drop away.
5. Compare against references in the same seat. Level-match two or three released tracks in your genre and flip between them and your mix. The room colours all of them the same way, so you’re judging the difference, which is the part that survives the trip to the car.
6. Read a meter that can’t hear your room. A spectrum view or a reference comparison reads the file, not the air. CoProducer’s reference match lines your bounce up against a reference metric by metric and shows where it diverges, and that answer doesn’t change when you roll your chair.
7. Then translate. Car, earbuds, phone. Last, not first, because by then you already know what the low end should be.
Here are the tones. Twelve notes from E1 to E3, two seconds each, at a safe −18 dBFS peak, with a cue list so you know what you’re hearing:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# bass_steps.sh: stepped sine tones for a by-ear room check (2 s each, 0.5 s gap, -18 dBFS peak).
#   ./bass_steps.sh            -> bass_steps.wav plus a cue list of which tone plays when
# Play it at a moderate level, sit still, and note which tones jump out or vanish.
# Then move 30 cm and play it again.
set -euo pipefail
notes=("E1 41.2" "F1 43.7" "G1 49.0" "A1 55.0" "B1 61.7" "C2 65.4" "D2 73.4" "E2 82.4" "G2 98.0" "A2 110.0" "C3 130.8" "E3 164.8")
inputs=(); filt=""; i=0; t10=0   # time in tenths of a second
for n in "${notes[@]}"; do
  set -- $n
  inputs+=(-f lavfi -i "aevalsrc=0.126*sin(2*PI*$2*t)*min(1\,min(t\,2-t)/0.02):s=48000:d=2")
  inputs+=(-f lavfi -i "anullsrc=r=48000:cl=mono:d=0.5")
  filt+="[$((2*i)):a][$((2*i+1)):a]"
  printf "%3d.%d s  %-3s %6s Hz\n" $((t10 / 10)) $((t10 % 10)) "$1" "$2"
  t10=$((t10 + 25)); i=$((i+1))
done
ffmpeg -v error -y "${inputs[@]}" -filter_complex "${filt}concat=n=$((2*i)):v=0:a=1[out]" -map "[out]" -c:a pcm_s24le bass_steps.wav
echo "wrote bass_steps.wav ($(ffprobe -v error -show_entries format=duration -of csv=p=0 bass_steps.wav) s)"
$ ./bass_steps.sh
  0.0 s  E1    41.2 Hz
  2.5 s  F1    43.7 Hz
  5.0 s  G1    49.0 Hz
  7.5 s  A1    55.0 Hz
 10.0 s  B1    61.7 Hz
 12.5 s  C2    65.4 Hz
 15.0 s  D2    73.4 Hz
 17.5 s  E2    82.4 Hz
 20.0 s  G2    98.0 Hz
 22.5 s  A2   110.0 Hz
 25.0 s  C3   130.8 Hz
 27.5 s  E3   164.8 Hz
wrote bass_steps.wav (30.000000 s)
Write down what jumps and what vanishes at your seat, then move 30 cm and do it again. In five minutes you’ll know which notes of your 808 line you can’t trust from that chair.

### Small fixes that actually help
- Don’t sit or put the desk at the dead centre of the length. It’s the one spot guaranteed to be in the first mode’s hole.
- Keep the speakers symmetric to the side walls. As the model showed, a symmetric pair with mono bass largely sidesteps the first width mode.
- Thick absorption in the corners helps most. Every mode has high pressure in the corners. Thin foam panels do very little at 50 Hz. Bass traps need real depth.
- Room-correction EQ can tame peaks, not fill holes. Cutting a boomy note works. Boosting a null doesn’t, because you’re pushing more energy into a spot where the room cancels it. You spend headroom and the hole stays.

### Genre notes
- Trap and drill. 808 lines from E1 to A1 (41–55 Hz) sit below or right on the first modes of most bedrooms, the region the room gets most wrong. Do the final 808 level on headphones and against references, and use the speakers for feel.
- R&B and neo-soul bass. Bass guitar and synth bass from 60 to 120 Hz walk right through the cluster of modes, so one note per bar can bloom or vanish. Stepped tones will tell you which ones before you start riding faders.
- House and techno. The kick fundamental around 50–60 Hz is the groove. If your seat sits in the first length mode’s hole, you’ll overcook the kick. Check it against a reference you know well in that genre.
- Rock and pop. Kick and bass weight around 80–100 Hz. In the example room, the gap between the 72 and 95 Hz modes is where the room gives bass the least help, which makes it an easy place to over-boost the bass guitar and then wonder why the master is wooly everywhere else.
Note: The room is a mic you can’t take off, so measure the file instead. Analyze a bounce, or line it up against a reference in the desktop app. Pro is $29 one-time. When the low end checks out but vanishes on small speakers, read why the 808 disappears on phones, and if the kick and 808 are still fighting, decide who owns the chair.
Q: Why does my bass sound different in different parts of the room?
A: Room modes. Low frequencies resonate between parallel walls at f = c ÷ 2L and its multiples, and each resonance is loud in some places and cancelled in others. In our computed example of a 3.6 m room, moving 30 cm front to back changed a 49 Hz note by 8 dB.
Q: Where should I sit to mix in an untreated room?
A: Start around 38% of the room length from the front wall, never at the exact centre, with the speakers symmetric to the side walls. Then test with stepped tones or a measurement mic and move until the low notes are most even. In our example room the best seat was at 32%.
Q: Can EQ fix room modes?
A: Partly. Cutting a peak that booms at your seat helps. Boosting a null does not, because the room cancels that frequency at that spot and the extra energy just costs headroom. Seat position, symmetry and thick bass trapping do more.
Q: Should I mix the low end on headphones?
A: Use them to check it. Headphones skip the room, so the level of each 808 note doesn’t change when you move. Combine that with level-matched references and a meter, then confirm the result on speakers, in the car and on a phone.

---

## Parallel compression sounds thin? Check the latency first
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/parallel-compression-sounds-thin-check-latency.html
Section: Mix craft · 16 October 2026 · 8 min
Summary: Parallel compression making drums or vocals thinner? The parallel bus is probably arriving late. Find the offset, fix the timing, then dial it in.

If bringing up a parallel compressor makes the drums thinner, hollower or flammy instead of bigger, the parallel bus is usually arriving late: a few samples to a few milliseconds of uncompensated latency turns the blend into a comb filter. Null-test the two paths, measure the offset, and fix the timing before you touch the compressor.
You know the move. Drum bus feeding a parallel aux, a compressor on it slammed at 10:1 with fast attack, and you ease that fader up expecting the kit to get thick and loud. Instead the snare loses its middle, the cymbals turn a little swishy, and the kick somehow feels smaller. So you swap compressors. Then you try a different attack. Same thing.
More often than not, the compressor isn’t the problem. The parallel copy is landing a few samples after the dry one, and two copies of the same drums, slightly apart in time, don’t add up. They comb.

### What a late copy does to the blend
Add a signal to a delayed copy of itself and some frequencies arrive in phase (louder) while others arrive opposite (cancelled). The cancellations fall at regular spacing, like the teeth of a comb. With a delay of N samples at sample rate fs, the first notch sits at fs / (2·N) and they repeat every fs / N above it.
With true parallel compression the copy isn’t identical (it’s squashed), so the notches aren’t bottomless. But their depth changes as the compressor breathes, because the level ratio between the two paths keeps moving. That’s the swishy, faintly flanged thing on cymbals and room mics. It’s not your compressor’s character. It’s timing.
Where the offset lands decides what you hear:
Offset at 48 kHz | First notch | What it usually sounds like
1–4 samples | 24–6 kHz | Top end a little duller than solo; easy to blame the compressor’s tone
8–64 samples (0.2–1.3 ms) | 3 kHz–375 Hz | Hollow snare, papery vocal, “phasey” overheads
128–512 samples (2.7–10.7 ms) | 188–47 Hz | Snare body and kick weight drop out; blend stops getting louder
1,000+ samples (20 ms+) | under 25 Hz | A flam or slap: you hear two hits, not one thicker one

### We measured it on a drum loop
To put numbers on it we built a synthetic drum loop (pitched-sine kick, noise-and-tone snare, hats, a small stereo room) at 48 kHz, ran a copy through a fast 10:1 compressor (about 9.4 dB of gain reduction on hits), matched its RMS to the dry loop, and blended it in at −4 dB. Then we slid the parallel path late by different amounts and compared each blend with the perfectly aligned one. Synthetic test signals, so read the shape rather than the decimals.
Parallel late by | First notch | Kick 40–120 | Body 150–400 | Crack 1.2–4k | Air 4–16k | Blend adds | L/R correlation
0 (aligned) | — | 0.0 | 0.0 | 0.0 | 0.0 | +4.0 dB | 0.89
1 sample | 24 kHz | 0.0 | 0.0 | −0.1 | −1.9 | +3.4 dB | 0.88
8 samples (0.17 ms) | 3 kHz | 0.0 | +0.1 | −6.0 | −2.7 | +3.4 dB | 0.89
32 samples (0.67 ms) | 750 Hz | −0.1 | −0.1 | −2.6 | −2.5 | +3.3 dB | 0.89
64 samples (1.33 ms) | 375 Hz | −0.3 | −1.5 | −2.5 | −2.6 | +3.1 dB | 0.89
128 samples (2.67 ms) | 188 Hz | −1.3 | −7.1 | −2.8 | −2.6 | +2.2 dB | 0.90
512 samples (10.7 ms) | 47 Hz | −3.8 | −1.1 | −2.6 | −2.6 | +0.8 dB | 0.86
1,024 samples (21.3 ms) | 23 Hz | −1.2 | −1.5 | −2.4 | −2.6 | +2.3 dB | 0.90
Band columns are dB relative to the aligned blend. Three things in there are worth carrying into your next session.
- Even one sample costs you air. Aligned, the parallel copy adds in phase all the way up. Late by anything, it adds in phase at some frequencies and against at others, so above the first few notches it only adds power, not amplitude. That’s the 2–3 dB of top end that went missing in every misaligned row, and individual notches dug 13–16 dB deep.
- The notch walks down as the offset grows. Eight samples took 6 dB out of the snare crack. A hundred and twenty-eight took 7 dB out of the body. Half a block of latency (512 samples) cancelled the kick fundamental. Each is a different “this compressor sounds wrong” complaint with the same cause.
- The blend stops getting louder. Aligned, the parallel bus added 4.0 dB. At 512 samples it added 0.8 dB, so you push the fader further, which digs the notches deeper. That feedback loop is how a drum bus ends up with the parallel aux at +6 and still sounding small.
The last column matters too. Correlation barely moved (0.86–0.90 in every row) because both channels comb the same way. A correlation meter, CoProducer’s phase row included, will pass this mix, and that’s honest: it answers whether left and right will cancel in mono, not whether two busses inside the session line up. Different question, different test.

### Where the latency sneaks in
Modern DAWs compensate plugin latency automatically, which is why this catches good engineers. It breaks in a handful of predictable places:
- Low-latency monitoring modes. Logic’s Low Latency Mode, Ableton’s Reduced Latency When Monitoring, Cubase’s Constrain Delay Compensation and friends trade compensation for tracking feel. Leave one on after a vocal session and your parallel paths drift.
- Lookahead and oversampling on one path only. A compressor in lookahead or high-quality mode, a linear-phase EQ, or a saturator with oversampling adds anywhere from a few samples to thousands. If the plugin reports it wrong, or changes it when you flip a quality switch mid-playback, compensation can be off until you stop and restart the transport.
- Hardware inserts. An outboard compressor through spare I/O needs its round trip measured (the ping or delay-compensation setting on the insert). An unpinged insert is the classic 1–3 ms parallel smear.
- Odd routing. Aux feeding aux, sidechain-fed chains, or a send taken from a different point than the dry signal. Not every DAW compensates every path the same way.
- Printed parallels. You bounced the crushed bus in place to save CPU and the print came back shifted or trimmed. Now there’s no plugin left to blame.

### Find it in one minute: the null test
Don’t bypass anything for this. In some DAWs a bypassed plugin drops its latency, which hides exactly what you’re looking for.
1. On the parallel bus, set the compressor so it does nothing: ratio 1:1 or threshold all the way up, make-up at 0 dB.
2. Flip polarity on the parallel bus and set its fader so its level matches the dry path (unity if the send is post-fader at 0 dB).
3. Play the drums. Aligned paths null to near silence. If you still hear a thin, fizzy version of the kit, the paths are apart.
On the loop above, aligned paths nulled to −175 dB (numerical floor). One sample of offset left a residual only 3.0 dB under the dry level, on this hat-heavy loop. Sixty-four samples left −0.8 dB, and 128 made the “null” 2.2 dB louder than the dry. There’s no such thing as nearly aligned. A miss is a miss.
If you’d rather have a number than a vibe, bounce the dry drums and the parallel bus soloed, same start point, and let this work out the lag. It cross-correlates the two files and tells you which path to delay:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""find_offset.py — how late is one bounce relative to another?
Bounce the dry track (or bus) soloed and the parallel bus soloed, same start point, then:
    python3 find_offset.py dry.wav parallel.wav
Prints the lag in samples and ms, the first comb notch it implies, and how well the two line up."""
import sys, subprocess, numpy as np

def load(path):   # any format ffmpeg reads -> mono float, plus its sample rate
    sr = int(subprocess.run(["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-select_streams", "a:0", "-show_entries", "stream=sample_rate",
                             "-of", "csv=p=0", path], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout)
    raw = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", path, "-ac", "1", "-f", "f32le", "-"], capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
    return np.frombuffer(raw, np.float32).astype(np.float64), sr

a, sr = load(sys.argv[1]); b, sr_b = load(sys.argv[2])
assert sr == sr_b, "bounce both files at the same sample rate"
n = min(len(a), len(b), sr * 30)                  # 30 s is plenty
a, b = a[:n] - a[:n].mean(), b[:n] - b[:n].mean()
size = 1 << int(np.ceil(np.log2(2 * n)))
xc = np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(b, size) * np.conj(np.fft.rfft(a, size)), size)
max_lag = sr // 10                                # search +/-100 ms
lags = np.r_[np.arange(0, max_lag), np.arange(-max_lag, 0)]
vals = np.r_[xc[:max_lag], xc[-max_lag:]]
k = int(np.argmax(np.abs(vals))); lag = int(lags[k])
score = abs(vals[k]) / np.sqrt(np.sum(a ** 2) * np.sum(b ** 2))
pol = "same" if vals[k] > 0 else "FLIPPED"
print(f"{sys.argv[2]} vs {sys.argv[1]}: {lag:+d} samples ({lag / sr * 1000:+.2f} ms) at {sr} Hz")
print(f"match {score:.2f} (1.00 = identical shape), polarity {pol}")
if lag:
    print(f"blending them comb-filters: first notch ~{sr / (2 * abs(lag)):.0f} Hz, then every {sr / abs(lag):.0f} Hz")
    print(f"fix: delay the {'dry path' if lag > 0 else 'parallel path'} by {abs(lag)} samples, or fix the plugin delay compensation")
else:
    print("aligned to the sample")
On our loop, with the parallel path deliberately 64 samples late:
wet_late.wav vs dry.wav: +64 samples (+1.33 ms) at 48000 Hz
match 0.86 (1.00 = identical shape), polarity same
blending them comb-filters: first notch ~375 Hz, then every 750 Hz
fix: delay the dry path by 64 samples, or fix the plugin delay compensation
A match score under 1.00 is expected here, since one side is compressed. The lag is what you came for.

### Fix order
1. Turn compensation back on fully and restart playback. That alone fixes most of these.
2. Ping any hardware inserts.
3. If the routing can’t be compensated, put the measured offset on the dry path’s track delay (most DAWs take it in samples or ms) and run the null test again until it disappears.
4. Only now dial the compressor. You’ll probably need less of the parallel fader than before, because the blend is finally adding up.
Once it’s aligned, the genre moves behave the way the tutorials promise. Rock and pop drum busses take a fast, hard-ratio parallel tucked well under the dry and get density without losing the snare’s crack. On R&B and pop vocals, a parallel tucked a few dB under the lead thickens the low-level detail without that papery phasiness. On trap 808s with parallel saturation, alignment protects the fundamental. Remember the 512-sample row: it cost the kick 3.8 dB.
And if you want two hits, do it on purpose. A parallel slap delayed 20 ms or more is a legitimate effect. The trouble is the 0.1–10 ms zone nobody chose.
Note: Plugins with a built-in mix knob usually avoid all this, because the dry and wet signals share the same internal latency. When a mix knob sounds fuller than the same compressor on an aux, the aux is probably late. For the stereo side of phase, read Phase correlation is a mono audition. If the bus is pumping rather than thinning, the sidechain filter essay is the one you want.
Q: Why does parallel compression make my drums sound thin?
A: Usually because the parallel bus arrives a few samples to a few milliseconds after the dry signal. The two copies comb-filter, cancelling some frequencies and losing top-end coherence, so the blend gets hollower instead of bigger. Null-test the paths and fix the latency before changing compressor settings.
Q: How much delay causes phasing in parallel compression?
A: Any. On our synthetic drum loop a single sample at 48 kHz cost about 2 dB in the 4–16 kHz band, 8 samples took 6 dB out of the 1.2–4 kHz crack, and 128 samples took 7 dB out of the snare body. The first notch sits at the sample rate divided by twice the offset.
Q: Does a compressor’s mix knob avoid the latency problem?
A: Usually, yes. With a built-in dry/wet control both signals go through the same plugin latency, so they stay aligned. The problem shows up when the dry and compressed signals take different routes through the session.
Q: Will a phase correlation meter catch a misaligned parallel bus?
A: No. Both channels comb-filter the same way, so left/right correlation barely moves. Our blends read 0.86–0.90 whether aligned or 1,024 samples late. Use a polarity-flip null test or cross-correlate soloed bounces instead.

## Why your gapless album gets gaps after MP3 or AAC
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/gapless-album-gaps-after-mp3-or-aac.html
Section: Delivery · 16 October 2026 · 7 min
Summary: MP3 and AAC encoders add silence at the start and padding at the end of every file. Why segues break, what we measured, and how to stay seamless.

Every MP3 and AAC encoder adds a little silence at the start of a file and pads the end out to a full frame, so two tracks that flowed perfectly as WAVs can play with a 5–30 ms hole or a tick between them unless the file carries gapless info and the player reads it. Render the album in one pass, split it at exact sample positions, deliver lossless, and count samples on anything you encode yourself.
Live record, DJ mix, ambient album, a concept project where track 4 pours into track 5 under a held chord. In the session it’s one long, beautiful sentence. Then you make MP3s for the press folder, or a client plays the AAC previews in a car, and right at the segue there’s a hiccup. A tiny hole, sometimes a tick. Nobody touched the transition. The files did.
Single-song releases don’t care about any of this. A few tens of milliseconds of silence before a single is inaudible. It only bites when one track is supposed to keep flowing into the next.

### Where the hole comes from
Lossy codecs work in frames, and the encoder needs a run-up before the first one. So every MP3 and AAC file starts with a short stretch of priming (encoder delay) and ends with padding that fills out the last frame. The file is a little longer than your audio, on both ends.
There’s a fix built into the formats, as long as everyone plays along. LAME writes the exact delay and padding into a header in the first frame (the LAME/Info tag). MP4 files use an edit list (Apple’s encoders also write an iTunSMPB tag). Opus stores a pre-skip in its header. A player that reads these trims the priming and padding and plays your audio sample for sample. A player that doesn’t plays the silence, and two of those silences back to back are your gap.

### What we measured
We rendered a synthetic 20-second segue at 44.1 kHz (a sustained pad chord, a low pulse, a little noise for air) and split it into two tracks at sample 441,123. That’s deliberately mid-note, at −12.4 dBFS, not on a zero crossing. Then we encoded both halves the common ways, decoded them back to back with ffmpeg the way a player would, and compared the join with the continuous original.
Delivery / playback | Lead-in | Extra at end | Track 2 arrives late | Dip at the join | Join null (mid-track)
24-bit WAV or FLAC, split from one render | 0 | 0 | 0 | none | −128.7 dB (−128.5)
Each track bounced separately, 10 ms edge fades | 0 | 0 | 0 | −6.0 dB | −10.2 dB (−184.6)
MP3 (LAME 320k), tag read | 0 | 0 | 0 | none | −36.7 dB (−36.5)
Same MP3, player ignores the tag | 1,105 | 140 | 28.2 ms | silence (−90 dB) | —
MP3 written without the tag | 1,105 | 140 | 28.2 ms | silence (−90 dB) | —
AAC .m4a (ffmpeg aac 256k), edit list read | 0 | 221 | 5.0 ms | −23.1 dB | −16.1 dB (−38.2)
Same .m4a, edit list ignored / raw .aac | 1,024 | 221 | 28.2 ms | −29.4 dB | −16.1 dB (−38.2)
Lead-in and extra are in samples. “Dip” is the quietest 2 ms right at the join compared with the same spot in the original. “Join null” re-aligns track 2 and nulls ±50 ms around the cut against the original, with the same measure from the middle of the track in brackets, so you can see whether the join is any worse than the codec already is.
- Lossless split from one render is perfect. The two WAVs put back together match the original to 24-bit rounding, even cut mid-note. You don’t need zero crossings when nothing is going to be re-encoded at the edges.
- A tagged MP3 is seamless, if the player reads the tag. With the tag honoured, the join nulled exactly as well as the middle of the track (−36.7 vs −36.5 dB), which means it’s only codec noise. Ignore the tag, or never write it, and you get 1,245 samples of pure digital silence: 28.2 ms, right in the middle of your held chord.
- AAC was the touchier one here. With ffmpeg’s built-in encoder the start was trimmed, but 221 samples of end padding stayed in, and the edges reconstructed noticeably worse than the middle of the file (−16 vs −38 dB). That reads as a small smeared tick rather than a clean hole. Other AAC encoders and players behave differently, which is exactly why you test the pair you’re shipping.
- You can break it before any codec gets near it. Bouncing each song as its own region with default edge fades gave a 6 dB dip at the join in a lossless WAV. No encoder will fix that.

### What’s yours to control
For streaming releases you upload WAV or FLAC and the platform does its own encoding and gapless playback. You can’t control their decoder, but you control whether the files you hand them are continuous to the sample, and that’s the part that breaks most often. If your distributor’s form asks whether the album should play continuously or gapless, say yes.
Anything you encode yourself is all on you: press MP3s, a DJ pool upload, the player on your own site, previews for a client. Use an encoder that writes gapless info (LAME does by default) and check the result.

### The workflow
1. Do the transitions in one session and render once. Crossfades, reverb tails, room tone between live songs: all of it lives in the long render. Dither once on that render if you’re going to 16-bit, then split.
2. Split at sample positions, not by bouncing regions. No auto-fades at the cut points, no per-track normalize, no tail trimming. The tracks should butt together and reassemble into the original exactly.
3. For CD, author from the continuous file. Red Book audio is addressed in frames of 1/75 s (588 samples at 44.1 kHz), and track marks in a DDP land on those frames. If a plant insists on individual WAVs, put the splits on 588-sample boundaries so the authoring tool has nothing to pad.
4. Encode with gapless metadata, then count samples. Every encoded track should decode to the same number of samples as its WAV.
Here’s steps 2 and 4 as a script. It cuts one album render at the sample positions you give it, writes 24-bit WAVs for delivery, and makes LAME-tagged MP3s for anything you hand out. The optional --cd flag snaps the splits to CD frames.
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# split_album.sh — cut one continuous album render into tracks at exact sample positions,
# write 24-bit WAVs for delivery plus gapless-tagged MP3s for anything you hand out yourself.
#   ./split_album.sh album_full.wav markers.txt [--cd]
# markers.txt: one track START per line, in samples (0 for track 1). --cd snaps starts to 588-sample CD frames.
set -euo pipefail
src=$1; markers=$2; cd_snap=${3:-}
sr=$(ffprobe -v error -select_streams a:0 -show_entries stream=sample_rate -of csv=p=0 "$src")
total=$(ffprobe -v error -select_streams a:0 -count_packets -show_entries stream=duration_ts -of csv=p=0 "$src")
mapfile -t starts < <(grep -v '^\s*$' "$markers")
[[ $cd_snap == --cd ]] && for i in "${!starts[@]}"; do starts[$i]=$(( (starts[$i] + 294) / 588 * 588 )); done
starts+=("$total")
for (( i = 0; i < ${#starts[@]} - 1; i++ )); do
  a=${starts[$i]}; b=${starts[$((i + 1))]}; n=$(printf "%02d" $((i + 1)))
  ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$src" -af "atrim=start_sample=$a:end_sample=$b,asetpts=N/SR/TB" -c:a pcm_s24le "track$n.wav"
  ffmpeg -v error -y -i "track$n.wav" -c:a libmp3lame -b:a 320k "track$n.mp3"   # LAME/Xing tag carries delay + padding
  echo "track$n  samples $a-$b  ($(( b - a )) samples, $(awk "BEGIN{printf \"%.3f\", ($b-$a)/$sr}") s)"
done
On our segue, with markers at 0 and 441123:
track01  samples 0-441123  (441123 samples, 10.003 s)
track02  samples 441123-882000  (440877 samples, 9.997 s)
Then the check. Each encoded file should decode to exactly the sample count of its WAV:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# count_samples.sh — does each encoded track decode to exactly as many samples as its WAV?
#   ./count_samples.sh track01 track02 ...   (expects trackNN.wav next to trackNN.mp3 / .m4a)
for t in "$@"; do
  wav=$(ffmpeg -v error -i "$t.wav" -f s16le -ac 1 - | wc -c)
  for enc in "$t".mp3 "$t".m4a; do
    [[ -f $enc ]] || continue
    dec=$(ffmpeg -v error -i "$enc" -f s16le -ac 1 - | wc -c)
    printf '%-14s %9d samples   wav %9d   extra %+d\n' "$enc" $((dec / 2)) $((wav / 2)) $(((dec - wav) / 2))
  done
done
From the split above (MP3 from the script, plus an ffmpeg AAC for comparison):
track01.mp3       441123 samples   wav    441123   extra +0
track01.m4a       441344 samples   wav    441123   extra +221
track02.mp3       440877 samples   wav    440877   extra +0
track02.m4a       441344 samples   wav    440877   extra +467
And the same MP3s written without the tag came back +1,245 and +1,491 samples longer. That’s the gap, measured in advance instead of discovered by a listener. +0 means the decoder knows where your audio starts and stops. Anything else is a gap waiting for a segue.
Screw tapes were continuous by design, and the rule carries over: whether the slowdowns come from ScrewAI or a turntable pass, blend the tape in one session, render it once and cut it after. Don’t bounce every song separately and hope the joins line up.
Note: Encoders change more than timing. Re-encoding eats true-peak headroom covers what they do to your peaks. And if a track’s leading silence is dragging its loudness reading down, that’s a different edge problem with its own fix.
Q: Why is there a gap between tracks on my album after converting to MP3?
A: MP3 encoders add priming silence at the start and padding at the end of every file. LAME records both in a header so players can trim them. If the tag is missing or the player ignores it, the silences play. In our test that was a 28.2 ms hole at 44.1 kHz.
Q: Do I need to split album tracks at zero crossings?
A: Not for lossless delivery. Two WAVs cut from one render reassemble exactly, even mid-note. What matters is cutting at a single sample position with no fades, trims or per-track processing at the cut.
Q: Do streaming platforms fix gapless playback for me?
A: They encode from your lossless files and handle playback themselves, so you can’t control their decoder. You do control whether the files you upload are continuous to the sample. A dip or fade baked into your WAVs survives every platform.
Q: How do I check that an MP3 or AAC file is gapless?
A: Decode it and compare its sample count with the WAV it came from. A tagged LAME MP3 decoded by ffmpeg matched exactly in our test. An untagged one was 1,245 samples longer, and an ffmpeg AAC .m4a kept 221 samples of end padding.

---

## Why your 808 disappears on phone speakers
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/808-disappears-on-phone-speakers.html
Section: Low end · 15 October 2026 · 8 min
Summary: Phone speakers barely play below 200–300 Hz, so a clean 808 vanishes. Add a parallel harmonic layer, then check it through a phone filter.

Most phone speakers barely play anything under about 200–300 Hz, so a clean 808 sitting at 40–60 Hz is mostly not there on a phone. What survives is its harmonics. Blend in a parallel layer of controlled harmonics between roughly 120 Hz and 1.5 kHz, check it through a phone-speaker filter, and the note comes back without touching the sub.
You know this one. In the studio the 808 is the whole record: long, round, rattling the desk. Then you send the bounce to your phone, hit play on the bus, and the hats, the snare and the vocal are all there, sitting on top of nothing. The beat feels like it lost a floor. Nothing is wrong with the file. The phone just can’t play the note you wrote.
The fix isn’t more sub. It’s giving the 808 something a tiny speaker can actually reproduce, and keeping the real low end exactly where it is for the systems that can play it.

### A phone hears the harmonics or nothing
A phone speaker is a driver about the size of a fingernail. It can’t move enough air to make much 50 Hz at any volume, so its output falls off hard somewhere in the low hundreds of hertz. Where exactly depends on the phone, but somewhere between 200 and 500 Hz is a fair rough picture. A laptop does a bit better and gives up closer to 100–150 Hz.
An 808 on G1 has a fundamental at 49 Hz. A1 is 55. Even an 808 riding high in the key rarely goes much past 80–90 Hz. So on a phone, the fundamental, which is most of the 808’s energy, simply doesn’t play. What you hear is whatever the 808 has above 200–300 Hz: its harmonics at 2×, 3×, 4× the note and up.
Here’s the part that makes the fix work. When your ear gets a stack of harmonics at 98, 147, 196, 245 Hz, your brain fills in the 49 Hz pitch that isn’t physically there. Psychoacoustics calls it the missing fundamental. A clean sine 808 has almost no harmonics, so there’s nothing to infer the note from. A saturated 808 carries its own pitch up into the range a phone can play.

### The test: same 808, five ways
We built a synthetic four-note 808 line (G1, G1, F1, A1, quick pitch drop into each note, long decay) and a stand-in for the rest of the mix: band-limited noise from 300 Hz to 8 kHz at a fixed level. Then we made four variants, matched all of them to the same full-range RMS so nobody wins by being louder, and ran each through two rough speaker models: a laptop (4th-order high-pass at 150 Hz) and a phone (4th-order high-pass at 300 Hz). These are synthetic test signals and simple filters, not a measurement of any real phone, but the gaps between versions are what you’ll hear.
Version | Full-range RMS | Sample peak | Laptop model | Phone model | 808 vs rest of mix, on the phone
A · clean sine 808 | −16.2 dB | −6.0 dB | −45.8 dB | −57.5 dB | −33.4 dB
B · parallel harmonics, −12 dB blend | −16.2 dB | −5.3 dB | −30.5 dB | −39.3 dB | −15.3 dB
B · parallel harmonics, −6 dB blend | −16.2 dB | −3.9 dB | −25.3 dB | −34.1 dB | −10.1 dB
C · whole 808 driven hard (tanh) | −16.2 dB | −11.1 dB | −35.1 dB | −47.7 dB | −23.7 dB
D · clean 808 slowed to 0.8× | −16.2 dB | −5.3 dB | −49.3 dB | −59.5 dB | −35.5 dB
Read the phone column. The clean 808 sits 33 dB under the rest of the mix: on a phone, it’s gone. A parallel harmonic layer blended 12 dB under the 808 brings it up by about 18 dB on the phone model and costs 0.7 dB of peak. Push the blend to −6 and the gain is about 23 dB, for 2.1 dB of peak. The full-range level didn’t move, because we matched it, so the sub is doing the same job it was doing before.
Version C is interesting for a different reason. Driving the whole 808 into saturation helps the phone by about 10 dB and drops the sample peak 5 dB at the same RMS, because it squares off the wave. That’s exactly why trap and drill engineers clip 808s on purpose: it buys loudness and headroom. But it changes the sub itself, and you can’t dial the phone layer separately from the weight. Parallel gives you two faders instead of one.
Here’s what the −6 dB blend actually added on the first note, before any speaker model:
Harmonic | Frequency | Level vs the 49 Hz fundamental | Does a phone play it?
2nd | 98 Hz | −14.2 dB | No
3rd | 147 Hz | −16.7 dB | Barely; a laptop does
4th | 196 Hz | −8.8 dB | Barely
5th | 245 Hz | −17.2 dB | Partly
6th | 294 Hz | −22.2 dB | Partly
7th | 343 Hz | −21.1 dB | Yes
9th | 441 Hz | −31.0 dB | Yes

### The parallel harmonics move, step by step
1. Send or duplicate the 808 to its own bus. Leave the original alone. That one keeps the sub.
2. Saturate the copy hard. Tape, tube, a soft clipper, a distortion: anything that makes harmonics. You’re not listening to this channel on its own, so don’t be shy. The ffmpeg version below drives it 24 dB into a soft clipper.
3. Band-limit the copy, roughly a high-pass at 100–150 Hz and a low-pass at 1–2 kHz. The high-pass keeps it from stacking on your sub; the low-pass keeps the fizz away from the vocal and hats.
