4. Blend it up with a phone filter on the monitor path (or just your phone) until each 808 note reads as a note, then back off a dB or two. Somewhere between −18 and −6 dB under the dry 808 is a good range to start in.
5. Check it full-range and in mono. The sub should feel identical. If the low mids feel thick, pull the blend back or move the low-pass down.
Flavor matters. Asymmetric saturation (tube- or tape-style) adds even harmonics: 2nd and 4th, which are octaves of the note and sit very musically. Symmetric clipping adds odd harmonics, the 3rd and 5th, which is where the bark and growl come from. Trap and drill usually want the bark. R&B, clean pop and anything with a sung bass line usually want the octaves, blended lower. In house and techno the kick tends to own the sub and the bass already lives higher, so this matters less there, but the phone check still tells you if the groove survives.
Note: The new harmonics land right where the kick’s knock, the snare body and the low end of the vocal live, around 150–500 Hz. If the mix gets cloudy after the blend, that’s the place to look. A small dip in the harmonic bus where the vocal sits, or a sidechain from the kick, usually clears it. More on sharing that space in the kick and 808 can’t sit in the same chair.

### Slowed versions make it worse
If you also put out a slowed edit, check the slowed one on a phone separately. Slowing to 0.8× by resampling drops every pitch with it: a G1 at 49 Hz lands near 39 Hz. In the test that cost another 2 dB on the phone model and 3.5 dB on the laptop model, on an 808 that was already barely there. A slowed version built from the harmonic-layered mix holds up far better than one built from a clean-sine mix. If you make your slowed edits in ScrewAI, run the result through the same phone check before it goes out. Tempo changes the low end too, and screw tempo still needs a legal peak covers the peak side of it.

### A phone check you can run on any bounce
This writes two files next to your bounce: .phone.wav (a rough phone-speaker filter you can just listen to) and .harm.wav (the parallel-harmonics move done in ffmpeg, so you can hear what it would give you before you touch the session). Then it prints the levels. It needs only ffmpeg.
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# phone_check.sh in.wav: writes in.phone.wav (rough phone speaker: 4th-order high-pass at 300 Hz)
# and in.harm.wav (parallel harmonics: copy driven 24 dB into a soft clipper, 120 Hz-1.5 kHz only, pulled down 12 dB, mixed back in).
set -euo pipefail
in="$1"; b="${in%.*}"
ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$in" -af "highpass=f=300:poles=2,highpass=f=300:poles=2" "$b.phone.wav"
ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$in" -filter_complex \
 "[0:a]asplit[dry][wet];[wet]volume=24dB,asoftclip=type=tanh,highpass=f=120:poles=2,highpass=f=120:poles=2,lowpass=f=1500:poles=2,volume=-12dB[h];[dry][h]amix=inputs=2:normalize=0" \
 -c:a pcm_f32le "$b.harm.wav"
ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$b.harm.wav" -af "highpass=f=300:poles=2,highpass=f=300:poles=2" "$b.harm.phone.wav"
for f in "$in" "$b.phone.wav" "$b.harm.wav" "$b.harm.phone.wav"; do
  ffmpeg -nostats -i "$f" -af astats=measure_overall=RMS_level+Peak_level:measure_perchannel=none -f null - 2>&1 \
   | awk -v f="$f" '/RMS level dB/{r=$NF} /Peak level dB/{p=$NF} END{printf "%-22s RMS %6.1f dB  peak %6.1f dB\n", f, r, p}'
done
On the synthetic 808 line it printed:
808_clean.wav          RMS  -16.2 dB  peak   -6.0 dB
808_clean.phone.wav    RMS  -59.4 dB  peak  -22.7 dB
808_clean.harm.wav     RMS  -15.8 dB  peak   -5.2 dB
808_clean.harm.phone.wav RMS  -39.0 dB  peak  -17.9 dB
About 20 dB more 808 on the phone, for 0.4 dB of full-range level and 0.8 dB of peak. (The ffmpeg filters and the Python model in the table disagree by a couple of dB on the clean file. That’s expected; both are rough speaker models. Compare versions through the same one.) The fuller Python version that produced the tables, with the laptop model and the harmonic breakdown, is phone808.py in the demo folder.
If you want to see it rather than run a script, drop the before and after bounces on CoProducer’s analyze page. It draws a spectral map of the file right in the browser, and you can see whether each 808 note lights up above the bottom rows or only down at the floor, where phones never reach.
Q: Why can I hear my 808 on headphones but not on my phone?
A: Headphones sit right at your ear and can reproduce 40–60 Hz easily. A phone speaker can’t, and its output falls off hard somewhere around 200–500 Hz depending on the model. If the 808 is mostly fundamental, the phone has nothing left to play. Harmonics above 200–300 Hz are what carry it.
Q: Should I just boost the 808 around 100 Hz?
A: It helps a laptop a little, but 100 Hz is still below what most phone speakers reproduce, and the boost eats headroom on every system that can play it. Adding harmonics higher up gives the phone something real to play without making the sub heavier.
Q: Does saturating the 808 hurt my master?
A: Not in the test. A parallel layer blended at −12 dB added 0.7 dB of sample peak at the same full-range level. Driving the whole 808 hard lowered the peak by 5 dB because it squares the wave, which is why clipping 808s is a common loudness move in trap. Just watch the 150–500 Hz area for build-up.

---

## How much headroom to leave for mastering (and why −6 dB isn’t the point)
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/how-much-headroom-to-leave-for-mastering.html
Section: Delivery · 15 October 2026 · 8 min
Summary: Headroom for mastering means no clipping and no mix-bus limiter. Peaks near −6 to −3 dBFS in 24-bit or float is convention; clipping can’t be undone.

Leave enough headroom that nothing clips, and send it with no limiter or clipper on the mix bus. Peaks somewhere around −6 to −3 dBFS in a 24-bit or 32-bit float file is a polite convention, not a rule: in 24-bit there’s no audible cost to leaving more, but a clipped fixed-point bounce can’t be undone.
The email says “please leave −6 dB of headroom.” So you pull the master fader until the meter peaks at −6 and export. Or, more often, the mix already sounds great with the limiter on the bus, so you leave it there and just turn the output down to −6. Both feel like you followed the instructions. Only one of them actually did.
The number is the least important part of that request. What the mastering engineer is really asking for is a file they can still make decisions on.

### What headroom actually protects
- No clipping baked in. Inside a modern DAW the mix bus runs in floating point, so it can go over 0 dBFS without damage. The moment you export to a fixed-point format like 24-bit WAV, anything over 0 is sliced flat. That damage is permanent.
- No mastering decision made early. A limiter or clipper on the mix bus sets how hard the peaks get pushed before the person whose job that is gets the file. Turning its output down to −6 afterwards leaves the squash in place.
- A little room between samples. The waveform between samples can peak higher than the samples themselves (inter-sample peaks). A few dB of space keeps the file honest on the way into the mastering chain.
What headroom does not do is change the quality of a 24-bit file. The engineer is going to set the gain anyway. A 24-bit file has a theoretical noise floor around −144 dBFS, so leaving 6 dB, 10 dB or even 20 dB of headroom costs nothing you’ll ever hear. The difference between peaking at −3 and peaking at −8 is just a gain knob.

### One mix, four exports
We summed a synthetic hot mix (kick, snare, bass, pad, hats) so its float peak landed at +4.5 dBFS, which is common when a mix bus is running hot and nobody’s looking. Then we exported it four ways and ran each file through the check script below. These are synthetic test signals, but the failure modes are the real ones.
Export | Sample peak | True peak | Integrated | Crest | Clipped runs | Check says
32-bit float, overs kept | +4.5 dBFS | +4.7 dBTP | −11.7 LUFS | 17.0 dB | — | Recoverable; say so
24-bit, overs clipped | +0.0 dBFS | +2.7 dBTP | −11.7 LUFS | 12.5 dB | 5 | Clipped
24-bit, limiter on the bus (−0.3 ceiling) | −0.3 dBFS | +1.1 dBTP | −12.4 LUFS | 12.6 dB | 0 | Limiter on the bus?
24-bit, turned down 10 dB first | −5.5 dBFS | −5.3 dBTP | −21.7 LUFS | 17.0 dB | 0 | OK to send
Then we did what a mastering engineer would do first: turn each file down 10 dB and compare it against the clean, unclipped original.
Export | Error vs the clean original | What that means
32-bit float, overs kept | −151.9 dB | Nothing lost. Float only rounds.
24-bit, turned down 10 dB first | −121.2 dB | 24-bit rounding, far below anything audible
24-bit, overs clipped | −33.4 dB | Flat-topped transients, permanently. At the worst moment the error is only 8 dB below the peak itself.
Three things jump out. The clipped file reads the same −11.7 LUFS as the float one, so a loudness meter won’t warn you. Its crest factor dropped from 17.0 to 12.5 dB: that’s the punch of the kick and snare, gone. And the file that peaked at −5.5 is the cleanest fixed-point export of the lot, even though it’s 10 dB “quieter.”
The limiter file needs its own sentence. It shows zero clipped runs, so a quick clip check passes it. But its crest dropped 4.4 dB, nearly as much as the clipped file, and the peaks keep landing on the same ceiling, about 9% of all 50 ms blocks, against roughly 1% in the untouched exports. That pattern is what the script flags. Also notice that a sample-peak limiter set to −0.3 still let a +1.1 dBTP true peak through. True peak is what codecs clip goes into why.

### The send-to-mastering checklist
1. Take the limiter, maximizer or clipper off the mix bus. If the mix depends on how it sounds through it, send two files: the clean premaster, and the limited version labeled as a vibe reference. A clipper on the 808 or drum bus is a mix choice and can stay; on the whole mix it’s a mastering choice.
2. Peak somewhere around −6 to −3 dBFS. That’s the convention most engineers ask for. Anything under 0 in 24-bit is technically fine; the range just leaves room for inter-sample peaks and stray overs.
3. Make headroom at the source, not after a bus processor. Pull the mix bus input trim, or lower the faders or a VCA. Pulling the master fader works in a float DAW only if no plugin after it clips internally.
4. Export 24-bit or 32-bit float at the session’s sample rate. No dither unless you’re going to 16-bit, no normalize box ticked, no MP3 preview as the master. Sample rate and bit depth are delivery hygiene has the details.
5. If you send float with overs, say so in the email. It’s recoverable, but only if the next person turns it down before anything fixed-point touches it.
6. Leave the reverb tail and a breath of room at the end. Don’t trim it tight; the engineer will set fades.

### A check you can run before you hit send
This reads any file ffmpeg can open and prints its format, sample peak, true peak, integrated loudness and crest, counts runs of three or more samples stuck at full scale (per channel, so stereo interleaving can’t hide them), and measures how often the peaks land on one ceiling, which is a hint that a limiter or clipper is on the bus. That last one is a heuristic, not a verdict. It needs Python 3, numpy and ffmpeg.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""premaster_check.py: is this bounce safe to send to mastering?
Usage: python3 premaster_check.py mix.wav [more.wav ...]   (needs ffmpeg + numpy)
Reports format, sample peak, true peak, integrated LUFS, clipped runs and how much
of the file sits pinned near its own ceiling (a hint that a limiter or clipper is on)."""
import sys, re, json, subprocess, numpy as np

def probe(p):
    j = json.loads(subprocess.run(["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-select_streams", "a:0", "-show_entries",
        "stream=codec_name,sample_rate,channels,bits_per_raw_sample,bits_per_sample", "-of", "json", p],
        capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout)["streams"][0]
    return j

def pcm(p):
    raw = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", p, "-f", "f32le", "-"], capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
    return np.frombuffer(raw, np.float32)

def loud(p):
    err = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-nostats", "-i", p, "-af", "ebur128=peak=true", "-f", "null", "-"],
                         capture_output=True, text=True).stderr
    I = float(re.findall(r"I:\s+(-?[\d.]+) LUFS", err)[-1]); tp = float(re.findall(r"Peak:\s+(-?[\d.]+) dBFS", err)[-1])
    return I, tp

def runs(x, thr, minlen=3):
    hot = np.abs(x) >= thr
    if not hot.any(): return 0
    d = np.diff(np.concatenate([[0], hot.astype(np.int8), [0]]))
    return int(np.sum((np.where(d == -1)[0] - np.where(d == 1)[0]) >= minlen))

for p in sys.argv[1:]:
    s = probe(p); x = pcm(p); pk = np.max(np.abs(x)); I, tp = loud(p)
    fmt = s["codec_name"]; floaty = fmt.startswith("pcm_f")
    ch = int(s["channels"])
    clip_runs = 0 if floaty else sum(runs(x[c::ch], 0.9999) for c in range(ch))   # 3+ samples in a row at full scale, per channel
    blk = int(int(s["sample_rate"]) * 0.05) * ch
    bp = np.abs(x[:len(x) // blk * blk]).reshape(-1, blk).max(1)
    pinned = 100 * np.mean(bp >= pk * 10 ** (-0.5 / 20))   # 50 ms blocks peaking within 0.5 dB of the max
    crest = 20 * np.log10(pk / np.sqrt(np.mean(x.astype(np.float64) ** 2)))
    notes = []
    if floaty and pk > 1: notes.append("overs kept in float: recoverable, but say so when you send it")
    if not floaty and clip_runs: notes.append("CLIPPED: flat tops baked into a fixed-point file")
    if pinned > 5 and not clip_runs: notes.append("peaks keep landing on one ceiling: limiter or clipper on the mix bus?")
    if pk < 10 ** (-24 / 20): notes.append("very quiet: fine in 24-bit/float, just check it's the right file")
    print(f"\n{p}\n  format {fmt}, {s['sample_rate']} Hz, {s['channels']} ch")
    print(f"  sample peak {20*np.log10(pk):+.1f} dBFS | true peak {tp:+.1f} dBTP | {I:.1f} LUFS | crest {crest:.1f} dB")
    print(f"  clipped runs (3+ samples at full scale) {clip_runs} | 50 ms blocks at the ceiling {pinned:.1f}%")
    print("  " + ("; ".join(notes) if notes else "OK to send"))
On the four exports above it printed (trimmed to the last line of each):
mix_float.wav        overs kept in float: recoverable, but say so when you send it
mix_24_clipped.wav   CLIPPED: flat tops baked into a fixed-point file
mix_24_limited.wav   peaks keep landing on one ceiling: limiter or clipper on the mix bus?
mix_24_headroom.wav  OK to send
If you’d rather not run Python, CoProducer’s analyze page reads clipped samples, true peak and crest for a bounce right in the browser, without uploading it anywhere. Drop the premaster there before it goes out. A zero in the clipped samples row plus a crest that looks like your mix (not like a master) is a good sign.
Note: Mastering your own mix? The same rule applies with one person playing both roles. Bounce the premaster clean, take a break, then master the bounce. More on resisting the bus limiter in when not to reach for the limiter.
Q: Is −6 dB of headroom required for mastering?
A: No. It’s a convention. What matters is that nothing clips and there’s no limiter on the mix bus. In a 24-bit file, peaking anywhere from about −10 to −3 dBFS gives the engineer the same quality to work with; they set the gain either way.
Q: Should I normalize my mix before sending it to mastering?
A: No. Normalizing just moves the peak to a fixed level, often right up to 0 dBFS, which removes the safety margin you were asked for. Leave the gain where your headroom puts it.
Q: Can I send a 32-bit float file that peaks over 0 dBFS?
A: Yes, the overs are still in the file and turning it down recovers them exactly. Tell the engineer, though, because any fixed-point step before that turn-down will clip it, and some tools convert on import.
Q: Should I send my mix with or without the limiter?
A: Without, as the main file. If the limiter is part of the sound you’ve been living with, include the limited bounce as a labeled reference so the engineer knows what you liked.

---

## Integrated LUFS hides how loud the chorus actually is
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/integrated-lufs-hides-the-chorus.html
Section: Meters · 14 October 2026 · 7 min
Summary: A master can read −14 LUFS integrated while its chorus runs 3–4 LU hotter. Measure integrated, short-term and momentary on one bounce first.

Integrated LUFS is a gated average of the whole song, so a master that reads −14 can carry a chorus running 3–4 LU hotter on the short-term meter — and that chorus is what your ears, your limiter, and the next track in the playlist actually meet. Measure I, S max and M max on the same bounce before you decide anything.
Here’s the session. The delivery sheet says −14.1 LUFS integrated. Right in the lane. Then you play the first chorus with a loudness meter open, and the short-term readout says −10.6. Momentary flicks up to −9.5 on the downbeat. First thought: one of these meters is broken. Neither is. They’re answering three different questions, and only one of them is the question the store asks.
Once you know which is which, the “is my master too loud or too quiet” argument gets a lot shorter.

### Three windows on the same file
All three readings come from the same BS.1770 measurement: K-weighting (a gentle low cut and a high-shelf lift that roughly track how loud things feel), then average power over a window. The only thing that changes is the window.
- Momentary (M) is a 400 ms sliding window with no gate. It’s the needle that jumps on a snare or an impact, which makes it good for spotting one hit that lands way above its bar.
- Short-term (S) is a 3-second sliding window with no gate, roughly a bar or two. It’s the honest answer to “how loud is this section?”
- Integrated (I) covers the whole program in 400 ms blocks, gated twice: an absolute gate drops anything under −70 LUFS, then a relative gate drops blocks more than 10 LU under the running level. This is the single number the stores normalize on.
Here’s the part that surprises people. Integrated isn’t an average of decibels. It’s an average of power, so loud sections count for far more than quiet ones. A chorus 9 LU over the verse carries roughly eight times the power per second. The integrated number leans hard toward the chorus, and the verses pull it down a few LU. That’s why, on a song with real sections, the loudest short-term window usually sits somewhere around 2–5 LU over integrated, and mastering louder barely closes it unless the limiter starts crushing the chorus.

### One bounce, three readings
We built a synthetic test song (a pink-noise bed, a few tones, a kick, verses about 9 dB under the chorus, and an impact on every chorus downbeat) and drove it into a plain limiter until the integrated number landed at −14. These are synthetic test signals, not a real record, but the relationships are the same ones you’ll find on your own bounces.
Reading | Window | Value | What it tells you
Integrated (I) | Whole song, gated | −14.1 LUFS | The number the store normalizes on
Short-term max (S max) | 3 s, first chorus | −10.6 LUFS | How loud the chorus plays: 3.5 LU over I
Momentary max (M max) | 400 ms, chorus downbeat | −9.5 LUFS | The hit itself: 4.6 LU over I
Verse (measured alone) | 28 s of verse | −19.8 LUFS | Above the gate, so it’s counted and drags I down
And all of the limiter’s work happened in the chorus: about 0.9 dB of average gain reduction there, effectively none in the verses. The number on the delivery sheet (−14.1) and the section your limiter is fighting (−10.6) are describing two different parts of the song.

### Why the store and your ears disagree
The store measures integrated, applies one gain to the whole track, and walks away. Spotify’s own artist docs say tracks are adjusted to −14 LUFS, and they point out that a dynamic track mastered to −14 keeps its peaks, so it can feel louder in contrast than a crushed one played at the same level. That’s this exact effect. On normalized playback, your chorus plays at the target plus your gap. Here that means about −10.5, on every normalized player.
Your ears don’t average a three-minute song. They hear your chorus, then the next song’s chorus. Your limiter doesn’t average either. It reacts to the loudest bars, which is why a master that “only” reads −14 integrated can still sound flattened in the hook. And if you ever deliver to a spec that caps max short-term (some broadcast and ad specs do), the gap is the number that fails, not the integrated one.

### The mistake that costs the most
The common slip goes the other way. You watch the short-term meter during the loudest part, pull the master down until the chorus reads −14, and bounce. We tried it. The chorus reads −14.0 short-term, and the integrated number falls to −17.6.
Now the store has a quiet track. Spotify only turns quiet tracks up as far as their peaks allow (they keep 1 dB for the encoder), and this master already peaks at −1.1 dBTP, so it gets about a tenth of a dB. YouTube doesn’t turn quiet tracks up at all. The chorus ends up playing around 3.4 LU under the same song mastered to −14 integrated. Nothing about the mix changed. Only the meter you trusted did.
Short-term is a great meter for the session. It’s the wrong meter for the delivery number.

### The call: tame the chorus, or accept the number
Once you have I, S max and M max side by side, there are really two honest moves. Here’s the same song four ways:
Version | I | S max | M max | LRA | Verse
As bounced | −14.1 | −10.6 | −9.5 | 12.1 LU | −19.8
Chorus −2.5 dB, re-mastered to −14 | −14.1 | −10.9 | −9.7 | 9.7 LU | −17.7
Kept the chorus, accepted −14.9 | −14.9 | −11.3 | −10.2 | 12.3 LU | −20.8
Chorus set to −14 short-term | −17.6 | −14.0 | −12.4 | 12.9 LU | −24.0
Tame the chorus when the limiter is grinding there, when the downbeat impact jumps out on the momentary meter, or when the hook sounds smaller than the verse in context. But look at what that row actually did. We pulled the chorus down 2.5 dB, chased −14 again, and the loudest three seconds moved only 0.3 LU. Because the integrated number is mostly made of the chorus, re-mastering to the same integrated hands most of the level straight back. What really changed was the verses: up 2.1 dB, with loudness range down from 12.1 to 9.7 LU. At a fixed integrated number, taming the chorus is a contrast decision. Make it on purpose, with the verse in your ears.
Accept the quieter integrated number when the chorus sounds right and the limiter is only there to catch it. Backing the input off 1 dB put the master at −14.9 with less limiting in the hook. On Apple’s Sound Check, which plays around −16, both versions get turned down to the same place, so it costs nothing there. On Spotify Normal it plays about 0.8 LU quieter, because the peaks leave no room for a lift. That’s a trade you can hear and choose, instead of one a meter chose for you.
What we wouldn’t do: push the whole master another dB into the limiter just to see −14.0 on the sheet, or pull it down until the chorus reads −14. Both let a meter make an arrangement decision.

### The check, in one pass
This prints all three readings, plus where the loudest 3 seconds sit, from a single ffmpeg pass. Give it several bounces at once to compare versions side by side.
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ism.sh — integrated, max short-term and max momentary loudness from one ffmpeg pass.
# Usage: ./ism.sh master.wav [another.wav ...]      Needs: ffmpeg
set -euo pipefail
for f in "$@"; do
  ffmpeg -nostats -hide_banner -i "$f" -af ebur128=peak=true -f null - 2>&1 |
  sed -E 's/(t|M|S|I):[[:space:]]*/\1: /g' |
  awk -v f="$f" '
    / M: / { for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) {
               if ($i == "t:") t = $(i+1); if ($i == "M:") m = $(i+1) + 0; if ($i == "S:") s = $(i+1) + 0 }
             if (mm == "" || m > mm) mm = m
             if (sm == "" || s > sm) { sm = s; at = t } }
    /Integrated loudness/ { sum = 1 }
    sum && $1 == "I:"    { I = $2 }
    sum && $1 == "LRA:"  { L = $2 }
    sum && $1 == "Peak:" { P = $2 }
    END { printf "%s\n  I %.1f LUFS | S max %.1f (at %.0f s) | M max %.1f | LRA %.1f LU | TP %s dBTP\n", f, I, sm, at, mm, L, P
          printf "  the loudest 3 seconds sit %.1f LU over the integrated number\n", sm - I }'
done
How to read it. If S max sits 2–5 LU over I and the chorus sounds right, you’re done. That’s a song with sections, and the store will play it the way you hear it. If the gap is a lot bigger, check the verse and the intro, because something is pulling integrated down hard. If M max sits more than 2–3 LU over S max, one hit is jumping out of its own bar, and that’s a transient or clipper job, not a loudness job.
Then drop the same bounce on CoProducer’s analyze page and read the LUFS row. That’s the integrated number the stores act on, measured the same BS.1770 way, so the two should agree within a tenth or so. The script tells you how far the chorus sits above it. Between them, you’ve got the whole picture.
Note: The gating math lives in the LUFS guide. If the store turn-down is new to you, start with Why streaming platforms turn loud masters down. Then measure the bounce and read the LUFS row next to your short-term max. The web form tells you the distance and doesn’t write a master.
Q: Why does my chorus read louder than my integrated LUFS?
A: Integrated is a gated average of the whole song, including verses and intros that sit under the chorus. Short-term only looks at the last 3 seconds. On a dynamic song the loudest short-term window usually runs 2–5 LU over integrated, and that’s normal.
Q: Should I master so the chorus reads −14 LUFS short-term?
A: No. Stores normalize on integrated, so a chorus at −14 short-term usually leaves the song around −17 or −18 integrated, and many platforms won’t turn it back up. Hit your integrated number, then make sure the chorus gap sounds intentional.

---

## Don’t match a streamed reference
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/dont-match-a-streamed-reference.html
Section: Workflow · 14 October 2026 · 7 min
Summary: A streamed reference was already turned down or up by the platform. Match it and you inherit an offset you never measured. Compare lossless files.

A streamed reference isn’t the master. It’s the master after the platform turned it down (or up), ran it through a codec, and sometimes through a limiter — so if you match your loudness to the stream, you’re matching an offset you never measured. Get a lossless file, measure both on the same meter, and compare there.
We’ve all done this one. The mix is nearly there, you pull up the record you love on Spotify or YouTube, flip between it and your bounce, and nudge the limiter until they feel the same. It’s fast, and it feels like the responsible move. The catch: what comes out of the app isn’t the file that engineer delivered. It’s that file plus a gain change the platform picked, plus a lossy encode, plus whatever your app and system volume are doing. You matched against all of it at once.
None of this is a reason to stop referencing. It’s a reason to reference the right file.

### What the stream did before you heard it
Every big store measures integrated loudness when the track comes in and applies one playback gain. Loud records get turned down. Quiet ones get turned up only sometimes, and only as far as their peaks allow. We built two synthetic references, one loud (−8.8 LUFS) and one dynamic (−17.4 LUFS), and simulated what each platform would hand you: the platform’s gain, then an encode and a decode.
Reference file | Spotify Normal | Apple Sound Check | YouTube | Spotify Loud
Loud: −8.8 LUFS, −0.3 dBTP | −14.0 (down 5.2 dB) | −16.0 (down 7.2) | −14.0 (down 5.2) | −11.0 (down 2.2)
Dynamic: −17.4 LUFS, −0.6 dBTP | −17.5 (no lift, peaks) | −17.4 (no lift) | −17.4 (never lifts) | −12.3 (up 6.4 into a limiter)
These are synthetic signals and simulated platform behavior, based on what the platforms document, so treat the tenths as illustration. The shape is the point. The loud reference came out of four players at three different levels, and none of them was its real −8.8. The dynamic one didn’t move on three of them, then got shoved through a limiter on the fourth.
Check the peaks, too. The loud reference’s Spotify capture measured −5.1 dBTP. The actual file runs at −0.3. Read peaks off a stream and you’ll decide the pros leave 5 dB of headroom. They don’t. You’re reading the turn-down.

### How it bites once you upload
Say you matched the loud reference by meter while it played with Sound Check on. The capture reads −16.0, so you master to −16.1 with a −1.1 dBTP ceiling. Then both records land on Spotify. The reference gets turned down to −14.0. Yours is quiet, and Spotify only lifts quiet tracks until their peaks reach −1 dBTP. You’re already there, so you get about a tenth of a dB. Your record plays around 2 LU under the one you matched. YouTube never turns up, so same story there.
It goes the other way just as easily. Say you referenced the dynamic record on Spotify with the Premium “Loud” setting on. That mode targets −11 regardless of peaks and runs a limiter to get there, so the dynamic reference came out at −12.3 with its peaks already squashed. You chase that and limit your master to −12.3. On Normal playback you get turned down to −14 while the reference plays at its real −17.4. You’re now 3.4 LU hotter than the record you were matching, and you paid for it with limiting you didn’t need.
Same ears, same mix decisions, a completely different result, purely because of which setting was on when you A/B’d. That’s the trap. It also bakes in the codec: lossy streams soften the very top end and smear transients a little, so an air-band or punch match against a stream is partly a match against the encoder.

### Platform targets, as guidance not gospel
Where it plays | Plays at about | Turns quiet tracks up? | Worth knowing
Spotify (Normal) | −14 LUFS | Only until peaks reach −1 dBTP | Premium listeners can pick Loud (−11, with a limiter) or Quiet (−19)
Apple Music (Sound Check) | ≈ −16 LUFS | Commonly reported as peak-limited | With Sound Check off you hear the file’s own level
YouTube | −14 LUFS | No | “Stats for nerds” shows content loudness, the turn-down in dB
Amazon Music | ≈ −14 LUFS | Not well documented | Often wants −2 dBTP on loud masters
TIDAL | ≈ −14 LUFS | Not well documented | Often normalizes per album, not per track
Bandcamp, downloads, DJ pools | No platform gain | — | The file is the playback level
Sources: Spotify for Artists, “Loudness normalization” (tracks adjusted to −14 LUFS per ITU 1770); Apple Support, “Sound Check” (Apple describes the feature but does not publish a LUFS figure there, so ≈ −16 is the commonly reported value); AES TD1008, the AES recommendations for streaming loudness; ITU-R BS.1770, the loudness and true-peak measurement. The YouTube, Amazon Music and TIDAL rows are commonly reported figures; we did not find an official published target to link.
These drift. Platforms change targets, apps change defaults, listeners change settings. Read the table as the shape of the problem, not a spec sheet. The one constant: the level you hear from a stream is the platform’s decision, not the engineer’s.

### The fix: compare files, not apps
The clean version takes about ten minutes:
1. Get a lossless file of the reference. A Bandcamp or Qobuz purchase, a label promo, or the WAV your mastering engineer worked from. A lossless stream beats a lossy one, but it’s still gain-shifted unless normalization is off.
2. If all you have is a stream, measure the offset. On YouTube, right-click the video, open Stats for nerds and read “content loudness”: 5.2 dB there means it’s playing 5.2 dB under its own file. In Spotify or Apple Music, switch off normalization (Normalize volume, Sound Check), set the app volume to full, and treat a loopback capture as a ballpark, not a measurement.
3. Measure both files on the same meter: integrated, short-term max, loudness range, true peak.
4. Loudness-match for listening with clean gain only, turning the louder file down so nothing clips. Then compare tone, punch and width at equal loudness.
5. Pick your delivery number separately. Matching a reference’s balance is the goal. Copying its loudness is optional. Copying its peaks is how you inherit someone else’s codec problem.
Here are steps 3 and 4 as a script. It measures both files on ffmpeg’s EBU R128 meter and writes a loudness-matched listening copy, gain only, so you hear balance instead of level.
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# refcheck.sh — measure your master and a lossless reference on the same meter,
# then write a loudness-matched listening copy (clean gain only, no limiter, no EQ).
# Usage: ./refcheck.sh my_master.wav reference.wav       Needs: ffmpeg
set -euo pipefail
mine="$1"; ref="$2"
meas(){ ffmpeg -nostats -hide_banner -i "$1" -af ebur128=peak=true -f null - 2>&1 |
  awk '/Integrated loudness/{s=1} s&&$1=="I:"{i=$2} s&&$1=="LRA:"{l=$2} s&&$1=="Peak:"{p=$2} END{print i, l, p}'; }
read -r mi ml mp < <(meas "$mine")
read -r ri rl rp < <(meas "$ref")
printf "mine  I %6s LUFS  LRA %5s LU  TP %5s dBTP\n" "$mi" "$ml" "$mp"
printf "ref   I %6s LUFS  LRA %5s LU  TP %5s dBTP\n" "$ri" "$rl" "$rp"
d=$(awk -v a="$ri" -v b="$mi" 'BEGIN{printf "%+.1f", a-b}')
echo "reference minus yours: ${d} LU"
# Turn the louder file DOWN, so nothing in the listening copy can clip.
if awk -v d="$d" 'BEGIN{exit !(d>0)}'; then src="$ref"; g="-${d#+}"; else src="$mine"; g="${d#+}"; fi
out="${src%.*}_listen.wav"
ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$src" -af "volume=${g}dB" -c:a pcm_f32le "$out"
echo "wrote $out (${g} dB). A/B it against the other file at one monitor level."
On our synthetic pair, a master at −14.9 against the loud reference file, it reports:
mine  I  -14.9 LUFS  LRA  12.3 LU  TP  -1.1 dBTP
ref   I   -8.8 LUFS  LRA   6.0 LU  TP  -0.3 dBTP
reference minus yours: +6.1 LU
wrote ref_loud_listen.wav (-6.1 dB). A/B it against the other file at one monitor level.
Six LU is the real distance between the two files, the number the Spotify capture hid by reading −14.0. Now A/B the listening copy against your master at one monitor level. If yours still sounds smaller at matched loudness, that’s a real mix note: low-mid density, transient shape, width. If it sounds the same or better, the gap you heard in the app was the app.
When you want more than loudness, CoProducer’s reference table does this same comparison on two local bounces, with loudness, peak, balance and the delivery gates side by side, so you’re reading divergence on files you control instead of on a stream. Meters only mean something when both sides came through the same door.
Note: If the divergence table is new to you, Reference matching without guesswork walks through it. For the turn-up side of this story, read Quiet masters get turned up — and so does the noise. Then measure your bounce before you reach for the limiter. The web form tells you the distance and doesn’t write a master.
Q: Can I use a Spotify or YouTube stream as a mix reference?
A: For arrangement and vibe, sure. For loudness or peaks, no: the stream has already been turned down or up by the platform and passed through a codec. Use a lossless file, or measure the stream’s offset and compensate for it.
Q: How do I loudness-match a reference track properly?
A: Measure the integrated LUFS of both lossless files on the same meter, then turn the louder one down by the difference with clean gain. Compare at equal loudness, and set your own delivery level separately.

---

## Short-term LUFS is not your target
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/short-term-lufs-is-not-your-target.html
Section: Loudness · 12 October 2026 · 8 min
Summary: Stores use integrated LUFS over the whole file. A hook at −9 short-term can still miss −14 integrated. Read both meters, then decide.

Streaming and stores care about integrated LUFS over the whole file. A drop that hits −9 short-term can still miss −14 integrated—or look “quiet” while the chorus is already crushed. Read both meters, then decide.
You’ve seen this one. The hook meter needles into the red, short-term sitting somewhere around −9, and it feels competitive. You bounce, upload, and the store report says −16 integrated. Or the opposite: the whole-song number looks soft, so you shove another dB into the limiter and suddenly the chorus is brickwalled while the verses still sit in the mud.
Neither meter lied. You asked them different questions and treated the answers as the same number.

### Three windows, three jobs
Loudness meters in the EBU R128 / BS.1770 family give you three reads that move at different speeds:
Meter | Window | What it’s for
Momentary | ~400 ms | Catching peaks and hits while you work. Not a delivery target.
Short-term | 3 seconds | Sectional truth—verse vs hook, drop vs breakdown.
Integrated | Whole file (gated) | What Spotify, YouTube, Apple Sound Check, and most stores use for playback gain.
Integrated is the delivery lane. Short-term is how the arrangement actually breathes. Momentary is the warning light on the desk. Chasing short-term on the hook and calling it done is how you either over-limit the whole song or leave the integrated number in the wrong place.
A quick mental model: if the chorus is 6 LU hotter than the verse on short-term, and the chorus is half the song, the integrated number will land somewhere between them—not at the chorus. Push the chorus to “competitive” short-term and the integrated reading can still look quiet. Leave the verses alone and the store average never catches the hook.

### Measure both before you touch the limiter
Here’s a small script that runs ffmpeg’s ebur128 meter on a bounce and prints integrated loudness, loudness range, true peak, max short-term, and the gap between the hottest short-term window and the whole-song average. That’s the number that tells you whether the hook is doing all the work.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""shortterm_check.py — integrated vs max short-term on one bounce.
Usage: python3 shortterm_check.py master.wav
Needs: ffmpeg on PATH. Uses ffmpeg's EBU R128 meter (same family as a LUFS plugin)."""
import re, subprocess, sys
def run(path):
    out = subprocess.run(
        ["ffmpeg", "-hide_banner", "-nostats", "-i", path,
         "-filter_complex",
         "ebur128=metadata=1:peak=true,ametadata=print:key=lavfi.r128.S:file=-",
         "-f", "null", "-"],
        capture_output=True, text=True, check=True,
    )
    # Live short-term samples (3 s windows, updated ~10×/sec)
    times = [float(t) for t in re.findall(r"pts_time:([\d.]+)", out.stdout)]
    shorts = [float(v) for v in re.findall(r"lavfi\.r128\.S=(-?[\d.]+|-inf)", out.stdout)]
    pairs = [(t, s) for t, s in zip(times, shorts) if s != float("-inf") and s > -70]
    # Summary block on stderr
    integ = float(re.findall(r"I:\s+(-?[\d.]+) LUFS", out.stderr)[-1])
    lra = float(re.findall(r"LRA:\s+([\d.]+) LU", out.stderr)[-1])
    tp = float(re.findall(r"Peak:\s+(-?[\d.]+) dBFS", out.stderr)[-1])
    return integ, lra, tp, pairs
def mmss(s):
    return f"{int(s // 60)}:{int(s % 60):02d}"
integ, lra, tp, pairs = run(sys.argv[1])
if not pairs:
    sys.exit("No short-term samples above −70 LUFS.")
max_s = max(pairs, key=lambda x: x[1])
# Skip the first ~3 s while the short-term window fills
usable = [(t, s) for t, s in pairs if t >= 3.0] or pairs
median_s = sorted(s for _, s in usable)[len(usable) // 2]
print(f"integrated     : {integ:6.1f} LUFS")
print(f"loudness range : {lra:6.1f} LU")
print(f"true peak      : {tp:6.1f} dBTP")
print(f"max short-term : {max_s[1]:6.1f} LUFS  at {mmss(max_s[0])}")
print(f"median short   : {median_s:6.1f} LUFS  (after window fill)")
print(f"hook vs song   : {max_s[1] - integ:+6.1f} LU  (max short-term minus integrated)")
if max_s[1] - integ >= 6:
    print("note           : hook is 6+ LU hotter than the whole-song average.")
    print("                 Don’t push the limiter to chase the hook number.")

Run it like python3 shortterm_check.py master.wav. On a synthetic two-minute file—verse at roughly −18 LUFS short-term for a minute, then a chorus 6 LU hotter—the script reports something like integrated around −15.5, max short-term near −12, and a “hook vs song” gap of about +3.5 LU. Same file, if you only watched short-term on the drop, you’d swear you were already competitive. The store would still turn you up a little, and the chorus would get louder than you meant.
The opposite synthetic—same average energy smashed flat so short-term barely moves—lands integrated near the short-term reading and a tiny LRA. That’s the crushed master that “hits −14” while the hook has nowhere left to go.

### When the hook is 6+ LU hotter than the verse
That’s not a bug. Arrangement is supposed to move. The mistake is treating the hook’s short-term as the delivery target.
If integrated is quiet and the hook is already hot. Don’t add more limiting. The verses are dragging the average down, which is often what you want for drama. Trim fake silence at the edges first (quiet intros that still count still pull integrated), then decide whether the arrangement needs a louder verse bed—or whether −15 integrated with a −9 short-term hook is the record you meant to make. Streaming will turn a quiet file up; the question is whether the noise floor and true-peak headroom survive that turn-up.
If integrated is already near −14 and the hook short-term is −8 or hotter. The chorus is doing almost all the loudness work. More limiter input gain will mostly crush the drop and barely move the song average. Pull a dB or two out of the hook bus, or shorten how long the biggest texture stays in, before you ask the master chain for another LU.
If short-term and integrated are almost the same. You’ve flattened the sectional contrast. That can be right for some club and hip-hop delivery, but it’s a choice—not an accident. Check crest / dynamic range next to the LUFS row so you know what you spent.
Across genres the gap looks different on purpose. A ballad can sit with 8–10 LU between verse and chorus short-term and still land a polite integrated number. Trap and drill often keep the short-term closer together because the 808 and hats never really leave. EDM drops can spike short-term hard for eight bars and still average near −14 if the breakdowns are long. None of those need the same limiter preset.

### Read the bounce, then decide
Once the mix bounce is done, measure integrated and true peak the way a store will. CoProducer’s analyze table puts integrated LUFS, true peak, and clips next to each other so you’re not chasing a short-term needle that the distributor never sees. If the hook feels soft next to a reference, match levels on short sections by ear—then confirm the whole-file number hasn’t left the lane.
Note: After the bounce, measure integrated and true peak before you upload. If sections feel uneven, split and listen on the A/B player at matched loudness instead of trusting the short-term needle alone.
Q: Should I master to −9 short-term LUFS?
A: No. Short-term is a sectional readout, not a delivery target. Aim the whole file near the store lane (often around −14 integrated, Apple closer to −16), and use short-term to see whether the hook is carrying the loudness or the arrangement still has contrast.
Q: Why does my chorus meter hot but the upload report says I’m quiet?
A: The store averages the gated whole file. A hot chorus over quieter verses, long intros that still count, or fades can pull integrated down even when short-term on the drop looks competitive. Measure both, trim fake edges, then decide.

---

## Turn the mix down before you limit
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/turn-the-mix-down-before-you-limit.html
Section: Mastering · 12 October 2026 · 8 min
Summary: If the mix already hits 0 dBFS into the limiter, extra loudness is distortion you can’t take back. Pull the bus down 3–6 dB, then limit.

If the mix already kisses 0 dBFS into the limiter, every dB of “loudness” is distortion and gain reduction you can’t take back. Pull the mix bus down 3–6 dB, then limit into clean headroom.
Here’s the chain that quietly ruins bounce after bounce. The mix bus is already kissing the red. A soft clipper is “warming” what’s left. Then a limiter, maybe two, trying to invent loudness from a signal that has nowhere to go. The meters look busy. The file comes back with clipped samples, a true-peak overshoot, and a chorus that feels smaller than the rough mix did at half the level.
The limiter didn’t fail. It never had headroom to work with.

### What “into the limiter” actually means
A limiter needs clean peaks below its ceiling so it can catch overs without living in constant gain reduction. If the mix bounce already hits 0 dBFS sample peak—or worse, already has flat-topped clips—every “extra dB of loudness” is either distortion you already printed or GR that ducks the punch you wanted to keep.
Check the level before the limiter, not after. Solo-safe ways:
1. Bypass the limiter (and any clipper stacked in front of it) and watch the mix-bus peak meter on the loudest section.
2. Bounce a quick mix without the master chain and measure sample peak and true peak on that file.
3. Put a peak meter insert before the first ceiling processor and leave it there while you mix.
You’re looking for something like −6 to −3 dBFS sample peak into the first limiter on a finished mix, depending on genre and how hard you plan to drive. Hitting −0.1 into the limiter is not “competitive.” It’s already out of runway.

### Measure the pre-limiter bounce
This script takes a mix bounce (ideally with the limiter bypassed), prints sample peak, a simple 4× true-peak estimate, ffmpeg’s true-peak reading, and how many dB you’d need to pull the file down to leave a chosen amount of headroom before a −1.0 dBFS ceiling.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""prelimit_headroom.py — how hot is the mix before the limiter?
Usage: python3 prelimit_headroom.py mix_no_limiter.wav [--headroom 6]
Needs: numpy + ffmpeg on PATH.
Prints sample peak, 4×-oversample peak estimate, ffmpeg true peak,
and the gain to pull so peak + headroom sits under a −1.0 dBFS ceiling.
Use a bounce with the master limiter/clipper bypassed."""
import argparse, re, subprocess, sys
import numpy as np
SR = 48000
def load_stereo(path):
    raw = subprocess.run(
        ["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", path, "-ac", "2", "-ar", str(SR),
         "-f", "f32le", "-"],
        capture_output=True, check=True,
    ).stdout
    return np.frombuffer(raw, dtype=np.float32).reshape(-1, 2)
def sample_peak_db(x):
    p = float(np.max(np.abs(x)))
    return 20 * np.log10(p + 1e-12)
def truepeak_4x(x):
    # Cheap 4× peak estimate via linear upsample of abs envelope peaks.
    # Good enough to show overs; trust ffmpeg's ebur128 for delivery numbers.
    mono = np.mean(x, axis=1)
    up = np.interp(np.linspace(0, len(mono) - 1, len(mono) * 4),
                   np.arange(len(mono)), mono)
    return 20 * np.log10(float(np.max(np.abs(up))) + 1e-12)
def ffmpeg_tp(path):
    err = subprocess.run(
        ["ffmpeg", "-hide_banner", "-nostats", "-i", path,
         "-af", "ebur128=peak=true", "-f", "null", "-"],
        capture_output=True, text=True, check=True,
    ).stderr
    return float(re.findall(r"Peak:\s+(-?[\d.]+) dBFS", err)[-1])
ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
ap.add_argument("wav")
ap.add_argument("--headroom", type=float, default=6.0,
                help="dB of clean headroom you want before a −1.0 dBFS ceiling")
ap.add_argument("--ceiling", type=float, default=-1.0)
args = ap.parse_args()
x = load_stereo(args.wav)
sp = sample_peak_db(x)
tp4 = truepeak_4x(x)
tp = ffmpeg_tp(args.wav)
target = args.ceiling - args.headroom          # e.g. −1 − 6 = −7 dBFS
pull = min(0.0, target - sp)                  # only pull down, never suggest boost
print(f"sample peak     : {sp:6.2f} dBFS")
print(f"~true peak (4×) : {tp4:6.2f} dBFS")
print(f"ffmpeg true peak: {tp:6.2f} dBTP")
print(f"want into limit : ≤ {target:.1f} dBFS  "
      f"({args.headroom:.0f} dB under {args.ceiling:.1f} ceiling)")
if pull < 0:
    print(f"pull mix bus    : {pull:6.2f} dB  (then limit into the open headroom)")
else:
    print("pull mix bus    : 0.00 dB  (already has the headroom you asked for)")
if sp > -0.5:
    print("note            : mix already kisses full scale. Limiting from here "
          "is mostly distortion and GR.")

Run python3 prelimit_headroom.py mix_no_limiter.wav. On a synthetic transient-heavy loop that already peaks at −0.2 dBFS, it suggests pulling about 6–7 dB so you have clean space under a −1.0 ceiling. Same loop with the bus already at −6 dBFS sample peak prints “0.00 dB” pull—and that’s the session that still has punch after you limit.

### Soft clippers, stacked limiters, already-clipped samples
Three patterns show up across genres:
Pattern | What you hear | First move
Mix bus already at 0 into one limiter | Constant GR, dull kicks, “loud but small” | Pull the mix bus (or the last 2–3 dB of group faders) 3–6 dB, then set ceiling
Soft clipper → limiter → second limiter | Thickened distortion, weird pumping on 808s / cymbals | Pick one ceiling tool for delivery; put taste saturation earlier and quieter
Clipped samples before any limiter | Flat tops that no limiter can restore | Fix the clip in the session or at the clip-gain stage; limiting hides overs, it doesn’t un-flatten them
Hip-hop / 808s. The 808 front and the kick click are the first things a starved limiter grabs. If the mix already hits zero, the limiter ducks the sub on every hit and the bounce feels smaller than the beat did in the session. Leave a few dB into the limiter and let a clipper (if you use one) work on purpose, not as damage control.
Rock drums. Snare and crash transients need height. Driving a full-scale bus into a brickwall turns the kit into a pad. Pull the bus, then limit lightly—or fix the overhead/bus compression that was already squashing the hits.
EDM drops. It’s fine to hit a clipper hard for tone. It is not fine to do that on a bus that’s already clipped, then stack a true-peak limiter on top and call the distortion “energy.” Print the drop with headroom, drive the taste processor, then cap true peak last.

### After the final bounce
Once the chain is honest—mix down, then limit into headroom—bounce and check clips and true peak. CoProducer’s analyze row for clip count and true peak is the quick tell: non-zero clips after a “safe” limiter usually means the signal was already broken on the way in, or the ceiling isn’t true-peak aware. Fix the input level first; another limiter stage rarely helps.
Note: Measure the bounce for clips and true peak after the final chain. If the mix still feels broken in sections, A/B the repair at matched loudness before you add another ceiling.
Q: How much should I pull the mix down before limiting?
A: Often 3–6 dB on a mix that was already near full scale. Aim for roughly −6 to −3 dBFS sample peak into the first limiter, then set your true-peak ceiling (commonly −1.0 dBTP). Measure the pre-limiter bounce instead of guessing from the post-limiter meter.
Q: Can a limiter fix clipped samples in the mix?
A: No. It can stop new overs past its ceiling. Flattened peaks stay flattened. Pull the bus down, repair or rebalance the clipped sources in the session, then limit into clean headroom.

---

## What 432 Hz actually changes in a finished master
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/what-432-hz-actually-changes-in-a-master.html
Section: Pitch · 8 October 2026 · 12 min
Summary: Retuning a master from 440 to 432 Hz scales every frequency by 0.981818 (−31.77 cents) and, with resampling, adds 1.85% length. Measured on real renders.

Moving a finished master from A=440 to A=432 multiplies every frequency in the file by 432/440 = 0.981818, which is about 31.77 cents lower, a little under a third of a semitone. Harmony, mix balance, and loudness stay where they were. With plain resampling the track also runs about 1.85% longer, so 120 BPM becomes 117.82.
Somebody always brings it up near the end of a session. The record is done, the master is approved, and then someone asks what it would sound like at 432. Half the room rolls their eyes. The other half has already heard a video saying it’s the frequency of the universe. And the person who actually has to render the file just wants to know what’s going to happen to it.
So let’s skip the mythology and the eye-rolling and look at what really changes in the file. Some of it is exact math. Some of it is measurable but small. Some of it is taste, and taste is a perfectly good reason to make a record. It just isn’t physics.

### What “440” actually refers to
When people say a record is “in 440,” they mean the tuning reference: the A above middle C (A4) sits at 440 cycles per second, and every other note in equal temperament is placed relative to it. That reference is the international standard, ISO 16, the standard tuning frequency. It doesn’t mean anything in the song actually is 440 Hz. A finished master holds fundamentals, overtones, kick resonances, room reflections, cymbal noise, and reverb tails spread across the whole audible range. The 440 is just where the grid is anchored.
Retuning a finished master to 432 doesn’t re-pitch notes one at a time the way Auto-Tune would. It slides the entire grid. Every component, from the sub to the hiss, gets multiplied by the same number:
- Ratio: 432 ÷ 440 = 0.981818 (exactly 54/55)
- Pitch: 1200 × log2(0.981818) ≈ −31.77 cents. A semitone is 100 cents, so this is less than a third of one.
- Length, with plain resampling: 440 ÷ 432 = 1.018519, so about 1.85% longer. A 3:00 song gains about 3.3 seconds.
- Tempo, with plain resampling: ×0.981818. 90 BPM becomes 88.36, 120 becomes 117.82, 140 becomes 137.45.
Because every frequency moves by the same ratio, every interval survives. A major third is still a major third. The chord is the same chord, played from a slightly lower floor.

### Follow one note through the conversion
Claims are cheap, so here’s a script that renders an exact 432 version and then shows you what moved. It finds the strongest partials before and after so you can watch A4 and its harmonics land where the math says they should. It also measures length, tempo, integrated loudness, and true peak. It writes a new 24-bit WAV and never touches your original.
One detail is worth a sentence. FFmpeg’s asetrate only takes whole numbers, and 48000 × 0.981818 = 47127.27. So the script first upsamples to a rate that divides cleanly by 55 (52.8 kHz for a 48 kHz file, 48.51 kHz for 44.1), relabels it at exactly 54/55 of that rate, and resamples back. That gives the exact ratio and no rounding.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""retune_check.py: render an exact 440 -> 432 classic retune and prove what moved.
Usage: python3 retune_check.py in.wav [out_432.wav]
Needs: numpy + ffmpeg on PATH. Works on any sample rate that is a multiple of 50 Hz
(44.1, 48, 88.2, 96 kHz...). Writes a 24-bit WAV; never touches the input.

Prints the ratio math, the strongest partials before and after (so you can follow A4
and its harmonics), duration, tempo, integrated loudness, and true peak."""
import re, subprocess, sys
import numpy as np

SRC, TGT = 440, 432
r = TGT / SRC
src = sys.argv[1]
out = sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else re.sub(r"\.\w+$", "", src) + "_432.wav"

def probe_sr(path):
    return int(subprocess.run(["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-select_streams", "a:0", "-show_entries",
                               "stream=sample_rate", "-of", "csv=p=0", path],
                              capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout.strip())

def decode(path, sr):
    raw = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", path, "-ac", "1", "-ar", str(sr), "-f", "f32le", "-"],
                         capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
    return np.frombuffer(raw, dtype=np.float32)

def loudness(path):
    err = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-nostats", "-hide_banner", "-i", path, "-af",
                          "ebur128=peak=true:framelog=quiet", "-f", "null", "-"],
                         capture_output=True, text=True).stderr
    s = err[err.rfind("Summary:"):]
    return (float(re.search(r"I:\s+(-?[\d.]+) LUFS", s).group(1)),
            float(re.search(r"Peak:\s+(-?[\d.]+) dBFS", s).group(1)))

def partials(x, sr, fmax=2000.0, top=8):
    """Strongest spectral peaks (Hann window, zero-padded FFT, parabolic interpolation)."""
    n = 1 << int(np.ceil(np.log2(len(x)))) + 1
    mag = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x * np.hanning(len(x)), n))
    lm = 20 * np.log10(mag + 1e-12)
    f = np.fft.rfftfreq(n, 1 / sr)
    k = np.where((f > 30) & (f < fmax))[0]
    pk = k[(lm[k] > lm[k - 1]) & (lm[k] >= lm[k + 1])]
    pk = pk[np.argsort(lm[pk])[::-1]]
    chosen = []
    for p in pk:                                   # skip side lobes within 3 Hz of a stronger peak
        if all(abs(f[p] - f[q]) > 3 for q in chosen):
            chosen.append(p)
        if len(chosen) == top:
            break
    res = []
    for p in sorted(chosen):
        a, b, c = lm[p - 1], lm[p], lm[p + 1]
        d = 0.5 * (a - c) / (a - 2 * b + c)
        res.append((f[p] + d * (f[1] - f[0]), b))
    return res

def tempo(x, sr):
    """BPM from the autocorrelation of an onset envelope (low band + high band, 2 ms hop).
    The beat-length peak is refined at 8 beats out, which makes the estimate 8x finer."""
    hop = int(0.002 * sr)
    spec = np.fft.rfft(x); f = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(x), 1 / sr)
    onset = 0
    for band in (f < 200, f > 2000):
        b = np.fft.irfft(spec * band, len(x))
        e = np.sqrt(np.mean(b[: len(b) // hop * hop].reshape(-1, hop) ** 2, axis=1))
        o = np.maximum(np.diff(e), 0)
        onset = onset + o / (o.max() + 1e-12)
    ac = np.correlate(onset, onset, "full")[len(onset) - 1:]
    fps = sr / hop
    ok = np.arange(int(fps * 60 / 180), int(fps * 60 / 70))
    i = ok[np.argmax(ac[ok])]                       # one beat
    j = 8 * i + np.argmax(ac[8 * i - 8: 8 * i + 9]) - 8  # eight beats
    d = 0.5 * (ac[j - 1] - ac[j + 1]) / (ac[j - 1] - 2 * ac[j] + ac[j + 1])
    return 60 * 8 / ((j + d) / fps)

sr = probe_sr(src)
if sr % 50:
    sys.exit("sample rate must be a multiple of 50 Hz for the exact chain")
up = sr * 11 // 10                      # 48000 -> 52800, 44100 -> 48510 (both divisible by 55)
chain = f"aresample={up},asetrate={up * 54 // 55},aresample={sr}"   # 54/55 == 432/440 exactly
subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-y", "-i", src, "-af", chain, "-c:a", "pcm_s24le", out], check=True)

x, y = decode(src, sr), decode(out, sr)
print(f"ratio          : {TGT}/{SRC} = {r:.6f}   shift = {1200 * np.log2(r):+.2f} cents")
print(f"ffmpeg chain   : {chain}")
print(f"duration       : {len(x) / sr:.3f} s -> {len(y) / sr:.3f} s  ({100 * (len(y) / len(x) - 1):+.2f}%, expect {100 * (1 / r - 1):+.2f}%)")
print("partials (Hz)  :  before   ->  after     ratio     cents")
after = partials(y, sr, top=16)
for fb, lvl in partials(x, sr):
    fa = min(after, key=lambda p: abs(p[0] - fb * r))[0]
    print(f"                {fb:8.2f} -> {fa:8.2f}   {fa / fb:.6f}  {1200 * np.log2(fa / fb):+7.2f}")
bi, bo = tempo(x, sr), tempo(y, sr)
print(f"tempo          : {bi:.2f} BPM -> {bo:.2f} BPM  (x{bo / bi:.4f}, expect x{r:.4f})")
(li, ti), (lo, to) = loudness(src), loudness(out)
print(f"integrated     : {li:.1f} LUFS -> {lo:.1f} LUFS")
print(f"true peak      : {ti:+.2f} dBTP -> {to:+.2f} dBTP")
print(f"wrote          : {out}")
Run it on your own bounce with python3 retune_check.py mix.wav. It needs Python with numpy, plus ffmpeg on your PATH.

### What it printed on a synthetic loop
The test file is synthetic. We built it on the box so the answers are known in advance, and it isn’t anyone’s record. It’s a 17-second, 48 kHz, 120 BPM loop with an A-major pad (A3, A4, C♯5, E5 with overtones), a 55 Hz sub note on every bar, a pitch-swept kick, and short high ticks on every eighth note. Here’s the real output, trimmed to the parts that matter:
ratio          : 432/440 = 0.981818   shift = -31.77 cents
ffmpeg chain   : aresample=52800,asetrate=51840,aresample=48000
duration       : 17.000 s -> 17.315 s  (+1.85%, expect +1.85%)
partials (Hz)  :  before   ->  after     ratio     cents
                   55.00 ->    54.00   0.981819   -31.77
                  220.00 ->   216.00   0.981818   -31.77
                  440.00 ->   432.00   0.981818   -31.77
                  554.37 ->   544.29   0.981818   -31.77
                  659.26 ->   647.27   0.981818   -31.77
                  880.00 ->   864.00   0.981818   -31.77
                 1108.73 ->  1088.57   0.981818   -31.77
tempo          : 120.00 BPM -> 117.82 BPM  (x0.9818, expect x0.9818)
integrated     : -15.1 LUFS -> -15.1 LUFS
true peak      : -3.00 dBTP -> -3.00 dBTP
Every partial moved by the same ratio to six decimal places. A4 landed on 432. Its octave, 880, landed on 864. The 55 Hz sub, which is A1, landed on 54. The third of the chord, C♯5, went from 554.37 to 544.29. Divide each by its A and you get 1.25993 both times, so the interval didn’t move at all. That’s the whole idea in one line: the chord keeps its shape and sits about a third of a semitone lower.
The tempo was measured from the audio, not just calculated: 120.00 BPM went in and 117.82 came out. Loudness and true peak didn’t move at the meter’s resolution.
We also ran the same loop after pushing it 12 dB into a limiter, so it looked more like a modern master. It measured −6.7 LUFS and −0.40 dBTP before, and −6.8 LUFS and −0.40 dBTP after. That’s close to unchanged, but notice we said measured. Resampling rebuilds the waveform, so on a real master inter-sample peaks can land a little differently. Measure the file you’re actually going to ship. It takes ten seconds.
About that rounding detail: if you skip the trick and just write asetrate=47127, the error is −0.01 cents and about one millisecond over a three-minute song. Nobody will hear it. It only matters if you document your masters like an archivist, and some of us do.

### What does not change
This is where most of the confusion lives, so here it is plainly. A 432 conversion is one operation. It doesn’t do any of the following.
- It isn’t EQ. Nothing gets warmer because a band was boosted. Spectral balance moves down with everything else, by the same ratio.
- It doesn’t change the mix. Vocal level, 808 balance, stereo width, and compression all carry over exactly as printed.
- It doesn’t change the temperament. Equal temperament stays equal temperament. Just intonation and other historical tunings change the relationships between notes, and a single global ratio can’t do that.
- It doesn’t master anything. If the source is clipped, the 432 version is clipped too, just a little lower. Loudness is a separate decision you make afterward.
- It doesn’t carry any medical or spiritual payload. There’s no credible evidence that 432 heals anything, changes your biology, or is more “natural” than any other reference. We’ll leave it there.
Note: What we can prove. Every frequency is multiplied by 0.981818, which is −31.77 cents. Intervals are preserved exactly. With plain resampling the file is 1.85% longer and the tempo is 1.85% slower. On our synthetic loop, loudness and true peak didn’t move at the meter’s resolution. All of that is measurable, and the script above shows it.What’s taste. Whether the lower version feels heavier, darker, calmer, or just less urgent. Whether the slight slowdown suits the groove. Whether your singer sounds better a third of a semitone down. Those are real reactions and good reasons to print an alternate master. They aren’t measurements, and they won’t hold for every song or every listener.

### Where you’ll actually hear it
Thirty-two cents is subtle, but it isn’t nothing. Most trained listeners can tell a shift that size when they A/B it directly. Where it shows up:
Material | What usually changes | How obvious
Exposed lead vocal | Chest weight drops slightly; bright vowels lose a touch of edge | Clear in a synced A/B
Sustained 808 / sub | The fundamental moves down (55 → 54 Hz on an A1); on small speakers it slides a bit further toward roll-off | Felt more than heard
Piano, pads, strings | The whole chord sits lower and decays read slightly longer with resampling | Clear on held chords
Dense distorted chorus | Pitch center is masked by saturation and drums | Often hard to call
Groove and pocket | With resampling the tempo drops 1.85%: 120 → 117.82, 140 → 137.45 | Some feel it as “laid back”
Hats and cymbals | Spectrum moves down by the same ratio and timing stretches slightly | Rarely noticed on its own
The sub row deserves a second look if you make 808 records. An 808 tuned to E1 (41.2 Hz) lands around 40.5 Hz after conversion. That won’t matter on a club system. On a phone that’s already rolling off below 100 Hz, you’re hearing harmonics anyway, and they move down by the same ratio. It’s worth one check on the small speaker before you commit.

### How to compare without fooling yourself
The fastest way to convince yourself of anything is a bad A/B. Everyone has done it: the new version is half a dB louder, or you restart it from the top while the old one was mid-chorus, and your brain hands you a winner. A few rules make the comparison honest.
1. Same source, rendered once. Use the approved WAV, not a stream rip. Change only the tuning.
2. Level-matched. Don’t normalize one side and leave the other. If the files measure differently, it’s because something else in the chain changed.
3. Same musical position. This is where plain resampling gets tricky. The 432 file is longer, so ten seconds into the original lines up with about 10.185 seconds into the retune. If your player switches by clock time, you drift a little further off the beat with every switch. By the end of a three-minute song you’re off by more than three seconds.
4. Short loops, reversed order, a break. Fifteen to thirty seconds of something exposed, switched every few bars. Take five minutes away, come back, and run it in the opposite order. If the preference survives that, it’s real for you.
That third rule is the one people trip on, and it’s why reTUNE[432] is built around a synced A/B player. It maps the same musical position between the 440 and 432 versions, so switching lands on the same syllable instead of the same clock reading. The retune happens locally in the browser, so your unreleased master never leaves your machine. When a song earns a full alternate, the $4 system adds full-length export and an offline Windows batch for folders, other reference targets, and optional LUFS delivery copies. If the comparison doesn’t win you over, keep the 440. That’s a perfectly good result.

### Shipping a 432 alternate like a professional
If the lower version wins, treat it as its own deliverable, not as a replacement:
- Never overwrite the approved master. Name the alternate plainly, something like Artist_Title_432Alt_48k_24b.wav.
- Render from the original, once. Don’t retune an MP3, and don’t retune something that’s already been retuned.
- Re-measure true peak and loudness on the new file. On ours they held. On yours, check. If it needs a delivery target, apply it afterward as its own step.
- Update anything that depends on time. A resampled alternate is 1.85% longer, so lyric videos, visualizers, DJ grids, and stems all need to follow it.
- Describe it honestly. “Retuned from A=440 to A=432 (−31.77 cents), classic resample” tells listeners exactly what they’re getting. Words like warmer and heavier are fine as artistic description. Health claims aren’t.
If the master is going out anyway, dropping both versions into CoProducer’s analyzer is a quick way to confirm that loudness and true peak are still legal side by side. Pitch is a choice. The delivery rules don’t change.
And if you need the alternate to keep the exact original runtime for picture lock, choreography, or a fixed DJ grid, that’s a different operation with different trade-offs. We measured those trade-offs in Resampling, pitch shifting, and tempo change are three different jobs.
Q: Does converting a song to 432 Hz change its key?
A: Not by name. The shift is −31.77 cents, less than a third of a semitone, so a song in A minor is still labeled A minor. It just sits lower than a 440-referenced A minor, and it will sound slightly flat next to unshifted instruments.
Q: Does 432 Hz make a song slower?
A: With plain resampling, yes. Length grows by 1.85% and tempo drops by the same ratio, so 120 BPM becomes 117.82. A time-preserving pitch shift keeps the original tempo but can add artifacts.
Q: Is 432 Hz better for your health or more natural?
A: There’s no reliable evidence for health benefits. ISO 16 sets A4 at 440 Hz as a shared reference for coordination, and 432 is a valid creative alternative. Prefer it if it sounds better to you. That’s the honest claim.
Q: Does retuning to 432 change LUFS or true peak?
A: Usually only slightly. On our synthetic loop, integrated loudness and true peak stayed within the meter’s 0.1 resolution. Resampling rebuilds the waveform, so always re-measure the final file before delivery.
Q: What is the exact ratio for 440 to 432?
A: 432/440 = 0.981818, which is exactly 54/55. That works out to −31.77 cents. In FFmpeg you can apply it exactly by upsampling to a rate divisible by 55, relabeling the rate at 54/55, then resampling back.

---

## Resampling, pitch shifting, and tempo change are three different jobs
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/resampling-vs-pitch-shift-vs-tempo.html
Section: Pitch · 8 October 2026 · 14 min
Summary: Resampling moves pitch and time together, pitch shifting rebuilds time, tempo change keeps pitch. Seven FFmpeg renders measured for pitch, BPM, and smearing.

Resampling moves pitch and time together, like slowing tape: 440 to 432 is −31.77 cents and 1.85% longer. Pitch shifting moves pitch and rebuilds the timeline so length stays fixed. Tempo change moves length and keeps pitch. They answer different questions, and the time-preserving ones always rebuild something you should listen to.
Every DAW, DJ app, and plugin has a knob for this, and most of them are labeled something vague like “speed,” “pitch,” “warp,” or “key lock.” Three different operations hide behind those labels. If you don’t know which one you’re using, you can’t predict what will happen to your hats, your reverb tails, or the runtime the video editor is counting on.
So we rendered one loop seven ways and measured all of them: length, where the held note lands, BPM, how far the last hit drifts, how sharp the transients stay, loudness, and true peak. Some results were what you’d expect. One of them surprised us.

### The one question that sorts them
Ask what stays fixed.
- Resampling (varispeed): nothing stays fixed. The samples are played back as if the clock ran slower, so every frequency drops by the ratio and every event arrives later by the inverse. For 440 → 432 that’s ×0.981818 on pitch and ×1.018519 on length. It’s the cleanest operation of the three because there’s nothing to invent. It’s just very good interpolation.
- Pitch shifting (time-preserving): length stays fixed and pitch moves. To do that, the algorithm has to take the audio apart and put it back together: phase vocoders split it into short FFT frames, and time-domain methods cut and overlap little grains. Something gets rebuilt, and rebuilding is where artifacts come from.
- Tempo change (time stretch): pitch stays fixed and length moves. It’s the same reconstruction problem pointed the other way. It’s what DJ key-lock and practice apps do, and it isn’t a 432 conversion, even though the slowdown can feel similar.
There’s also a combined recipe you’ll see in batch tools: resample first, then time-stretch back to the original length. On paper that equals a pitch shift. In practice its artifacts come from the stretcher, not the resampler.

### The FFmpeg lines, so you know what you’re running
These are the exact filters we measured. They run the same in any terminal: Windows, macOS, or Linux. The rubberband lines need an FFmpeg built with librubberband. Most “full” builds include it. Run ffmpeg -filters and look for it.
# A  resample, exact 54/55 (48 kHz source; for 44.1 kHz use 48510 / 47628 / 44100)
ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "aresample=52800,asetrate=51840,aresample=48000" -c:a pcm_s24le A_resample.wav

# B/C/D  time-preserving pitch shift (Rubber Band), default "crisp", then mixed, then smooth
ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "rubberband=pitch=0.9818181818" -c:a pcm_s24le B_rb_crisp.wav
ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "rubberband=pitch=0.9818181818:transients=mixed" -c:a pcm_s24le C_rb_mixed.wav
ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "rubberband=pitch=0.9818181818:transients=smooth" -c:a pcm_s24le D_rb_smooth.wav

# E  resample, then stretch back to the original length (WSOLA-style atempo)
ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "aresample=52800,asetrate=51840,aresample=48000,atempo=1.0185185185" -c:a pcm_s24le E_resample_atempo.wav

# F/G  tempo only: 1.85% slower, pitch kept
ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "atempo=0.9818181818" -c:a pcm_s24le F_atempo.wav
ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "rubberband=tempo=0.9818181818" -c:a pcm_s24le G_rb_tempo.wav
Watch for one trap. asetrate and aresample only accept plain whole numbers. Something like asetrate=sample_rate*432/440 looks reasonable, but FFmpeg rejects it with “Undefined constant” and renders nothing. Work out the number yourself, or use the exact 52800 → 51840 trick above.

### A script that measures all seven
This runs every render above on one file and measures each result against the source. Pitch is measured by sliding the spectrum on a log-frequency axis, in one-second frames taken at the same musical position, so a longer render is compared bar for bar instead of by clock time. The “match” column shows how cleanly the shifted spectrum lines up with the original, where 1.000 is identical in shape. Hits are found above 3 kHz. Width is how long each hit stays within 12 dB of its peak. Pre-echo is the loudest level in the 2–20 ms before each hit.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""three_ways.py: resampling vs pitch shifting vs tempo change, measured on one file.
Usage: python3 three_ways.py in.wav [source_bpm]
Needs: numpy + ffmpeg on PATH. Rows that need librubberband are skipped if your build lacks it.
Sample rate must be a multiple of 50 Hz (44.1/48/88.2/96 kHz). Renders are written next to
the input as 32-bit float WAVs; the input is never modified.

Per render: length change; pitch change (log-frequency cross-correlation of 1 s frames:
median, spread in cents, and "match", how cleanly the shifted spectrum lines up, 1.000 = perfect); time scale from matched high-band hits (and BPM if you pass it);
drift of the last hit; hit width and pre-echo in the band above 3 kHz; loudness; true peak."""
import re, subprocess, sys
import numpy as np

r = 432 / 440
src = sys.argv[1]
bpm_in = float(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else None
base = re.sub(r"\.\w+$", "", src)
sr = int(subprocess.run(["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-select_streams", "a:0", "-show_entries",
                         "stream=sample_rate", "-of", "csv=p=0", src], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout)
up = sr * 11 // 10
exact = f"aresample={up},asetrate={up * 54 // 55},aresample={sr}"      # 54/55 == 432/440 exactly
RENDERS = [  # (label, filter, what the textbook says should happen: pitch factor, time factor)
    ("A classic resample",          exact,                                         r, 1 / r),
    ("B rubberband pitch, crisp",   f"rubberband=pitch={r:.10f}",                  r, 1),
    ("C rubberband pitch, mixed",   f"rubberband=pitch={r:.10f}:transients=mixed", r, 1),
    ("D rubberband pitch, smooth",  f"rubberband=pitch={r:.10f}:transients=smooth", r, 1),
    ("E resample + atempo",         f"{exact},atempo={1 / r:.10f}",                r, 1),
    ("F atempo only",               f"atempo={r:.10f}",                            1, 1 / r),
    ("G rubberband tempo only",     f"rubberband=tempo={r:.10f}",                  1, 1 / r),
]

def decode(path):
    raw = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", path, "-ac", "1", "-ar", str(sr), "-f", "f32le", "-"],
                         capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
    return np.frombuffer(raw, dtype=np.float32).astype(np.float64)

def loud(path):
    e = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-nostats", "-hide_banner", "-i", path, "-af", "ebur128=peak=true:framelog=quiet",
                        "-f", "null", "-"], capture_output=True, text=True).stderr
    s = e[e.rfind("Summary:"):]
    return float(re.search(r"I:\s+(-?[\d.]+) LUFS", s).group(1)), float(re.search(r"Peak:\s+(-?[\d.]+) dBFS", s).group(1))

def logspec(x, lo=100.0, hi=2000.0, step=0.25):
    n = 1 << 18
    mag = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x * np.hanning(len(x)), n)); f = np.fft.rfftfreq(n, 1 / sr)
    return np.interp(lo * 2 ** (np.arange(0, 1200 * np.log2(hi / lo), step) / 1200), f, mag)

def xcorr_cents(A, B, step=0.25, span=60):
    """Shift (cents) that best lines B's spectrum up with A's, and how well it lines up (1.0 = identical shape)."""
    lags = np.arange(-int(span / step), int(span / step) + 1)
    c = np.array([np.dot(A[max(0, -k):len(A) - max(0, k)], B[max(0, k):len(B) - max(0, -k)]) for k in lags])
    i = int(np.clip(np.argmax(c), 1, len(c) - 2)); d = 0.5 * (c[i - 1] - c[i + 1]) / (c[i - 1] - 2 * c[i] + c[i + 1])
    return (lags[i] + d) * step, c[i] / (np.linalg.norm(A) * np.linalg.norm(B) + 1e-20)

def pitch(x, y, tf):
    """Compare 1 s frames at the SAME musical position (source time t maps to t*tf in the render)."""
    out = []
    for t in np.arange(0.5, len(x) / sr - 1.5, 1.0):
        a = x[int(t * sr): int((t + 1) * sr)]; b = y[int(t * tf * sr): int(t * tf * sr) + sr]
        if len(b) == sr:
            out.append(xcorr_cents(logspec(a), logspec(b)))
    c, m = np.array(out).T
    return np.median(c), c.max() - c.min(), np.median(m)

def match_hits(h0, h):
    """Pair source hits with render hits (allowing a dropped hit at either end), fit time = a*t + b.
    Returns time scale a, drift of the last paired hit in ms, and how many hits were paired."""
    best = None
    for k in range(-3, 4):
        a0, a1 = h0[max(0, -k):], h[max(0, k):]; n = min(len(a0), len(a1)); a0, a1 = a0[:n], a1[:n]
        fit = np.polyfit(a0, a1, 1)
        if best is None or abs(fit[1]) < best[0]:          # the pairing whose first hit lines up at t = 0
            best = (abs(fit[1]), fit[0], (a1[-1] - a0[-1]) * 1000, n)
    return best[1:]

def hf_env(x):
    spec = np.fft.rfft(x); f = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(x), 1 / sr)
    edge = np.clip((f - 2200) / 800, 0, 1); edge = 0.5 - 0.5 * np.cos(np.pi * edge)  # smooth 2.2-3.0 kHz high-pass
    h = np.r_[1, 2 * np.ones(len(spec) - 1)]                                             # analytic signal
    env = np.abs(np.fft.ifft(np.r_[spec * edge * h, np.zeros(len(x) - len(spec))]))
    k = max(int(0.0002 * sr), 1)
    return np.convolve(env, np.ones(k) / k, "same")

def hits(x):
    env = hf_env(x); thr = env.max() * 0.1; gap = int(0.05 * sr)
    cand = np.where(env > thr)[0]; peaks, i = [], 0
    while i < len(cand):
        j = cand[i]; p = j + int(np.argmax(env[j:j + gap])); peaks.append(p)
        i = np.searchsorted(cand, p + gap)
    widths, pre = [], []
    for p in peaks:
        lvl = env[p] * 10 ** (-12 / 20); a = b = p
        while a > 0 and env[a] > lvl: a -= 1
        while b < len(env) - 1 and env[b] > lvl: b += 1
        widths.append((b - a) / sr * 1000)
        w = env[max(0, p - int(0.020 * sr)): max(1, p - int(0.002 * sr))]
        pre.append(20 * np.log10(w.max() / env[p] + 1e-9))
    return np.array(peaks) / sr, float(np.median(widths)), float(np.median(pre))

x = decode(src); li, ti = loud(src); h0, w0, p0 = hits(x)
