print(f"source : {src} (SYNTHETIC if it came from synth.py)  {len(x) / sr:.3f} s, {len(h0)} hits, "
      f"width {w0:.2f} ms, pre-echo {p0:.1f} dB, {li:.1f} LUFS, {ti:+.2f} dBTP")
print(f"target : pitch x{r:.6f} ({1200 * np.log2(r):+.2f} c); classic resample length x{1 / r:.6f} ({100 * (1 / r - 1):+.2f}%)")
print(f"{'render':27s} {'length':>7s} {'pitch c':>8s} {'spread':>6s} {'match':>6s} {'time x':>8s} {'BPM':>7s} {'drift':>8s} "
      f"{'hits':>4s} {'width':>7s} {'pre':>7s} {'LUFS':>6s} {'dBTP':>6s}")
for name, af, pf, tf in RENDERS:
    out = f"{base}__{re.sub(r'[^a-z]+', '_', name.lower()[2:]).strip('_')}.wav"
    run = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-y", "-i", src, "-af", af, "-c:a", "pcm_f32le", out],
                         capture_output=True, text=True)
    if run.returncode:
        print(f"{name:27s} skipped: {run.stderr.strip().splitlines()[-1][:70]}"); continue
    y = decode(out); lo_, to_ = loud(out); h, w, p = hits(y)
    med, spread, match = pitch(x, y, tf)
    scale, drift, paired = match_hits(h0, h)
    tempo = f"{bpm_in / scale:7.2f}" if bpm_in else "    n/a"
    print(f"{name:27s} {100 * (len(y) / len(x) - 1):+6.2f}% {med:+8.2f} {spread:6.2f} {match:6.3f} {scale:8.5f} {tempo} "
          f"{drift:+7.1f}ms {len(h):4d} {w:5.2f}ms {p:5.1f}dB {lo_:6.1f} {to_:+6.2f}")
Usage: python3 three_ways.py mix.wav 120. The BPM argument is optional and only used to turn the measured time scale into a tempo.

### What it measured on a synthetic loop
The source is synthetic, built on the box from formulas so every answer is known: 17 seconds at 48 kHz and 120 BPM, with an A-major pad including a held A4, a 55 Hz sub on every bar, a swept kick on 1 and 3, and 1 ms high ticks on every eighth note standing in for hats and snare. It isn’t a real record. The table below combines the script’s output with a second check, a4_track.py, which reads the held A4 in each of 15 one-second frames.
Render | Length | Held A4, 15 frames | Tempo (120 in) | Last hit drift | Hit width / pre-echo | LUFS / dBTP
Source | 17.000 s | 440.0 | 120.00 | 0 | 0.67 ms / −64.7 dB | −15.1 / −3.00
A · Resample | +1.85% | 432.0 in 15/15 | 117.82 | +291.7 ms | 0.69 ms / −64.1 dB | −15.1 / −3.00
B · Rubber Band pitch, crisp (default) | 0.00% | 0/15 at 432, read 426.4–439.9 | 120.00 | +1.0 ms | 0.69 ms / −15.6 dB | −15.5 / −3.20
C · Rubber Band pitch, mixed | 0.00% | 432.0 in 15/15 | 120.00 | +1.0 ms | 0.69 ms / −15.6 dB | −15.2 / −3.20
D · Rubber Band pitch, smooth | 0.00% | 432.0 in 15/15 | 120.00 | +3.3 ms | 2.60 ms / −2.6 dB | −15.7 / −4.00
E · Resample + atempo | −0.12% | 432.0–432.2 in 15/15 | 119.99 | +6.5 ms | 0.69 ms / −64.1 dB | −15.1 / −3.00
F · atempo only | +1.72% | 439.7–440.0 in 15/15 | 117.82 | +285.9 ms | 0.67 ms / −64.7 dB | −15.1 / −3.00
G · Rubber Band tempo only | +1.85% | 0/15 at 440, read 431.9–447.5 | 117.82 | +290.4 ms | 0.71 ms / −14.4 dB | −15.6 / −3.60
Here’s how to read it.
Resampling did exactly what the math says. The length grew 1.85%, the held A4 read 432.0 in every frame, and the tempo measured from the hits was 117.82. Transients came through essentially untouched: 0.69 ms wide with no pre-echo to speak of. Loudness and true peak didn’t move. We also built the mathematically ideal 432 version of the loop from the same formulas and subtracted it. The residual was −44.5 dB, which is about as close as our sample-quantized reference can show. No other render can pass that test, because the time-preserving methods rebuild phase in their own way. They came in between −0.2 and −3.3 dB, which tells you they’re reconstructions, not that they’re bad.
Watch the last-hit drift. After 15.75 seconds, the resampled loop’s final hit lands 291.7 ms late. At 120 BPM a sixteenth note is 125 ms, so the two versions are a full sixteenth apart about 6.75 seconds in. That’s why a resampled 432 version can’t share stems, a beat grid, or a video timeline with the original, and why an A/B player that switches by clock time sends you to the wrong syllable.
The surprise was Rubber Band’s default in FFmpeg. With transients=crisp, which is what you get if you type nothing else, the held A4 never read 432 in a single frame. It read 426 to 429 most of the time and 439.9 once. The match score fell to 0.674, while every clean render scored above 0.97. Rubber Band documents crisp mode as resetting phase at transients. Our loop has a hit every eighth note, four per second, and what we measured looks like the held chord being reset four times a second: its energy splits into sidebands a few hertz either side of where it belongs. The tempo-only version (G) did the same thing around 440. Switching to transients=mixed fixed the pitch completely, 432.0 in every frame. That’s on a synthetic loop with very sharp ticks, so your music may behave better. But it’s exactly the kind of thing you should test before trusting a preset.
Smooth mode buys stable pitch with blurry hits. D held 432 perfectly, but the hits got almost four times wider (2.60 ms against 0.69) and the 2–20 ms before each hit came up to −2.6 dB of the hit itself. That’s the soft, chorus-like attack people describe as “phasey,” and it pulled true peak down by a full dB. All three Rubber Band pitch renders also dropped the very first hit at 0:00, so leave a little silence at the top of anything you process this way.
The resample-plus-atempo recipe held up better than its reputation. E kept the original length to within 0.12% (atempo trimmed about 20 ms off the end), held A4 at 432.0–432.2, and kept transients as sharp as the source. FFmpeg’s atempo is a time-domain splicer, and on dense polyphonic material those splices can turn into audible flutter or doubling. Our loop is simple enough that they mostly didn’t. The 0.2 Hz wobble in its A4 readings is the trace they left.
Note: What we can prove. Resampling scales pitch and time by the same exact ratio and reproduces the textbook result. Pitch shifters keep the length and rebuild phase. On this loop, Rubber Band’s default crisp mode didn’t hold a sustained note at its target pitch, mixed mode did, and smooth mode widened every hit almost fourfold. Tempo change slows the music without moving the pitch.What’s taste. Whether the 1.85% slowdown of a resampled 432 sounds relaxed or just slow. Whether a slightly soft attack from a pitch shifter bothers you on a piano ballad (probably not) or on a drill hat pattern (probably yes). Which artifacts you can live with is a listening decision, and the right answer changes from song to song.

### Choosing the mode from the job, not the label
If the job is… | Use | Because | Then check
A 432 listening alternate of a finished master | Resample | Nothing gets rebuilt, and the slight slowdown is part of the sound people expect | New runtime, true peak, metadata
A 432 version locked to picture, choreography, or a DJ grid | Resample + stretch back, or a pitch shifter in a mode you’ve tested | The length has to match to the frame | Hats, reverb tails, held chords in a synced A/B
Matching a sample to a 432 session | Resample the sample | One-shots and loops can take the 1.85% length change, and it stays clean | Loop points and the grid
Practice, DJ key-lock, a slower edit | Tempo change only | The pitch has to stay at concert reference | Transient doubling on drums
Stems that must stay in sync with the full mix | Process every stem with the same operation and settings | Different algorithms drift and phase differently | Null the summed stems against the processed mix

### A render routine that doesn’t bite later
1. Start from the approved lossless master and render once. Re-processing a render stacks one algorithm’s artifacts on another’s.
2. Write down the operation, not just the number. “432, resample, 54/55 exact” and “432, Rubber Band mixed, length locked” are different masters.
3. Check the length. A resample should come out at about the original duration ÷ 0.981818. Anything else means a second operation snuck in.
4. Listen where reconstruction fails: the first transient, sustained cymbals, a held chord under busy drums, reverb tails, and the widest stereo moment.
5. Re-measure loudness and true peak on the file you’ll actually ship. In our test the pitch shifters moved integrated loudness by up to 0.6 LU and true peak by up to 1 dB.
For the common case, a 432 alternate of a finished record, reTUNE[432] keeps it simple. The browser engine does an exact-ratio resample locally, and its synced A/B player maps musical position across the longer timeline, so switching lands on the same beat. The $4 full system adds full-length export and an offline Windows batch with a classic mode and a preserve-duration mode, so you can render both, compare them, and decide by ear. If you want the background on what the conversion itself does to a master, start with What 432 Hz actually changes in a finished master.
Q: What is the difference between resampling and pitch shifting?
A: Resampling changes pitch and length together, like varispeed tape: 440 to 432 is −31.77 cents and 1.85% longer. Pitch shifting changes pitch while rebuilding the timeline so the length stays the same, which can add smearing or phasey artifacts.
Q: Does converting to 432 Hz change the BPM?
A: With resampling, yes. Tempo drops by the ratio 0.981818, so 120 BPM becomes 117.82. With a time-preserving pitch shift, the BPM stays the same.
Q: Is FFmpeg atempo or rubberband better for pitch shifting?
A: It depends on the material. On our synthetic loop, resample plus atempo kept transients sharp, while Rubber Band in its default crisp mode didn’t hold a sustained note at pitch and needed transients=mixed. Test both on your hardest passage.
Q: Why does my pitch-shifted audio sound phasey or smeared?
A: Time-preserving algorithms rebuild phase in short frames or splice short grains. Transients can spread out and sustained notes can pick up sidebands. Try a different transient mode, or resample if a change in length is acceptable.
Q: Can I do an exact 440 to 432 conversion in FFmpeg?
A: Yes. At 48 kHz, use aresample=52800,asetrate=51840,aresample=48000, which is exactly 54/55. The asetrate and aresample options take plain whole numbers, so expressions like sample_rate*432/440 fail.

---

## Concert pitch before A=440: a history that never stood still
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/concert-pitch-history-before-a440.html
Section: History · 8 October 2026 · 12 min
Summary: Before A=440, concert pitch ran from about 415 to 457 Hz. The dated record from Shore's 1711 fork to ISO 16, the temperature fights, and the 432 math.

There was never one ancient concert pitch. Surviving organs, forks, and written reports put the A above middle C anywhere from below 400 Hz to above 450 Hz depending on the city, the instrument, and the decade. France fixed A=435 by law in 1859, a London conference recommended A=440 in 1939, and ISO published it as ISO 16 in 1975. Nothing in that record shows a universal 432 standard that 440 replaced.
Somebody sends you a clip. Soft synth pad, slow zoom on a cathedral, a voice telling you music used to be tuned to 432 until someone changed it. You've probably seen a version of it. Before we argue with it, it's worth doing the more interesting thing, which is looking at what the instruments themselves say. They kept better records than the comment sections did.
The short version: pitch wandered for centuries, it wandered upward for most of the nineteenth, and 440 won mostly because it was measurable, broadcastable, and close to where a lot of people already were. That's a less cinematic story than a villain flipping a switch. It's also a lot more useful when you're deciding what to do with a master.

### Pitch used to be a local fact
For most of musical history, "what is A?" had the same answer as "which organ are we playing with?" Organs were the fixed, expensive anchor in a town, and everything else bent around them. Lynn Cavanagh's short history of how A=440 was established, drawing on Alexander Ellis's nineteenth-century surveys, gives a startling spread for German organs before 1600: from around A=567 Hz on early medieval instruments down to about A=377 Hz around 1511. ISO's own magazine, in Tor Halmrast's "Tune in to ISO 16!" feature (ISO Focus+, Nov.-Dec. 2012), notes that organs in the same city could differ by up to five semitones.
That sounds like chaos, but musicians handled it the way session players handle a capo. They transposed at sight, or composers wrote parts in more than one key. Nobody needed a global number because nobody was trying to make an orchestra in one city sound identical to an orchestra in another on the same night. The need for a standard arrived with travel, printed scores that outlived their towns, and later, radio.

### 1711: the fork that made pitch portable
The tuning fork is younger than people assume. According to the Whipple Museum at Cambridge, in its brief chronicle of the tuning fork, it was invented in 1711 by John Shore, trumpeter to the English court and a favourite of Handel. Before that, a "standard" pitch usually came from a wooden pitch pipe, which drifted with temperature and humidity. A fork held its note and produced a nearly pure tone. ISO Focus+ puts Shore's fork at A=423.5 Hz.
Sit with that number for a second. The first portable pitch reference we can point to is about 34 cents below 432 and about 66 cents below 440. Around 1800, the article continues, the most common reference was a "Classical pitch" near A=422 Hz, the level often associated with Mozart. Cavanagh, again via Ellis, gives Handel about 423 and Mozart about 422 in modern terms. If you wanted to make a historical argument for a lower A, the documents point you nearer 422 than 432.

### The nineteenth-century climb
Then pitch went up, and kept going. The explanation Cavanagh draws from Ellis feels very familiar to anyone who has watched the loudness war: bigger halls wanted more brilliance, wind-instrument makers sold horns pitched a little higher so they'd sound brighter than the competition, and improved strings could be tightened to match. Two forks from the Dresden opera house show the drift in a single building, A=423.2 in 1815 and A=435 by 1826.
London went further. ISO Focus+ describes Philharmonic Society forks stamped at A=433.2 still being sold around 1846, by which time the Society's actual performing pitch had reached a "High Pitch" of about 452.5 Hz. Military bands went higher again, with American military pitch sometimes landing near 457. Singers paid for it. Roles written for a voice at roughly 422 were being sung half a semitone or more higher, and the people with the most to lose started lobbying.

### Stuttgart, 1834: where 440 actually starts
Here's the part that tends to get skipped. Johann Heinrich Scheibler, a German silk manufacturer with a serious amateur obsession with acoustics, built a tonometer: a calibrated set of precision forks used with beat counting to measure pitch far more accurately than anyone had managed before. The Whipple Museum credits him with showing that the average concert A of Viennese pianos in the 1830s was 440 Hz, and with having his pitch endorsed in 1834 as a German standard, the so-called Stuttgart pitch. The Concise Oxford Dictionary of Music entry on Scheibler records that he proposed 440 vibrations for A at 69°F.
So 440 is not a twentieth-century invention. It's a nineteenth-century measurement of where good pianos already sat, proposed more than a century before the conference that people like to argue about.

### Paris, 1859: 435 by law, and a temperature argument
France moved first on a national rule. In 1859, a government commission fixed the diapason normal at A=435 Hz, defined at a temperature of 15 degrees, as a compromise between the strained high pitches and the older, lower ones. The Whipple chronicle notes that the physicist Jules Lissajous worked on the French standard fork and invented his famous optical calibration method along the way. Other countries gradually followed; ISO Focus+ says Queen Victoria sanctioned the French standard for her private band in 1885.
Britain then did something wonderfully British. Both Cavanagh and ISO Focus+ describe the Philharmonic Society's 1896 decision to adopt A=439 at 68°F, reasoning that the French 435 had been specified at a cooler temperature, so the same instrument in a warmer room would play higher. Cavanagh calls the derivation dubious, and the history of what "15 degrees" originally meant is genuinely tangled. The physics underneath it is real, though, and you can check it.

### Broadcasting finishes the job
By the 1930s the problem had changed shape. Radio could put an orchestra in London and one in New York side by side in a listener's living room, and the broadcasting industry pushed hard for one reference. Cavanagh, citing Llewelyn Lloyd's 1949 account, describes an international conference in London in May 1939, with the British Standards Institution handling the arrangements, agreeing on A=440. She also flags a real disagreement in the literature: the New Grove dictionary dates the British endorsement to 1938, which she argues is the same conference with the wrong year.
There's a lovely engineering detail in Lloyd's account. The BBC's tuning note came from a crystal oscillator at one million hertz, divided down to 1,000 Hz, then multiplied by 11 and divided by 25. That gives exactly 440. Because 439 is a prime number, you can't get it that cleanly from a 1,000 Hz base. A practical reason, not a mystical one, nudged the world from 439 to 440.
Across the Atlantic, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology notes in its time and frequency glossary that station WWV has broadcast an A440 tone since 1936. ISO followed with a recommendation in 1955 and then ISO 16:1975, a one-page standard that sets A at 440 Hz and asks that tuning instruments hold it within 0.5 Hz. ISO lists it as last reviewed and confirmed in 2022.

### Put every reference on one ruler
Hertz values are hard to feel. Cents aren't. A semitone is 100 cents, and the 440-to-432 move is 1200 × log2(432/440) ≈ −31.77 cents, a ratio of 0.981818. So I wrote a small script that takes the documented references above, converts each one into cents against both 440 and 432, and shows what a 3:30 master would run if you resampled a 440 version to that reference. It also checks the temperature story behind London's 439, and then renders a synthetic tone ladder with ffmpeg and measures every step back out of the file, so you can trust the ruler itself.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""pitch_history.py: put historical A4 references on one musical ruler.
Usage: python3 pitch_history.py
Needs: numpy, ffmpeg on PATH.

Part 1 converts documented historical references into cents against
A=440 and A=432, plus what a 3:30 song would run if a 440 master were
resampled to that reference. Part 2 checks the temperature story behind
Britain's 1896 A=439. Part 3 renders a SYNTHETIC pitch ladder with
ffmpeg and measures every tone back out of the file."""
import math, subprocess
import numpy as np

REFS = [  # (label, A4 Hz, source note)
    ("Shore tuning fork, 1711",             423.5, "ISO Focus+ 2012"),
    ("'Classical pitch', c.1800",           422.0, "ISO Focus+ / Cavanagh"),
    ("Dresden opera fork, 1815",            423.2, "ISO Focus+ 2012"),
    ("Dresden opera fork, 1826",            435.0, "ISO Focus+ 2012"),
    ("Stuttgart pitch (Scheibler), 1834",   440.0, "Whipple Museum"),
    ("Philharmonic forks, to 1846",         433.2, "ISO Focus+ 2012"),
    ("London 'High Pitch', c.1846",         452.5, "ISO Focus+ 2012"),
    ("Diapason normal, France 1859",        435.0, "ISO Focus+ / Cavanagh"),
    ("New Philharmonic, London 1896",       439.0, "ISO Focus+ / Cavanagh"),
    ("US military high pitch",              457.0, "ISO Focus+ 2012"),
    ("London conference 1939 / ISO 16",     440.0, "Cavanagh / ISO"),
    ("NY orchestra habit, c.1950 (Mendel)", 444.0, "Cavanagh"),
    ("Cammer-ton grouping (Haynes)",        415.0, "ISO Focus+ 2012"),
    ("Modern 432 alternate",                432.0, "reference"),
]

cents = lambda f, ref: 1200 * math.log2(f / ref)
SONG = 210.0  # a 3:30 master at 440

def mmss(s):
    return f"{int(s // 60)}:{s % 60:05.2f}"

print("PART 1  Historical references on one ruler")
print(f"{'reference':38s} {'A4 Hz':>7s} {'vs 440':>9s} {'vs 432':>9s} {'3:30 resampled':>15s}")
for label, f, _ in sorted(REFS, key=lambda r: r[1]):
    dur = SONG * 440.0 / f
    print(f"{label:38s} {f:7.1f} {cents(f,440):+8.2f}c {cents(f,432):+8.2f}c {mmss(dur):>15s}")
lo, hi = min(r[1] for r in REFS), max(r[1] for r in REFS)
print(f"spread of this list: {lo} to {hi} Hz = {cents(hi,lo):.1f} cents = {cents(hi,lo)/100:.2f} semitones")
print(f"432/440 = {432/440:.6f}  ->  {cents(432,440):+.2f} cents, duration x{440/432:.5f} (+{(440/432-1)*100:.2f}%)")

print("\nPART 2  Temperature and the 1896 A=439")
# 1896 Philharmonic reasoning as reported by Cavanagh (linear 1/1000 per degree F)
lin = 435 + (68 - 59) / 1000 * 435
print(f"Philharmonic linear rule 435 + 9/1000*435      = {lin:.3f} Hz")
# Physics: a pipe's pitch tracks the speed of sound, c ~ sqrt(T in kelvin)
def pipe(f0, t0c, t1c):
    return f0 * math.sqrt((t1c + 273.15) / (t0c + 273.15))
print(f"pipe tuned 435 at 15.0 C, played at 20.0 C     = {pipe(435,15,20):.3f} Hz")
print(f"pipe tuned 435 at 15.0 C, played at 25.0 C     = {pipe(435,15,25):.3f} Hz")
print(f"if '15 degrees' meant Reaumur (18.75 C) -> 20 C = {pipe(435,18.75,20):.3f} Hz")
print(f"cents per degree C near room temp              = {cents(pipe(440,20,21),440):+.2f} c/C")

print("\nPART 3  SYNTHETIC pitch ladder, rendered then measured")
SR, SEG = 48000, 2.0
ladder = [415.0, 422.0, 432.0, 435.0, 440.0, 452.5]
parts = "".join(f"sine=f={f}:r={SR}:d={SEG}[s{i}];" for i, f in enumerate(ladder))
graph = parts + "".join(f"[s{i}]" for i in range(len(ladder))) + f"concat=n={len(ladder)}:v=0:a=1,volume=0.5[out]"
subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-y", "-filter_complex", graph, "-map", "[out]",
                "-c:a", "pcm_s24le", "synthetic_pitch_ladder.wav"], check=True)
raw = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", "synthetic_pitch_ladder.wav", "-f", "f32le", "-ac", "1", "-"],
                     capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
x = np.frombuffer(raw, dtype=np.float32)
n = int(SR * SEG)
for i, f in enumerate(ladder):
    seg = x[i * n + n // 4: i * n + n // 4 + n // 2] * np.hanning(n // 2)
    spec = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(seg, 1 << 20))
    k = int(np.argmax(spec))
    a, b, c = np.log(spec[k - 1:k + 2])
    k_ref = k + 0.5 * (a - c) / (a - 2 * b + c)       # parabolic peak interpolation
    est = k_ref * SR / (1 << 20)
    print(f"rendered {f:6.1f} Hz -> measured {est:8.3f} Hz  (error {est-f:+.3f} Hz, ISO tolerance +/-0.5)")

import os
os.remove("synthetic_pitch_ladder.wav")  # keep the demo folder clean

Here's the real output from running it. The audio in part 3 is synthetic sine tones generated on the spot, not a recording of any instrument.

rendered  435.0 Hz -> measured  435.000 Hz  (error -0.000 Hz, ISO tolerance +/-0.5)
rendered  440.0 Hz -> measured  440.000 Hz  (error +0.000 Hz, ISO tolerance +/-0.5)
rendered  452.5 Hz -> measured  452.500 Hz  (error +0.000 Hz, ISO tolerance +/-0.5)
A few things jump out. The references in this short list alone span about 167 cents, more than a semitone and a half. The modern 432 alternate sits between the Classical-era forks and the Philharmonic's 433.2, but it isn't any of them. And the temperature check is the quiet star: a wind pipe tuned to 435 at 15°C plays about 438.8 at 20°C, close to the 439 the British settled on. That's roughly 3 cents per degree near room temperature, which is why organs and oboes were such unreliable anchors and why a steel fork, or a crystal, won.

### What the evidence is, and what it isn't
Date | Reference | Kind of evidence | What it shows | What it doesn't
Pre-1600 | c. 377 to 567 Hz | Surviving and replica German organs | Pitch was local and could be wildly different | What singers or other instruments in that town did
1711 | 423.5 Hz | Shore's tuning fork | A stable, portable reference existed | That all of England used it
1815 / 1826 | 423.2 / 435 Hz | Two Dresden opera forks | Pitch rose inside one house within a decade | A Europe-wide rate of change
1834 | 440 Hz | Scheibler's tonometer measurements | Viennese pianos already averaged 440 | That 440 became universal then
1859 | 435 Hz | French government decree | A national legal standard | Compliance outside France
1896 | 439 Hz | Philharmonic Society decision | Temperature arguments shaped standards | That the correction was historically right
1939 | 440 Hz | London international conference | Broad international agreement | Overnight change in every orchestra
1975 | 440 ± 0.5 Hz | ISO 16 | The formal standard still in force | That other references are wrong
That last column matters. A single fork tells you what one fork was. Forks can be altered, organs get re-pitched, and written reports use different conditions. Historians compare many objects and records and end up with ranges, not a sacred number. Even after 1939, Cavanagh quotes the musicologist Arthur Mendel tuning a continuo organ in New York around 1950 and finding he had to set it near 444 to stay in tune with orchestral players who drifted up from 440. Standards describe an agreement. Musicians are still people with ears and habits.

### A standard is a handshake, not a law of music
This is the bit I'd want you to carry into a session. A=440 earned its place by solving coordination problems: instrument makers building compatible products, broadcasters sending a reproducible tone, touring players arriving without surprises, schools teaching from one starting point. None of that makes 440 artistically superior. It just makes it convenient and shared.
Which also means nothing stops you from choosing something else. Period ensembles play at 415 because it suits the instruments and repertoire. Plenty of orchestras sit a little above 440. Producers detune samples, synths, and whole masters for character all the time. A 432 alternate of a finished record is part of that same long habit of moving the reference, as long as you're honest that it's a creative choice and not a restoration of some lost universal pitch.
The working rules are simple. Keep the approved 440 master untouched. Render the alternate from it once, label it clearly, and write down the ratio and method. If you want to understand exactly what that conversion does to a mix, What 432 Hz actually changes in a finished master walks through it, and Resampling, pitch shifting, and tempo change are three different jobs covers why the method changes the runtime. Slowing a record is a close cousin of this, and When to slow the bounce deals with the delivery side of that.
Note: If the history leaves you curious how a lower reference actually sounds on a record you own, the reTUNE[432] synced A/B player switches between 440 and 432 at the same musical position, right in your browser, so you can judge it by ear instead of by legend.

### Sources worth reading
- Lynn Cavanagh, "A brief history of the establishment of international standard pitch a=440 hertz" (PDF), drawing on Ellis, Lloyd, and New Grove.
- Tor Halmrast, "Tune in to ISO 16! The long and oscillating history of standard tuning frequency", ISO Focus+, Nov.-Dec. 2012 (PDF).
- Whipple Museum of the History of Science, University of Cambridge, "Historical notes: a brief chronicle of the tuning fork".
- ISO, ISO 16:1975 Acoustics, standard tuning frequency.
- NIST, Time and Frequency from A to Z, entry for A440.
Q: When did A=440 become the standard?
A: Johann Scheibler proposed 440 in 1834 and it was endorsed at Stuttgart that year. An international conference in London recommended it in 1939, ISO issued a recommendation in 1955, and ISO 16 made it a published standard in 1975.
Q: Was music tuned to 432 Hz before 440?
A: No single 432 standard appears in the historical record. Surviving forks and organs show references from below 400 to above 450 Hz. The common 'Classical pitch' of about 422 Hz sits roughly 40 cents below 432.
Q: Why did France choose 435 Hz in 1859?
A: Pitch had been rising and singers were straining. A government commission fixed the diapason normal at 435 Hz as a lower, shared reference, and many institutions outside France later adopted it.
Q: Why do some orchestras tune higher than 440?
A: A standard coordinates instruments and broadcasts; it does not forbid an ensemble from agreeing on another reference. Many orchestras choose a slightly higher A for brightness and projection, and period groups often use 415.
Q: Does temperature change concert pitch?
A: Yes for wind instruments and organ pipes, whose pitch follows the speed of sound in the air inside them. Near room temperature that is roughly 3 cents per degree Celsius. A steel tuning fork barely moves.

---

## The 432 Hz conspiracy theories, checked against the record
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/432-hz-conspiracy-theories-fact-check.html
Section: Rumor file · 8 October 2026 · 13 min
Summary: Did the Nazis or the Rockefellers change music from 432 to 440 Hz? Where each 432 rumor started, what the dated record shows, and how to read health studies.

There is no documented evidence that the Nazis, Joseph Goebbels, the Rockefeller Foundation, or any hidden group moved music from 432 to 440 Hz. A=440 was proposed in 1834, broadcast by the U.S. government from 1936, recommended at a London conference in 1939, and standardized by ISO in 1975. The Goebbels story traces to a 1988 political publication. The health studies so far are small pilots. Preferring 432 is fine on its own terms.
I want to be upfront about the tone here, because this topic usually gets one of two treatments. Either someone posts a dramatic video with a cathedral and a drone pad, or someone else dunks on everyone who ever liked a 432 version. Neither helps you decide anything about your record. What helps is doing it the way you'd troubleshoot a weird noise in a mix: name the claim, find where it came from, check it against what's documented, and work out what evidence would actually settle it.
So that's what this is. A rumor file, labeled as rumors, with receipts.

### The Goebbels story, and where it actually starts
The most repeated version says Joseph Goebbels, or the Nazi propaganda apparatus generally, pushed the world to 440 to make people anxious or easier to control. It's sticky because part of it is true in general: propaganda ministries really did manipulate media. But a general truth isn't evidence for a specific acoustic claim.
It turns out we can trace this one. Ruth E. Rosenberg's article "Perfect Pitch: 432 Hz Music and the Promise of Frequency" in the Journal of Popular Music Studies (2021) follows the claim back to a 1988 article by Laurent Rosenfeld in a publication of Lyndon LaRouche's organization, titled "How the Nazis Ruined Musical Tuning." It argued that Goebbels, through Radio Berlin, was instrumental in the 1939 conference where 440 was agreed. The same network's Schiller Institute says on its own campaign page that it launched a drive in Milan in April 1988 to restore a pitch based on middle C at 256 Hz, which it tied to A=432 and to Verdi. So the Nazi story and the 432 campaign arrived together, from the same political source, in the same year.
Now line it up against the record covered in our history of concert pitch. Johann Scheibler proposed 440 in 1834, and the Whipple Museum at Cambridge records it being endorsed at Stuttgart that year. ISO's own magazine dates the American Federation of Musicians' adoption of 440 to 1917. NIST notes that WWV has broadcast A440 since 1936. Lynn Cavanagh's history of the A=440 standard, citing a 1949 account by Llewelyn Lloyd of the British Standards Institution, describes the 1939 London conference with the BSI handling the arrangements. And the final standard came from ISO in 1955 and 1975, long after the war, from an international body.
For the Goebbels version to hold up, you'd want primary policy documents showing intent, a physiological mechanism, controlled evidence that 440 does what's claimed, and a chain connecting a Nazi decision to an ISO standard published three decades later. None of those pieces has surfaced in the sources that keep repeating it.

### Rockefeller, Rothschild, and the swap-a-villain pattern
The second family of stories keeps the plot and changes the villain. A research note from Middlebury's Center on Terrorism, Extremism, and Counterterrorism, "Fashwave (432 hz): How Audio Frequencies Take on Meaning in Neofascist Communities" (2024), quotes one widely viewed video claiming a 1953 worldwide agreement, based on a Rockefeller Foundation idea, moved music to a "consciousness suppressing" 440. It also quotes a top comment blaming the Rothschilds, and points out the familiar antisemitic shape of that accusation.
The dates don't even line up with the story they're telling. Nothing in the standards record happened in 1953; the milestones are 1834, 1859, 1939, 1955, and 1975. And the structure is worth noticing on its own: a messy, decades-long process involving instrument makers, broadcasters, musicians' unions, and standards bodies gets collapsed into one switch and one motive. That's emotionally satisfying. It just isn't how standards get made.
It's also worth knowing, gently, what company some of these stories keep. The same Middlebury note documents fashwave channels labeling tracks "(432 hz)" alongside extremist imagery. Liking a 432 version of a song doesn't make anyone part of that, obviously. But it's a good reason to be careful about which explanations you repeat when you share one.

### Cosmic numbers, checked with a calculator
The third family is mathematical: 432 shows up in astronomy, ancient measures, and geometry, so it must be the universe's frequency. Some of the arithmetic is real. The jump from "this number appears in patterns" to "music tuned to it does something to your body" is where it falls apart, and you can see why with a short script. It does five things: shows that hertz depends on the human-defined second, scores every integer from 400 to 480 against two equally arbitrary sets of "pattern" tests, checks the C=256 claim, repeats the BBC's crystal-divider arithmetic, and simulates a small study where the true effect is zero.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""rumor_math.py: test the arithmetic that 432 Hz stories lean on.
Usage: python3 rumor_math.py
Needs: numpy, scipy.

Part 1 shows a hertz value depends on the human-defined second.
Part 2 scores every integer 400..480 against two equally arbitrary
'pattern' test sets, to show that whoever picks the tests picks the winner.
Part 3 checks the C=256 / A=432 claim under equal temperament.
Part 4 repeats the BBC crystal-divider arithmetic for 432, 439, 440.
Part 5 simulates a small cross-over study with NO real effect to see
how often at least one outcome still comes out 'significant'."""
import math
from fractions import Fraction
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

print("PART 1  A hertz is cycles per *second*, and the second is a convention")
for name, sec in [("SI second", 1.0), ("minute", 60.0), ("French decimal second (0.864 s)", 0.864)]:
    print(f"  A=432 expressed per {name:32s}: {432*sec:9.2f}   A=440: {440*sec:9.2f}")

def factors(n):
    f, p = [], 2
    while p * p <= n:
        while n % p == 0: f.append(p); n //= p
        p += 1
    return f + ([n] if n > 1 else [])
FIB = {5, 8, 13, 21, 34, 55, 89, 144, 233, 377}
dsum = lambda n: sum(map(int, str(n)))
SET_A = {  # the tests 432 enthusiasts tend to reach for
    "digit sum 9":          lambda n: dsum(n) == 9,
    "divisible by 12":      lambda n: n % 12 == 0,
    "divisible by 8":       lambda n: n % 8 == 0,
    "only 2s and 3s":       lambda n: set(factors(n)) <= {2, 3},
    "Fibonacci factor":     lambda n: any(n % f == 0 for f in FIB),
}
SET_B = {  # equally arbitrary tests, chosen by someone else
    "divisible by 11":      lambda n: n % 11 == 0,
    "multiple of 10":       lambda n: n % 10 == 0,
    "divisible by 55 (Fib)":lambda n: n % 55 == 0,
    "digit sum 8":          lambda n: dsum(n) == 8,
    "divisible by 8":       lambda n: n % 8 == 0,
}
print("\nPART 2  Pattern scores for every integer 400..480")
for label, T in (("test set A", SET_A), ("test set B", SET_B)):
    sc = {n: sum(t(n) for t in T.values()) for n in range(400, 481)}
    best = max(sc.values())
    winners = [n for n, s in sc.items() if s == best]
    print(f"  {label}: top score {best}/5 -> {winners};  432 scores {sc[432]}, 440 scores {sc[440]}")

print("\nPART 3  Does C=256 give A=432?")
print(f"  equal temperament, A = 256 x 2^(9/12)  = {256 * 2 ** (9/12):.2f} Hz")
print(f"  Pythagorean sixth, A = 256 x 27/16     = {256 * 27/16:.2f} Hz")
print(f"  an equal-tempered master retuned to A=432 puts C4 at {432 / 2 ** (9/12):.2f} Hz")
print(f"  a 440 master puts C4 at {440 / 2 ** (9/12):.2f} Hz")

print("\nPART 4  Crystal-divider arithmetic from a 1,000 Hz base")
for f in (432, 439, 440):
    r = Fraction(f, 1000)
    print(f"  {f} Hz = 1000 x {r.numerator}/{r.denominator}   prime: {factors(f) == [f]}")

print("\nPART 5  Small study, no true effect: how often does *something* hit p<0.05?")
rng = np.random.default_rng(432440)
N, SIMS = 33, 20000
for k in (1, 4, 8):
    a = rng.normal(size=(SIMS, N, k)); b = rng.normal(size=(SIMS, N, k))
    p = stats.ttest_rel(a, b, axis=1).pvalue
    rate = np.mean(np.any(p < 0.05, axis=1))
    print(f"  {k} outcome(s), n={N}: at least one p<0.05 in {100*rate:5.1f}% of null studies"
          f"  (theory {100*(1-0.95**k):.1f}%)")
df = N - 1; tcrit = stats.t.ppf(0.975, df)
for d in (0.2, 0.35, 0.5):
    nc = d * math.sqrt(N)
    power = 1 - stats.nct.cdf(tcrit, df, nc) + stats.nct.cdf(-tcrit, df, nc)
    print(f"  paired n={N}, true effect size d={d}: power {100*power:4.1f}%")

Real output from running it on this machine. No audio is involved; part 5 uses simulated random data.
PART 1  A hertz is cycles per *second*, and the second is a convention
  A=432 expressed per SI second                       :    432.00   A=440:    440.00
  A=432 expressed per minute                          :  25920.00   A=440:  26400.00
  A=432 expressed per French decimal second (0.864 s) :    373.25   A=440:    380.16

PART 2  Pattern scores for every integer 400..480
  test set A: top score 5/5 -> [432];  432 scores 5, 440 scores 2
  test set B: top score 5/5 -> [440];  432 scores 1, 440 scores 5

PART 3  Does C=256 give A=432?
  equal temperament, A = 256 x 2^(9/12)  = 430.54 Hz
  Pythagorean sixth, A = 256 x 27/16     = 432.00 Hz
  an equal-tempered master retuned to A=432 puts C4 at 256.87 Hz
  a 440 master puts C4 at 261.63 Hz

PART 4  Crystal-divider arithmetic from a 1,000 Hz base
  432 Hz = 1000 x 54/125   prime: False
  439 Hz = 1000 x 439/1000   prime: True
  440 Hz = 1000 x 11/25   prime: False

PART 5  Small study, no true effect: how often does *something* hit p<0.05?
  1 outcome(s), n=33: at least one p<0.05 in   4.8% of null studies  (theory 5.0%)
  4 outcome(s), n=33: at least one p<0.05 in  18.1% of null studies  (theory 18.5%)
  8 outcome(s), n=33: at least one p<0.05 in  33.4% of null studies  (theory 33.7%)
  paired n=33, true effect size d=0.2: power 20.0%
  paired n=33, true effect size d=0.35: power 49.6%
  paired n=33, true effect size d=0.5: power 79.5%
Part 2 is my favourite result in this whole series. With test set A, the kind of patterns 432 fans reach for, 432 is the unique winner out of 81 numbers. With test set B, just as arbitrary and picked by someone else, 440 is the unique winner. Whoever picks the tests picks the winner. That's not a trick against 432; it's how pattern-hunting works for any number.
Part 3 matters for the "scientific pitch" argument. Middle C at 256 Hz gives A=432 only if you use a Pythagorean major sixth (27/16). In the equal temperament that almost every modern record uses, C=256 gives A of about 430.54. Retune an equal-tempered master to A=432 and its middle C lands near 256.87, not 256. And part 4 kills a tidy story I've seen in both directions: 432 is just as easy to derive from a 1,000 Hz crystal base as 440 is (54/125 versus 11/25). The awkward number was 439, which is prime. That's why Britain's 439 lost, not because 432 was hidden.
One more point that people miss: a hertz is cycles per second, and the second is a human convention. Express the same notes per minute, or per old French decimal second, and every "sacred" number changes while the music doesn't.

### The health claims, read carefully
This is where I'd ask for the most care, because people make real decisions on it. The study cited most often is Calamassi and Pomponi's "Music Tuned to 440 Hz Versus 432 Hz and the Health Effects: A Double-blind Cross-over Pilot Study" in Explore (2019). Thirty-three healthy volunteers listened to the same film soundtracks for 20 minutes on two days, once at each tuning. The 432 sessions showed a mean heart-rate drop of 4.79 bpm at p=0.05, a non-significant dip in blood pressure, and a respiratory change at p=0.06. Listeners also reported feeling more focused and satisfied. The authors themselves conclude the experiment should be repeated with a larger sample and randomized controlled trials.
That's an honest pilot, and the right reading is "interesting, unconfirmed." Part 5 of the script shows why. With 33 people and no real effect at all, measuring one outcome gives a false "significant" hit about 5% of the time. Measure four outcomes and at least one hits in about 18% of null studies. Measure eight and it's about a third. And if a real effect were small (d=0.2), a study this size would only detect it about 20% of the time. Small samples cut both ways: they miss real effects and they flag fake ones.
There's an engineering confound too. A 432 version made by classic resampling isn't only lower, it's about 1.85% slower, as What 432 Hz actually changes in a finished master explains. A study that wants to say anything about pitch needs to separate pitch from tempo, which means a time-preserving shift on one arm, and the trade-offs of that are covered in Resampling, pitch shifting, and tempo change are three different jobs. Nothing here supports claims that 432 heals, repairs DNA, or that 440 harms anyone.

### The rumor file at a glance
Claim | Earliest traceable source | What the record shows | What would change the verdict
Goebbels chose 440 | 1988 LaRouche-network article | 440 proposed 1834, broadcast 1936, BSI-arranged 1939 conference, ISO 1955/1975 | Primary Nazi policy documents linked to the standards chain
Rockefeller "1953 agreement" | Viral social video (per Middlebury CTEC) | No standards milestone in 1953 | Any document of a 1953 agreement
432 is the universe's frequency | Numerology posts, C=256 campaign | Hertz depends on the second; pattern tests can crown any number | A unit-independent physical mechanism
C=256 means A=432 | 1988 Schiller Institute campaign | True only with a Pythagorean sixth; equal temperament gives 430.54 | Not applicable; it's arithmetic
432 is measurably healthier | Small pilot studies | One 33-person pilot, borderline heart-rate result, authors call for larger trials | Large, preregistered, randomized trials that separate pitch from tempo

### Why these stories feel true
The persuasive frequency rumors all share a recipe. Start with a true fragment: standards did change, institutions were involved, propaganda has used music, and people really do feel different when a song is lower and slower. Then add a dramatic missing cause, a villain with a motive, without the documents or mechanism that would connect the dots. Then repeat it until it feels remembered rather than demonstrated. Numbers add a coat of authority on top.
A quick source check that works for this topic and most others:
- Is there a primary document, a dated record, or a named study you can open yourself?
- Does the timeline fit the events it claims to explain?
- Is a mechanism proposed, and has anyone tested it with controls?
- Does the claim depend on a unit, a rounding choice, or a cherry-picked pattern?
- Who first said it, and what were they campaigning for at the time?

### The reasonable middle
Here's what's solid. 440 is a documented standard with a long, boring, practical history. Pitch varied enormously before it. An exact 432 retune is audible and measurable: 31.77 cents lower, and 1.85% longer if you resample. And personal preference is a perfectly good reason to make one. If a lower version of your record sounds better to you, that's enough. It doesn't need a conspiracy behind it, and it's stronger without one.
The best antidote to a scary story is a fair test. How to run a 432 vs 440 listening test you can trust walks through level matching, blind switching, and scoring, the same discipline Reference matching without guesswork applies to mix references.
Note: When you want to hear the difference rather than read about it, the reTUNE[432] synced A/B player switches between 440 and 432 at the same musical position on audio you own, processed locally in your browser. It makes no health claims, just the conversion.

### Sources worth reading
- Ruth E. Rosenberg, "Perfect Pitch: 432 Hz Music and the Promise of Frequency", Journal of Popular Music Studies 33(1), 2021.
- Calamassi and Pomponi, "Music Tuned to 440 Hz Versus 432 Hz and the Health Effects", Explore, 2019 (PubMed abstract).
- Middlebury Institute CTEC, "Fashwave (432 hz): How Audio Frequencies Take on Meaning in Neofascist Communities", 2024.
- Lynn Cavanagh, "A brief history of the establishment of international standard pitch a=440 hertz" (PDF).
- ISO, ISO 16:1975 standard tuning frequency, and NIST's A440 glossary entry.
Q: Who changed the tuning standard from 432 Hz to 440 Hz?
A: Nobody, because there was no 432 standard to change. 440 was proposed by Johann Scheibler in 1834, broadcast by NIST's WWV from 1936, recommended at a London conference in 1939, and published by ISO in 1975. Earlier pitch varied widely.
Q: Did Joseph Goebbels or the Nazis choose 440 Hz?
A: No primary evidence supports it. The claim traces to a 1988 article in a publication tied to Lyndon LaRouche. The 1939 London conference was arranged through the British Standards Institution, and 440 was in use well before the Nazi era.
Q: Is 432 Hz the frequency of the universe?
A: A hertz is cycles per second, and the second is a human-defined unit. Change the unit and the number changes. Number patterns around 432 depend on which patterns you choose to look for.
Q: Is there scientific evidence that 432 Hz music is healthier?
A: There are small pilot studies, including a 33-person cross-over study that found a borderline heart-rate difference. Its own authors called for larger trials. That is a hypothesis worth testing, not proof of a health benefit.
Q: Is it wrong to prefer 432 Hz?
A: Not at all. Preferring a lower, slightly slower version of a song is a legitimate taste. It just doesn't need a conspiracy or a medical claim to be valid. Judge it with a fair, level-matched A/B test.

---

## How to run a 432 vs 440 listening test you can trust
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/432-vs-440-blind-listening-test.html
Section: Listening lab · 8 October 2026 · 12 min
Summary: 432 Hz vs 440 Hz, tested fairly: level-match within 0.1 LU, switch at the same note, run a blind ABX round, and score it so placebo and loudness can't win.

A fair 432 vs 440 test uses one approved master rendered two ways, level-matched within 0.1 LU, compared at the same musical position rather than the same clock time, with the labels hidden. Run a blind ABX round first to see if you can tell them apart, then a blind preference round. With 10 trials you need 9 correct before chance stops being a good explanation.
You know the scene. It's late, the session's been good, someone bounces a 432 version and hits play, and everybody in the room nods. "Yeah. Warmer." Maybe it is. But the file was also a touch louder, started on a better chord, and had a label on the screen that said 432. Every one of those things can make a version win before pitch gets a vote.
This essay is about removing those other votes. It's the same discipline you'd use to compare two limiters or two mix revisions, applied to a small pitch move. It costs about fifteen minutes and saves you from making an alternate master on a hunch.

### What you're really comparing
Be clear about the variables first. A classic 440-to-432 conversion scales every frequency by 432/440, or 0.981818, which is about 31.77 cents lower. If it's done by resampling, it also runs about 1.85% longer, so a 120 BPM record lands near 117.8 BPM. What 432 Hz actually changes in a finished master covers the full picture, and Resampling, pitch shifting, and tempo change are three different jobs explains when you'd keep the runtime instead.
That means a "432 test" with a classic render is really a test of lower-and-slightly-slower. That's fine, it's what most people actually want to hear. Just know it, and don't credit pitch alone for something that might be tempo.
Then there are the variables that shouldn't be in the test at all: loudness, the chord you start on, the playback chain, the file format, and the label. Anyone who has done mix work knows the slightly louder version sounds clearer, wider, and more expensive for the first few seconds. That bias alone can decide a comparison.

### Build both files from one source, then measure them
Use the same approved master for both sides, lossless, with identical processing except the retune. Don't compare a streaming rip against a fresh WAV, and don't compare a 432 file someone posted online against your own 440 bounce. Different masters, different encodes, different everything.
Then measure. Resampling barely changes perceived loudness, but "barely" isn't "zero," and sample peaks can move as the waveform is reconstructed. Turn the louder side down to match the quieter one. Never boost the version you're secretly rooting for.

### Switch at the same note, not the same second
Here's the trap that catches most homemade tests. Because the classic 432 render is longer, the same syllable happens later in that file. If your player switches by clock time, you jump to a slightly different place in the music every time, and the error grows the further in you go. Your ear then compares two different moments and calls the difference "tone."
The fix is to map the position: the 432 time for a given note is the 440 time divided by 0.981818. A purpose-built synchronized player does that for you. If you're rigging it yourself in a DAW, put both files on separate tracks, time-stretch nothing, and align a downbeat near your test loop instead of the song start.

### A runnable rehearsal
This script rehearses the whole method on synthetic audio: it renders a 30-second clip with a pad chord, a vibrato tone in the vocal range, an 808, and hats, makes a classic 432 version with ffmpeg's soxr resampler, measures both, gain-matches them, prints the clock-drift table, and then does the statistics for scoring a blind round.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""listening_test.py: build a fair 440 vs 432 listening test and score it.
Usage: python3 listening_test.py
Needs: numpy, scipy, ffmpeg (with soxr) on PATH.

1. Renders a 30 s SYNTHETIC clip (pad chord, vocal-like tone, 808, hats).
2. Makes a classic 432 version (asetrate + soxr resample), measures both.
3. Gain-matches the 432 side to the 440 side within 0.1 LU.
4. Shows why switching by clock time drifts, and the mapped position.
5. Scores a blind ABX run: how many correct you need, and how often a
   guesser or a genuinely hearing listener passes."""
import re, subprocess
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

SR, DUR, BPM = 48000, 30.0, 120
R = 432 / 440

def ffmpeg(*args):
    subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-y", *args], check=True)

def measure(path):
    err = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-nostats", "-hide_banner", "-i", path, "-af",
                          "ebur128=peak=true:framelog=quiet", "-f", "null", "-"],
                         capture_output=True, text=True).stderr
    s = err[err.rfind("Summary:"):]
    i = float(re.search(r"I:\s+(-?[\d.]+) LUFS", s).group(1))
    tp = float(re.search(r"Peak:\s+(-?[\d.]+) dBFS", s).group(1))
    dur = float(subprocess.run(["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-show_entries", "format=duration",
                                "-of", "csv=p=0", path], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout)
    return i, tp, dur

# 1. synthetic clip -------------------------------------------------------
t = np.arange(int(SR * DUR)) / SR
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
def tone(f, amp, harmonics=6, decay=0.0):
    ph = 2 * np.pi * (np.cumsum(f) / SR if np.ndim(f) else f * t)   # integrate frequency -> phase
    y = sum(amp / h * np.sin(h * ph) for h in range(1, harmonics + 1))
    return y * (np.exp(-decay * (t % 2.0)) if decay else 1)
pad = tone(220.0, .10) + tone(277.18, .08) + tone(329.63, .08)          # A3 C#4 E4
vox = tone(440.0 * (1 + 0.004 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 5.5 * t)), .12, 10)   # A4 with vibrato
beat = (t * BPM / 60) % 1.0
e808 = 0.45 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 55.0 * t) * np.exp(-3.0 * beat)          # A1 808 on every beat
hats = 0.05 * rng.standard_normal(t.size) * np.exp(-60 * ((t * BPM / 30) % 1.0))
mix = pad + vox + e808 + hats
mix = 0.7 * mix / np.max(np.abs(mix))
stereo = np.stack([mix, np.roll(mix, 24)], axis=1).astype(np.float32)
stereo.tofile("syn_raw.f32")
ffmpeg("-f", "f32le", "-ar", str(SR), "-ac", "2", "-i", "syn_raw.f32", "-c:a", "pcm_s24le", "synthetic_440.wav")

# 2. classic 432 render ----------------------------------------------------
ffmpeg("-i", "synthetic_440.wav", "-af",
       f"asetrate={SR*R:.6f},aresample={SR}:resampler=soxr:precision=28",
       "-c:a", "pcm_s24le", "synthetic_432.wav")
i440, tp440, d440 = measure("synthetic_440.wav")
i432, tp432, d432 = measure("synthetic_432.wav")
print("STEP 2  Same synthetic source, two renders")
print(f"  440: {i440:6.1f} LUFS  {tp440:+5.1f} dBTP  {d440:7.3f} s")
print(f"  432: {i432:6.1f} LUFS  {tp432:+5.1f} dBTP  {d432:7.3f} s   (ratio {d432/d440:.5f}, expected {1/R:.5f})")
print(f"  loudness gap before matching: {i432 - i440:+.2f} LU")

# 3. gain match -----------------------------------------------------------
g = i440 - i432
ffmpeg("-i", "synthetic_432.wav", "-af", f"volume={g:.3f}dB", "-c:a", "pcm_s24le", "synthetic_432_matched.wav")
im, tpm, _ = measure("synthetic_432_matched.wav")
print(f"\nSTEP 3  Apply {g:+.2f} dB to the 432 side")
print(f"  432 matched: {im:6.1f} LUFS  {tpm:+5.1f} dBTP  -> gap now {im - i440:+.2f} LU (target within 0.1)")

# 4. clock drift vs mapped position ----------------------------------------
print("\nSTEP 4  Switching by clock time vs by musical position (120 BPM)")
print("  440 time   432 same-note time   clock-switch error   error in beats")
for s in (10, 30, 60, 120, 180):
    m = s / R
    print(f"  {s:6.1f} s   {m:10.3f} s          {1000*(m - s):8.0f} ms          {(m - s) * BPM / 60:6.2f}")

# 5. scoring a blind ABX run -----------------------------------------------
print("\nSTEP 5  Blind ABX scoring (one-sided binomial, chance = 50%)")
for n in (8, 10, 12, 16, 20):
    k = next(k for k in range(n + 1) if stats.binom.sf(k - 1, n, 0.5) < 0.05)
    print(f"  {n:2d} trials: need {k:2d} correct for p<0.05   (P(guess 7/10 or better) = "
          f"{stats.binom.sf(6, 10, 0.5):.3f})" if n == 10 else f"  {n:2d} trials: need {k:2d} correct for p<0.05")
rng = np.random.default_rng(440432)
order = rng.choice(["X=A(440)", "X=B(432)"], size=12)
print("  example randomized 12-trial key:", " ".join(o[2] for o in order))
for p_true in (0.5, 0.65, 0.75, 0.9):
    k12 = next(k for k in range(13) if stats.binom.sf(k - 1, 12, 0.5) < 0.05)
    passes = np.mean(rng.binomial(12, p_true, size=100000) >= k12)
    print(f"  listener right {int(p_true*100)}% of the time: passes a 12-trial test in {100*passes:5.1f}% of sessions")

for f in ("syn_raw.f32", "synthetic_440.wav", "synthetic_432.wav", "synthetic_432_matched.wav"):
    subprocess.run(["rm", "-f", f])

Real output from this machine. The clip is synthetic, generated by the script, not a commercial recording.
STEP 2  Same synthetic source, two renders
  440:  -14.5 LUFS   -3.1 dBTP   30.000 s
  432:  -14.5 LUFS   -3.1 dBTP   30.556 s   (ratio 1.01852, expected 1.01852)
  loudness gap before matching: +0.00 LU

STEP 3  Apply +0.00 dB to the 432 side
  432 matched:  -14.5 LUFS   -3.1 dBTP  -> gap now +0.00 LU (target within 0.1)

STEP 4  Switching by clock time vs by musical position (120 BPM)
  440 time   432 same-note time   clock-switch error   error in beats
    10.0 s       10.185 s               185 ms            0.37
    30.0 s       30.556 s               556 ms            1.11
    60.0 s       61.111 s              1111 ms            2.22
   120.0 s      122.222 s              2222 ms            4.44
   180.0 s      183.333 s              3333 ms            6.67

STEP 5  Blind ABX scoring (one-sided binomial, chance = 50%)
   8 trials: need  7 correct for p<0.05
  10 trials: need  9 correct for p<0.05   (P(guess 7/10 or better) = 0.172)
  12 trials: need 10 correct for p<0.05
  16 trials: need 12 correct for p<0.05
  20 trials: need 15 correct for p<0.05
  example randomized 12-trial key: A B B B B A B B A A B B
  listener right 50% of the time: passes a 12-trial test in   2.0% of sessions
  listener right 65% of the time: passes a 12-trial test in  15.1% of sessions
  listener right 75% of the time: passes a 12-trial test in  39.0% of sessions
  listener right 90% of the time: passes a 12-trial test in  89.1% of sessions
Three things to take from that. First, on this clip the loudness gap after resampling rounded to zero and true peak didn't move, so the gain-match step applied nothing. That won't always be true for a dense, limited master, and the only way to know for your track is to measure it. Second, look at the drift table: switching by clock time is 185 ms off at ten seconds, over a full second off at one minute, and more than six beats off at three minutes. That's not a subtle bias, it's a different part of the song. Third, the statistics are stricter than intuition. Getting 7 out of 10 right feels convincing, but a coin does that or better about 17% of the time.

### No synced player? Cut matched loops instead
If you're working from files, the simplest fair setup is two short loops that contain exactly the same notes, level-matched, with neutral names. This little script does it with ffmpeg. You give it the 440 master, the 432 render, a start time, and a length in 440 time. It works out where those same notes live in the 432 file, cuts both, turns only the louder one down, then shuffles them into blind_1.wav and blind_2.wav with the answer in a key file you hand to your helper.
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# make_blind_pair.sh: cut the SAME musical passage from a 440 master and its
# classic 432 render, level-match them, and hide which is which.
# Usage: ./make_blind_pair.sh master_440.wav master_432.wav START_SEC LENGTH_SEC
set -euo pipefail
A="$1"; B="$2"; S="$3"; L="$4"
R=$(python3 -c "print(432/440)")
S432=$(python3 -c "print($S/$R)"); L432=$(python3 -c "print($L/$R)")   # same notes, later and longer
lufs() { ffmpeg -nostats -hide_banner -i "$1" -af ebur128=framelog=quiet -f null - 2>&1 \
         | awk '/Summary:/{f=1} f&&/ I:/{print $2; exit}'; }
ffmpeg -v error -y -ss "$S"    -t "$L"    -i "$A" -c:a pcm_s24le loop_440.wav
ffmpeg -v error -y -ss "$S432" -t "$L432" -i "$B" -c:a pcm_s24le loop_432.wav
IA=$(lufs loop_440.wav); IB=$(lufs loop_432.wav)
G=$(python3 -c "print(round(min(0.0, $IA-$IB),2))")       # only ever turn the 432 side DOWN
H=$(python3 -c "print(round(min(0.0, $IB-$IA),2))")       # ...or the 440 side down
ffmpeg -v error -y -i loop_440.wav -af "volume=${H}dB" -c:a pcm_s24le loop_440_m.wav
ffmpeg -v error -y -i loop_432.wav -af "volume=${G}dB" -c:a pcm_s24le loop_432_m.wav
if [ $((RANDOM % 2)) -eq 0 ]; then X=loop_440_m.wav; Y=loop_432_m.wav; K="1=440 2=432"
else X=loop_432_m.wav; Y=loop_440_m.wav; K="1=432 2=440"; fi
mv "$X" blind_1.wav; mv "$Y" blind_2.wav; echo "$K" > KEY_dont_peek.txt
rm -f loop_440.wav loop_432.wav loop_440_m.wav loop_432_m.wav
echo "440 loop: start ${S}s len ${L}s   ${IA} LUFS"
echo "432 loop: start ${S432}s len ${L432}s   ${IB} LUFS"
echo "blind_1: $(lufs blind_1.wav) LUFS   blind_2: $(lufs blind_2.wav) LUFS   key saved to KEY_dont_peek.txt"

Here's the real run, on a synthetic 90-second pair (a sustained chord, a vibrato tone, and an 808 pulse generated by ffmpeg, then resampled to 432):
$ ./make_blind_pair.sh synthetic_master_440.wav synthetic_master_432.wav 60 20
440 loop: start 60s len 20s   -12.9 LUFS
432 loop: start 61.111111111111114s len 20.37037037037037s   -13.0 LUFS
blind_1: -13.0 LUFS   blind_2: -13.0 LUFS   key saved to KEY_dont_peek.txt
durations: blind_1 20.370375s  blind_2 20.000000s
Notice that the 432 loop starts at 61.1 seconds, not 60, and runs 20.37 seconds instead of 20. That's the same passage; it just takes longer to play. Hide the timeline while you listen, because the loop length is the one giveaway left once the levels are matched.

### Pick a passage that can actually reveal it
Choose 15 to 30 seconds of a song you know well, ideally one you made or have the rights to. Exposed vocals, sustained chords, piano tails, strings, pads, and long sub notes show pitch movement clearly. A dense, distorted chorus full of percussion can hide a third of a semitone almost completely. Which songs reveal a 432 Hz retune, and which hide it goes deep on choosing material, including why your own catalog beats famous examples.
Loop that passage. Short loops beat full-song playthroughs because auditory memory for fine pitch and tone fades in seconds.

### Round one: can you tell them apart at all?
Before asking which is better, find out whether you can reliably hear a difference under blind conditions. That's what an ABX test does. You hear A (440) and B (432) labeled, then an unlabeled X that is secretly one of them, and you say which. Repeat at least ten times with the key randomized.
- Get a friend to drive the switch, or use a tool that hides the label. If you can see which is which, it isn't blind.
- Keep the monitor volume fixed for the whole session.
- Use a randomized key like the one the script prints, written down before you start.
- Score honestly: 9 of 10, 10 of 12, 12 of 16, or 15 of 20 clears p<0.05.
The last block of the output is worth a second look, because it cuts both ways. A listener who really hears the difference 75% of the time only passes a 12-trial test in about 39% of sessions. So one failed run doesn't prove you can't hear it. Run another session another day. If you pass repeatedly, the difference is real for you on that material.

### Round two: which do you prefer?
Now the question you actually care about. Keep it blind. Have your helper play the two in random order and ask you only which you prefer and how confident you are, on a simple 1 to 5 scale. Record preference and confidence separately. A string of low-confidence "B, I guess" answers tells you something very different from a string of confident ones.
Describe what you hear in concrete words before you name a winner: vocal chest weight, cymbal edge, bass sustain, piano brightness, perceived pace, tension. Avoid "better," "natural," or "healing" in your notes. Those words decide the answer before the listening does.
Then reverse the order, take five minutes of silence, and come back. Repeated switching creates fatigue and false certainty fast. A preference that only exists after twenty minutes of flipping is usually exhaustion talking. Test again the next day at a moderate level, on headphones and on speakers.

### The biases and their controls
Bias | How it fools you | Control
Loudness | The louder side sounds clearer and wider | Measure both, match within 0.1 LU, lower the louder side
Labels | "432" or "healing" primes the answer | Hidden labels, helper drives the switch
Position drift | Clock-time switching compares different notes | Map position, or align a downbeat near the loop
Source mismatch | Different masters or encodes differ in many ways | Both sides rendered from one lossless master
Order and fatigue | Whatever plays second, or last, can win | Reverse order, short sessions, silence between rounds
Small samples | A lucky streak feels like proof | At least 10 trials, score against chance, repeat another day

### The fifteen-minute protocol
1. Render 440 and 432 from the same lossless master. Measure both and match within 0.1 LU.
2. Pick one revealing 15 to 30 second loop from a song you know.
3. Write a randomized key for 10 to 12 ABX trials. Have someone else run it.
4. Score it against chance. If you can't pass, stop here and keep the original.
5. If you can, run 10 blind preference trials, logging preference and confidence separately.
6. Break for five minutes. Reverse the order. Repeat on a second playback system tomorrow.
7. Save the loop location, system, date, and source file with your notes.

### What to do with the answer
No reliable difference, or no consistent preference? That's a good result. It means the record is fine as it is, and you just saved yourself from managing a second master. If the 432 version keeps winning blind, across days and systems, it has earned a full render. At that point it becomes a delivery job, and 432 Hz mastering: LUFS and true peak after a retune covers getting it out the door without clipping or cheating the comparison.
The same habits pay off everywhere else in your work. Level-matched, position-aligned comparison is the backbone of Reference matching without guesswork, and it's also why streaming platforms turn loud masters down: they remove the loudness vote for listeners, so you might as well remove it for yourself first.
Note: If you'd rather not rig this in a DAW, the reTUNE[432] synced A/B player derives both versions from one decoded file in your browser, maps the musical position when you switch, and lets you drag a loop on the waveform. Nothing gets uploaded.
Q: Can you actually hear the difference between 432 and 440 Hz?
A: Often, yes, on a sustained vocal or chord when you switch quickly at the same musical position. The change is about 31.77 cents, a third of a semitone. Whether you prefer it is a separate question, and a blind test is the only fair way to answer either.
Q: How many trials does a blind ABX test need?
A: Ten is a practical minimum. With 10 trials you need 9 correct for p<0.05 against guessing; 7 out of 10 happens by pure chance about 17% of the time. Sixteen trials need 12 correct.
Q: How closely should the two versions be level-matched?
A: Within 0.1 LU of integrated loudness. Measure both renders and turn the louder one down to match. Never boost the side you want to win, and never touch the monitor knob between switches.
Q: Why does the 432 version drift out of sync?
A: A classic resampled 432 version is about 1.85% longer, so the same note arrives later. At one minute in, switching by clock time lands about 1.1 seconds off. A good player maps the musical position instead.
Q: What if I don't hear a reliable difference?
A: That's a valid result. Keep the original master. A preference that doesn't survive blind switching, reversed order, and a break isn't a strong enough reason to make an alternate.
