## 432, 435, 442 and the reference pitch you actually started from
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/432-vs-435-vs-442-hz-reference-pitch-guide.html
Section: Reference · 8 October 2026 · 10 min
Summary: 432, 435, 438, 442, and custom A4 references compared: exact ratios, cents, runtime and BPM changes, documented history, and why the source reference matters.

An alternate reference is just a ratio: target divided by the source the recording was actually made at. 432 from 440 is −31.77 cents, 435 is −19.79, 438 is −7.89. A 442 source needs 432/442, which is −39.62 cents. Only 435, 439, and 440 have documented standards history. The rest are taste. Render each target from the untouched original.
Once you've heard a 432 version of something you love, the internet will offer you a whole menu. 435, 436, 438, 444, "Verdi pitch," "scientific pitch," a custom number someone swears by for vocals. It can start to feel like there's a correct frequency out there and you just haven't found it. There isn't one. What there is, is a simple piece of math, a little real history, and one question that matters more than the target: what reference was the recording made against in the first place?
This is the field guide I'd want handed to me. What the numbers do, which ones have documented history behind them, which are just taste (taste is allowed), and the two mistakes that quietly ruin alternate versions: assuming every source is 440, and stacking one conversion on another.

### The formula is target over source
Changing the A4 reference scales the whole note map by one ratio: target divided by source. Every fundamental, every harmonic, every room resonance moves by the same proportion, so the harmony stays intact and the whole record sits a little higher or lower. To compare references on a musical scale instead of a hertz scale, convert the ratio to cents. Cents = 1200 × log2(target ÷ source). A semitone is 100 cents.
From a verified 440 source, 432 is a ratio of 0.981818, about −31.77 cents. In classic resampling, where pitch and time move together like tape, the record also runs about 1.85% longer. If you want the full anatomy of that one move, What 432 Hz actually changes in a finished master covers it. Here we're widening the lens.
One thing worth noticing: equal steps in hertz aren't equal steps in cents. 440 to 438 is −7.89 cents. 440 to 432 is −31.77. And 442 to 432 is −39.62. Those last two are only 2 Hz apart at the source, but that's nearly 8 cents of difference in where you land.

### Every reference, side by side
Here's the menu with the context that actually applies to each number. "Evidence status" means whether there's a documented historical or standards role. It's not a verdict on whether the number sounds good. That part is yours.
A4 target | Ratio from 440 | Cents | 4:00 song becomes | 120 BPM becomes | Where it comes from | Evidence status
430 | 0.977273 | −39.80 | 4:05.58 | 117.27 | Custom sound design | Taste; no standards role
432 | 0.981818 | −31.77 | 4:04.44 | 117.82 | Popular alternate-listening reference | Preference; health claims unsupported
435 | 0.988636 | −19.79 | 4:02.76 | 118.64 | French government commission, 1859 | Documented historical standard
436 | 0.990909 | −15.81 | 4:02.20 | 118.91 | Custom sound design | Taste; no standards role
438 | 0.995455 | −7.89 | 4:01.10 | 119.45 | Subtle custom darkening | Taste; no standards role
439 | 0.997727 | −3.94 | 4:00.55 | 119.73 | London Philharmonic Society, 1896 | Documented, oddly derived
440 | 1.000000 | 0.00 | 4:00.00 | 120.00 | London conference 1939; ISO 16:1975 | Current international standard
442 | 1.004545 | +7.85 | 3:58.91 | 120.55 | Sharper reference some ensembles choose | Practice varies; verify per recording
443 | 1.006818 | +11.76 | 3:58.37 | 120.82 | Sharper still | Practice varies; verify per recording
444 | 1.009091 | +15.67 | 3:57.84 | 121.09 | Alternate-tuning communities | Preference only
Every ratio, cents value, runtime, and BPM in that table comes straight from the demo script below, computed on the box rather than typed in.

### The history that actually checks out
Pitch used to be local. Before electronic references, an orchestra's A depended on its instruments, its organ, its city, and the temperature of the room. Cavanagh's short history of A=440 lays out the arc with sources. Nineteenth-century instrument makers pushed pitch upward because higher sounded more brilliant, until singers were straining at references near 450. In 1859 a French government commission made A=435 law in France. It was a compromise, and it was adopted for a time in some other European houses.
Britain went its own way. In 1896 the Philharmonic Society in London settled on 439. Cavanagh describes it as coming from a common but mistaken belief that the French 435 had been specified at 59°F, and then adjusting it for a warmer room. Broadcasting then forced the question internationally. A 1939 conference in London agreed on A=440, and ISO 16:1975 still specifies 440 Hz for the A in the treble stave. Cavanagh also notes that in practice pitch kept creeping upward in some places after 1939.
Two honest takeaways. First, 435 and 439 have real, documented histories, which makes them interesting listening references. Second, putting a modern record at 435 does not recreate a nineteenth-century performance. Period sound also depends on temperament, instrument construction, playing technique, the room, and the repertoire. One global ratio is one ingredient, not a time machine.

### Reference pitch is not temperament
This is where a lot of online discussion goes sideways. Changing A4 moves the anchor. It doesn't change the relationships between notes. An equal-tempered major third is 400 cents wide whether A is 440 or 432. A pure "just" third (a 5:4 ratio) is about 386 cents. Turning one into the other means retuning individual notes relative to each other, which a single ratio applied to a finished stereo master cannot do. If someone tells you a 432 conversion "puts the song in natural tuning," the math says otherwise, and section C of the demo below measures it.

### The source reference comes first
Batch software can't infer intent from a filename. It also can't hear that a recording was tracked against something other than 440. Maybe it's a sharper ensemble, an older session, a detuned production, or a file somebody already retuned. If the source was 442 and you apply the default 432/440, you don't land on 432. You land a couple of hertz above it, at a reference nobody chose.
How do you find out? Ask the session notes first. Failing that, put a good tuner (set to A=440) on a long, stable, exposed note, like a sustained piano chord, a held vocal, or a synth pad. If it consistently reads around +8 cents, you're probably looking at a 442 source, because 442 is +7.85 cents. Around −20 cents suggests 435. Around −32, it's already been retuned to 432, and the right move is to leave it alone. Write the number down before anything renders. This exact case is built into the folder workflow in Batch retune a folder to 432 Hz without damaging a master.

### Proof on the box
Synthetic signals only: sines and filtered noise generated in code, so the measurements are clean and nothing here is anyone's record. The script prints the reference table, converts a 442 tone with the right and the wrong ratio, checks that an equal-tempered third keeps its size through a 432 conversion, and compares rendering 432 directly against stacking 440→435→432, once through lossless files and once through an MP3 in the middle. The renders use the same exact-ratio chain as the rest of this series: resample to 200 times the source reference, relabel as 200 times the target, come back to 48 kHz.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""10_reference_math.py: alternate A4 references by the numbers, plus three render checks.
SYNTHETIC AUDIO ONLY (tones and noise generated below).
Needs: python3 + numpy, ffmpeg on PATH.  Usage: python3 10_reference_math.py"""
import math, os, subprocess, tempfile
import numpy as np

SR = 48000
tmp = tempfile.mkdtemp()

def cents(r): return 1200 * math.log2(r)
def mmss(s): return f"{int(s // 60)}:{s % 60:05.2f}"

print("A) reference table from a verified 440 source (classic resample: pitch and time move together)")
print(f"{'target':>7} {'ratio':>9} {'cents':>8} {'4:00 song':>10} {'120 BPM':>8}")
for t in (430, 432, 435, 436, 438, 439, 440, 442, 443, 444):
    r = t / 440
    print(f"{t:>7} {r:>9.6f} {cents(r):>+8.2f} {mmss(240 / r):>10} {120 * r:>8.2f}")

def write(x, path, rate=SR):
    subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-y", "-v", "error", "-f", "f32le", "-ar", str(rate), "-ac", "1", "-i", "-",
                    "-c:a", "pcm_f32le", path], input=x.astype(np.float32).tobytes(), check=True)

def read(path):
    raw = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", path, "-f", "f32le", "-ac", "1", "-ar", str(SR), "-"],
                         capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
    return np.frombuffer(raw, np.float32).astype(np.float64)

def retune(src, dst, source_hz, target_hz, codec="pcm_f32le"):
    chain = (f"aresample={int(source_hz*200)}:resampler=soxr:precision=28,asetrate={int(target_hz*200)},"
             f"aresample={SR}:resampler=soxr:precision=28")
    subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-y", "-v", "error", "-i", src, "-af", chain, "-c:a", codec, dst], check=True)

def peaks(x, lo, hi, n=1):
    w = x[: SR * 4] * np.hanning(SR * 4)
    sp = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(w, 32 * len(w))); f = np.fft.rfftfreq(32 * len(w), 1 / SR)
    out = []
    for a, b in ([(lo, hi)] if n == 1 else [(lo, (lo + hi) / 2), ((lo + hi) / 2, hi)]):
        m = (f > a) & (f < b); out.append(f[m][np.argmax(sp[m])])
    return out

t = np.arange(SR * 6) / SR
print("\nB) a file recorded against A=442, converted two ways")
write(0.4 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 442 * t), f"{tmp}/a442.wav")
retune(f"{tmp}/a442.wav", f"{tmp}/right.wav", 442, 432)
retune(f"{tmp}/a442.wav", f"{tmp}/wrong.wav", 440, 432)
print(f"  source A4 measured        : {peaks(read(f'{tmp}/a442.wav'), 420, 460)[0]:.2f} Hz")
print(f"  432/442 (documented)      : {peaks(read(f'{tmp}/right.wav'), 420, 460)[0]:.2f} Hz  ({cents(432/442):+.2f} c)")
print(f"  432/440 (assumed default) : {peaks(read(f'{tmp}/wrong.wav'), 420, 460)[0]:.2f} Hz  ({cents(432/440):+.2f} c)")

print("\nC) reference vs temperament: an equal-tempered major third keeps its size")
third = 440 * 2 ** (4 / 12)
write(0.3 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 440 * t) + 0.3 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * third * t), f"{tmp}/third.wav")
retune(f"{tmp}/third.wav", f"{tmp}/third432.wav", 440, 432)
for name in ("third", "third432"):
    a, b = peaks(read(f"{tmp}/{name}.wav"), 400, 600, n=2)
    print(f"  {name:9s}: {a:7.2f} Hz + {b:7.2f} Hz -> interval {cents(b / a):.2f} c "
          f"(just third would be {cents(5 / 4):.2f} c)")

print("\nD) render every target from the original, or stack them? (broadband synthetic test)")
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
x = 0.2 * rng.standard_normal(SR * 6)
x = np.convolve(x, np.ones(4) / 4, "same") + 0.2 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 440 * t)
write(x, f"{tmp}/src.wav")
retune(f"{tmp}/src.wav", f"{tmp}/direct.wav", 440, 432)
retune(f"{tmp}/src.wav", f"{tmp}/s435.wav", 440, 435)
retune(f"{tmp}/s435.wav", f"{tmp}/stacked.wav", 435, 432)
retune(f"{tmp}/src.wav", f"{tmp}/s435.mp3", 440, 435, codec="libmp3lame")  # ffmpeg default 128 kbps
retune(f"{tmp}/s435.mp3", f"{tmp}/stacked_mp3.wav", 435, 432)
d = read(f"{tmp}/direct.wav")

def residual(y):
    best = None
    for lag in range(-2000, 2001):          # align, since encoders add delay
        a = d[max(0, lag):]; b = y[max(0, -lag):]; n = min(len(a), len(b)) - 4000
        e = a[2000:n] - b[2000:n]
        r = 10 * np.log10(np.mean(e ** 2) / np.mean(a[2000:n] ** 2))
        if best is None or r < best[0]: best = (r, lag)
    return best

def lowpass(v, hz=16000):                  # brick-wall FFT low-pass, for a "band you can hear" view
    V = np.fft.rfft(v); V[np.fft.rfftfreq(len(v), 1 / SR) > hz] = 0
    return np.fft.irfft(V, len(v))

def band_residual(y, lag):
    a = lowpass(d[max(0, lag):]); b = lowpass(y[max(0, -lag):]); n = min(len(a), len(b)) - 4000
    e = a[2000:n] - b[2000:n]
    return 10 * np.log10(np.mean(e ** 2) / np.mean(a[2000:n] ** 2))

print("  (difference = how far each stacked render sits from a direct 440->432 render; lower is closer)")
for name, path in (("440->435->432 lossless", "stacked.wav"), ("440->435 mp3 128k ->432", "stacked_mp3.wav")):
    y = read(f"{tmp}/{path}")
    r, lag = residual(y)
    print(f"  {name:24s}: A4 {peaks(y, 420, 460)[0]:.2f} Hz | full band {r:6.1f} dB | "
          f"below 16 kHz {band_residual(y, lag):6.1f} dB | lag {lag}")
What it printed:
A) reference table from a verified 440 source (classic resample: pitch and time move together)
 target     ratio    cents  4:00 song  120 BPM
    430  0.977273   -39.80    4:05.58   117.27
    432  0.981818   -31.77    4:04.44   117.82
    435  0.988636   -19.79    4:02.76   118.64
    436  0.990909   -15.81    4:02.20   118.91
    438  0.995455    -7.89    4:01.10   119.45
    439  0.997727    -3.94    4:00.55   119.73
    440  1.000000    +0.00    4:00.00   120.00
    442  1.004545    +7.85    3:58.91   120.55
    443  1.006818   +11.76    3:58.37   120.82
    444  1.009091   +15.67    3:57.84   121.09

B) a file recorded against A=442, converted two ways
  source A4 measured        : 442.00 Hz
  432/442 (documented)      : 432.00 Hz  (-39.62 c)
  432/440 (assumed default) : 433.96 Hz  (-31.77 c)

C) reference vs temperament: an equal-tempered major third keeps its size
  third    :  440.00 Hz +  554.37 Hz -> interval 400.01 c (just third would be 386.31 c)
  third432 :  432.00 Hz +  544.29 Hz -> interval 400.01 c (just third would be 386.31 c)

D) render every target from the original, or stack them? (broadband synthetic test)
  (difference = how far each stacked render sits from a direct 440->432 render; lower is closer)
  440->435->432 lossless  : A4 432.00 Hz | full band  -58.4 dB | below 16 kHz -130.7 dB | lag 0
  440->435 mp3 128k ->432 : A4 432.00 Hz | full band  -12.7 dB | below 16 kHz  -14.3 dB | lag 0

### What those numbers say
B is the expensive mistake. The 442 tone converted with the documented ratio landed at exactly 432.00 Hz. Converted with the assumed 440 default, it landed at 433.96, almost 8 cents sharp of the target. That's not a disaster you'd hear on a phone. But it means the file's label is wrong, and every later version built from it inherits the error.
C settles the temperament question. Before conversion: 440.00 and 554.37 Hz, 400.01 cents apart. After: 432.00 and 544.29 Hz, still 400.01 cents apart. The extra hundredth is the FFT's measurement resolution, not the conversion. The whole chord moved and its internal shape didn't change. A just third would be 386.31 cents, and nothing about a reference conversion gets you there.
D is subtler and worth reading carefully. Stacking two lossless conversions landed on the same 432.00 Hz, and below 16 kHz it was indistinguishable from a direct render: −130.7 dB of difference, which is numerically nothing. The full-band figure of −58.4 dB comes from the very top octave near the Nyquist limit, where each resampling pass applies its own steep anti-aliasing filter. So stacking lossless renders isn't a sonic catastrophe. It's a documentation catastrophe, because the file's history now has two steps nobody wrote down.
The MP3-in-the-middle path is different. The difference against a direct render was −14.3 dB below 16 kHz. Be careful reading that. Broadband noise is the hardest possible material for a perceptual codec, and codecs are designed to throw away what they predict you won't hear, so a big null difference isn't the same as a big audible difference. What it does prove is that the stacked file is no longer the same signal. It also carries the encoder's choices forward into every version built on top of it. That's the same reason re-encoding eats true-peak headroom.
The rule falls out on its own: render every target from the untouched original. If you want 435 and 432 versions, that's two renders from the 440 master. It is not one render from the other.

### Custom targets are sound design, and that's fine
Sometimes 438 just suits the singer better. Sometimes a sample sits sweeter at 436 against the rest of the arrangement, or a slowed, darker 430 is exactly the mood. None of those numbers needs a mythology. They need a known source, an intentional target, a written ratio, and an honest A/B at matched level. Remember that classic mode moves time too: a 430 version of a four-minute song runs 4:05.58, and that slower pace is part of what you're hearing, the same way it is when you slow the bounce on purpose. If runtime has to stay fixed, a time-preserving shift is the alternative, with its own trade-offs, covered in Resampling, pitch shifting, and tempo change are three different jobs.
Write the cents value in your notes, not just the hertz. "Slightly lower" is not a production instruction. "−15.81 cents from a verified 440 source, classic mode" is.
Note: The full reTUNE[432] system adds named alternate references and custom targets on top of the 432 preview, so you can render 435 or 438 straight from the original and let the record decide instead of a slogan.
Q: What is the difference between 432 Hz and 435 Hz tuning?
A: Both lower A4 from 440. 432 is about −31.77 cents and 435 is about −19.79 cents. A=435 has documented history as the French standard set in 1859, while 432 is a modern alternate-listening preference without a standards role.
Q: How do I convert a 442 Hz recording to 432 Hz?
A: Use 432 divided by 442, a ratio of 0.977376 or about −39.62 cents. Applying the usual 432/440 ratio to a 442 source lands near 433.96 Hz instead of 432.
Q: How do I calculate cents between two reference pitches?
A: Cents = 1200 × log2(target ÷ source). From 440, 438 is −7.89 cents, 435 is −19.79 cents, 432 is −31.77 cents, and 444 is +15.67 cents.
Q: Does changing to 432 Hz change the tuning system or temperament?
A: No. A reference change scales every note by the same ratio, so an equal-tempered major third stays 400 cents wide. Converting to just intonation or another temperament requires changing note relationships, which one ratio cannot do.
Q: Can I convert a 432 Hz file to 435 Hz?
A: You can, but render every target from the untouched original instead. In our synthetic test, stacking lossless conversions was numerically harmless below 16 kHz, but an MP3 step in the middle left the file measurably different, and stacked versions are hard to document.
Q: Which reference frequency is correct?
A: There is no universally correct one. 440 is the current ISO standard, 435 and 439 have documented history, and other targets are creative choices. Pick by matched-level listening on the record itself.

---

## Keeping an unreleased master on your own machine, honestly
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/local-audio-processing-for-unreleased-masters.html
Section: Privacy · 8 October 2026 · 10 min
Summary: What browser-local and offline audio processing protect for unreleased music, what they don't, the metadata that leaks anyway, and privacy claims to defend.

Local processing means the audio you select is converted on your device instead of being uploaded, which removes the biggest exposure for an unreleased master. It does not make you invisible: pages still load over the network, synced folders still upload outputs, and tags inside the file still travel. Process locally, strip metadata from delivery copies, and promise only what is true.
There's a specific kind of nervous you feel holding an unreleased record. It might be a client's single under embargo, a feature verse you were trusted with, or a vocal that hasn't been registered or cleared yet. Then you want to try something small on it, like a 432 alternate or a quick check, and the tool you find wants you to upload the file first. For a job that's basically one ratio applied to some samples, that's a strange trade.
This essay is about what local processing actually protects, what it doesn't, and how to talk about it without overpromising, to a client or to yourself. If you've read Should you upload an unreleased master to the cloud?, this is the next layer down: not whether to upload, but what "it stays on your machine" really means once you look closely.

### Why a retune doesn't need a server
Some jobs genuinely need someone else's computer. Large AI models, collaborative sessions, and human mastering engineers all qualify. A pitch-reference conversion isn't one of them. Moving 440 to 432 is a resample by 432/440. On an ordinary laptop it usually finishes before an upload of the same file would. In a browser, the Web Audio API can decode a file you choose, render it offline at a new rate, and hand you back a WAV, all inside the tab.
So the honest default flips. If the operation is narrow and deterministic, the burden of proof is on the upload, not on keeping it local. Every transfer adds another copy, another storage policy to read, another retention window you don't control, and another place a file can surface before release day.

### What "local" protects, and what it doesn't
Here's the part privacy copy usually skips. When a web tool processes audio in the browser, the bytes of the song you pick don't need to go to an application server for the conversion. That's real, and it removes the biggest single exposure. It isn't invisibility.
- The page still came over the internet. The host's normal logs can record that your browser requested the page and its assets, along with the network details any website sees.
- Your device is still your device. Browser extensions with broad permissions, malware, screen recorders, and backups all operate outside the tool's control.
- The output lands somewhere. If your Downloads folder syncs to a cloud drive, the rendered file gets uploaded anyway, just by a different program.
- Paying isn't processing. A checkout or license system may receive your email and a payment record. That identity doesn't need to contain the music, and it shouldn't.
The defensible sentence is narrow: the selected audio is processed on this device, and it isn't intentionally uploaded for conversion. That's meaningful, it's checkable, and it doesn't pretend to be more.

### Where the copies go, path by path
Workflow | Audio leaves the device? | Who else may hold a copy | Works offline? | Your remaining job
Upload-based online converter | Yes, by design | The service, its storage and processing vendors, per its terms | No | Read retention and training terms before uploading
Browser-local tool (Web Audio) | No, for the conversion | Nobody, unless extensions or sync grab it | Once the page is loaded, often | Trusted browser, controlled download folder
Offline desktop batch | No | Nobody, unless backup or sync tools copy it | Yes | Trusted install, read-only inputs, backups
Cloud-synced output folder | Yes, after render | The sync provider | N/A | Render outside synced folders, or accept it knowingly
Handoff by chat or email | Yes | The platform, every recipient, their devices | N/A | Use the client-approved channel, strip tags, send hashes
Read the table top to bottom and something becomes obvious. Local processing fixes one link in the chain. It's an important link, but the leaks that actually hurt people tend to happen at the edges: the synced Downloads folder, the forwarded email, the file whose tags announce what it is.

### The leak nobody checks: what's written inside the file
Audio files carry text. Titles, artist names, comments, copyright lines, and encoder names ride along in the container. DAWs and assistants fill them in helpfully, with things like "v7 for Label X" or "do not share before the 20th." Most conversion tools copy those tags forward by default, because usually that's what you want. With an unreleased record, it's the opposite of what you want. You can strip every identifying word from the file name and still send a WAV whose comment field names the label and the embargo date.

### Proving it on the box
This script does three things with a synthetic file: a decaying 440 Hz tone generated in code, tagged like a real unreleased mix so you can see what happens to the tags. First, it renders the 432 version inside a Linux sandbox with no network at all (unshare -rn), and tells FFmpeg to accept only local files and pipes. Then it tries to feed the same sandboxed FFmpeg a remote URL, to show the refusal. Second, it follows the tags through a default render, an MP3 made from that render, and a render with metadata stripped. Third, it writes a short hash manifest and confirms that stripping tags didn't change a single audio sample.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""11_local_private_render.py: prove a 432 render needs no network, and catch the metadata
that quietly travels with an "unreleased" file. SYNTHETIC AUDIO ONLY.
Needs: python3 + numpy, ffmpeg/ffprobe on PATH. Part 1 uses Linux `unshare -rn` (no network
namespace); on other systems, switch the network off and run the same ffmpeg command.
Usage: python3 11_local_private_render.py [workdir]"""
import hashlib, json, os, shutil, subprocess, sys
import numpy as np

SR = 48000
work = os.path.abspath(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "private_demo")
shutil.rmtree(work, ignore_errors=True); os.makedirs(work)
src = os.path.join(work, "client_unreleased_v7.wav")
CHAIN = "aresample=88000:resampler=soxr:precision=28,asetrate=86400,aresample=48000:resampler=soxr:precision=28"

def sh(cmd, **kw):
    return subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, **kw)

def tags(p):
    j = json.loads(sh(["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-show_entries", "format_tags", "-of", "json", p]).stdout)
    return j.get("format", {}).get("tags", {})

# a synthetic "unreleased" mix with the kind of tags DAWs and assistants leave behind
t = np.arange(SR * 6) / SR
x = (0.3 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 440 * t) * np.exp(-((t % 1.5) * 1.2))).astype(np.float32)
subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-y", "-v", "error", "-f", "f32le", "-ar", str(SR), "-ac", "1", "-i", "-",
                "-metadata", "title=SECRET SINGLE (unreleased) v7",
                "-metadata", "artist=Client Artist",
                "-metadata", "comment=mix v7 for Label X, embargo until 2026-11-20, do not share",
                "-metadata", "copyright=Client Artist / Label X",
                "-c:a", "pcm_s24le", src], input=x.tobytes(), check=True)

print("1) render with the network switched off")
offline = os.path.join(work, "offline_432.wav")
r = sh(["unshare", "-rn", "sh", "-c",
        "ip -o link show | awk '{print $2, $9}'; "
        f"ffmpeg -y -v error -protocol_whitelist file,pipe -i '{src}' -af '{CHAIN}' -c:a pcm_s24le '{offline}' "
        "&& echo render: ok"])
print("   interfaces inside sandbox:", " | ".join(l for l in r.stdout.splitlines() if not l.startswith("render")))
print("  ", [l for l in r.stdout.splitlines() if l.startswith("render")][0], "| stderr:", r.stderr.strip() or "none")
r = sh(["unshare", "-rn", "ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-protocol_whitelist", "file,pipe",
        "-i", "https://example.com/upload.wav", "-f", "null", "-"])
print("   same sandbox, remote URL as input:", (r.stderr.strip().splitlines() or ["(no error)"])[0].split("] ")[-1])

print("\n2) what travels inside the file")
default = os.path.join(work, "default_432.wav")
sh(["ffmpeg", "-y", "-v", "error", "-i", src, "-af", CHAIN, "-c:a", "pcm_s24le", default], check=True)
mp3 = os.path.join(work, "default_432.mp3")
sh(["ffmpeg", "-y", "-v", "error", "-i", default, "-c:a", "libmp3lame", "-b:a", "320k", mp3], check=True)
clean = os.path.join(work, "clean_432.wav")
sh(["ffmpeg", "-y", "-v", "error", "-i", src, "-map_metadata", "-1", "-fflags", "+bitexact",
    "-flags:a", "+bitexact", "-af", CHAIN, "-c:a", "pcm_s24le", clean], check=True)
for label, p in (("source", src), ("default render", default), ("mp3 of render", mp3), ("stripped render", clean)):
    tg = tags(p)
    print(f"   {label:16s}: {len(tg)} tags")
    for k, v in sorted(tg.items()):
        print(f"      {k:10s} = {v}")

print("\n3) handoff manifest (hash what you send, so the receiver can verify it arrived intact)")
for p in (src, clean):
    h = hashlib.sha256(open(p, "rb").read()).hexdigest()
    print(f"   {h[:20]}...  {os.path.getsize(p):>8d} B  {os.path.basename(p)}")
same_audio = sh(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", default, "-f", "md5", "-"]).stdout.strip() == \
             sh(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", clean, "-f", "md5", "-"]).stdout.strip()
print("   audio identical between default and stripped render:", same_audio)
Unedited output:
1) render with the network switched off
   interfaces inside sandbox: lo: DOWN
   render: ok | stderr: none
   same sandbox, remote URL as input: Protocol 'https' not on whitelist 'file,pipe'!

2) what travels inside the file
   source          : 5 tags
      artist     = Client Artist
      comment    = mix v7 for Label X, embargo until 2026-11-20, do not share
      copyright  = Client Artist / Label X
      encoder    = Lavf61.7.103
      title      = SECRET SINGLE (unreleased) v7
   default render  : 5 tags
      artist     = Client Artist
      comment    = mix v7 for Label X, embargo until 2026-11-20, do not share
      copyright  = Client Artist / Label X
      encoder    = Lavf61.7.103
      title      = SECRET SINGLE (unreleased) v7
   mp3 of render   : 5 tags
      artist     = Client Artist
      comment    = mix v7 for Label X, embargo until 2026-11-20, do not share
      copyright  = Client Artist / Label X
      encoder    = Lavf61.7.103
      title      = SECRET SINGLE (unreleased) v7
   stripped render : 0 tags

3) handoff manifest (hash what you send, so the receiver can verify it arrived intact)
   75aa39c178c3534007fa...    864262 B  client_unreleased_v7.wav
   382857b0c59010a731c6...    880068 B  clean_432.wav
   audio identical between default and stripped render: True

### What that output means for a real session
The render finished with the only network interface down. Inside the sandbox, the loopback interface was the only one, and it was down. The 432 render still completed with no errors. That's the cleanest possible evidence that this job never needed the internet. On a Mac or Windows machine you can run the same test the low-tech way: turn Wi-Fi off, render, check the file.
The whitelist turned away a remote input. -protocol_whitelist file,pipe made FFmpeg refuse an https address outright, before it even tried the network. It's a small belt-and-braces flag for scripts that handle sensitive material, because it means a typo or a pasted URL can't quietly make a local job reach out.
The tags survived everything. The default render carried all five tags, including the embargo comment. The MP3 made from it carried all five too, even though it was a separate encode of a separate file. That's the point to remember: conversion doesn't launder metadata. Only the explicit strip, -map_metadata -1 plus the bitexact flags (which also drop FFmpeg's own encoder tag), produced a file with zero tags.
The audio didn't change when the tags did. The default and stripped renders have identical decoded audio, checked by an MD5 of the samples, not the file. Stripping is a container change, not a sound change, so there's no quality excuse for skipping it.
The hashes are for the person on the other end. Send the SHA-256 alongside the file through a different channel. The receiver can confirm they got exactly what you sent, not a re-encode some chat app made "to save space." It also gives your notes a fingerprint that says which file left the room on which day.

### Offline goes one step further
A browser tool removes the upload. A downloadable offline tool also removes the dependency on a live web page. It works on a plane, behind a studio firewall, on a machine that's never logged into anything, and it keeps working if the website changes or disappears. For catalog work, it also keeps the files right next to the storage they already live on instead of shuttling them anywhere. That ties into why local tools beat upload queues on speed as well as privacy.
It still isn't a security system. Offline means nobody else is involved in the conversion. It doesn't mean you have backups, permission, malware protection, or a sane delivery plan. Those were always your job.

### A private workflow for someone else's record
1. Confirm you're allowed. Before any tool question, make sure you have permission to process this audio. A private test of someone else's unreleased master is still their master.
2. Work from a copy. Keep the original where it lives and process a duplicate in a local, non-synced working folder. Check your Downloads and Desktop sync settings once and you'll know for good.
3. Use a trusted environment. An updated browser and a short list of extensions, ideally a clean profile for client work. Close the tab full of random plugins before you drop in an embargoed file.
4. Render locally, strip tags on delivery copies. Keep full internal tags in your archive copy if they help you. Strip them from anything that leaves the room, unless the client asked for specific tags, and then write only those.
5. Hand off through the approved channel. Whatever the client or label specified, with a hash manifest sent separately.
6. Clean up. Delete temp renders and stray exports you don't need. An old test file in a forgotten folder is how a record leaks a year later.

### How to say it without overpromising
Privacy language gets a studio in trouble when it's broader than the truth. "Your music never touches the internet" is a promise about your whole device, network, and future behavior, and nobody can make it. "This tool processes the selected audio on your device and doesn't upload it for conversion" is a promise about one code path, and you can stand behind it. The same goes for what you tell a client: "I render alternates locally, strip metadata from delivery copies, and send through the channel you specified." Specific beats sweeping, every time.
None of this needs to be paranoid. It's the same habit as checking true peak before delivery: a few small, boring steps that make the bad day much less likely. The unreleased record is often the most valuable file in the room. It deserves a workflow that treats it that way.
Note: reTUNE[432] follows that pattern for the 440-to-432 job: the browser engine decodes and renders the file you pick in the tab, and the full system adds an offline Windows batch engine for complete files and folders, no catalog account needed.
Q: Does browser-based audio processing upload my file?
A: Not necessarily. Tools built on the Web Audio API can decode and render a file you select inside the browser tab, without sending it to a server for conversion. The page itself still loads over the network, so check how a specific tool works before trusting it.
Q: Is local audio processing completely private?
A: No. It removes the upload for the conversion, but extensions, malware, backups, and cloud-synced download folders can still copy files, and the page request is still logged like any website visit. It protects one important link, not the whole chain.
Q: Do audio files contain hidden metadata?
A: Yes. WAV and MP3 files can carry titles, artist names, comments, copyright lines, and encoder tags. In our synthetic test, an embargo comment survived both a 432 render and an MP3 made from it until the metadata was explicitly stripped.
Q: How do I remove metadata from an audio file with FFmpeg?
A: Add -map_metadata -1 to drop copied tags, and -fflags +bitexact with -flags:a +bitexact to stop FFmpeg writing its own encoder tag. This changes the container, not the audio samples.
Q: Can I retune audio to 432 Hz without an internet connection?
A: Yes. A 432 conversion is a resample by 432/440 and needs no server. Our demo rendered it inside a sandbox with no network at all. Offline desktop tools do the same for whole folders.

## Before a 432 version ships: the release checklist
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/432-hz-release-checklist.html
Section: Checklist · 8 October 2026 · 10 min
Summary: Before releasing a 432 Hz version: rights, the right source reference, a QC gate for clipping and true peak, runtime fixes, honest copy, an archive.

Before you release a 432 Hz version, confirm you have the rights, render once from the approved lossless master at the correct source reference, and run a real QC gate. Check runtime, pitch, clipping, true peak on the WAV and the encode, and loudness change. Re-time anything synced to the old runtime, label it clearly, describe it honestly, and archive everything.
The A/B went well. The artist wants the 432 version out. It's rendered, it sounds right in the car, and the distributor upload form is open in another tab. This is the moment where a good creative idea turns into a sloppy release. Not because anyone did anything wrong, but because "it sounds good" quietly stood in for a dozen smaller questions nobody asked.
This is the list I'd want taped to the monitor before an alternate version goes public. It's not homework. Most items take a minute. A few of them, like rights, the source reference, the true peak, and the words you use to describe it, are the difference between a version people trust and one that causes a takedown, a rejected upload, or an awkward correction. If you haven't built the alternate yet, start with A 432 alternate master should never cost you the original. This picks up where that leaves off.

### 1. Rights first, before anything technical
Only release an altered version of a recording you own or are authorized to alter. A private listening test on your own machine is one thing. Publishing a retuned copy of someone else's master is another, and pitch-shifting it doesn't make it yours. The U.S. Copyright Office's overview of musical works and sound recordings is a good reminder that the composition and the recording are separate rights, often held by different people. For collaborations, get explicit permission from whoever controls the master. A thumbs-up emoji in a group chat doesn't count.
Then name the purpose: deluxe bonus track, standalone listening edition, slowed companion, DJ tool, client request. The purpose decides everything else, including how long it can run, whether loudness should match the original, what the title says, and how you talk about it.

### 2. Start from the approved source, at the right reference
Use the best lossless master you have, the one that was actually signed off, not a download of the streaming version. Confirm what A4 reference it was made against. Most modern records are 440, but not all, and a file that was already retuned must never be retuned again. The ratio is always target over the real source; 432, 435, 442 and the reference pitch you actually started from covers why that matters. Render once, to a 24-bit WAV, and keep the original untouched beside it.

### 3. Run a real QC gate, not a vibe check
Here's a pre-release gate you can run. It builds a synthetic master, a pad with a held A4 and very bright hats, generated in code and deliberately mastered too hot, the way plenty of real records are. It renders the 432 version, makes an AAC delivery encode from it, and checks eleven things. Then it does it again with a documented gain trim applied before the resample.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""12_release_qc.py: a pre-release gate for a 432 alternate master and its delivery encode.
SYNTHETIC AUDIO ONLY: a deliberately hot synthetic master is generated below.
Needs: python3 + numpy, ffmpeg/ffprobe on PATH.  Usage: python3 12_release_qc.py [workdir]"""
import hashlib, json, math, os, re, shutil, subprocess, sys
import numpy as np

SR, SRC_HZ, TGT_HZ = 48000, 440, 432
RATIO = TGT_HZ / SRC_HZ
work = os.path.abspath(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "release_qc")
shutil.rmtree(work, ignore_errors=True); os.makedirs(work)
CHAIN = (f"aresample={SRC_HZ*200}:resampler=soxr:precision=28,asetrate={TGT_HZ*200},"
         f"aresample={SR}:resampler=soxr:precision=28")

def sh(cmd, **kw): return subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, **{"text": True, **kw})
def sha(p): return hashlib.sha256(open(p, "rb").read()).hexdigest()

def probe(p):
    j = json.loads(sh(["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-show_streams", "-show_format", "-of", "json", p]).stdout)
    s = j["streams"][0]
    return dict(dur=float(j["format"]["duration"]), rate=int(s["sample_rate"]), ch=s["channels"],
                bits=s.get("bits_per_raw_sample") or s.get("bits_per_sample"), codec=s["codec_name"],
                title=j["format"].get("tags", {}).get("title", ""))

def loud(p):
    e = sh(["ffmpeg", "-nostats", "-hide_banner", "-i", p, "-af", "ebur128=peak=true:framelog=quiet",
            "-f", "null", "-"]).stderr
    s = e[e.rfind("Summary:"):]
    return float(re.search(r"I:\s+(-?[\d.]+) LUFS", s).group(1)), float(re.search(r"Peak:\s+(-?[\d.]+) dBFS", s).group(1))

def decode(p):
    raw = sh(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", p, "-f", "f32le", "-ac", "1", "-ar", str(SR), "-"], text=False).stdout
    return np.frombuffer(raw, np.float32).astype(np.float64)

def decode_stereo(p):
    raw = sh(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", p, "-f", "f32le", "-"], text=False).stdout
    return np.frombuffer(raw, np.float32)

def a4(x):
    w = x[SR:SR * 5] * np.hanning(SR * 4)
    sp = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(w, 32 * len(w))); f = np.fft.rfftfreq(32 * len(w), 1 / SR)
    m = (f > 420) & (f < 460); return f[m][np.argmax(sp[m])]

def edges(x):
    db = lambda v: 20 * math.log10(max(v, 1e-9))
    lead = np.argmax(np.abs(x) > 10 ** (-60 / 20)) / SR
    tail = db(np.sqrt(np.mean(x[-SR // 10:] ** 2)))
    return lead, tail

# synthetic hot master: pad + held A4 + bright clicky hats, peak-normalized to -0.2 dBFS
t = np.arange(SR * 20) / SR
x = sum(a * np.sin(2 * np.pi * f * t) for f, a in ((110, .3), (220, .2), (440, .25), (554.37, .12)))
hat = np.zeros_like(t)
for n in range(80):
    i = int(n * 0.25 * SR); hat[i:i + 96] += np.sign(np.sin(np.arange(96) * 1.9)) * 0.6
x = (x + hat) * np.minimum(1, (20 - t) / 3)              # 3 s fade so the tail is musical
x = np.stack([x, x * 0.97], 1); x *= 10 ** (-0.2 / 20) / np.abs(x).max()
src = os.path.join(work, "Artist_Title_Master_440_48k_24b.wav")
subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-y", "-v", "error", "-f", "f32le", "-ar", str(SR), "-ac", "2", "-i", "-",
                "-c:a", "pcm_s24le", src], input=x.astype(np.float32).tobytes(), check=True)
src_hash = sha(src)

def build(tag, trim_db):
    wav = os.path.join(work, f"Artist_Title_432Master{tag}_48k_24b.wav")
    af = (f"volume={trim_db}dB," if trim_db else "") + CHAIN   # trim BEFORE the resample, never after a clip
    sh(["ffmpeg", "-y", "-v", "error", "-i", src, "-af", af, "-c:a", "pcm_s24le",
        "-metadata", "title=Title (432 Hz Alternate Master)", wav], check=True)
    aac = wav.replace("_48k_24b.wav", "_256k.m4a")
    sh(["ffmpeg", "-y", "-v", "error", "-i", wav, "-c:a", "aac", "-b:a", "256k", aac], check=True)
    return wav, aac

def gate(label, wav, aac):
    ps, pw, pa = probe(src), probe(wav), probe(aac)
    ls, lw, la = loud(src), loud(wav), loud(aac)
    xs, xw = decode(src), decode(wav)
    lead, tail = edges(xw)
    clipped = int((np.abs(decode_stereo(wav)) >= 0.99999).sum())
    checks = [
        ("Runtime = source / 0.981818 (±5 ms)", abs(pw["dur"] - ps["dur"] / RATIO) < .005,
         f'{ps["dur"]:.3f} -> {pw["dur"]:.3f} s (expect {ps["dur"] / RATIO:.3f})'),
        ("Format kept: rate, depth, channels", (pw["rate"], pw["bits"], pw["ch"]) == (ps["rate"], ps["bits"], ps["ch"]),
         f'{pw["rate"]} Hz / {pw["bits"]}-bit / {pw["ch"]} ch'),
        ("Held A4 measures 432 Hz (±0.05)", abs(a4(xw) - 432) < .05, f"{a4(xs):.2f} -> {a4(xw):.2f} Hz"),
        ("Starts on time (first audio within 50 ms)", lead <= .05, f"first audio at {lead * 1000:.1f} ms"),
        ("Tail decays, not cut (last 100 ms < -40 dBFS)", tail < -40, f"last 100 ms at {tail:.1f} dBFS"),
        ("No full-scale (clipped) samples in the WAV", clipped == 0, f"{clipped} samples at full scale"),
        ("Lossless true peak <= -1.0 dBTP", lw[1] <= -1.0, f"{lw[1]:+.1f} dBTP (source {ls[1]:+.1f})"),
        ("Encoded AAC true peak <= -1.0 dBTP", la[1] <= -1.0, f"{la[1]:+.1f} dBTP"),
        ("Loudness change documented", True, f"{ls[0]:.1f} -> {lw[0]:.1f} LUFS ({lw[0] - ls[0]:+.1f} LU)"),
        ("Version title says 432", "432" in pw["title"] and "432" in pa["title"], pa["title"]),
        ("Approved 440 master untouched", sha(src) == src_hash, "sha256 matches"),
    ]
    print(f"\n{label}")
    for name, ok, note in checks:
        print(f"  [{'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}] {name:46s} {note}")
    print(f"  => {sum(ok for _, ok, _ in checks)}/{len(checks)} passed")

gate("Render A: straight 432 render of the hot master", *build("", 0))
gate("Render B: documented -4.0 dB trim applied before the resample", *build("_trim-4dB", -4.0))
Real output from the box:

Render A: straight 432 render of the hot master
  [PASS] Runtime = source / 0.981818 (±5 ms)            20.000 -> 20.370 s (expect 20.370)
  [PASS] Format kept: rate, depth, channels             48000 Hz / 24-bit / 2 ch
  [PASS] Held A4 measures 432 Hz (±0.05)                440.00 -> 432.00 Hz
  [PASS] Starts on time (first audio within 50 ms)      first audio at 0.0 ms
  [PASS] Tail decays, not cut (last 100 ms < -40 dBFS)  last 100 ms at -43.8 dBFS
  [FAIL] No full-scale (clipped) samples in the WAV     323 samples at full scale
  [FAIL] Lossless true peak <= -1.0 dBTP                +1.0 dBTP (source +2.5)
  [FAIL] Encoded AAC true peak <= -1.0 dBTP             +1.0 dBTP
  [PASS] Loudness change documented                     -10.2 -> -10.3 LUFS (-0.1 LU)
  [PASS] Version title says 432                         Title (432 Hz Alternate Master)
  [PASS] Approved 440 master untouched                  sha256 matches
  => 8/11 passed

Render B: documented -4.0 dB trim applied before the resample
  [PASS] Runtime = source / 0.981818 (±5 ms)            20.000 -> 20.370 s (expect 20.370)
  [PASS] Format kept: rate, depth, channels             48000 Hz / 24-bit / 2 ch
  [PASS] Held A4 measures 432 Hz (±0.05)                440.00 -> 432.00 Hz
  [PASS] Starts on time (first audio within 50 ms)      first audio at 0.0 ms
  [PASS] Tail decays, not cut (last 100 ms < -40 dBFS)  last 100 ms at -47.8 dBFS
  [PASS] No full-scale (clipped) samples in the WAV     0 samples at full scale
  [PASS] Lossless true peak <= -1.0 dBTP                -1.7 dBTP (source +2.5)
  [PASS] Encoded AAC true peak <= -1.0 dBTP             -1.7 dBTP
  [PASS] Loudness change documented                     -10.2 -> -14.3 LUFS (-4.1 LU)
  [PASS] Version title says 432                         Title (432 Hz Alternate Master)
  [PASS] Approved 440 master untouched                  sha256 matches
  => 11/11 passed

### What that gate caught
Most of the list passed on the first try, and that's normal. The ratio, runtime, format, pitch, head, tail, title, and untouched source were all fine. The interesting part is the three failures, because they show something people don't expect.
The source master was already illegal. Its sample peak sat at −0.2 dBFS, which looks fine on a basic meter, but its true peak read +2.5 dBTP. The bright, clicky hats create big peaks between the samples, which is exactly what true peak is what codecs clip is about. The alternate inherited that problem. Retuning doesn't create headroom.
The resample clipped 323 samples. A resample rebuilds the waveform between the original sample points. Some of those intersample peaks became real samples above full scale, and a 24-bit WAV can't store anything above full scale, so they were flattened. That's why Render A's true peak reads +1.0 instead of the source's +2.5. It isn't better. The tops were cut off. A lower true-peak number caused by clipping is a warning, not a win.
The fix went in before the resample, not after. Render B applied a −4.0 dB trim first, then converted. No clipped samples, true peak at −1.7 dBTP on both the WAV and the AAC encode, all eleven checks passing. The cost is honest and visible: 4.1 LU quieter than the original master. On a streaming service that normalizes playback, that may not matter much. On a platform that doesn't, the alternate will sound quieter than the original, and the real fix is to go back to the master and give it some peak headroom, not to hit the alternate with a limiter and call it the same record. Whatever you choose, write it in the notes and in the file name, as the script does with _trim-4dB.
The ceiling here, −1.0 dBTP, is the maximum true peak the EBU R 128 loudness recommendation sets for broadcast programmes, and a sensible default for music delivery that will be encoded downstream.

### 4. The checklist, in one place
Stage | Check | Pass looks like | If it fails
Rights | Owner or written permission for the master and composition | Name and date in notes | Stop. Private tests only
Purpose | Deluxe, listening edition, companion, DJ tool, client request | One sentence in notes | Decide before rendering
Source | Approved lossless master, verified A4 reference | Hash recorded, reference written | Find the real master; measure the reference
Render | Single exact-ratio render to 24-bit WAV | A4 at 432.00, runtime ÷ 0.981818 | Check the ratio and for a second operation
Clipping | No full-scale samples in the WAV | 0 clipped samples | Trim before the resample; don't limit after
True peak | WAV and encoded file ≤ −1.0 dBTP | Both under the ceiling | Documented trim, or fix the source master
Loudness | Change vs original measured and intended | Delta written in notes | Don't let a loudness edge sell the version
Time-based assets | Video, lyrics, cues, sequencing re-timed | Everything lands on the new runtime | Re-time, or use a time-preserving shift and audition
Full playback | Start to finish, headphones, speakers, phone, low volume | No clicks, cut tails, swapped channels | Re-render from source
Metadata | Title, version field, identifiers | "(432 Hz Alternate Master)" everywhere | Fix before upload, not after
Copy | Description states facts and intent | No health or cosmic claims | Rewrite
Archive | Source, render, encodes, notes, permissions together | Someone else could rebuild it | Assemble it now, while you remember

### 5. Fix everything that was timed against the old runtime
A classic 432 render runs about 1.85% longer, so every time-based asset built for the original is now slightly wrong. Lyric videos and visualizers drift a little more each bar. Synced lyrics on streaming platforms land early. Album transitions and gapless sequences shift. Live cues fire ahead of the music. Re-time them to the new file, or if picture must stay locked, render with a time-preserving pitch shift instead and audition the percussion, reverb tails, and stereo effects for artifacts. And re-check the identifier question with your distributor. The ISRC rules around length changes are covered in the alternate-master essay linked above.

### 6. Listen to the actual encoded file
Not the WAV, not the session: the encoded file the platform will receive. Start to finish, on headphones, on speakers, on a phone, and once at low volume in a quiet room. That last one reveals more than people expect. Then do a short synchronized A/B against the original at matched level, on a passage you know cold. You're not trying to prove anything. You're confirming the version going out is the version that won the room.

### 7. Describe it like a professional
The title should be unambiguous: Title (432 Hz Alternate Master), or another clear version name. Don't call it a remaster unless remastering happened. The description can say exactly what changed, and that's more persuasive than any promise. Something like this:
"An alternate version of [Title], retuned from the original A=440 reference to A=432. The whole recording sits about a third of a semitone lower and, because it was resampled like tape, runs about 1.85% longer. No other mixing or mastering changes. Same song, heavier and a little more suspended. Listen to both and see which one you live with."
What you leave out matters just as much. Don't promise healing, guaranteed calm, DNA repair, or "natural" tuning. Don't imply the standard version is harmful. None of it is supported, it invites exactly the wrong kind of attention, and it cheapens a version that can stand on how it sounds. Lower, warmer, heavier, slower, more suspended are all fair as artistic description, because they describe intent, not physiology. If anyone wants the math, What 432 Hz actually changes in a finished master is there.
A clear release note also does something quieter. It gives writers, curators, and fans a real reason to talk about the version. "The artist wanted a heavier companion to the single" is a story. "Frequency of the universe" is a slogan, and people can tell the difference.

### 8. Archive enough to rebuild it
Put it all in one folder: the approved source and its hash, the 432 render, every encode, the notes (source and target reference, ratio, render mode, any trim, loudness and true-peak readings, tool and version, date, who did it), the artwork, the metadata as submitted, and the permissions. If the file ever has to be replaced, this is what tells a correction apart from an accidental new master. Keep the delivery copies stripped of internal tags, and keep the archive copy complete. The privacy side of that is in Keeping an unreleased master on your own machine, honestly.
Then do the last check that matters: confirm the original 440 master is still there, still the approved file, still the primary release. The alternate is a companion. It shouldn't replace anything by accident.
If you want a second set of eyes before upload, run the final WAV through CoProducer's Analyze for a true-peak and loudness readout against the same delivery gates, the way a release checklist that matches the meter describes.
Note: Still deciding whether the record wants a 432 version at all? reTUNE[432] gives you the synchronized A/B in the browser on audio you own, and the full system adds full-length output, offline batch rendering, and optional LUFS targets once the answer is yes.
Q: Can I release a 432 Hz version of someone else's song?
A: Only with permission from whoever controls the recording, and the composition rights still apply. Retuning a recording does not make it yours. Private listening tests and public releases are different things.
Q: Does retuning to 432 Hz change the true peak?
A: It can. A resample rebuilds the waveform, so intersample peaks can become real samples. In our synthetic test, a hot master clipped 323 samples during a straight 432 render. Trim the gain before the resample and re-measure both the WAV and the encoded file.
Q: What should I call a 432 Hz version on streaming platforms?
A: Use a clear version name such as Title (432 Hz Alternate Master). Don't call it a remaster unless remastering happened, and keep the original 440 release as the primary version.
Q: What can I honestly say about a 432 Hz release?
A: State the facts: retuned from A=440 to A=432, about a third of a semitone lower, and about 1.85% longer if resampled. Describe the creative intent in words like heavier or warmer. Don't promise healing, relaxation, or natural tuning.
Q: Do I need to update lyrics and videos for a 432 Hz version?
A: Yes, if it was made with classic resampling. It runs about 1.85% longer, so synced lyrics, videos, visualizers, cues, and gapless transitions drift unless you re-time them or use a time-preserving pitch shift.
