## Splitting stems from YouTube audio you own starts with the cleanest copy
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/split-stems-from-youtube-audio-you-own.html
Section: Stems · 8 October 2026 · 11 min
Summary: Want stems from a song you uploaded to YouTube? The copy you feed the separator sets the ceiling. Find the first-generation file, then split locally.

If the song is yours and the only copy you can find is the one on YouTube, you can still get usable stems out of it. But the separator can’t give back what the codec already threw away. Before you split anything, hunt down the earliest-generation file you have, check that it really is lossless, decode it to WAV exactly once, and then split on your own machine. The kick and bass will survive a lossy copy fine. The cymbals and air won’t.
Most of us have been here. A track you made three laptops ago, the session folder gone with a dead drive, and the record still sitting on your channel with a few thousand plays. Or a live set your band filmed, you have the rights to it, and the multitrack never got exported. You want the vocal out of it for a remix, or the drums for a new edit, or just the bassline so you can finally figure out what you played.
Stem separation can do that now, and it does it well. What it can’t do is undo the trip your audio took to get to you. That trip is the part people skip, and it’s where most of the “AI stems sound watery” complaints actually start.

### First, whose audio is it
This essay is about your own music, or music you’ve been given rights to. That isn’t a disclaimer bolted onto the end. It changes what you’re allowed to do and where you should look for the file. YouTube’s Terms of Service say you can’t download content except where the service expressly authorizes it, or with prior written permission from YouTube and the rights holders. Pulling someone else’s single off a video page so you can strip the vocal falls outside that, and the copyright problem follows you into anything you release.
For your own uploads there’s a sanctioned route. YouTube’s help page on downloading videos you’ve uploaded describes it: open YouTube Studio, go to Content, choose the video, and pick Download from its menu. You get an MP4 at 720p or 360p. Google Takeout can export everything you’ve uploaded in one go. That MP4 is your fallback, but it isn’t your first choice, for reasons the numbers below make clear.

### What a separator is really doing
Modern separators like Demucs and the MDX-Net family learn, from thousands of multitrack songs, how to estimate each source from a mix. Many of them work, at least partly, by building a mask over a time-frequency picture of the song: for every small tile of time and frequency, how much of it belongs to the vocal, the drums, the bass. The rest is detail, and we go deep on the differences in the Demucs vs MDX-Net essay.
The detail that matters here is simpler. Whatever lands in those tiles gets handed to some stem. If a codec replaced the top octave of your hi-hats with smeared, quantized noise, the separator can’t tell that noise from cymbal. It just does its best with it. The source copy sets a ceiling, and no model, however good, gets above it.

### Measuring the ceiling
We wanted to put a number on that, so we built a test with no real record in it at all. lab.py synthesizes a short 92 BPM groove: a pitch-swept kick, a band-limited saw bass, a detuned pad, a vowel-like lead standing in for a voice, and noise-burst hats. Because we made every stem ourselves, we know the truth exactly.
Then we push the mix through the lossy chains a real song tends to pass through: a single AAC or Opus encode, an MP3, and the classic “downloaded it, then a converter re-exported it” double hop. Every decoded copy gets split with the same oracle soft masks, built from the true stems. That’s the best any mask could ever do, a perfect separator. So any drop in quality is damage done by the copy, not by the separator.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""source_ceiling.py: how much separation quality a lossy copy costs you
before any AI model touches it.

SYNTHETIC test: a 92 BPM groove (kick, bass, pad, vowel-like lead, hats) built
in lab.py. We push the mix (as 2-channel, like a real stereo file) through common lossy chains with ffmpeg, then split
every decoded copy with the SAME oracle soft masks (computed from the true
stems, the best a mask can ever do). Any drop in SDR is damage the source copy
did, not the separator.

Usage: python3 source_ceiling.py            (needs numpy + ffmpeg)
"""
import numpy as np
import lab

N_FFT = 4096
stems = lab.synth_stems(seed=7)
mix, stems = lab.mixdown(stems)
masks = lab.ratio_masks(stems, N_FFT, power=2.0)

AAC = lambda k: ("m4a", ["-ac", "2", "-c:a", "aac", "-b:a", k])
MP3 = lambda k: ("mp3", ["-ac", "2", "-c:a", "libmp3lame", "-b:a", k])
OPUS = lambda k: ("opus", ["-ac", "2", "-c:a", "libopus", "-b:a", k])
chains = [
    ("lossless WAV (your bounce)", []),
    ("AAC 256k", [AAC("256k")]),
    ("AAC 128k", [AAC("128k")]),
    ("Opus 128k", [OPUS("128k")]),
    ("MP3 128k", [MP3("128k")]),
    ("AAC 128k -> MP3 192k", [AAC("128k"), MP3("192k")]),
    ("AAC 128k -> MP3 128k -> AAC 128k", [AAC("128k"), MP3("128k"), AAC("128k")]),
]

def hf_share(x, lo=15000):
    X = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x)) ** 2
    f = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(x), 1 / lab.SR)
    return X[f >= lo].sum() / (X.sum() + 1e-20)

hf_ref = hf_share(mix)
names = list(stems)
print(f"synthetic mix: {len(mix)/lab.SR:.1f} s mono @ {lab.SR} Hz, oracle masks n_fft={N_FFT}")
print(f"{'source copy':36s} {'mix SNR':>8s} {'>15k kept':>9s} " +
      " ".join(f"{n:>6s}" for n in names) + f" {'mean':>6s}")
for label, chain in chains:
    if chain:
        y, lag = lab.codec_roundtrip(mix, chain)
    else:
        y, lag = mix.copy(), 0
    est = lab.separate_with_masks(y, masks, N_FFT)
    s = [lab.sdr(stems[n], est[n]) for n in names]
    snr = lab.sdr(mix, y)
    kept = 100 * hf_share(y) / hf_ref
    snr_txt = "   inf" if not chain else f"{snr:6.1f}"
    print(f"{label:36s} {snr_txt:>8s} {kept:8.0f}% " +
          " ".join(f"{v:6.1f}" for v in s) + f" {np.mean(s):6.1f}")
print("SDR in dB against the true synthetic stems (MDX-2021 definition). Higher is better.")
This is the real output from the box. The shared helpers (synthesis, STFT, SDR, codec round-trip with delay alignment) are in lab.py in the demos folder.
synthetic mix: 8.0 s mono @ 44100 Hz, oracle masks n_fft=4096
source copy                           mix SNR >15k kept   kick   bass    pad   lead   hats   mean
lossless WAV (your bounce)                inf      100%    9.6    9.1    9.1   16.9   18.1   12.6
AAC 256k                                 30.0       98%    9.6    9.0    9.1   16.9   13.7   11.7
AAC 128k                                 25.1       20%    9.6    9.0    9.0   16.9    2.4    9.4
Opus 128k                                23.7       65%    9.6    8.9    9.0   16.8    5.2    9.9
MP3 128k                                 23.0       20%    9.4    8.9    9.0   16.4    2.8    9.3
AAC 128k -> MP3 192k                     23.8       21%    9.5    9.0    9.0   16.7    2.4    9.3
AAC 128k -> MP3 128k -> AAC 128k         21.3       17%    9.4    8.8    8.9   16.2    1.5    9.0
SDR in dB against the true synthetic stems (MDX-2021 definition). Higher is better.

#### Reading it like an engineer
Source copy (synthetic test) | Mix SNR vs bounce | Energy kept above 15 kHz | Kick SDR | Lead SDR | Hats SDR
Lossless WAV bounce | reference | 100% | 9.6 dB | 16.9 dB | 18.1 dB
AAC 256k | 30.0 dB | 98% | 9.6 dB | 16.9 dB | 13.7 dB
AAC 128k | 25.1 dB | 20% | 9.6 dB | 16.9 dB | 2.4 dB
MP3 128k | 23.0 dB | 20% | 9.4 dB | 16.4 dB | 2.8 dB
AAC → MP3 → AAC, all 128k | 21.3 dB | 17% | 9.4 dB | 16.2 dB | 1.5 dB
Look at the columns, not the averages. The kick, bass, pad and lead hardly notice. They live where codecs spend their bits, and at 128 kbps their stems stay within a few tenths of a dB of the lossless result. The hats tell the other story. They go from 18.1 dB SDR on the bounce to 2.4 dB through a single 128k AAC encode, and to 1.5 dB after three generations. At 128k on a stereo file, both AAC and MP3 kept only about a fifth of the energy above 15 kHz.
A 2–3 dB SDR stem is the swirly, sandy cymbal you’ve heard out of every quick YouTube split. The separator didn’t invent that. The copy handed it a top end that was mostly codec.
Two honest caveats. This is one synthetic groove in mono, run through ffmpeg’s encoders. YouTube’s own encoder settings aren’t public in a form we can reproduce, so read these as directions, not as a measurement of YouTube itself. And the kick’s ceiling of about 9.6 dB is a limit of the 4096-point mask, not the codec. Long analysis windows blur transients. That’s a story for the model comparison.

### Find out what you actually have
The worst file in your archive is the one that says .wav and isn’t. A WAV decoded from an MP3 keeps the codec’s low-pass shelf forever, and nothing in the file name or the header will tell you. This little checker prints what ffprobe sees and then finds where the long-term spectrum drops off a cliff:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""fake_lossless_check.py: is this "WAV" really a first-generation file?

A WAV that was decoded from an MP3/AAC keeps the codec's low-pass shelf.
This prints the codec ffprobe sees, plus the frequency where the long-term
spectrum falls off a cliff. Usage: python3 fake_lossless_check.py file [file...]
With no arguments it builds SYNTHETIC test files from lab.py and checks those.
"""
import json, os, subprocess, sys, tempfile
import numpy as np
import lab

def probe(path):
    out = subprocess.run(["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-select_streams", "a:0", "-show_entries",
                          "stream=codec_name,sample_rate,bits_per_raw_sample,bit_rate",
                          "-of", "json", path], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout
    return json.loads(out)["streams"][0]

def cliff(path):
    x = lab.read_audio(path)
    n = 8192
    frames = [x[i:i + n] * np.hanning(n) for i in range(0, len(x) - n, n // 2)]
    P = np.mean([np.abs(np.fft.rfft(f)) ** 2 for f in frames], axis=0)
    f = np.fft.rfftfreq(n, 1 / lab.SR)
    PdB = 10 * np.log10(P + 1e-20)
    ref = np.median(PdB[(f > 2000) & (f < 8000)])
    # walk 250 Hz bands from 10 kHz up; the cliff is the last band within 30 dB of the mids
    top = 10000.0
    for lo in np.arange(10000, lab.SR / 2 - 250, 250):
        band = PdB[(f >= lo) & (f < lo + 250)]
        if band.size and band.mean() > ref - 30:
            top = lo + 250
    return top, None

def report(path):
    p = probe(path)
    top, shelf = cliff(path)
    verdict = "looks full-band" if top > 19500 else "LOW-PASS SHELF: probably decoded from a lossy file"
    print(f"{os.path.basename(path):28s} codec={p.get('codec_name'):10s} sr={p.get('sample_rate')} "
          f"content to ~{top/1000:4.1f} kHz  -> {verdict}")

if len(sys.argv) > 1:
    for pth in sys.argv[1:]:
        report(pth)
else:
    stems = lab.synth_stems(seed=7)
    mix, _ = lab.mixdown(stems)
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
        wav = os.path.join(d, "bounce_24bit.wav"); lab.write_wav(wav, mix)
        mp3 = os.path.join(d, "tmp.mp3")
        subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-y", "-i", wav, "-ac", "2", "-c:a", "libmp3lame", "-b:a", "128k", mp3], check=True)
        fake = os.path.join(d, "fake_lossless_from_mp3.wav")
        subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-y", "-i", mp3, "-ac", "1", "-c:a", "pcm_s24le", fake], check=True)
        m4a = os.path.join(d, "tmp.m4a")
        subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-y", "-i", wav, "-ac", "2", "-c:a", "aac", "-b:a", "128k", m4a], check=True)
        fake2 = os.path.join(d, "fake_lossless_from_aac.wav")
        subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-y", "-i", m4a, "-ac", "1", "-c:a", "pcm_s24le", fake2], check=True)
        print("SYNTHETIC files (built from lab.py):")
        for pth in (wav, fake, fake2):
            report(pth)
SYNTHETIC files (built from lab.py):
bounce_24bit.wav             codec=pcm_s24le  sr=44100 content to ~22.0 kHz  -> looks full-band
fake_lossless_from_mp3.wav   codec=pcm_s24le  sr=44100 content to ~16.8 kHz  -> LOW-PASS SHELF: probably decoded from a lossy file
fake_lossless_from_aac.wav   codec=pcm_s24le  sr=44100 content to ~17.5 kHz  -> LOW-PASS SHELF: probably decoded from a lossy file
All three files say pcm_s24le, 44.1 kHz. The header has no idea. The spectrum knows: real content to 22 kHz on the true bounce, and a hard shelf around 17 kHz on the two that came from 128k lossy files. Run it on anything you find before you trust it. A shelf near 16–20 kHz means a lossy ancestor somewhere.

### The order that gets you the best stems
1. Dig for the first generation. Check old bounce folders and external drives. Search your sent mail for the WAV you sent the mastering engineer. Look at your distributor’s dashboard, since some keep the file you delivered. Ask collaborators and the studio that tracked you. A 16-bit master from 2014 beats a 2024 upload every time.
2. If YouTube really is all that’s left, use the official download. YouTube Studio for your own channel, Takeout for the whole archive. For a band or label channel, ask whoever controls it. Don’t point a ripper at a video you don’t control.
3. Decode once, to WAV, and archive that file. ffmpeg -i upload.mp4 -vn -c:a pcm_s24le song.wav. Converting doesn’t add quality back. It stops the next tool from encoding it again. Every “export as MP3 to save space” in the chain is another row down that table.
4. Ask for the fewest stems that do the job. Vocals, drums, bass and other is the most mature split in published benchmarks. Separate guitar and piano stems are handy, but similar timbres bleed into each other more.
5. Split locally, audition, then null-test. Sum the stems back together and subtract the original. The leftover tells you what the separator dropped or invented, and it’s often a quick read on how much the source copy hurt.
6. Export stems as WAV. They’re working files. Compress the delivery, never the parts.
For the splitting step, a local tool keeps the whole thing in your room. DeepSplit runs Demucs- and MDX-style models on your own computer, from two stems up to drum sub-separation, and writes lossless stems. If you’re working from an upload of your own unreleased demo, that matters. The file never has to go to someone else’s server just to be taken apart.

### When the lossy copy is all you’ll ever have
Sometimes the master is truly gone. Then you’re working with the stems the copy allows, and a few habits help.
- Trust the low and mid stems. Vocal, bass, kick and most of the snare body came through our test nearly untouched. Build the remix around those.
- Replace, don’t rescue, the top end. Swirly hats are codec damage. Re-program them, or layer a clean shaker or ride over a filtered version of the original, instead of boosting 12 kHz on something that’s mostly noise.
- Don’t high-shelf the vocal to “restore air.” You’ll be turning up quantization noise. A gentle exciter driven from the 3–6 kHz region tends to sound more honest than EQ above the shelf.
- Measure after you rebuild. A remix built from separated parts still has to hit the same delivery numbers. Re-encoding it on the way out costs peak headroom again, as Re-encoding eats true-peak headroom shows. Leave margin for it.
When the new version is printed, a pass through CoProducer’s analyzer is a good last look: loudness, true peak and the stereo picture, measured on your own machine, before the file heads back to the platform it came from.
Note: The short version: your rights, then your earliest copy, then one decode to WAV, then a local split. Everything after that is taste.
Q: Is it legal to split stems from a YouTube video?
A: It depends on whose audio it is. YouTube’s Terms don’t allow downloading content unless the service expressly authorizes it or you have permission from YouTube and the rights holders. For your own uploads, YouTube Studio offers a download. For anyone else’s song, get permission or a licensed copy first.
Q: How do I download a video I uploaded myself?
A: Sign in to YouTube Studio, open Content, pick the video, and choose Download from its menu. YouTube’s help page says you get an MP4 at 720p or 360p. Google Takeout can export all your uploads at once.
Q: Why do my separated hi-hats sound swirly?
A: Most of the time it’s the source copy. Lossy codecs drop or coarsen the top octave, and the separator then has to assign codec noise to some stem. In our synthetic test the hats lost most of their SDR at 128 kbps while kick and bass barely moved.
Q: Will converting the MP4 audio to WAV improve the stems?
A: No. Converting to WAV only stops further damage. Decode once to WAV and work from that file so you don’t stack another lossy generation on top.
Q: How many stems should I ask for?
A: Ask for the fewest that do the job. Four stems (vocals, drums, bass, other) are the most mature in published benchmarks. Extra guitar or piano stems are useful, but expect more bleed between similar instruments.

---

## Demucs vs MDX-Net: what each separator gets wrong, and why
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/demucs-vs-mdx-net-stem-separation-compared.html
Section: Stems · 8 October 2026 · 11 min
Summary: Demucs vs MDX-Net from the published benchmarks and a runnable window test: who wins drums and bass, who wins vocals, and how to hear it.

Demucs and MDX-Net each fail in their own way. In the published 2021 Music Demixing Challenge numbers, Hybrid Demucs led on drums and bass, and KUIELab-MDX-Net led on vocals and the catch-all “other” stem. The reason is representation. A model that thinks in long spectrogram windows resolves pitch beautifully and smears attacks. A model that thinks in waveforms keeps the hit and fights with sustained harmony. Choose by the stem you need, and judge the result with your ears and a null test, not with a single score.
Every forum thread on this question ends the same way. Someone posts “Demucs for drums, MDX for vocals,” someone else says the opposite, and nobody shows their work. The truth is more interesting than a tier list. These two families are two answers to one hard trade-off, and once you can hear that trade-off, you can choose a model per stem instead of picking a team.

### Two families, and how they blurred
The original Demucs from Meta’s research team was a waveform model. It was a U-Net that took raw samples in and put raw samples out, with a recurrent layer in the middle for longer context. Spectrogram models came at the problem from the other side. They look at a time-frequency picture of the mix and predict how much of each tile belongs to each source.
That neat split didn’t last. Hybrid Demucs (Défossez, 2021) runs a waveform branch and a spectrogram branch side by side, shares a core between them, and sums their outputs. The paper reports that it won the Sony-organized Music Demixing Challenge 2021. Hybrid Transformer Demucs (Rouard, Massa and Défossez, 2022), the “htdemucs” you see in most tools today, swaps the innermost layers for a cross-domain Transformer. With extra training data and per-source fine-tuning it reached 9.0 dB SDR on MUSDB HQ, and 9.2 dB with sparse attention.
KUIELab-MDX-Net (Kim, Choi and colleagues), the model behind the “MDX” name, was blended from the start. It uses four spectrogram U-Nets, one per source, plus a small mixer network, and blends the result with a pretrained Demucs for the time-domain side. Per the authors, it placed second on leaderboard A and third on leaderboard B of the same challenge. So “Demucs versus MDX” really means “a waveform-first hybrid versus a spectrogram-first blend.”

### What the published numbers say
Here are the MDX 2021 hidden-test results for Track A (MUSDB-only training), as reported in the Hybrid Demucs paper. The scores are in the challenge’s SDR, higher is better:
Model (MDX 2021, Track A) | Overall | Drums | Bass | Other | Vocals
Hybrid Demucs | 7.33 | 8.04 | 8.12 | 5.19 | 7.97
KUIELab-MDX-Net | 7.24 | 7.17 | 7.23 | 5.63 | 8.90
Almost a dB apart on drums and bass, almost a dB the other way on vocals, and nearly tied overall. The same paper ran a listening test on MUSDB. Listeners rated KUIELab-MDX-Net best for vocal quality, and rated Hybrid Demucs much better for low bleed across sources. Défossez also names each family’s signature flaw plainly: phase inconsistency in spectrogram methods can make attacks sound hollow, and waveform Demucs vocals can carry a crunchy static.
That’s the whole forum argument, settled by the people who built the models. The rest of this essay is about why it happens, and how to check it on your own material.

### The trade-off you can run
Any time-frequency method has to choose a window. Long windows separate close pitches, like a 48 Hz kick tail and a 55 Hz bass note, but they spread each event across their whole length. Short windows pin events in time but blur pitch. MDX-Net leans into this openly: the paper lists a different FFT size per source, 6144 for vocals, 4096 for drums, 16384 for bass and 8192 for other.
To isolate the effect of the window from any model’s mistakes, this script uses oracle masks. They’re built from the true stems of a synthetic mix, so they’re the best a mask can ever do at each window size. It also measures kick pre-echo, the energy that leaks into the 20 ms before each hit, and shows why researchers moved to scale-invariant SDR.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""window_tradeoff.py: why spectrogram separators and waveform separators fail
differently, shown with oracle masks on a SYNTHETIC mix (lab.py).

For each STFT size we build the best possible soft mask from the true stems
and score every stem. Short windows keep the kick's attack; long windows
resolve the bass and pad harmonics. Then we measure kick pre-echo (energy
smeared into the 20 ms before each hit) and show why SI-SDR exists.
Usage: python3 window_tradeoff.py   (numpy + lab.py)
"""
import numpy as np
import lab

stems = lab.synth_stems(seed=7)
mix, stems = lab.mixdown(stems)
names = list(stems)
sizes = [512, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192, 16384]
best = {n: (-99, None, None) for n in names}

print("oracle soft-mask SDR (dB) by STFT size, SYNTHETIC 92 BPM mix")
print(f"{'n_fft':>6s} {'ms':>6s} " + " ".join(f"{n:>6s}" for n in names) + f" {'mean':>6s}")
for nf in sizes:
    est = lab.separate_with_masks(mix, lab.ratio_masks(stems, nf), nf)
    s = [lab.sdr(stems[n], est[n]) for n in names]
    for n, v in zip(names, s):
        if v > best[n][0]:
            best[n] = (v, nf, est[n])
    print(f"{nf:6d} {1000*nf/lab.SR:6.1f} " + " ".join(f"{v:6.1f}" for v in s) + f" {np.mean(s):6.1f}")

print("\nper-stem best window (the MDX-Net idea: a different n_fft per source)")
for n in names:
    print(f"  {n:5s} best at n_fft={best[n][1]:5d}  SDR {best[n][0]:5.1f} dB")
print(f"  mean of per-stem bests: {np.mean([best[n][0] for n in names]):.1f} dB")

# kick pre-echo: energy in the 20 ms before each onset, relative to the 20 ms after
k = stems["kick"]
on = np.where((np.abs(k[1:]) > 0.05) & (np.abs(k[:-1]) <= 0.05))[0]
on = [o for i, o in enumerate(on) if i == 0 or o - on[i - 1] > lab.SR // 4]
w = int(0.02 * lab.SR)
def pre_echo(x):
    pre = sum(np.sum(x[o - w:o] ** 2) for o in on if o > w)
    post = sum(np.sum(x[o:o + w] ** 2) for o in on)
    return 10 * np.log10(pre / post + 1e-12)
print("\nkick pre-echo (20 ms before hit vs 20 ms after; lower is cleaner)")
print(f"  true kick stem          : {pre_echo(k):6.1f} dB")
for nf in (512, 4096, 16384):
    e = lab.separate_with_masks(mix, lab.ratio_masks(stems, nf), nf)["kick"]
    print(f"  oracle mask n_fft={nf:5d} : {pre_echo(e):6.1f} dB")

# SDR vs SI-SDR: turn a good estimate down 6 dB
e = best["lead"][2]
print("\nscale check on the lead estimate")
print(f"  as is      : SDR {lab.sdr(stems['lead'], e):5.1f} dB   SI-SDR {lab.si_sdr(stems['lead'], e):5.1f} dB")
print(f"  -6 dB gain : SDR {lab.sdr(stems['lead'], 0.5*e):5.1f} dB   SI-SDR {lab.si_sdr(stems['lead'], 0.5*e):5.1f} dB")
Real output, synthetic audio (the groove from lab.py: kick, bass, pad, vowel-like lead, hats):
oracle soft-mask SDR (dB) by STFT size, SYNTHETIC 92 BPM mix
 n_fft     ms   kick   bass    pad   lead   hats   mean
   512   11.6    7.8    7.9    8.7   13.5   18.0   11.2
  1024   23.2    7.8    7.7    8.9   15.5   18.1   11.6
  2048   46.4    8.5    8.2    8.8   16.3   18.1   12.0
  4096   92.9    9.6    9.1    9.1   16.9   18.1   12.6
  8192  185.8   10.5    9.7    9.3   16.9   18.1   12.9
 16384  371.5   10.8   10.0    9.5   16.7   17.7   12.9

per-stem best window (the MDX-Net idea: a different n_fft per source)
  kick  best at n_fft=16384  SDR  10.8 dB
  bass  best at n_fft=16384  SDR  10.0 dB
  pad   best at n_fft=16384  SDR   9.5 dB
  lead  best at n_fft= 8192  SDR  16.9 dB
  hats  best at n_fft= 4096  SDR  18.1 dB
  mean of per-stem bests: 13.1 dB

kick pre-echo (20 ms before hit vs 20 ms after; lower is cleaner)
  true kick stem          : -120.0 dB
  oracle mask n_fft=  512 :  -22.8 dB
  oracle mask n_fft= 4096 :  -18.2 dB
  oracle mask n_fft=16384 :  -17.2 dB

scale check on the lead estimate
  as is      : SDR  16.9 dB   SI-SDR  16.9 dB
  -6 dB gain : SDR   5.8 dB   SI-SDR  16.9 dB

#### What that tells you
SDR loves long windows, even for the kick. Kick SDR climbs from 7.8 dB at 512 points to 10.8 dB at 16384. That’s because most of a kick’s energy is its low sine tail, and a long window is what pulls that tail apart from the bass. Bass and pad follow the same curve. The hats don’t care at all, about 18 dB everywhere.
Your ears hear the other column. The true kick has no energy before the hit (the −120 dB is just our floor). A 512-point mask leaks a ghost at −22.8 dB, and a 16384-point mask leaks one at −17.2 dB. That’s the soft “fff-THUMP” pre-echo on separated drums, and the window that won on SDR made it worse. A score that sums error energy over the whole file will happily trade a smeared transient for a cleaner tail.
Choosing per stem helps. Taking the best window for each stem raises the mean from 12.9 dB, the best single size, to 13.1 dB. It’s a small gain with oracle masks. With real models it’s the logic behind per-source FFT sizes and blending.
Watch how a score is defined. Turning a perfectly good lead estimate down 6 dB drops plain SDR from 16.9 dB to 5.8 dB, while SI-SDR stays at 16.9 dB. Le Roux and colleagues argue the case in “SDR – half-baked or well done?”. If a tool’s marketing quotes an SDR, ask which one, and on what test set.
A caveat that should keep everyone humble. Oracle masks are a ceiling for masking, not for models. The HT Demucs paper lists an ideal-ratio-mask oracle at 8.22 dB on MUSDB HQ, and its best model at 9.20 dB. Hybrid models that predict complex spectra or waveforms can beat a magnitude mask. Our synthetic groove shows you the trade-off. It doesn’t rank real models.

### Choosing by stem, in practice
You need | Lean toward | Listen for | Quick fix
Acapella, vocal for a remix | MDX-style vocal model | Snare ghosts, hollow “s” sounds | Gate between phrases, de-ess gently
Drum loop or breaks | htdemucs | Pre-echo before hits, cymbal swirl | Transient shaper, short fade-in on each chop
Bassline | htdemucs | Kick thump riding the bass | Sidechain-style ducking keyed from the drum stem
Instrumental or karaoke | Either; blend if you can | Reverb tails left behind from the vocal | Null test, then decide if the leftover matters
Pads, keys, “other” | MDX-style | Watery, phasey sustain | Accept a little bleed; it often glues
None of this replaces your ears. Separators are trained on particular data, and a dense trap mix, a jazz trio and a live rock room will each surprise you. Treat the table as a place to start.

### Decoding the model names in a menu
Stem tools tend to show you a menu of names that sound like firmware versions, so here’s a quick translation. “htdemucs” is Hybrid Transformer Demucs, the v4 release. “htdemucs_ft” is the per-source fine-tuned version: four models, one per stem, slower and usually a bit cleaner. “htdemucs_6s” adds guitar and piano stems. The Demucs README calls that six-source model experimental and warns of a lot of bleeding in the piano stem, so treat it that way. “MDX” on its own usually means a model descended from the KUIELab challenge work. “MDX23C” is a later, community-trained successor, and “Roformer” names usually point to band-split Transformer designs, the line of work that grew out of Band-Split RNN, which the HT Demucs paper itself names as its strongest competitor.
Two practical rules come out of that. More stems doesn’t mean better stems. Each extra source is another chance for two similar timbres to trade energy, so start with four and only go wider when you actually need the guitar on its own. And the newest name isn’t automatically the best one for your record. The benchmarks are averages over pop and rock multitracks. A sparse 808 record or a bowed-string arrangement can rank models differently, and that’s exactly why the five-minute audition below beats any chart.

### How to audition two models without fooling yourself
1. Use the same source. Same WAV, same sample rate, no re-encode between runs. A lossy source takes away more than the model difference adds back.
2. Level-match the stems. A stem that’s 1 dB louder sounds “better.” Match by RMS or LUFS before you compare. This is the SI-SDR lesson in practice.
3. Solo the transients first. Loop two bars of drums and listen right before each hit. Pre-echo is the fastest tell between the families.
4. Then listen in the mix. A stem that sounds rough soloed can sit perfectly once the rest of the track is playing.
5. Null-test. Add all the stems up, flip polarity, sum with the original. A loud residual means the model dropped or invented something.
If you’d rather not wire this up by hand, DeepSplit runs htdemucs-, MDX23C- and Roformer-class models locally, so you can split the same file several ways on your own machine and compare the results without any upload in between.
Once a rebuild is done, the transient you were fighting is still what the limiter sees. Crest factor is not loudness covers what a softened attack does to your master, and checking the summed stems in mono with a phase-correlation pass catches the phasey sustain that spectrogram bleed leaves behind.
Note: The one-line answer: Demucs-family for the hits and the low end, MDX-family for the voice, a blend when it matters. Then trust the null test over the leaderboard.
Q: Is Demucs or MDX-Net better?
A: Neither wins everywhere. In the MDX 2021 challenge results, Hybrid Demucs scored higher on drums and bass, and KUIELab-MDX-Net scored higher on vocals and the ‘other’ stem. Choose by the stem you need.
Q: Is Demucs a waveform model or a spectrogram model?
A: Both, these days. The original Demucs worked on waveforms. Hybrid Demucs (v3) and Hybrid Transformer Demucs (v4) run a waveform branch and a spectrogram branch together and add their outputs.
Q: What does SDR actually measure?
A: It compares the energy of the true stem with the energy of the error, in dB. Higher is better. It doesn’t weight errors by how audible they are, so a transient smeared before the hit can hide inside a good score.
Q: Why do separated drums sound hollow?
A: Spectrogram masking smears energy across the analysis window, and estimating phase is hard. The Hybrid Demucs paper notes that phase inconsistency in spectrogram methods can make attacks sound hollow.
Q: Should I ensemble two models?
A: Blending is a sound idea, and it’s what KUIELab-MDX-Net itself does with Demucs for drums and bass. Null-test the blend against the mix and listen to transients before you trust it.

---

## Before a cloud stem splitter gets your unreleased song, read four clauses
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/cloud-stem-splitter-privacy-unreleased-music.html
Section: Local-first · 8 October 2026 · 10 min
Summary: Uploading an unreleased track to a cloud stem splitter is a rights decision. Four terms clauses to read, and how to prove a split stays local.

A cloud stem splitter needs your whole song on its servers, and an unreleased song is the most sensitive file you own. Before you upload one, read four clauses in the terms: the license you grant, how long they keep the file, whether they can train on it, and who else processes it. Don’t count on a renamed file to hide anything, because audio can be identified from its content. If the track isn’t out yet, split it on your own machine, and prove that “local” really is local by running the split with the network turned off.
You know the moment. It’s late, the record is almost done, and you want the acapella to send a remixer, or the drum stem to check a collision. A browser tab promises stems in ninety seconds. You drag the bounce in, and the progress bar starts. Somewhere in that bar, a copy of a song nobody else has heard just landed on a computer you’ll never see.
That might be fine. Plenty of services handle files carefully, and for released music the risk is small. But this site already has an essay on uploading an unreleased master for mastering, and stem splitting raises the stakes in a specific way. You aren’t just sending the mix. You’re asking the service to produce the most reusable pieces of it: the clean vocal, the isolated beat. That’s the stuff that gets leaked, bootlegged or flipped.

### The four clauses worth five minutes
We aren’t going to quote any one company here. Terms change, and a quote that was accurate in spring is wrong by fall. What doesn’t change is where the important sentences live. Open the terms of service and the privacy policy, search for these words, and read the paragraph around each hit.
Clause | Search for | Reassuring wording | Wording that should slow you down
License you grant | “license”, “royalty-free”, “sublicensable” | A license limited to processing your request | Worldwide, sublicensable, “to operate and improve our services”
Retention | “retain”, “delete”, “days” | Deleted automatically after a stated short period, including backups | “As long as necessary” or no period at all; deletion only on request
Training | “train”, “machine learning”, “improve” | An explicit statement that uploads are never used for training | “Improve our models,” or an opt-out buried in settings
Sub-processors | “third parties”, “sub-processors”, “service providers” | A named list, with storage regions | Unnamed partners; a broad right to share with affiliates
Two habits make this quicker. Screenshot or save the page on the day you upload, because a future edit doesn’t change what you agreed to then. And remember the license and the retention clause work together. A narrow license on a file kept forever, or a broad license on a file deleted in an hour, are very different risks from a broad license on a file kept forever.
Even the big platforms spell out how broad an upload license can be. YouTube’s Terms, for instance, take a worldwide, non-exclusive, royalty-free, sublicensable and transferable license to content you provide, and say YouTube may keep server copies of removed videos. That’s a reasonable deal for publishing. It would be a strange deal for “please split this demo.” Read for the deal you actually want.

### Renaming the file doesn’t hide the song
A common instinct is to upload as untitled_v2.wav and assume nobody can tell what it is. File names and hashes only identify exact bytes. Content identification works on the sound itself, and it survives the things we do to files every day. To show how little it takes, here’s a landmark fingerprint in about fifty lines. It pairs strong spectral peaks, the idea popularized by audio ID services. Everything it tests is synthetic.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""fingerprint_leak.py: renaming or re-encoding a file doesn't make it anonymous.

SYNTHETIC test. We build an "unreleased song" with lab.py, then make the kinds
of copies that end up on servers: a renamed copy, a 128k AAC transcode, a
12-second excerpt, a 6 dB quieter bounce, and its isolated lead stem. A
50-line landmark fingerprint (the peak-pair idea behind audio ID services)
still finds every one of them, while SHA-256 only catches the exact bytes.
An unrelated synthetic song is the control.
Usage: python3 fingerprint_leak.py   (numpy + ffmpeg + lab.py)
"""
import hashlib, os, shutil, tempfile
from collections import Counter
import numpy as np
import lab

def landmarks(x, n_fft=2048, hop=512):
    X, _ = lab.stft(x, n_fft, hop)
    S = np.log(np.abs(X) + 1e-9)
    peaks = []
    for t in range(S.shape[0]):
        row = S[t, 10:700]                       # ~200 Hz .. 15 kHz
        for f in np.argsort(row)[-5:]:           # 5 strongest bins per frame
            peaks.append((t, int(f) + 10))
    peaks.sort()
    hashes = []
    for i, (t1, f1) in enumerate(peaks):
        for t2, f2 in peaks[i + 1:i + 40]:
            dt = t2 - t1
            if 1 <= dt <= 32:
                hashes.append(((f1, f2, dt), t1))
    return hashes

def index(h):
    d = {}
    for k, t in h:
        d.setdefault(k, []).append(t)
    return d

def match(db, q):
    offs = Counter()
    for k, t in q:
        for t0 in db.get(k, ()):
            offs[t0 - t] += 1
    return offs.most_common(1)[0] if offs else (0, 0)

sha = lambda p: hashlib.sha256(open(p, "rb").read()).hexdigest()[:12]

song_stems = lab.synth_stems(seed=7)
song, song_stems = lab.mixdown(song_stems)
other, _ = lab.mixdown(lab.synth_stems(seed=99, bpm=128.0, key_shift=-5))
db = index(landmarks(song))

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    master = os.path.join(d, "unreleased_master.wav"); lab.write_wav(master, song)
    renamed = os.path.join(d, "untitled_final_v2.wav"); shutil.copy(master, renamed)
    aac, _ = lab.codec_roundtrip(song, [("m4a", ["-ac", "2", "-c:a", "aac", "-b:a", "128k"])])
    variants = [
        ("renamed copy (same bytes)", lab.read_audio(renamed), sha(renamed)),
        ("AAC 128k transcode", aac, "differs"),
        ("5 s excerpt from 1.5 s", song[int(1.5 * lab.SR):int(6.5 * lab.SR)], "differs"),
        ("-6 dB quieter bounce", 0.5 * song, "differs"),
        ("isolated lead stem only", song_stems["lead"], "differs"),
        ("CONTROL: unrelated song", other, "differs"),
    ]
    print(f"master sha256 {sha(master)}  landmarks indexed: {sum(len(v) for v in db.values())}")
    print(f"{'query':28s} {'sha256':>12s} {'score':>6s} {'offset(s)':>9s}  verdict")
    for name, x, h in variants:
        q = landmarks(x)
        off, votes = match(db, q)
        score = votes / max(len(q), 1)
        hit = score > 0.10
        print(f"{name:28s} {h:>12s} {score:6.3f} {off*512/lab.SR:9.2f}  {'IDENTIFIED' if hit else 'no match'}")
master sha256 b407e6fad71d  landmarks indexed: 128350
query                              sha256  score offset(s)  verdict
renamed copy (same bytes)    b407e6fad71d  1.000      0.00  IDENTIFIED
AAC 128k transcode                differs  0.978      0.00  IDENTIFIED
5 s excerpt from 1.5 s            differs  0.891      1.50  IDENTIFIED
-6 dB quieter bounce              differs  1.000      0.00  IDENTIFIED
isolated lead stem only           differs  0.157      0.00  IDENTIFIED
CONTROL: unrelated song           differs  0.062      0.00  no match
The SHA-256 column shows why hashing isn’t protection. Change a single sample and the hash is a different string. The score column shows the other side. The transcode scored 0.98, the excerpt was found at its real position, 1.50 s, and the quieter bounce matched perfectly. Even the isolated lead stem scored 0.157 against the full mix, while an unrelated control song scored 0.062.
Be honest about that last margin. A lone stem against a toy fingerprint is a thin match, and production systems are far better tuned in both directions. But the takeaway holds. Once a server has heard your song, it can recognize that song again, in new copies, in clips, sometimes in pieces. That isn’t an accusation against anyone. It’s just what audio is.

### Why stems raise the stakes
A finished mix is hard to reuse. A clean acapella or an isolated drum break is the most portable thing in your session. It drops into someone else’s project in seconds. When a cloud splitter keeps outputs as well as inputs, the most leak-ready version of your record now sits beside the original. So check whether the retention clause covers generated files too. They’re often treated separately, and sometimes they’re kept longer so you can download them again.
There’s a quieter point about registration, too. Unreleased music often isn’t registered with your PRO, your distributor or a copyright office yet. Proving the song was yours first is easier when the only copies are on your drives and your collaborators’ drives. Every extra copy adds a little noise to that story.
And think about the people on the record. A featured vocalist agreed to be on your song, not to have their dry voice sitting on a third-party server as a separate file. If someone else’s performance is in the bounce, uploading it is partly their decision too. A short text before you hit upload costs nothing and keeps a collaboration friendly.

### Prove “local” with the network off
“Offline” and “on-device” are easy words to put on a landing page. The test is easy too: take the network away and see whether the split still finishes. On Linux, unshare -rn starts a process in a fresh network namespace with nothing but a loopback interface, and it’s down. No root needed on most distros.
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# airplane_mode_test.sh: prove a local split needs no network.
# Runs a command inside a fresh Linux network namespace (unshare -rn, no root
# needed on most distros) after showing the network really is gone.
# Usage: ./airplane_mode_test.sh [your separator command...]
# Default: python3 offline_split.py (a SYNTHETIC oracle-mask split)
set -euo pipefail
if [ $# -eq 0 ]; then set -- python3 offline_split.py; fi
unshare -rn bash -c '
  echo "interfaces: $(ip -br link | awk "{print \$1, \$2}" | tr "\n" " ")"
  if curl -s -m 3 https://example.com >/dev/null; then
    echo "network: REACHABLE (test invalid)"; exit 1
  else
    echo "network: unreachable"
  fi
  "$@"
' _ "$@"
Real output from the box, running the synthetic split in offline_split.py:
interfaces: lo DOWN 
network: unreachable
split ok: kick=9.6dB bass=9.1dB pad=9.1dB lead=16.9dB hats=18.1dB
Swap in your own separator command and run it the same way. If it finishes, the split happened on your machine. If it hangs or errors, something wanted to phone home, maybe just a model download or a license check. Find out which before you trust it with a demo. On macOS or Windows, the low-tech version works: download the models once, pull the Ethernet cable, turn off Wi-Fi, and split.
One more check that matters: what part of a tool is local. Many products ship a desktop app and a web version side by side. The app may run everything on-device, while the web page sends audio to a server. Both can be honest products. Just know which one you’re using.

### If you decide to upload anyway
Sometimes the cloud is the right answer. Your laptop can’t run the model, the deadline is in an hour, the terms read fine. Then shrink the exposure instead of pretending there isn’t any.
- Strip the tags. Exported WAVs and MP3s can carry title, artist, ISRC, even your DAW’s project path in the metadata. ffmpeg -i in.wav -map_metadata -1 -c copy clean.wav removes them without touching the audio. It won’t stop fingerprinting, as the test above shows, but it stops you from labeling the file for them.
- Send only the section you need. If the job is the hook vocal, upload the hook. The excerpt is still identifiable, but it’s less of the song.
- Use the deletion controls, then ask in writing. Delete inputs and outputs in the dashboard. Where privacy law gives you a right to erasure, a short email asking for deletion of both the upload and the generated stems leaves a record.
- Keep a ledger. One line per upload: date, service, file hash, terms URL, and the screenshot you saved. If a stem ever surfaces somewhere it shouldn’t, you’ll know where it went and what you agreed to.
None of these make an upload private. They make it smaller, labeled, and on the record. For a song that isn’t out yet, that’s the difference between a known risk and a vague one.

### A sane default for unreleased work
1. Released music: cloud is fine if you’re comfortable with the terms. The song is already public.
2. Unreleased, solo project: split locally. You lose nothing but a little setup.
3. Unreleased, collaborators involved: split locally and send stems directly, or through storage your team already uses and controls.
4. Label or client work: check your contract before anything leaves the room. Many agreements restrict third-party processing of unreleased masters outright.
For the local path, DeepSplit’s desktop app runs its separation models on your own computer, on GPU if you have one, and is built to work fully offline once installed. Run it through the network-off test above and you’ll know for sure. Its web-based YouTube splitter is a different path that goes through a server, so keep unreleased songs on the desktop side.
None of this is paranoia. It’s the same posture as keeping measurement local: the job doesn’t need a stranger’s disk, so don’t give it one by default. When the job really does, upload deliberately, after reading the four paragraphs that matter.
Note: Released? Use whatever you like. Unreleased? Read four clauses, or don’t upload at all, and prove “local” by pulling the plug.
Q: Do cloud stem splitters train on my uploads?
A: Some terms allow it and some forbid it, and the wording changes. Read the license, retention, training and sub-processor clauses for the specific service on the day you upload, and assume the broadest reading unless a contract says otherwise.
Q: If I rename the file, is it anonymous?
A: No. Audio can be identified from its content. In our synthetic test, a simple landmark fingerprint matched a renamed copy, a 128k AAC transcode, a 5-second excerpt and a quieter bounce, while a file hash only matched the identical bytes.
Q: Is uploading just the vocal stem safer?
A: It’s less of the song, but it isn’t anonymous either. The isolated lead still matched the full mix in our test, though with a much thinner margin than the full-mix copies.
Q: How do I know a ‘local’ app is really local?
A: Run it with the network off. On Linux, unshare -rn gives a process no network at all. On any OS, disconnect Wi-Fi and Ethernet, split a file, and see whether it finishes.
Q: Is cloud ever the right call?
A: Yes, for released material, for a machine that can’t run the models, or when you’ve read and accepted the terms. The point is to upload deliberately, not by default.

## Sampling from separated stems: chop around the bleed, not through it
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/sampling-from-separated-stems-workflow.html
Section: Sampling · 8 October 2026 · 11 min
Summary: A producer’s workflow for sampling from AI-separated stems: audit the bleed, restore the attack, null-test, match key, clear what you don’t own.

A separated stem is a great sample source, as long as you treat it like a recording with a known flaw. Before you chop, find out where the bleed lives. In drum stems it’s mostly the bass, under 120 Hz. Put the attack back that the mask softened. Null-test so you know exactly what any processing removed. Match the key with a clean pitch ratio. And clear anything you don’t own, because how you got the stem doesn’t change whose recording it is.
Chopping a full mix used to mean choosing the least-bad two bars: the break where the vocal drops out, the intro before the bass comes in. Separation changed that. Now you can lift the drums from bar 37, where the drummer finally opens the hats, or the bassline from the chorus without the singer on top. It’s a huge creative unlock, and it comes with a catch nobody puts on the box. The stem isn’t the original track. It’s an estimate, and estimates have fingerprints.
The good news is that those fingerprints are predictable. Once you know where to look, the cleanup takes minutes.

### First, what you’re allowed to sample
Quickly, because it matters more than any EQ move. The separator doesn’t launder anything. Pull a drum stem out of a commercial record and you’re still copying that record. US courts don’t even agree on how small a sample can be before it counts. In Bridgeport Music v. Dimension Films (6th Cir. 2005), the court wrote “Get a license or do not sample” about a two-second sample. In 2016 the Ninth Circuit called that reasoning unpersuasive in VMG Salsoul v. Ciccone. A split like that is exactly why clearance is the only answer that works everywhere.
So this workflow is for sources you have a right to: your own old records and sessions, recordings you’ve licensed, a collaborator’s track they’ve said yes to, sample packs whose license covers it, and genuinely public-domain recordings. That covers a lot of ground. Some of the best flips come from your own catalog, where you no longer have the session.

### A stand-in for a real model
To show the flaws honestly, we needed a separator that makes mistakes the way real ones do. Oracle masks are too perfect, so sampling_lab.py takes the oracle mask for a synthetic groove, blurs it by about 70 ms and three frequency bins, and pulls it 25% toward an even split. The result is a believable imitation of a model: decent on the voice, soft on transients, smeary on hats. Everything below is measured on that synthetic stand-in.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""sampling_lab.py: three checks before you chop a separated stem.

SYNTHETIC audio only (lab.py). A real model makes mistakes an oracle mask
doesn't, so we fake a model: the oracle mask blurred over ~70 ms and ~3 bins,
then pulled 25% toward an even split. Then:
  1. bleed audit: where the other instruments hide inside the "drum" stem, by band
  2. transient check: kick attack in the true vs separated drums, and after a
     simple transient restore
  3. null test + residual: stems sum back to the mix; mix minus a processed
     stem gives you back exactly what you removed
  4. key match: rubberband pitch shift of the bass stem, verified by FFT
Usage: python3 sampling_lab.py   (numpy + ffmpeg with rubberband + lab.py)
"""
import os, subprocess, tempfile
import numpy as np
import lab

NF = 4096
stems = lab.synth_stems(seed=7)
mix, stems = lab.mixdown(stems)
names = list(stems)

def blur(M, t=3, f=3):
    k = np.ones(t) / t
    M = np.apply_along_axis(lambda c: np.convolve(c, k, "same"), 0, M)
    k = np.ones(f) / f
    return np.apply_along_axis(lambda r: np.convolve(r, k, "same"), 1, M)

oracle = lab.ratio_masks(stems, NF)
imperfect = {k: 0.75 * blur(m) + 0.25 / len(names) for k, m in oracle.items()}
tot = sum(imperfect.values())
imperfect = {k: m / tot for k, m in imperfect.items()}
est = lab.separate_with_masks(mix, imperfect, NF)
print("imperfect-mask stems (stand-in for a real model), SDR dB:",
      " ".join(f"{k}={lab.sdr(stems[k], est[k]):.1f}" for k in names))

# 1. bleed audit in the drum stem (kick + hats)
drums_true = stems["kick"] + stems["hats"]
drums_est = est["kick"] + est["hats"]
X, meta = lab.stft(mix, NF)
Md = imperfect["kick"] + imperfect["hats"]
contrib = {k: lab.istft(lab.stft(v, NF)[0] * Md, meta) for k, v in stems.items()}
bleed = sum(contrib[k] for k in ("bass", "pad", "lead"))
target = contrib["kick"] + contrib["hats"]
f = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(mix), 1 / lab.SR)
B = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(bleed)) ** 2; T = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(target)) ** 2
print("\n1) bleed audit, drum stem: drums-to-bleed ratio by band (higher = cleaner)")
for lo, hi in [(20, 60), (60, 120), (120, 250), (250, 1000), (1000, 4000), (4000, 20000)]:
    sel = (f >= lo) & (f < hi)
    r = 10 * np.log10(T[sel].sum() / (B[sel].sum() + 1e-20) + 1e-20)
    share = 100 * B[sel].sum() / B.sum()
    print(f"   {lo:5d}-{hi:<5d} Hz  drums/bleed {r:6.1f} dB   {share:5.1f}% of all bleed")

# 2. transient check on kick hits
k = stems["kick"]
on = np.where((np.abs(k[1:]) > 0.05) & (np.abs(k[:-1]) <= 0.05))[0]
on = [o for i, o in enumerate(on) if i == 0 or o - on[i - 1] > lab.SR // 4]
def attack(x):
    a = int(0.005 * lab.SR); b = int(0.05 * lab.SR); p = int(0.02 * lab.SR)
    early = np.mean([np.sum(x[o:o + a] ** 2) for o in on])
    body = np.mean([np.sum(x[o:o + b] ** 2) for o in on])
    pre = np.mean([np.sum(x[o - p:o] ** 2) for o in on if o > p])
    return 10 * np.log10(early / body), 10 * np.log10(pre / body + 1e-12)
def restore(x, fast=0.0005, slow=0.02, amount=1.5):
    env = np.abs(x)
    def follow(e, tau):
        a = np.exp(-1 / (tau * lab.SR)); y = np.empty_like(e); s = 0.0
        for i, v in enumerate(e):
            s = a * s + (1 - a) * v; y[i] = s
        return y
    ef, es = follow(env, fast), follow(env, slow)
    g = np.clip((ef / (es + 1e-6)) ** (amount - 1), 1.0, 4.0)  # boost only where the hit outruns the body
    return x * g
print("\n2) kick attack: first 5 ms vs first 50 ms (higher = punchier); 20 ms pre-echo vs body (lower = cleaner)")
for label, x in [("true drums", drums_true), ("separated drums", drums_est),
                 ("separated + transient restore", restore(drums_est))]:
    a, p = attack(x)
    print(f"   {label:30s} attack {a:6.1f} dB   pre-echo {p:6.1f} dB")

# 3. null test and residual recovery
recon = sum(est.values())
print(f"\n3) null test: mix - sum(stems) peak = {lab.db(np.abs(mix - recon).max()):.1f} dBFS")
hp = np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(est["kick"] + est["hats"]) * (f > 150), n=len(mix))
other = recon - (est["kick"] + est["hats"])
removed = mix - other - hp
print(f"   high-passed the drum stem at 150 Hz; mix - (other stems + HP drums) = what you cut:")
print(f"   residual RMS {lab.db(np.sqrt(np.mean(removed**2))):.1f} dBFS, of which "
      f"{100*np.sum(np.abs(np.fft.rfft(removed))[f<150]**2)/np.sum(np.abs(np.fft.rfft(removed))**2):.1f}% sits below 150 Hz")

# 4. key match with rubberband
def peak_hz(x, lo=30, hi=90):
    X = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x[: 4 * int(lab.SR * 60 / 92)] * np.hanning(4 * int(lab.SR * 60 / 92))))
    fr = np.fft.rfftfreq(4 * int(lab.SR * 60 / 92), 1 / lab.SR)
    sel = (fr > lo) & (fr < hi)
    return fr[sel][np.argmax(X[sel])]
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    src = os.path.join(d, "bass.wav"); dst = os.path.join(d, "bass_up2.wav")
    lab.write_wav(src, est["bass"])
    subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-y", "-i", src, "-af",
                    f"rubberband=pitch={2**(2/12):.6f}", dst], check=True)
    up = lab.read_audio(dst)
print(f"\n4) key match: bass bar 1 fundamental {peak_hz(est['bass']):.1f} Hz -> "
      f"{peak_hz(up):.1f} Hz after +2 semitones (expected x{2**(2/12):.4f} = {peak_hz(est['bass'])*2**(2/12):.1f} Hz)")
Real output from the box:
imperfect-mask stems (stand-in for a real model), SDR dB: kick=6.8 bass=6.9 pad=7.3 lead=11.0 hats=2.2

1) bleed audit, drum stem: drums-to-bleed ratio by band (higher = cleaner)
      20-60    Hz  drums/bleed    4.5 dB    48.9% of all bleed
      60-120   Hz  drums/bleed   10.3 dB    28.9% of all bleed
     120-250   Hz  drums/bleed    8.3 dB     9.3% of all bleed
     250-1000  Hz  drums/bleed  -13.5 dB    10.9% of all bleed
    1000-4000  Hz  drums/bleed   -9.4 dB     1.7% of all bleed
    4000-20000 Hz  drums/bleed   19.0 dB     0.1% of all bleed

2) kick attack: first 5 ms vs first 50 ms (higher = punchier); 20 ms pre-echo vs body (lower = cleaner)
   true drums                     attack   -7.7 dB   pre-echo -120.0 dB
   separated drums                attack   -8.9 dB   pre-echo  -19.8 dB
   separated + transient restore  attack   -5.2 dB   pre-echo  -19.8 dB

3) null test: mix - sum(stems) peak = -240.0 dBFS
   high-passed the drum stem at 150 Hz; mix - (other stems + HP drums) = what you cut:
   residual RMS -27.8 dBFS, of which 100.0% sits below 150 Hz

4) key match: bass bar 1 fundamental 54.8 Hz -> 61.3 Hz after +2 semitones (expected x1.1225 = 61.5 Hz)

### 1. Audit the bleed before you chop
The audit splits the drum stem into what truly came from the drums and what leaked in from bass, pad and lead, then reports it band by band. The pattern is the one you’ll hear on almost every real drum stem: 78% of the bleed sits under 120 Hz, where the bass lives right under the kick. In the low mids, 250 Hz to 4 kHz, the bleed actually outweighs the drums by 9–14 dB. That isn’t a lot of energy, but it’s the pad and voice ghosting between hits. Above 4 kHz the stem is clean.
Band (synthetic drum stem) | Drums vs bleed | Share of all bleed | What to do with the chop
20–60 Hz | 4.5 dB | 48.9% | High-pass, then layer your own sub or kick
60–120 Hz | 10.3 dB | 28.9% | Keep the punch; duck it against your new bass
120–250 Hz | 8.3 dB | 9.3% | Usually fine; a narrow cut if the old bass note rings
250 Hz–4 kHz | −13.5 to −9.4 dB | 12.6% | Gate or trim between hits; this is the ghost pad and voice
4–20 kHz | 19.0 dB | 0.1% | Leave it; this is your snap and air
The practical lesson is to chop around the bleed, not through it. Start each slice right on the hit and end it before the next ghost swells up. Take the low end out of the chop and put your own underneath, which is the same chair problem as in Your kick and 808 are arguing in the same chair, just with an old bassline as the second person. If the old bass note under the kick is in a different key from your track, no amount of EQ will make it sit. High-pass it and move on.

### 2. Put the attack back, carefully
Masks smear energy across their window, so separated hits come out softer and get a faint pre-echo. In the test, attack (the first 5 ms against the first 50 ms) dropped from −7.7 dB on the true drums to −8.9 dB on the separated stem, and a ghost appeared at −19.8 dB in the 20 ms before each kick, where the original had nothing.
The simple transient restore in the script compares a fast and a slow envelope and boosts only where the hit outruns the body. It lifted attack to −5.2 dB, which is past the original. That overshoot is the warning. Transient shapers on separated drums are easy to overdo, and the result sounds clicky and fake. Dial it in by ear against the source. Notice too that the pre-echo didn’t move. A shaper can’t remove energy that sits before the transient. Only editing can: start the slice on the hit, with a 1–2 ms fade-in.

### 3. Null-test, then use the residual
With mask-based separation the stems sum back to the mix. The test shows a null at −240 dBFS, which is numerical silence. That gives you a superpower most producers never use: whatever you take away from a stem, you can get back exactly. After high-passing the drum stem at 150 Hz, the mix minus the other stems minus the processed drums is precisely the part you cut. In the test that was −27.8 dBFS RMS, all of it below 150 Hz.
Print that residual as its own track. Sometimes the “bleed” you removed is the thing that made the loop feel like a record: a room tone, the old bass breathing under the kick. Now it’s a fader instead of a loss. One caveat: not every model is mask-based. Some predict waveforms directly, and their stems may not null perfectly. Run the test anyway. The size of the residual tells you how much the model made up.

### 4. Match the key with a real ratio
A semitone is a frequency ratio of 21/12, so n semitones is 2n/12. Two up is ×1.1225. In the test, Rubber Band through ffmpeg’s rubberband filter moved the separated bass from 54.8 Hz to 61.3 Hz, against an expected 61.5 Hz. That’s within the FFT’s resolution and close enough for any tuner. Use a formant-aware shifter for vocals so a +3 doesn’t turn the singer into a cartoon. Keep shifts within a few semitones when you can, because bleed shifts along with the target and gets more noticeable the further you go.
Tempo works the same way, as a ratio. To pull a 92 BPM loop up to 100 BPM, stretch by 100/92 = 1.087. In ffmpeg, rubberband=tempo=1.087 changes the timing and leaves the pitch alone, and atempo does the same with a simpler algorithm that’s fine for small moves. Do the tempo stretch and the pitch shift as separate, deliberate steps, and print each one to a new file. If you only change the sample rate, the old turntable way, pitch and tempo move together. That can be exactly the color you want for a chipmunked soul flip, but then choose it on purpose, not by accident.

### The routine, start to finish
1. Confirm the rights. Yours, licensed, cleared or public domain. Write down which.
2. Use the best source you can get. A first-generation WAV, not a lossy copy. The cleanest-copy essay in this series shows why.
3. Split to four stems first. Go wider only when a part really needs its own lane.
4. Audit, then chop. Slice on the hits, clear the low end, trim the ghosts.
5. Restore the attack by ear, stopping before it clicks.
6. Null-test and keep the residual as an optional layer.
7. Key-match with clean ratios and check with a tuner.
8. Bounce the chops as WAV with the source noted in the file name or metadata, so clearance questions later take a minute instead of a week.
For the split itself, DeepSplit runs locally, does everything from two stems to separate kick, snare and hat lanes, and includes per-stem effects presets if you want a starting point before you do the careful work by hand. On your own catalog, keeping the files on your machine is the natural fit.
Once the beat is built, remember the separated parts were only ever a diagnosis of someone’s mix. Stems diagnose mixes — they do not replace them is the reminder. The chops are raw material. The record is still yours to mix.
Note: Rights, then the cleanest source. Audit, chop on the hit, restore by ear, null, key-match. Every flip after that is your taste, not the separator’s.
Q: Is sampling from a separated stem legal?
A: How you got the stem doesn’t change the copyright. If the recording isn’t yours, licensed, or public domain, clear it. In the Sixth Circuit, Bridgeport v. Dimension Films said ‘Get a license or do not sample’; the Ninth Circuit disagreed in VMG Salsoul v. Ciccone, so the law isn’t uniform. Clearance avoids the argument.
Q: Why does my separated drum loop have a ghost bassline?
A: The kick and bass share the same low frequencies, so a separator can’t fully pull them apart. In our synthetic audit, about 78% of the bleed in the drum stem sat below 120 Hz. A high-pass or a layered kick usually fixes it.
Q: How do I get the punch back on separated drums?
A: Use a transient shaper, gently. In our test it lifted attack from −8.9 dB to −5.2 dB, which is past the original −7.7 dB, so go by ear. It doesn’t remove pre-echo, so trim each chop’s start to the hit.
Q: What is a null test for stems?
A: Sum all the stems, flip polarity, and add the original mix. With mask-based separation the result should be near silence. After you process a stem, the same subtraction gives you exactly what you removed.
Q: How do I change the key of a sampled bassline?
A: Shift by a ratio of 2^(n/12) for n semitones, with a formant-aware pitch shifter such as Rubber Band. Check the result with a tuner or FFT. Our +2 semitone shift moved 54.8 Hz to 61.3 Hz, against an expected 61.5 Hz.

---

## Rumble you can’t hear is eating your limiter
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/subsonic-rumble-steals-limiter-headroom.html
Section: Low end · 7 October 2026 · 8 min
Summary: Subsonic rumble and DC offset barely move LUFS but still count toward peaks. Check under 20–30 Hz and filter gently before the limiter to win headroom back.

Subsonic rumble and DC offset barely register on a LUFS meter, but they still count toward your peaks, so the limiter works harder for loudness you can’t hear. Check what lives under 20–30 Hz, filter it gently before the limiter, and you get headroom back without changing the song.
Here’s the session. The mix sounds clean. The meter says the master is sitting where you want it. But the limiter is pumping more than it should for how loud the record actually feels, and every time you push for another dB the kick gets smaller. You solo things, you check the vocal, you blame the 808. Nothing sounds wrong.
That’s the tell. When the limiter is busy and your ears can’t find the reason, the reason is often below where your ears and most speakers go. A mic stand getting bumped. HVAC in the vocal booth. A sample pulled off vinyl with the turntable wobble still in it. A plugin that leaves a little DC offset behind. You can’t hear 9 Hz, and the loudness meter mostly ignores it too, because K-weighting rolls off the deep lows. Your peak meter counts every bit of it.

### Why the meter and the limiter disagree
Integrated LUFS is built to track how loud something feels, so it rolls off the low end on purpose. A peak limiter doesn’t care how anything feels. It sees a sample value and turns the whole mix down when that value crosses the ceiling. So a slow swell riding under the beat lifts every transient on top of it closer to the ceiling. The limiter hits harder on the hits that ride that swell, and you pay for it in punch.
DC offset is the same problem in its simplest form. If the whole waveform sits a little above zero, the positive peaks reach the ceiling early. It’s a few tenths of a dB on a mild case and more on a bad one, and you get nothing musical in return.

### A quick check before you blame the mix
This script reads a bounce and tells you the DC offset, how much of the file’s energy sits under 20 Hz and under your cutoff, and what a gentle 25 Hz high-pass would do to peaks and loudness. It only reports. It doesn’t change your file.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""rumble_check.py: find the low end you can't hear but your limiter can.
Usage: python3 rumble_check.py mix.wav [cutoff_hz]
Needs: numpy + ffmpeg on PATH.

Prints DC offset, how much of the file's energy sits under 20 Hz and
under the cutoff, and how much peak headroom a gentle high-pass gives
back while integrated loudness barely moves."""
import re, subprocess, sys
import numpy as np

SR = 48000
path = sys.argv[1]
cut = float(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 25.0
HPF = f"highpass=f={cut}:poles=2,highpass=f={cut}:poles=2"  # ~24 dB/oct, removes DC too

def decode(af=None):
    cmd = ["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", path, "-ac", "2", "-ar", str(SR)]
    if af:
        cmd += ["-af", af]
    raw = subprocess.run(cmd + ["-f", "f32le", "-"], capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
    return np.frombuffer(raw, dtype=np.float32).reshape(-1, 2)

def lufs(af=None):
    chain = (af + "," if af else "") + "ebur128=peak=true:framelog=quiet"
    err = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-nostats", "-hide_banner", "-i", path, "-af", chain,
                          "-f", "null", "-"], capture_output=True, text=True).stderr
    summ = err[err.rfind("Summary:"):]
    i = float(re.search(r"I:\s+(-?[\d.]+) LUFS", summ).group(1))
    tp = float(re.search(r"Peak:\s+(-?[\d.]+) dBFS", summ).group(1))
    return i, tp

db = lambda v: 20 * np.log10(max(v, 1e-12))
x = decode()
dc = x.mean(axis=0)
mono = x.mean(axis=1) - x.mean()
spec = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(mono)) ** 2
freqs = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(mono), 1 / SR)
total = spec[1:].sum() + 1e-20
share20 = spec[(freqs > 0) & (freqs < 20)].sum() / total
sharecut = spec[(freqs > 0) & (freqs < cut)].sum() / total

y = decode(HPF)
pk_in, pk_out = np.abs(x).max(), np.abs(y).max()
i_in, tp_in = lufs()
i_out, tp_out = lufs(HPF)

print(f"file              : {path}")
print(f"DC offset L/R     : {dc[0]:+.4f} / {dc[1]:+.4f}  ({db(abs(dc).max()):.1f} dBFS)")
print(f"energy < 20 Hz    : {100 * share20:.1f}% of the file")
print(f"energy < {cut:g} Hz    : {100 * sharecut:.1f}%")
print(f"sample peak       : {db(pk_in):+.2f} dBFS -> {db(pk_out):+.2f} dBFS after {cut:g} Hz HPF")
print(f"true peak         : {tp_in:+.1f} dBTP -> {tp_out:+.1f} dBTP")
print(f"integrated        : {i_in:.1f} LUFS -> {i_out:.1f} LUFS")
print(f"headroom returned : {db(pk_in) - db(pk_out):+.2f} dB of peak for {i_in - i_out:+.1f} LU of loudness")
if abs(dc).max() > 0.001 or sharecut > 0.02:
    print("verdict           : low end you can't hear is spending headroom. Filter before the limiter.")
else:
    print("verdict           : sub-audio looks clean. Leave the low end alone.")


### What it found on test signals
These are synthetic WAVs built on the box, labeled that way on purpose so nobody mistakes them for a real record. The base is a 140 BPM trap-style loop with a kick, a 49 Hz 808, a snare, and hats. The second version is the same loop with a 9 Hz swell, a few 18 Hz mic-stand bumps, and a small DC offset added.
Measurement | Clean loop | Loop + rumble
Integrated loudness | −23.3 LUFS | −23.2 LUFS
Sample peak | −6.9 dBFS | −4.1 dBFS
True peak | −6.9 dBTP | −3.4 dBTP
DC offset | −66 dBFS | −30 dBFS
Energy under 20 Hz | 0.2% | 76%
Read that again. The loudness meter says the two files are the same, within a tenth of a LU. The peak meter says the rumble version has 3.5 dB less true-peak headroom. Three quarters of the file’s energy is something nobody will ever hear.
Then we pushed both into the same limiter: +12 dB of drive into a −2.0 dBFS sample-peak ceiling. The rumble version came out at −14.1 LUFS with about 1.7 dB of average gain reduction. The same file with a 20 Hz high-pass first came out at −13.1 LUFS with about 0.7 dB of average gain reduction. Same drive and same ceiling, but a full LU louder, and the limiter worked less than half as hard. The clean loop, for reference, landed at −12.9.
One honest footnote. The limiter in that test held a sample-peak ceiling, and the synthetic hats still pushed true peak over it. That’s a separate fight, and it’s covered in True peak is what codecs clip. Rumble doesn’t cause it, but it does eat the margin you’d otherwise have for it.

### The catch: filtering isn’t free
On the clean loop, the same 25 Hz filter raised the peak by about 1 dB. Nothing was wrong down there to remove. All the filter did was shift the phase of the 49 Hz 808 and kick, and the waveform stacked a little differently. That’s why the script gives a verdict instead of telling you to always filter.
- If there’s real sub-audio junk (DC, energy under 20 Hz above a couple of percent, a peak that drops when you filter), filter it.
- If the low end is already clean, leave it alone. A reflexive 30 Hz cut on every master can cost a little weight and a little headroom for nothing.
- Mind your fundamentals. A tuned 808 can go down to E1 (41 Hz) or lower. Keep the cutoff well below the lowest note. Around 18–25 Hz is a safe start for most hip-hop and electronic records. Acoustic and orchestral sessions can usually sit a bit higher, around 25–30 Hz.

### Where to fix it, in order
1. At the source. Put a high-pass on the vocal, the acoustic guitar, the room mics, and any sample you lifted from vinyl. They have no business under 40–80 Hz anyway. That’s where most rumble comes from.
2. On the mix bus, gently. A 12–24 dB/oct high-pass around 20 Hz cleans up whatever is left without touching the 808. Linear-phase is an option if you hear the low end shift, but listen for pre-ringing on the kick.
3. Then the limiter. Re-check peak headroom and gain reduction. If the limiter suddenly relaxes, you just found free loudness.
4. Re-measure after any slow or screwed version. Slowing a track down moves everything lower, including rumble that used to sit at 25 Hz and is now down at 17. Check the ScrewAI render separately instead of trusting the full-speed numbers.
When the master is printed, dropping it into CoProducer is a good last look. It looks for DC and rumble evidence next to the true-peak and loudness readings, and only suggests a cautious high-pass when that evidence is strong, so you can see whether the limiter was fighting the song or the floor.
Note: Measure the bounce, split out the stem that’s carrying the rumble with StemSplit when you don’t have the session, and re-check the low end on the ScrewAI render before you ship the slowed version.
Q: Should I always high-pass my master at 30 Hz?
A: No. Filter when there’s measurable DC or sub-audio energy. On a clean mix a high-pass can shift low-end phase and even raise peaks slightly. Measure first.
Q: Will a high-pass make my 808 weaker?
A: Not if the cutoff sits well below the 808’s lowest note. Around 18–25 Hz with a gentle slope leaves a tuned 808 alone and removes rumble under it.
Q: Does DC offset really matter?
A: It shifts the whole waveform off center, so one side of it reaches the ceiling sooner. It’s small, but it’s headroom you get back for free.
