## Crest factor is not loudness
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/crest-factor-is-not-loudness.html
Section: Dynamics · 21 August 2026 · 7 min
Summary: Crest factor is peak-to-RMS height. LUFS is perceived loudness over time. You can raise crest and still miss −14 LUFS — or hit −14 with a crushed crest.

Crest factor describes peak-to-RMS height. LUFS describes perceived loudness over time. You can raise crest and still miss −14 LUFS, or hit −14 LUFS with a crushed crest. They answer different questions.

### Two numbers, two jobs
Integrated LUFS is what stores use to decide playback gain. Crest (and the related dynamic-range readouts in CoProducer) tell you whether the mix still has punch after you chase that lane. Treating them as synonyms is how people print a flat −14 and call it musical.
On Drippin, the repair moved LUFS from −11.92 toward −14.12 while clip count fell from 231,310 to 0. The crest story changed because overs were no longer glued to full scale — not because the arrangement grew taller.

### A faster diagnostic
If LUFS is hot and crest is already low, do not add another bus limiter. Take gain out. If LUFS is quiet and crest is huge, you may still be fine for streaming — quiet files can be turned up, which then reveals noise floor problems.
Measure both before you open a new plugin. That order saves the hour you would spend “making it slap” into a turn-down.
Note: Hear the public A/B on the homepage, then run your bounce through Analyze. Pro is $29 one-time if you already like the meter.
Q: Is higher crest always better?
A: No. Extreme crest can mean unused headroom or a mix that will jump when normalized. Aim for intentional dynamics inside a legal loudness lane.
Q: Where does CoProducer show this?
A: Dynamic range and related crest-style readouts sit beside LUFS and true peak in the report. Use them together.

---

## Phase correlation is a mono audition
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/phase-correlation-and-mono.html
Section: Stereo · 21 August 2026 · 7 min
Summary: Phase near 0 or negative means the mix thins or cancels in mono. CoProducer fails values under about 0.2. Auto-repair will not flip polarity for you.

Phase correlation near 0 or negative means the mix will thin or cancel in mono. CoProducer treats values under about 0.2 as a fail. Auto-repair will not flip polarity for you — that is mix work.

### Why stores still care
Phones, clubs, and some smart speakers collapse channels. A wide chorus that disappears in mono is not “creative stereo.” It is a delivery risk. Correlation is a cheap proxy for that audition.
If correlation fails, check doubled vocals, misaligned layers, and mid/side tricks that emptied the mid. Do not buy a loudness tool to fix a polarity problem.

### Order of operations
Fix phase in the session. Then print. Then measure LUFS and true peak. Reversing that order wastes renders.
CoProducer will caution on phase and leave it alone in the automatic plan. That restraint is intentional.
Note: The release checklist keeps phase ≥ 0.2 next to the loudness gates. Read it beside the meter checklist.
Q: Can a stereo widener pass correlation?
A: Sometimes on the meter, rarely in a real mono fold. Audition mono after every width move.
Q: Is 1.0 required?
A: No. Fully correlated mono sits near 1.0. Most finished stereo records sit comfortably above 0.2 without being mono.

---

## Quiet masters get turned up — and so does the noise
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/quiet-masters-and-noise-floor.html
Section: Noise · 21 August 2026 · 6 min
Summary: Streaming turn-up lifts quiet files. A −20 LUFS master may be gained up, which also lifts hiss, rumble, and room tone. Quiet is not a free pass.

Streaming turn-up applies to quiet files as well as turn-down to hot ones. A −20 LUFS master may be gained up, which lifts hiss, rumble, and room tone with it. Measure noise floor before you celebrate “dynamic.”

### Both directions of normalization
Engineers obsess over hot masters getting turned down. The other side matters: sparse, quiet prints get lifted. If your noise floor sits near −40 dBFS in a sparse verse, turn-up makes it obvious on earbuds.
CoProducer reports noise floor beside LUFS. Use it when the arrangement has long gaps.

### What auto-repair will try
A cautious high-pass may appear when rumble or DC evidence is strong. It will not invent a denoiser for air hiss. That is still mix or restoration work.
If the floor is the story, clean the session before you chase −14.
Note: Upload a quiet bounce to Analyze and read noise floor next to LUFS before you ship.
Q: Is −14 always louder than −16 after normalization?
A: Not in the way people mean. Playback gain aims for a similar lane; crest and spectrum still decide punch.
Q: Should I raise the master to avoid turn-up?
A: Raise intentional signal, not noise. Fix the floor first.

---

## When not to reach for the limiter
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/when-not-to-reach-for-the-limiter.html
Section: Limiting · 21 August 2026 · 8 min
Summary: Skip another limiter when clips are already non-zero, LUFS is only slightly hot, or the real problem is arrangement, noise, or a bad edit — not peak height.

Do not reach for another limiter when clipped samples are already non-zero, when LUFS is only slightly hot, or when the mix problem is arrangement. A limiter can park true peak; it cannot restore flattened transients.

### Three stops
If clips exist and you still have the session, fix the clip at the source. If true peak is high and clips are zero, a final true-peak cap is enough. If LUFS is hot and crest is gone, take gain out — more limiting only spends punch the store will not return.
Crazy Stacy’s public pair cleared 831 clips. BeatGoHard needed the ceiling more than a new mix. Different medicine.

### What CoProducer projects
The web analyzer projects post-repair stats from the same plan the desktop app would apply. It does not download a mastered WAV. That honesty keeps you from treating a website form like a mastering house.
Desktop is where Pedalboard/FFmpeg write the file.
Note: A/B the public pairs on the homepage, then decide whether your bounce needs a cap, a gain change, or a session recall. Pro is $29 one-time if that is the next step.
Q: Is a limiter always last?
A: For delivery true-peak control, yes — after loudness moves. In the mix, stop earlier.
Q: Can repair un-clip a vocal?
A: No. It can stop new overs. Flattened peaks stay flattened.

## Sample rate and bit depth are delivery hygiene
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/sample-rate-and-bit-depth-for-delivery.html
Section: Delivery · 21 August 2026 · 8 min
Summary: CoProducer fails sample rates under 44.1 kHz. Why 32 kHz fails delivery, when 44.1/48/96 are fine, what bit depth distributors want, and how to verify the bounce.

CoProducer fails sample rates under 44.1 kHz. A 32 kHz MP3 labeled MASTER is not a master. Bit depth and rate mistakes are cheap to prevent and expensive to explain to a distributor.
You already know the loudness and true-peak story. This gate is quieter. It does not change how the chorus hits. It decides whether the portal accepts the upload on Monday. Treat rate and depth like file naming: boring, visible, non-negotiable.

### Why 32 kHz fails — and what CoProducer flags
Most storefronts expect at least 44.1 kHz. Anything under that is usually a bounced-down preview, a voice-memo export, or an MP3 someone renamed. CoProducer’s release gate matches the checklist: sample rate ≥ 44.1 kHz. Fail it in private before the distributor fails you in public.
Wrong rate does not always sound broken on laptop speakers. Nyquist for 32 kHz is 16 kHz, so air and cymbals are already gone or aliased. The bigger problem is process: the file is not what the storefront asked for. If the report paints sample rate red, re-export from the session at a legal rate — do not argue with the meter.

### 44.1 vs 48 vs 96: when each is fine
44.1 kHz is still the music default — CD heritage, most sample libraries, and a huge chunk of distributor templates. If you mixed at 44.1 and the storefront says 44.1, deliver 44.1.
48 kHz is the video / game / broadcast lane, and plenty of producers work there for everything. Fine for music when the portal accepts it. If a partner insists on 44.1, convert once with a high-quality SRC on the final bounce — not three times across assistants’ laptops.
96 kHz helps when you are stacking nonlinear plugins, pitching, or archiving. It is not a loudness upgrade and it is not required for streaming. Shipping 96 when the portal wants 44.1/48 just means someone else resamples you, often worse than you would. Consistency beats fetish.
Rate | Fine when | Cargo cult when
44.1 kHz | Music delivery, matching a 44.1 session | You upsampled a 32 kHz MP3 and called it high-res
48 kHz | Video, games, portals that list 48 | You convert “just in case” without asking
96 kHz | Heavy processing, archive, clients who asked | You think the stream will sound “more 96”

### Bit depth: 16 vs 24 vs 32-float
Bit depth is headroom and noise floor while you work, not a vibe knob. Rough numbers: 16-bit theoretical noise floor sits around −96 dBFS; 24-bit around −144 dBFS. In a real room you never hear the bottom of 24-bit. What you hear is whether you clipped, or truncated without dither on the way down.
32-bit float forgives overs inside the box — keep it for mixing, stems, and archives. Most distributors want integer PCM, usually 24-bit WAV or FLAC, sometimes 16-bit for CD / legacy paths. Check the portal. When you go to 16-bit, dither. Truncation without dither adds grain on quiet fades. Staying at 24-bit for delivery usually needs no dither.

### Bounce checklist
Check | Target | Notes
Sample rate | ≥ 44.1 kHz; match the portal | Convert once, high-quality SRC
Bit depth | 24-bit PCM typical; 16-bit if asked | Dither only when reducing depth
File type | WAV or FLAC as required | Not an MP3 labeled MASTER
True peak / LUFS | Same six-gate checklist | Rate and depth do not fix clips
Naming | Include rate and depth in the filename | Stops assistants guessing
A bounce named Title_master_48k_24b.wav beats a folder of FINAL_FINAL2.mp3. Hygiene is half engineering and half labeling.

### Common traps
MP3 labeled MASTER. Lossy encode is a distribution format after the master exists, not the master. Export PCM first.
Resampling twice. Session at 48 → “preview” at 44.1 → “fix” back to 48. Each pass costs fidelity. Convert once on the ship bounce.
Cheap SRC. Real-time device converters are not all equal. For a release convert, use a known-good offline SRC, then re-measure.
Upsampling junk. Turning a 32 kHz voice memo into 96 kHz does not restore missing air. Fix the source session.

### How to verify
Read the file properties before you open the portal. ffprobe is enough:
ffprobe -v error -select_streams a:0 \
  -show_entries stream=sample_rate,bits_per_raw_sample,bits_per_sample,codec_name \
  -of default=nw=1 MASTER.wav
You want sample_rate=44100 or 48000, a PCM codec, and bit depth that matches the portal. If ffprobe shows mp3 or 32000, stop. Drop the same file on CoProducer’s analyze table — sample rate under 44.1 kHz fails the gate on purpose, beside LUFS, true peak, clips, phase, and score. Private red is cheaper than Monday morning email.
Note: Run the six-gate checklist in this essay before you open the distributor portal. Handbook version: audio quality checklist. Measure a file: Analyze.
Q: Is 96 kHz required?
A: No for most music delivery. Consistency and legality beat fetish sample rates. Deliver at the rate the storefront asks for, usually 44.1 or 48 kHz.
Q: Does CoProducer convert for you?
A: It measures and reports. Conversion is a separate bounce decision — fix the session or re-export at the right rate and depth.
Q: Should I deliver 32-bit float?
A: Keep 32-bit float for session and archive work. Most distributors want 16- or 24-bit PCM WAV/FLAC. Dither when you go to 16-bit.
Q: Why does CoProducer fail under 44.1 kHz?
A: Because most storefronts reject or silently upsample junk rates. A 32 kHz file is not a master, even if the filename says MASTER.

---

## How to use a reference track when mixing: match the loudness first, then compare
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/reference-matching-without-guesswork.html
Section: Reference · 21 August 2026 · 7 min
Summary: Turn the louder track down before you compare, or you’ll pick it every time. Then compare tonal balance and true peak, and copy the balance, not the peak.

To use a reference track well, turn it down to the same loudness as your mix before you compare anything. A louder track almost always sounds better, so an unmatched A/B tells you nothing. Once they’re matched, compare tonal balance, how loud the vocal sits and how big the low end is. Copy the balance. Don’t copy the reference’s peak level, because plenty of commercial masters are hotter than streaming will ever play them.
“Make it sound like that song” is the most common note in music, and the hardest one to act on by ear. You flip to the reference, it sounds huge, you flip back, your mix sounds small, and you start adding EQ and limiting until something breaks. Most of that frustration is a measuring problem, and it’s easy to fix.

### What is a reference track for?
A reference is a finished song you trust, used as a ruler. It tells you where your mix sits on the things you’ve stopped hearing after hours in the session: how bright the top end is, how much low end there is compared with everything else, and how forward the vocal sits.
It isn’t a template. Your song has a different key, arrangement and singer, so matching it number for number would be strange even if you could do it. What you want is to be in the same neighbourhood on the big things, so nothing about your mix sounds wrong next to it on a playlist.
Pick one or two references in the same genre and tempo range, released recently enough that they reflect how records in your lane sound now. Get the best file you can: a purchased WAV, FLAC or high-bitrate download. A stream has already been turned up or down and run through a codec, which is a whole topic of its own (don’t match a streamed reference).

### Why does the reference always sound better?
Because it’s louder. When two versions of the same thing are a couple of dB apart, we tend to hear the louder one as fuller, brighter and more exciting. That’s simply how our hearing works at different levels; the equal-loudness contours show that our sensitivity to bass and treble changes with level. So a reference that’s 5 dB hotter than your mix wins every blind test before you’ve listened for anything specific. It’s the same trap as mixing at a different volume every day.
The fix is to measure both in integrated LUFS (loudness units relative to full scale, measured the ITU-R BS.1770 way) and turn the reference down by the difference. Then switch between them quickly, a few seconds each, at the same spot in the song. Now whatever difference you hear is a real difference.

### How do I compare my mix to a reference by the numbers?
Here’s a small script that does the measuring and writes a level-matched copy of the reference for you. It needs Python 3, NumPy and FFmpeg. It reads loudness, loudness range and true peak with FFmpeg’s ebur128 filter, then compares tonal balance in six bands. Each band is shown relative to that file’s own total energy, so it doesn’t matter which file is louder.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""ref_compare.py: compare your mix with a reference track by the numbers, at matched loudness.
Usage: python3 ref_compare.py MIX REFERENCE [--write-matched]
Prints integrated loudness, loudness range (LRA), true peak and peak-to-loudness ratio (PLR) for both
(FFmpeg ebur128, ITU-R BS.1770 / EBU Tech 3342), then tonal balance per band relative to each file's
own total, so the comparison doesn't depend on which one is louder. With --write-matched it writes
reference_matched.wav: the reference turned down (or up) to your mix's loudness, for honest A/B listening.
Your files are only read. Needs: Python 3, NumPy, FFmpeg on PATH."""
import re, subprocess, sys
import numpy as np

BANDS = [("sub", 20, 60), ("bass", 60, 250), ("lowmid", 250, 800), ("mid", 800, 2500), ("pres", 2500, 6000), ("air", 6000, 18000)]

def meter(path):
    err = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-hide_banner", "-nostats", "-i", path, "-af", "ebur128=peak=true", "-f", "null", "-"],
                         capture_output=True, text=True).stderr
    g = lambda pat: float(re.findall(pat, err)[-1])
    return dict(I=g(r"I:\s+(-?[\d.]+) LUFS"), LRA=g(r"LRA:\s+([\d.]+) LU"), TP=g(r"Peak:\s+(-?[\d.]+) dBFS"))

def balance(path):
    raw = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", path, "-f", "f32le", "-ac", "1", "-ar", "48000", "-"],
                         capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
    x = np.frombuffer(raw, np.float32).astype(np.float64)
    P = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x)) ** 2; f = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(x), 1 / 48000)
    tot = P[(f >= 20) & (f < 18000)].sum()
    return [10 * np.log10(P[(f >= lo) & (f < hi)].sum() / tot + 1e-12) for _, lo, hi in BANDS]

def main(mix, ref, write=False):
    a, b = meter(mix), meter(ref)
    for d in (a, b): d["PLR"] = d["TP"] - d["I"]
    print(f"{'':12}{'LUFS':>8}{'LRA LU':>8}{'TP dBTP':>9}{'PLR dB':>8}")
    for name, d in (("your mix", a), ("reference", b)):
        print(f"{name:12}{d['I']:8.1f}{d['LRA']:8.1f}{d['TP']:+9.1f}{d['PLR']:8.1f}")
    gain = a["I"] - b["I"]
    print(f"\nreference is {-gain:+.1f} LU vs your mix. To A/B fairly, play it at {gain:+.1f} dB.")
    if b["TP"] > -1.0:
        print(f"reference true peak {b['TP']:+.1f} dBTP is over -1 dBTP: copy its balance, not its peak.")
    need = b["I"] - a["I"]
    print(f"matching its loudness would push your mix {need:+.1f} dB: true peak {a['TP'] + need:+.1f} dBTP before any limiting")
    print(f"\ntonal balance, dB relative to each file's total (loudness-independent)")
    ba, bb = balance(mix), balance(ref)
    print(f"{'band':8}{'Hz':>12}{'mix':>8}{'ref':>8}{'diff':>8}")
    for (n, lo, hi), x, y in zip(BANDS, ba, bb):
        flag = "  <-- look here" if abs(x - y) >= 3 else ""
        print(f"{n:8}{f'{lo}-{hi}':>12}{x:8.1f}{y:8.1f}{x - y:+8.1f}{flag}")
    if write:
        subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-y", "-i", ref, "-af", f"volume={gain:.2f}dB", "-c:a", "pcm_f32le", "reference_matched.wav"], check=True)
        print(f"\nwrote reference_matched.wav ({gain:+.1f} dB, 32-bit float so nothing clips)")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    args = [x for x in sys.argv[1:] if not x.startswith("--")]
    main(*args, write="--write-matched" in sys.argv)
To show it working without anybody’s real song, we generated two synthetic 30-second beats at 140 BPM. The “reference” is bright and driven hard into a simple limiter, the way plenty of commercial masters are. “Your mix” is the same kind of beat, darker, with a low shelf boosting the bottom and no limiter. This is what the script printed:
$ python3 ref_compare.py refs/mix.wav refs/reference.wav --write-matched
                LUFS  LRA LU  TP dBTP  PLR dB
your mix       -14.0     0.2     -3.6    10.4
reference       -8.6     0.3     +1.6    10.2

reference is +5.4 LU vs your mix. To A/B fairly, play it at -5.4 dB.
reference true peak +1.6 dBTP is over -1 dBTP: copy its balance, not its peak.
matching its loudness would push your mix +5.4 dB: true peak +1.8 dBTP before any limiting

tonal balance, dB relative to each file's total (loudness-independent)
band              Hz     mix     ref    diff
sub            20-60    -0.8    -1.0    +0.1
bass          60-250    -7.8    -7.7    -0.1
lowmid       250-800   -23.0   -18.6    -4.4  <-- look here
mid         800-2500   -28.3   -23.3    -5.0  <-- look here
pres       2500-6000   -29.4   -25.0    -4.3  <-- look here
air       6000-18000   -25.3   -21.0    -4.4  <-- look here

wrote reference_matched.wav (-5.4 dB, 32-bit float so nothing clips)

### How do I read the comparison?
Start at the top. The reference is 5.4 LU louder than the mix. Before you change a single EQ band, that alone explains why it sounded bigger. The script wrote reference_matched.wav, the reference turned down 5.4 dB to −14.0 LUFS, the same as your mix. Use that file for listening.
Next, the reference’s true peak. Its highest sample sits at −0.1 dBFS, which looks safe on a normal peak meter, but its true peak is +1.6 dBTP. True peak estimates the level of the real waveform between the samples, which is what a converter or a lossy encoder has to reproduce. Spotify’s guidance asks for masters below −1 dBTP, and below −2 dBTP for masters louder than −14 LUFS. This reference fails both. That’s fine for a reference you listen to, but it’s not something to copy (more on why in true peak is what codecs clip).
The last line of the top section shows what happens if you try anyway. Pushing your mix up 5.4 dB to match the reference’s loudness would put your true peak at +1.8 dBTP before any limiter touched it. You’d need several dB of limiting just to make it legal, and you’d be squashing your song to match a number that streaming will turn down again.
Then the tonal balance table. The sub and bass rows match within a dB, but everything from 250 Hz up sits 4 to 5 dB lower in your mix than in the reference. Because each column is relative to its own total, that doesn’t mean your mids are quiet in absolute terms. It means the low end is taking too big a share of the mix. That’s the classic home-studio balance problem, and it’s why a mix can sound dull and small next to a reference at the same loudness.

### What should I copy from a reference, and what should I leave alone?
Copy the relationships, because those survive every playback system:
- Tonal balance. If your low end takes a much bigger share than the reference’s, pull the low shelf down or tighten the bass and kick, then re-measure. Don’t try to fix it by boosting everything else, which just adds level.
- Vocal level against the beat. Listen at matched loudness to how far forward the vocal sits in the hook. This is easier to judge by ear than by meter.
- Low end against everything. How much the kick and 808 or bass fill the speakers compared with the rest of the song.
- Movement. Whether the chorus lifts over the verse, and by how much.
Leave these alone:
- Peak level and true peak. Keep your master under −1 dBTP, whatever the reference does.
- Integrated loudness, as a target. Pick the loudness lane your master needs (streaming turns loud masters down anyway). Use the reference’s loudness only to set your listening level.
- Exact EQ curves. A difference of 1 or 2 dB in a band is usually the song, not a problem. Fix differences of 3 dB or more first, and only if you can hear them at matched loudness.

### What’s a good reference workflow in the session?
1. Put the reference on its own track routed straight to the output, so your mix bus processing doesn’t touch it.
2. Measure both and turn the reference down to your mix’s integrated loudness. Re-check whenever your mix level changes a lot.
3. Loop the same section of both songs, usually the first chorus, and switch every few seconds.
4. Write down the one or two biggest differences. Fix those, bounce, and measure again.
5. Stop referencing once the big things match. Past that point you’re mixing someone else’s song.
That last step matters. References are best used for a few minutes at the start of a session and again at the end, not as a constant comparison that keeps you second-guessing.
Note: CoProducer’s desktop app can lay your bounce next to a reference metric by metric, so you can see the gaps on loudness, peak and balance without running scripts. The Pro license includes it. The script above does the core of it for free.
Q: How do I use a reference track when mixing?
A: Pick one or two finished songs in the same lane as yours, get the best files you can, and drop them into your session on their own track that skips your mix bus. Turn the reference down until it measures the same integrated LUFS as your mix, then flip between them for a few seconds at a time. Compare tonal balance, how loud the vocal sits and how big the low end is. Don’t chase its peak level.
Q: Should I match the LUFS of my reference track?
A: Match it for listening, not for your master. Turn the reference down to your mix’s loudness so you can compare fairly. Many commercial references are mastered louder than streaming plays them back, and some have true peaks over 0 dBTP. Copy the balance and keep your own master under −1 dBTP.
Q: Why does my mix sound worse than the reference?
A: Often it’s just quieter. A track that’s a few dB louder usually sounds fuller and brighter to us, so an unmatched A/B is rigged before you start. Level-match first. If it still sounds worse, look at the biggest tonal balance difference, which is usually too much low end or a buried midrange.
Q: Can I use a YouTube or Spotify rip as a reference?
A: It works for rough balance, but the levels are wrong. A streamed or ripped file has been turned down or up by the platform and run through a lossy codec, so its loudness and peaks no longer match the master. Buy or download a lossless file when you can, and measure both on the same meter.

---

## How loud should each song on an album be? Measure the record as a set
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/album-consistency-in-one-meter.html
Section: Albums · 21 August 2026 · 6 min
Summary: Album tracks don’t all need −14 LUFS. Measure the record as a set, keep loud songs close, let quiet ones sit lower on purpose, and keep every true peak legal.

Songs on an album don’t all need to hit the same LUFS. They need to sound right in running order and each one has to be legal on its own. In practice, keep the songs that should feel equally loud within a LU or two of each other, let intros and ballads sit lower on purpose, and keep every true peak under −1 dBTP. The way to check that is to measure the whole record as a set, not one bounce at a time.
Most album loudness problems aren’t about any single master. Each song got finished on a different night, with a different limiter setting and a different idea of “loud enough.” Each one sounds fine solo. Then you play the record top to bottom and the closer jumps out of the speakers, or the ballad is so quiet people skip it. You only see that when you look at all the numbers side by side.

### Does every track on an album need to be −14 LUFS?
No, and the reason is in how streaming plays albums back. Spotify’s loudness normalization page says it normalizes an entire album at the same time, “so gain compensation doesn’t change between tracks,” and the softer tracks stay as soft as you intended. When someone shuffles or plays a song in a playlist, it adjusts each track on its own instead.
So your record has to work two ways. In album mode, the level differences you master in are exactly what listeners hear. In playlist mode, every track gets pulled toward −14 LUFS on its own, and a quiet track is only lifted as far as its true peak allows (Spotify keeps 1 dB of headroom). The older ReplayGain standard for music players works the same way, with a separate “album gain” that keeps the volume differences between tracks.
That means −14 isn’t a number each song has to hit. It’s roughly where streaming will put the album as a whole. What you control is how the songs sit next to each other.

### What does a consistent album look like in numbers?
Here are the four things worth measuring for each track, on the same meter:
- Integrated LUFS. The loudness of the whole song, measured the ITU-R BS.1770 way.
- True peak. The level between the samples, which lossy encoders have to reproduce. Keep it under −1 dBTP, and under −2 dBTP for songs louder than −14 LUFS, as Spotify recommends.
- Loudness range (LRA). How much the loudness moves within the song, defined in EBU Tech 3342 as the spread between the 10th and 95th percentile of short-term loudness. A ballad with a big build will have a wider range than a wall-to-wall club track.
- The step from the previous track. This is the one listeners actually feel. Two songs that are meant to feel equally loud shouldn’t be more than a LU or two apart.

### How do I check a whole album at once?
Here’s a script that measures every file in a folder in running order. It needs Python 3, NumPy and FFmpeg, and it only reads your files. It also estimates how each track will play on Spotify in playlist mode and in album mode. Spotify doesn’t publish exactly how it measures an album’s loudness, so the album column assumes the loudness of all tracks played back to back, like ReplayGain’s album gain. Treat that column as an estimate.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""album_check.py: measure an album (or EP, or beat tape) as one set.
Usage: python3 album_check.py FOLDER   (WAV/FLAC/AIFF files, in running order by file name)
For each track: integrated loudness, loudness range (LRA), true peak (FFmpeg ebur128, ITU-R BS.1770 /
EBU Tech 3342), distance from the album's median loudness, the step from the previous track, and flags. Then a rough picture of playback
on Spotify: shuffle/playlist mode (each track adjusted to -14 LUFS, quiet tracks lifted only as far as
-1 dBTP allows) versus album mode (one gain for the whole album). Spotify doesn't publish how it measures
an album's loudness, so album mode here ASSUMES the loudness of all tracks played back to back, the way
ReplayGain's album gain works. Treat that column as an estimate. Your files are only read.
Needs: Python 3, NumPy, FFmpeg on PATH."""
import re, subprocess, sys, tempfile, os
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np

def decode(p):
    raw = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", str(p), "-f", "f32le", "-ac", "2", "-ar", "48000", "-"],
                         capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
    return np.frombuffer(raw, np.float32).reshape(-1, 2)

def meter_file(p):
    err = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-hide_banner", "-nostats", "-i", str(p), "-af", "ebur128=peak=true", "-f", "null", "-"],
                         capture_output=True, text=True).stderr
    g = lambda pat: float(re.findall(pat, err)[-1])
    return g(r"I:\s+(-?[\d.]+) LUFS"), g(r"LRA:\s+([\d.]+) LU"), g(r"Peak:\s+(-?[\d.]+) dBFS")

def track_gain(I, TP, target=-14.0, ceiling=-1.0):
    g = target - I
    return min(g, ceiling - TP) if g > 0 else g

def main(folder):
    files = sorted(p for p in Path(folder).iterdir() if p.suffix.lower() in (".wav", ".flac", ".aif", ".aiff"))
    rows = [(p.stem, *meter_file(p)) for p in files]
    med = float(np.median([r[1] for r in rows]))
    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix=".wav", delete=False) as fh: tmp = fh.name
    subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-y", "-f", "f32le", "-ar", "48000", "-ac", "2", "-i", "-", "-c:a", "pcm_f32le", tmp],
                   input=np.concatenate([decode(p) for p in files]).tobytes(), check=True)
    AI, ALRA, ATP = meter_file(tmp); os.unlink(tmp)
    ag = track_gain(AI, ATP)
    print(f"album: {len(rows)} tracks, median {med:.1f} LUFS, whole album {AI:.1f} LUFS, max true peak {ATP:+.1f} dBTP\n")
    print(f"{'track':14}{'LUFS':>7}{'LRA':>6}{'TP':>7}{'vs med':>8}{'step':>7}   {'shuffle':>8}{'album*':>8}  flags")
    prev = None
    for name, I, LRA, TP in rows:
        flags = []
        if TP > -1.0: flags.append("TP over -1")
        if TP > -2.0 and I > -14.0 and TP <= -1.0: flags.append("loud: Spotify asks TP < -2")
        if abs(I - med) > 4: flags.append("outlier: intended?")
        step = "" if prev is None else f"{I - prev:+7.1f}"
        if prev is not None and abs(I - prev) > 6: flags.append("big jump from last track")
        prev = I
        s = I + track_gain(I, TP); a = I + ag
        print(f"{name:14}{I:7.1f}{LRA:6.1f}{TP:+7.1f}{I - med:+8.1f}{step:>7}   {s:8.1f}{a:8.1f}  {', '.join(flags)}")
    print(f"\nshuffle = loudness each track plays at in a playlist; album* = estimated loudness in album mode (one gain, {ag:+.1f} dB)")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(sys.argv[1])
To show it without anybody’s real record, we generated a synthetic six-track “album”: an ambient intro, an opener, a single, a deep cut, a ballad and a closer, each bounced at whatever level its session ended at. It’s the way a lot of records look the day before mastering. Here’s what the script printed:
$ python3 album_check.py album
album: 6 tracks, median -10.1 LUFS, whole album -9.6 LUFS, max true peak +1.9 dBTP

track            LUFS   LRA     TP  vs med   step    shuffle  album*  flags
01_intro        -20.0   0.7   -5.8    -9.9             -15.2   -24.4  outlier: intended?
02_opener        -8.4   0.5   +1.9    +1.7  +11.6      -14.0   -12.8  TP over -1, big jump from last track
03_single        -8.9   0.3   +1.4    +1.2   -0.5      -14.0   -13.3  TP over -1
04_deep_cut     -11.2   0.4   +0.4    -1.1   -2.3      -14.0   -15.6  TP over -1
05_ballad       -17.5   0.6   -2.6    -7.4   -6.3      -15.9   -21.9  outlier: intended?, big jump from last track
06_closer        -6.9   0.5   +0.9    +3.2  +10.6      -14.0   -11.3  TP over -1, big jump from last track

shuffle = loudness each track plays at in a playlist; album* = estimated loudness in album mode (one gain, -4.4 dB)

### What is this album doing wrong?
Three things, and only one of them is about loudness taste.
Four tracks have illegal true peaks. The opener, single, deep cut and closer all sit over −1 dBTP, the worst at +1.9. Their highest samples were limited to −0.1 dBFS, which looks fine on a sample-peak meter, but the waveform between samples goes higher. That’s a problem for every song on its own, before you think about the album.
The steps are wild. Ballad to closer is a jump of 10.6 LU. In album mode the closer would come in at around −11.3 LUFS straight after a ballad at −21.9. Nobody intended that; the closer’s session just ended with a hot limiter. In playlist mode both get pulled to similar levels, so you’d never notice it from a single-track check.
The ballad is quieter than it needs to be. At −17.5 LUFS it sits 7.4 LU under the album’s median. Some of that may be the point. But in album mode it lands near −22, which is quiet enough that a listener in a car or on earbuds will turn it up and then get blasted by the closer.
The intro is flagged as an outlier too, and that one probably is intentional. A quiet intro is fine. The flag is there so you look at it and decide, not so you flatten it.

### How do I fix album loudness without remastering everything?
Plan the lanes first, then fix the outliers. Write down where each song should sit in the running order: the loud songs together, the ballad a few LU under, the intro lower again. Then move only the tracks that miss their lane, and keep every true peak legal.
Here’s that plan applied to the synthetic album with gain only, capped so that loud tracks stay under −2 dBTP and the rest under −1:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""fix_album.py: SYNTHETIC demo of planning album lanes with gain only.
Each track gets a planned loudness; the gain is capped so true peak stays at or under -1.0 dBTP, or -2.0 dBTP
for tracks louder than -14 LUFS (Spotify's advice for loud masters).
Writes album_fixed/. In a real session you'd re-master into a true-peak limiter instead of only
turning down, but the plan (which track sits where) is the same. Needs NumPy and FFmpeg."""
import subprocess, os
from pathlib import Path
from album_check import meter_file
PLAN = {"01_intro": -18.0, "02_opener": -11.0, "03_single": -11.0, "04_deep_cut": -12.0, "05_ballad": -15.0, "06_closer": -11.5}
os.makedirs("album_fixed", exist_ok=True)
for p in sorted(Path("album").glob("*.wav")):
    I, LRA, TP = meter_file(p)
    g = PLAN[p.stem] - I
    ceiling = -2.0 if I + g > -14.0 else -1.0
    g = min(g, ceiling - TP)
    subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-y", "-i", str(p), "-af", f"volume={g:.2f}dB", "-c:a", "pcm_f32le", f"album_fixed/{p.name}"], check=True)
    print(f"{p.stem:14} plan {PLAN[p.stem]:6.1f}  gain {g:+5.1f} dB")
$ python3 fix_album.py && python3 album_check.py album_fixed
01_intro       plan  -18.0  gain  +2.0 dB
02_opener      plan  -11.0  gain  -3.9 dB
03_single      plan  -11.0  gain  -3.4 dB
04_deep_cut    plan  -12.0  gain  -2.4 dB
05_ballad      plan  -15.0  gain  +1.6 dB
06_closer      plan  -11.5  gain  -4.6 dB
album: 6 tracks, median -12.9 LUFS, whole album -13.2 LUFS, max true peak -1.0 dBTP

track            LUFS   LRA     TP  vs med   step    shuffle  album*  flags
01_intro        -18.0   0.7   -3.8    -5.1             -15.2   -18.8  outlier: intended?
02_opener       -12.3   0.5   -2.0    +0.6   +5.7      -14.0   -13.1  
03_single       -12.3   0.3   -2.0    +0.6   +0.0      -14.0   -13.1  
04_deep_cut     -13.6   0.4   -2.0    -0.7   -1.3      -14.0   -14.4  
05_ballad       -15.9   0.6   -1.0    -3.0   -2.3      -15.9   -16.7  
06_closer       -11.5   0.5   -3.7    +1.4   +4.4      -14.0   -12.3  

shuffle = loudness each track plays at in a playlist; album* = estimated loudness in album mode (one gain, -0.8 dB)
Every true peak is now legal, the loud songs sit within about 2 LU of each other, and the ballad-to-closer step shrank from 10.6 LU to 4.4. The ballad couldn’t reach its planned −15 because its peaks hit the ceiling first, so it settled at −15.9, which is still a reasonable distance under the loud songs. The jump from intro to opener is still 5.7 LU, and that’s the drop we want.
In a real session you’d usually re-master the loud tracks into a true-peak limiter rather than just turning them down, which keeps more loudness for the same peak. The plan stays the same either way: decide where each song sits, then change only what misses.

### What should I listen for once the numbers look right?
Numbers get you close, and your ears finish the job. Play the last 20 seconds of each song into the first 20 seconds of the next, in order, at one fixed monitor level. Listen for any step that makes you want to reach for the volume. Check the gaps and fades too, because the space between songs changes how big a level change feels (and if the album is gapless, lossy encoding can add gaps you didn’t master in).
Then play two songs on shuffle, from different spots in the album. If each one holds up next to the other at −14, you’re covered both ways.
Note: If you’d rather not run scripts, CoProducer’s desktop analyzer can write an HTML, JSON and TXT report beside every bounce in a folder, so the whole record’s numbers are in one place. More on the batch analyzer.
Q: Should every song on an album be the same LUFS?
A: No. Spotify plays an album with one gain for the whole record, so the differences you master in are the differences listeners hear. A ballad a few LU under the loud songs sounds intentional. What you want to avoid is accidental jumps, like a 10 LU step between two songs that should feel similar.
Q: Does Spotify normalize every track on an album separately?
A: Only when tracks play outside the album. Spotify says it normalizes a whole album at once, so the gain doesn’t change between tracks, and adjusts tracks individually when you shuffle or play a playlist. That means each song needs to work on its own and in running order.
Q: How loud should a ballad be compared with the rest of the album?
A: There’s no rule. A few LU under the main songs is a common starting point, because it sounds softer without making the listener reach for the volume. Check it in running order: listen to the end of the song before it, then the ballad. If the change feels like a mistake, it’s too big.
Q: How do I check loudness for a whole album at once?
A: Measure every track with the same meter and put the numbers side by side: integrated LUFS, true peak and loudness range, plus the step from each song to the next. A batch script or a batch report tool does this in one pass, so you aren’t copying numbers by hand.

---

## What should a loudness report include? Why HTML, JSON and TXT all matter
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/why-three-report-formats.html
Section: Reports · 21 August 2026 · 7 min
Summary: A loudness report should name the exact file, its hash, LUFS, true peak and LRA. Keep HTML for people, JSON for scripts and TXT for chat. Script included.

A useful loudness report names the exact file it measured (its name plus a hash of the audio), says when it was measured, and lists the numbers delivery cares about: integrated loudness in LUFS, true peak in dBTP, loudness range, sample rate, channels and length. Keep it in three forms because it has three kinds of reader. HTML is for people, JSON is for scripts, and a one-line TXT is for chat and tickets. They hold the same facts, written once by the meter, so nobody has to retype a number.

### Loudness report checklist
Before you trust a loudness report, check that it carries these. Each one is a measurement the standards define, so any decent meter can produce it.
1. Integrated loudness (LUFS) for the whole file, gated as ITU-R BS.1770 describes.
2. Loudness range (LRA, in LU), as defined in EBU Tech 3342.
3. Maximum momentary and maximum short-term loudness, the loudest 0.4 s and 3 s windows (EBU Tech 3341). The integrated number can hide a section that is far louder than the rest.
4. True peak per channel, in dBTP, not one number for the pair. A single figure hides which side is closer to the limit.
5. Meter and settings: the tool and its version, the standard it follows, the channel layout, and whether it measured the whole file or a selection.
6. The target and a pass or fail against it, with the target written down. EBU R 128 uses −23 LUFS integrated with −1 dBTP as the maximum true peak for broadcast; streaming platforms use their own numbers.
The file name, a hash of the audio and the measurement date, covered below, tie the numbers to one exact file. Sources: EBU R 128, ITU-R BS.1770, EBU Tech 3341 and EBU Tech 3342.
Here’s the situation it prevents. Someone in the group chat asks “is the single legal yet?” You’ve got single_master_v3.wav, single_master_v3_FINAL.wav and a screenshot of your meter from Tuesday. Which file did the screenshot measure? Was that before or after you pulled the limiter back? Nobody can say for sure, so somebody re-checks it, and somebody else asks again tomorrow. A report that travels with the file answers the question once.

### What should a loudness report include?
Keep it short. Every field should answer a question someone will actually ask:
- File name and a hash. The name tells people what it is. The hash (a SHA-256 fingerprint of the file’s bytes) proves which file it is. Rename it and the hash stays the same. Re-bounce it and the hash changes, even if the numbers barely move. That’s the only way to know a report belongs to the file in your hand.
- When it was measured, with the time zone. A date written like 2026-10-22T10:04:56-04:00 (the RFC 3339 format) sorts correctly and reads the same everywhere.
- Integrated loudness (LUFS). The average loudness of the whole track, measured the way ITU-R BS.1770 defines it. It’s the number streaming services use when they turn tracks up or down.
- True peak (dBTP). The highest point of the waveform once it’s rebuilt between samples, which is where codecs and converters clip. Also in BS.1770.
- Sample peak (dBFS). Worth keeping beside true peak because the gap between them tells a story. A master at −0.1 dBFS sample peak and +1.2 dBTP true peak was limited by sample peak only.
- Loudness range (LU). How much the loudness moves across the track, defined in EBU Tech 3342. When a revision suddenly drops in range, something squashed it.
- Format facts. Sample rate, channels, codec and length. They catch the boring mistakes, like a 44.1 kHz file where the label asked for 48, or a bounce that stopped eight seconds early.
Notice what isn’t on the list: opinions. A report says what the file measures. Whether −9 LUFS is right for the record is a creative call, and it belongs in your notes, not in the numbers.

### Why not just send a screenshot of the meter?
Screenshots are fine for a glance and bad for a record. Three problems:
- No identity. A screenshot doesn’t say which file it measured. Two weeks later, neither do you.
- Retyping. Someone will copy “−9.8” into a spreadsheet as “−8.9”. Every copy by hand is a chance to flip digits or units, and LUFS, LU, dBFS and dBTP are easy to mix up.
- No history. You can’t search a folder of screenshots for “every master with true peak above −1”. You can do that with text in about one line.

### Who reads the HTML, the JSON and the TXT?
Format | Who reads it | What it’s good at | Where it falls short
HTML | Artists, A&R, clients, you on your phone | Opens in any browser, can show a clear pass/check line, easy to forward | Awkward for scripts to read back
JSON | Your scripts, spreadsheets, a release checklist | Every number has a name and a type, so tools can compare and filter without guessing (RFC 8259 is the spec) | Nobody wants to read it in a group chat
TXT | Chats, tickets, email, notes apps | One line you can paste anywhere, readable with no app at all | Not built for tools to read back reliably
The point isn’t the formats, it’s that the meter writes all three at the same moment from the same measurement. Three files that were typed separately can disagree. Three files written by one run can’t.

### What does a three-format report look like in practice?
Here’s a small script that measures a file with FFmpeg’s ebur128 meter and writes all three reports next to it. It needs Python 3 and FFmpeg. Nothing leaves your computer.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""report.py: measure one bounce and write the same facts three ways.
    python3 report.py my_mix_v2.wav
Writes my_mix_v2.report.json (for scripts), .txt (for chat and tickets) and .html (for people)
next to the audio. Needs ffmpeg/ffprobe on your PATH. Nothing is uploaded anywhere."""
import hashlib, html, json, re, subprocess, sys, datetime
from pathlib import Path

def measure(path):
    err = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-hide_banner", "-nostats", "-i", str(path), "-vn",
                          "-af", "ebur128=peak=sample+true", "-f", "null", "-"],
                         capture_output=True, text=True).stderr
    summary = err[err.rindex("Summary:"):]
    num = lambda pat: float(re.search(pat, summary, re.S).group(1))
    probe = json.loads(subprocess.run(["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-select_streams", "a:0", "-show_entries",
        "stream=sample_rate,channels,codec_name,bits_per_raw_sample:format=duration", "-of", "json", str(path)],
        capture_output=True, text=True).stdout)
    st, fmt = probe["streams"][0], probe["format"]
    return {
        "file": path.name,
        "sha256": hashlib.sha256(path.read_bytes()).hexdigest(),
        "measured_at": datetime.datetime.now().astimezone().isoformat(timespec="seconds"),
        "duration_s": round(float(fmt["duration"]), 2),
        "codec": st["codec_name"], "sample_rate_hz": int(st["sample_rate"]), "channels": st["channels"],
        "integrated_lufs": num(r"I:\s+(-?[\d.]+) LUFS"),
        "loudness_range_lu": num(r"LRA:\s+(-?[\d.]+) LU"),
        "true_peak_dbtp": num(r"True peak:\s+Peak:\s+(-?[\d.]+) dBFS"),
        "sample_peak_dbfs": num(r"Sample peak:\s+Peak:\s+(-?[\d.]+) dBFS"),
    }

def verdict(r, tp_max=-1.0):
    return "PASS" if r["true_peak_dbtp"] <= tp_max else f"CHECK: true peak above {tp_max} dBTP"

def write_all(r, stem):
    stem.with_suffix(".report.json").write_text(json.dumps(r, indent=2) + "\n")
    txt = (f"{r['file']}  {r['integrated_lufs']:.1f} LUFS | TP {r['true_peak_dbtp']:+.1f} dBTP | "
           f"LRA {r['loudness_range_lu']:.1f} LU | {r['sample_rate_hz']/1000:g} kHz | {verdict(r)} | "
           f"sha256 {r['sha256'][:12]}")
    stem.with_suffix(".report.txt").write_text(txt + "\n")
    rows = "".join(f"<tr><th>{html.escape(k)}</th><td>{html.escape(str(v))}</td></tr>" for k, v in r.items())
    stem.with_suffix(".report.html").write_text(
        f"<!doctype html><meta charset=utf-8><title>{html.escape(r['file'])}</title>"
        f"<h1>{html.escape(r['file'])}</h1><p><b>{html.escape(verdict(r))}</b></p><table>{rows}</table>\n")
    return txt

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for arg in sys.argv[1:]:
        p = Path(arg); print(write_all(measure(p), p.with_suffix("")))
To show it working, we made two synthetic test files (a 30-second generated beat, no real song). mix_v1.wav was pushed 6 dB into a sample-peak limiter set to −0.1 dBFS, the way plenty of loud masters get made. mix_v2.wav is the same audio turned down so its true peak lands at −1.0 dBTP. Here are the two TXT lines the script printed:
$ python3 report.py mix_v1.wav mix_v2.wav
mix_v1.wav  -7.6 LUFS | TP +1.2 dBTP | LRA 0.3 LU | 48 kHz | CHECK: true peak above -1.0 dBTP | sha256 65c5ad9b4035
mix_v2.wav  -9.8 LUFS | TP -1.0 dBTP | LRA 0.3 LU | 48 kHz | PASS | sha256 4cca0dbad305
And here’s the JSON for the fixed version, exactly as written:
{
  "file": "mix_v2.wav",
  "sha256": "4cca0dbad305bdaed6978829aa13fcff9fd6e80253834131490bace296e46c07",
  "measured_at": "2026-10-22T10:04:56-04:00",
  "duration_s": 31.0,
  "codec": "pcm_f32le",
  "sample_rate_hz": 48000,
  "channels": 2,
  "integrated_lufs": -9.8,
  "loudness_range_lu": 0.3,
  "true_peak_dbtp": -1.0,
  "sample_peak_dbfs": -2.3
}
A few things worth reading out of that:
- v1 looked clean and wasn’t. Its sample peak was −0.1 dBFS, so an ordinary peak meter showed no problem. True peak was +1.2 dBTP, over full scale, and the TXT line flags it. Spotify’s loudness guidance asks for true peak below −1 dBTP, and below −2 dBTP for masters louder than −14 LUFS like this one. That’s why the PASS rule in the script is only a starting point.
- The hashes are different (65c5ad9b… and 4cca0dba…), so nobody can confuse the reports even if the files get renamed.
- The loudness range is tiny (0.3 LU) because the test beat is a short loop that never changes. A real song with a verse and a chorus usually reads several LU. Don’t copy that number as a target.

### What a fuller report looks like
This is a fuller version of the report above, for a synthetic 30-second stereo test file we made and measured with FFmpeg. It is not a real song, and the target is an example, not a recommendation. The short script in this essay writes the core fields; the per-channel peaks and maximum momentary and short-term values come from the same meter and are added here.
{
  "file": "demo_master.wav",
  "sha256": "cb73442ce914098e9cebe5fc627ac44f11f6f6cc3b62177e448887c1db39630b",
  "measured_at": "2026-11-04T19:48:00-05:00",
  "duration_s": 30.0,
  "sample_rate_hz": 48000,
  "channels": 2,
  "meter": {
    "tool": "ffmpeg 7.1 ebur128",
    "standard": "ITU-R BS.1770 / EBU R 128",
    "gating": "-70 LUFS absolute, -10 LU relative",
    "true_peak": "peak=true"
  },
  "integrated_lufs": -10.9,
  "loudness_range_lu": 1.9,
  "max_momentary_lufs": -9.2,
  "max_short_term_lufs": -10.0,
  "true_peak_dbtp": {
    "L": -0.7,
    "R": -2.2
  },
  "target": {
    "integrated_lufs": -14.0,
    "tolerance_lu": 1.0,
    "true_peak_max_dbtp": -1.0
  },
  "verdict": {
    "integrated": "fail (3.1 LU above target)",
    "true_peak": "fail (L channel 0.3 dB over)",
    "overall": "fail"
  }
}
The right channel is quieter than the left, so a single combined true-peak figure would show only the louder side and hide the difference. In this example the file fails on both integrated loudness and left-channel true peak, and the report says why.

### How do I compare two versions of a master?
This is where JSON pays for itself. A second tiny script reads two reports and prints only what changed:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""compare.py: what changed between two versions? Reads two .report.json files.
    python3 compare.py mix_v1.report.json mix_v2.report.json"""
import json, sys
a, b = (json.load(open(p)) for p in sys.argv[1:3])
print(f"{a['file']} -> {b['file']}")
if a["sha256"] == b["sha256"]:
    print("  same audio bytes: nothing changed")
for k in ("integrated_lufs", "true_peak_dbtp", "sample_peak_dbfs", "loudness_range_lu", "duration_s", "sample_rate_hz"):
    if a[k] != b[k]:
        print(f"  {k:18} {a[k]:>8} -> {b[k]:>8}  ({b[k] - a[k]:+.1f})")
On the synthetic pair it printed:
$ python3 compare.py mix_v1.report.json mix_v2.report.json
mix_v1.wav -> mix_v2.wav
  integrated_lufs        -7.6 ->     -9.8  (-2.2)
  true_peak_dbtp          1.2 ->     -1.0  (-2.2)
  sample_peak_dbfs       -0.1 ->     -2.3  (-2.2)
Integrated loudness, true peak and sample peak all moved by exactly −2.2 dB, and loudness range didn’t move at all. That pattern means the only change was a gain trim. If the range had dropped too, you’d know something compressed or limited the new version harder, and that’s worth a listen before anyone signs off. If the two hashes had matched, the script would say “same audio bytes”, which settles the classic “did you actually send me the new one?” question in a second.
When you want a spreadsheet, jq turns a folder of JSON reports into CSV rows in one line:
$ jq -r '[.file, .integrated_lufs, .true_peak_dbtp, .sha256[0:12]] | @csv' *.report.json
"mix_v1.wav",-7.6,1.2,"65c5ad9b4035"
"mix_v2.wav",-9.8,-1.0,"4cca0dbad305"

### Where should the reports live?
- Beside the bounce, with the same name. single_master_v4.wav sits next to single_master_v4.report.json, .txt and .html. Move the folder and everything moves together.
- Never edit a report by hand. If a number looks wrong, measure again. A report you edited is a note, not a measurement.
- Re-measure after every render that changes the audio. That includes sample-rate conversion, a new limiter setting, a slowed or sped-up version and an encoded preview. Each is a new file with a new hash and its own peaks.
- Archive them with the release. When a distributor, a sync house or a collaborator asks a year from now what you delivered, the JSON and the hash answer it.
Use the same meter for every version you compare. Meters that follow BS.1770 should agree closely on integrated loudness, but true-peak readings can differ a little with the oversampling each meter uses. Comparing v1 from one tool with v2 from another adds noise you don’t need. EBU Tech 3341 describes the test signals meters are checked against, if you ever want to test one yourself.

### What should a report never claim?
That a track is “good”. A report can tell you a file is −9.8 LUFS with −1.0 dBTP true peak at 48 kHz. It can’t tell you whether the vocal sits right or whether the chorus lifts. It also can’t promise how a platform will play it, since each service applies its own normalization and encoding. Keep the numbers honest and narrow, and keep the taste in your ears.
If you’d rather not keep scripts around, CoProducer’s analyzer works the same way. It writes HTML, JSON and TXT beside each bounce, so the facts travel with the file.
Note: Short version: one measurement, three formats, a hash in every one. HTML for people, JSON for tools, TXT for the chat. For what the numbers mean, see how to read a CoProducer score and true peak is what codecs clip.
Q: What should a loudness report include?
A: The file name and a hash of the audio, the date it was measured, integrated loudness in LUFS, true peak in dBTP, loudness range in LU, sample rate, channels and length. The hash ties the numbers to one exact file, so a renamed or re-bounced version can’t borrow an old report.
Q: Why keep a report in three formats?
A: Because three kinds of reader need the same facts. HTML is for people who open it in a browser, JSON is for scripts that compare versions or check a target, and a one-line TXT is for pasting into a chat or ticket. When the meter writes all three at once, nobody retypes a number.
Q: Can I just send a screenshot of my meter?
A: It works for a quick look, but a screenshot doesn’t say which file it measured, can’t be searched or compared, and invites someone to retype the numbers wrong. A text report with a file hash is easier to trust and keeps working months later.
Q: How do I compare two versions of a master?
A: Measure both with the same meter and compare the JSON reports field by field. If the hashes match, the audio is identical. If loudness, true peak and sample peak all moved by the same amount, the only change was gain. If loudness range changed too, something compressed or expanded the track.

---

## How to check LUFS without uploading your song: local tools beat upload queues
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/local-tools-beat-upload-queues.html
Section: Local-first · 21 August 2026 · 7 min
Summary: You don’t need to upload a track to measure LUFS or true peak. A free meter plugin or one FFmpeg command does it in seconds, and your unreleased song stays put.

Use a meter that runs in your browser or your DAW, and nothing leaves your computer. Integrated LUFS and true peak come from a published method (ITU-R BS.1770) that any laptop can run, so a free meter plug-in, one FFmpeg command or the CoProducer analyzer in your browser will read a finished bounce in seconds, with no queue, no account and no copy of your unreleased song on someone else’s server.
It’s an easy habit to fall into. You finish a bounce at 1 a.m., you want to know if it’s too loud for Spotify, and the first search result is a site that asks you to upload. So you sign up, wait for the progress bar, wait in a queue, and get back a number your own computer could have worked out before the upload finished. Meanwhile a song nobody has heard yet is now sitting on a disk you don’t control, under terms you probably didn’t read.

### Why would I avoid uploading a song just to check its loudness?
- It’s slower. Measuring is fast. Moving a big WAV over a home upload connection is not. The numbers are below.
- You lose track of the file. Once it’s uploaded, how long it’s kept, who can see it and what it may be used for is up to that service’s terms. Some are clear and fair. You still have to go and read them, for every site, every time they change.
- Unreleased means unreleased. A leak before release can cost you the rollout you planned. The fewer copies exist, the fewer can leak.
- Friction adds up. Accounts, logins, credits, per-track limits, “pick a genre preset” screens. None of it changes the math of a loudness measurement.
None of that makes online tools bad. It just means “I want a number” is the wrong reason to use one.

### How long does uploading a song actually take?
Here’s the plain arithmetic. A four-minute stereo WAV at 48 kHz and 24-bit is 4 × 60 × 48,000 × 3 bytes × 2 channels, which is about 69 MB. Upload time is just size divided by your upload speed. These are example speeds, not anyone’s actual connection, and real uploads add overhead and queue time on top:
Upload speed (example) | One 4-minute WAV (69 MB) | A 12-track album (829 MB)
5 Mbps | about 1 min 51 s | about 22 min
20 Mbps | about 28 s | about 5.5 min
50 Mbps | about 11 s | about 2.2 min
Upload speeds on home connections are often much lower than download speeds, so run a test at Speedtest and look at the “Upload” number for your real figure. Now compare that with measuring locally. On our test machine, FFmpeg measured four minutes of synthetic audio across four files (92 MB) in about one second, including true peak. Your computer may be slower or faster, but the measurement is rarely the slow part.

### How do I check LUFS on my own computer?
Three ways, from no setup to fully automatic.
1. A meter plugin in your DAW. Put a loudness meter on the master bus and play the whole song through. The Youlean Loudness Meter has a free version that runs as a VST, AU or AAX plugin and shows integrated LUFS, short-term loudness and true peak. Most DAWs also ship a meter of their own. Play the song start to finish, because integrated loudness only means something once it has heard the whole track.
2. One FFmpeg command. FFmpeg is free and runs on Windows, macOS and Linux. Its ebur128 filter follows the EBU R 128 method, which uses BS.1770 loudness. It reads the file faster than real time, so you don’t sit through playback. Here it is on a synthetic test file, trimmed to the summary it prints at the end:
$ ffmpeg -hide_banner -nostats -i mix_v2.wav -af ebur128=peak=true -f null -
...
Summary:

  Integrated loudness:
    I:          -9.8 LUFS
    Threshold: -19.8 LUFS

  Loudness range:
    LRA:         0.3 LU
    Threshold: -29.7 LUFS
    LRA low:    -9.9 LUFS
    LRA high:   -9.6 LUFS

  True peak:
    Peak:       -1.0 dBFS
“I” is integrated loudness. “LRA” is loudness range. With peak=true, the “Peak” line under “True peak” is the true peak; FFmpeg labels it dBFS, but it’s the true-peak value, so read it as dBTP.
3. A whole folder at once. When you’re checking an album, an EP or a pile of alternate mixes, measure them all in one go. This script runs the same FFmpeg meter over every audio file in a folder, prints a table and saves a CSV next to the songs:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""measure_folder.py: loudness for every audio file in a folder, measured on this machine.
    python3 measure_folder.py ./bounces
Prints a table and writes loudness.csv into the folder. Uses ffmpeg's EBU R128 meter
(integrated LUFS, loudness range, true peak). No account, no upload, no network."""
import csv, re, subprocess, sys, time
from pathlib import Path

AUDIO = {".wav", ".aif", ".aiff", ".flac", ".mp3", ".m4a", ".ogg", ".opus"}

def measure(path):
    err = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-hide_banner", "-nostats", "-i", str(path), "-vn",
                          "-af", "ebur128=peak=true", "-f", "null", "-"],
                         capture_output=True, text=True).stderr
    s = err[err.rindex("Summary:"):]
    f = lambda pat: float(re.search(pat, s, re.S).group(1))
    return f(r"I:\s+(-?[\d.]+) LUFS"), f(r"LRA:\s+(-?[\d.]+) LU"), f(r"Peak:\s+(-?[\d.]+) dBFS")

folder = Path(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else ".")
files = sorted(p for p in folder.iterdir() if p.suffix.lower() in AUDIO)
rows, t0 = [], time.perf_counter()
for p in files:
    I, lra, tp = measure(p)
    rows.append((p.name, I, lra, tp, "check peak" if tp > -1.0 else ""))
    print(f"{p.name:22} {I:6.1f} LUFS  LRA {lra:4.1f} LU  TP {tp:+5.1f} dBTP  {rows[-1][4]}")
loud = [r[1] for r in rows]
if loud:
    print(f"spread: {max(loud) - min(loud):.1f} LU between loudest and quietest")
print(f"{len(rows)} files, {sum(p.stat().st_size for p in files) / 1e6:.0f} MB, "
      f"measured in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")
with open(folder / "loudness.csv", "w", newline="") as fh:
    w = csv.writer(fh); w.writerow(["file", "integrated_lufs", "lra_lu", "true_peak_dbtp", "note"]); w.writerows(rows)
We ran it on a folder of four synthetic one-minute tracks made to be deliberately inconsistent, the way a rough album folder often is:
$ python3 measure_folder.py album
01_intro.wav            -15.1 LUFS  LRA  0.9 LU  TP  -2.6 dBTP  
02_single.wav            -8.3 LUFS  LRA  0.3 LU  TP  +1.5 dBTP  check peak
03_ballad.wav           -19.1 LUFS  LRA  0.8 LU  TP  -5.9 dBTP  
04_closer.wav            -9.7 LUFS  LRA  0.4 LU  TP  +0.1 dBTP  check peak
spread: 10.8 LU between loudest and quietest
4 files, 92 MB, measured in 1.0 s
Two things jump out without listening to a note. The tracks sit 10.8 LU apart, so on an album the ballad would land like a different record unless that’s the intent. And two tracks have true peaks above −1 dBTP, one of them at +1.5, which is the kind of file that can clip once it’s encoded. That took about a second, and nothing left the folder.

### Is a local meter as accurate as an online one?
It’s the same math. Any meter that follows BS.1770 (and the EBU’s R 128 recommendation built on it) applies the same weighting filter, the same 400 ms blocks and the same gating to work out integrated loudness. Two compliant meters should agree closely on integrated LUFS. True peak can differ by a small amount between meters, because each one estimates the waveform between samples with its own oversampling. The EBU publishes test signals and tolerances in Tech 3341 that meters are checked against.
The bigger source of disagreement is usually not the meter at all. It’s measuring a different file: the MP3 preview instead of the WAV, the version before the last limiter tweak, or 30 seconds instead of the whole song. Measuring locally, on the exact file you’ll deliver, removes most of that.
And remember what the number is for. Spotify’s loudness normalization plays tracks at around −14 LUFS by default and turns louder masters down, so the target isn’t “as loud as possible”. It’s knowing where you are, and keeping true peak below −1 dBTP (−2 dBTP if the master is louder than −14 LUFS).

### Which local LUFS meters are worth trying?
All of these read a file you already have, on your machine. Features and free tiers change, so check the vendor page before you rely on one. We make the CoProducer analyzer, so weigh that row accordingly.
Meter | Where it runs | Cost | What it shows | The catch
Youlean Loudness Meter 2 | Plug-in (VST, AU, AAX) or standalone app | Free version; paid Pro adds more (free vs Pro) | Momentary, short-term and integrated loudness, loudness range, true peak | Check which features sit behind Pro before you plan a workflow around it
FFmpeg ebur128 filter | Command line | Free | Integrated loudness, loudness range and, with peak=true, true peak | No graphs, and you read the numbers out of a text log
Logic Pro Loudness Meter | Inside Logic Pro | Included with Logic | Momentary, short-term and integrated loudness, LU range, EBU R128 mode | It is not a true-peak meter; use MultiMeter in true-peak mode for that
REAPER JS: Loudness Meter and render statistics | Inside REAPER | Included with REAPER | Momentary, short-term and integrated LUFS, loudness range, true peak | You get numbers, not a report you can hand to someone
Klangfreund LUFS Meter | Plug-in (VST, AU, AAX) | Paid; the free demo is limited to under a minute per measurement and non-commercial use | Loudness and true peak | The demo cannot measure a whole song
CoProducer analyzer | In your browser | Free to use on the web | LUFS, true peak, clipped samples and phase against a target | One file at a time on the web; batch and album passes are in CoProducer PRO
Whichever you choose, measure the exported file rather than the session, and use the same meter for every version so the numbers are comparable.

### What about stem separation and other heavy jobs?
This is where the trade gets real. Measuring loudness is light work. Splitting a song into vocals, drums and bass with a neural network is heavy, and it runs much faster on a decent graphics card. Open-source separators such as Demucs run locally (its repository is archived now, but the code still works), and on an older laptop without a GPU a split can take a few minutes per song rather than seconds.
So the honest question is whether a few minutes of your own computer’s time is worth keeping the song at home. For an unreleased record, it usually is. For a public song you just want to study, a cloud tool you trust can be fine. Either way, it’s your decision to make on purpose, not the default because a website asked first.

### When is uploading the right call?
Plenty of times. Uploading is the whole point when:
- You’re sending the mix to a mastering engineer or collaborator you’ve chosen.
- You’re delivering to your distributor. That upload has to happen, and it’s the one that counts.
- You’ve picked a cloud service to do creative work, such as an online master, and you’re comfortable with its terms.
Before uploading something unreleased, do three quick things. Read the part of the terms about how long files are kept, who can access them and whether they can be used for anything else. Keep your original WAV and session where they are, since an upload is a copy, not a backup. And upload once, the final file, rather than every rough version you’re testing.
For day-to-day checks, keep the meter on your own machine. That’s how CoProducer’s analyzer is built: the page talks to an engine on your own computer, and if that isn’t running, it measures in the browser, so the file stays on your device.
Note: Short version: measure locally, upload deliberately. If you’re weighing an online mastering service, our CoProducer vs LANDR notes lay out the trade-offs, and should you upload an unreleased master? goes deeper on the privacy side.
Q: Can I check LUFS without uploading my song?
A: Yes. LUFS and true peak are defined by a public standard (ITU-R BS.1770) that any computer can calculate. A free meter plugin in your DAW, or FFmpeg’s ebur128 filter from the command line, measures the file on your own machine without an account or an upload.
Q: Is a local LUFS meter as accurate as an online one?
A: If both follow ITU-R BS.1770, they should agree closely on integrated loudness, usually within a tenth of a dB or so. True-peak readings can differ slightly because meters oversample differently. Pick one meter and use it for every version you compare.
Q: Is local always higher quality?
A: Not automatically. A local tool isn’t smarter, it’s just better defined: you keep the original WAV, you know which settings ran, and you can run it again tomorrow and get the same answer.
Q: Does the CoProducer site upload my song when I analyze it?
A: No. The analyzer on the CoProducer page sends your file to an engine running on your own computer (at 127.0.0.1) if you’ve started one. If that engine isn’t running, the page measures the file in your browser, so it stays on your device either way.
Q: Which free LUFS meters run locally?
A: Youlean Loudness Meter 2 has a free plug-in and standalone app, FFmpeg’s ebur128 filter is free on the command line, and many DAWs include a meter, such as Logic Pro’s Loudness Meter or REAPER’s JS: Loudness Meter. The CoProducer analyzer reads a file in your browser. Whichever you pick, measure the exported file and use the same meter for every version.
Q: Can I check LUFS without uploading my song?
A: Yes. A loudness meter in your DAW, a free plug-in, an FFmpeg command or a browser-based analyzer measures integrated LUFS and true peak on your own computer, so the file never leaves it.

---

## Can stem separation fix a bad mix? Stems diagnose mixes, they don’t replace them
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/stems-diagnose-mixes-do-not-replace-them.html
Section: Stems · 21 August 2026 · 7 min
Summary: Stem separation can’t fix a bad mix, but it shows what’s wrong. Mute or lower one stem at a time to find what eats your headroom, then fix it in the session.

Stem separation won’t fix a bad mix, but it’s one of the fastest ways to find out what’s wrong with one. Pull the track apart, mute or turn down one part at a time, and re-measure. The part that moves the true peak or clears the mud is your suspect. Then go back to the session and fix it there. Separated stems carry bleed and artifacts, so they make a good flashlight and a poor replacement for the mix.
Here’s the situation it’s good for. A mix keeps slamming the limiter, or the vocal disappears in the hook, and you can’t tell why by ear any more because you’ve heard it 300 times. Maybe it’s a beat you bought as a two-track, or an old bounce whose session is gone. A separator gives you four handles on a file that used to have one. That’s really useful, as long as you’re clear about what those handles are.

### What can stems actually tell me about my mix?
Two kinds of things: where the energy is, and what each part does to the whole.
- Collisions in level. Which parts peak at the same moment and use up the ceiling together. Kick and 808 are the classic pair.
- Collisions in frequency. Which parts pile into the same band. A chord pad and a vocal both living at 200–400 Hz is how a vocal goes muddy without being quiet.
- Whether a problem is level or tone. If soloing the drums shows clean hits and the clipping only shows up when the bass comes in, the fix is balance, not a new kick sample.
What stems can’t tell you is what the arrangement should have been. They show you what’s there. Deciding what goes is still your job.

### How do I find which part is eating my headroom?
The test is simple: leave one out and measure again. Mute one stem, sum the others, read the true peak and loudness. Then try the same stem 3 dB down instead of muted, because that’s closer to a real mix move. If muting a part barely changes the true peak, that part isn’t your problem, however loud it sounds.
To show it working without anybody’s real song, we built a synthetic test: a generated 30-second beat at 140 BPM with four stems (drums, an 808, a synth “voice” lead and chords). We know exactly what went into it, so we can check whether the method finds the right answer. We summed them with one gain so the mix’s highest sample sat at −0.3 dBFS, which looks safe on a sample meter. Its true peak, measured to the ITU-R BS.1770 method with FFmpeg’s ebur128 filter, is 0.0 dBTP. That’s a full dB over the −1 dBTP that Spotify recommends for masters.
The script below does the leave-one-out test on any folder of stems. It needs Python 3, NumPy and FFmpeg, and it only reads your files.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""stem_check.py: use stems to find which part of a mix is causing a problem.
Usage: python3 stem_check.py FOLDER   (FOLDER holds the stem WAVs, plus mix.wav if you have it)
For each stem it prints loudness and true peak (FFmpeg ebur128, ITU-R BS.1770), where its energy
sits (sub / bass / low-mid / mid / presence / high), and what the summed mix does to true peak
and loudness if that stem is muted or turned down 3 dB. Nothing is written over your files.
Needs: Python 3, NumPy, FFmpeg on PATH."""
import re, subprocess, sys, tempfile, os
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np

BANDS = [("sub", 20, 60), ("bass", 60, 150), ("lowmid", 150, 400), ("mid", 400, 1200), ("pres", 1200, 4000), ("high", 4000, 18000)]

def read(path):
    """Decode any audio file to 48 kHz stereo float with FFmpeg."""
    raw = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", str(path), "-f", "f32le", "-ac", "2", "-ar", "48000", "-"],
                         capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
    return np.frombuffer(raw, np.float32).reshape(-1, 2).astype(np.float64)

def meter(x):
    """Integrated LUFS and true peak (dBTP) of a float array, measured by FFmpeg ebur128."""
    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix=".wav", delete=False) as fh: p = fh.name
    subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-y", "-f", "f32le", "-ar", "48000", "-ac", "2", "-i", "-", "-c:a", "pcm_f32le", p],
                   input=x.astype(np.float32).tobytes(), check=True)
    err = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-hide_banner", "-nostats", "-i", p, "-af", "ebur128=peak=true", "-f", "null", "-"],
                         capture_output=True, text=True).stderr
    os.unlink(p)
    lufs = float(re.findall(r"I:\s+(-?[\d.]+|-inf) LUFS", err)[-1])
    tp = float(re.findall(r"Peak:\s+(-?[\d.]+|-inf) dBFS", err)[-1])
    return lufs, tp

def bands(x):
    """Share of the stem's energy in each band, in percent."""
    m = x.mean(1); P = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(m)) ** 2; f = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(m), 1 / 48000)
    tot = P[(f >= 20) & (f < 18000)].sum() or 1.0
    return [100 * P[(f >= lo) & (f < hi)].sum() / tot for _, lo, hi in BANDS]

def main(folder):
    folder = Path(folder)
    files = sorted(p for p in folder.iterdir() if p.suffix.lower() in (".wav", ".flac", ".aif", ".aiff") and p.stem != "mix")
    stems = {p.stem: read(p) for p in files}
    n = min(len(x) for x in stems.values()); stems = {k: x[:n] for k, x in stems.items()}
    total = sum(stems.values())
    if (folder / "mix.wav").exists():
        mix = read(folder / "mix.wav")[:n]
        res = 20 * np.log10(np.sqrt(np.mean((mix - total) ** 2)) / np.sqrt(np.mean(mix ** 2)) + 1e-12)
        print(f"stems vs mix.wav: residual {res:.1f} dB (below -60 dB means the stems add back up to the mix)")
    L, T = meter(total)
    print(f"summed mix: {L:.1f} LUFS, true peak {T:+.1f} dBTP\n")
    print(f"{'stem':8} {'LUFS':>6} {'TP dBTP':>8} | " + " ".join(f"{b:>6}" for b, _, _ in BANDS) + " | mute: TP / LUFS   | -3 dB: TP / LUFS")
    for k, x in stems.items():
        l, tp = meter(x); sh = bands(x)
        mt, ml = meter(total - x)[::-1]
        dt, dl = meter(total - x + x * 10 ** (-3 / 20))[::-1]
        print(f"{k:8} {l:6.1f} {tp:+8.1f} | " + " ".join(f"{s:5.0f}%" for s in sh) + f" | {mt:+6.1f} / {ml:6.1f} | {dt:+6.1f} / {dl:6.1f}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "stems")
Here’s what it printed for the known stems:
$ python3 stem_check.py stems
stems vs mix.wav: residual -148.7 dB (below -60 dB means the stems add back up to the mix)
summed mix: -15.8 LUFS, true peak -0.0 dBTP

stem       LUFS  TP dBTP |    sub   bass lowmid    mid   pres   high | mute: TP / LUFS   | -3 dB: TP / LUFS
bass      -17.6    -10.4 |    94%     6%     0%     0%     0%     0% |   -1.9 /  -19.2 |   -0.5 /  -17.3
drums     -19.5     -2.1 |    34%    57%     5%     0%     0%     2% |   -8.0 /  -17.4 |   -2.3 /  -16.7
other     -34.3    -26.8 |     0%     0%    80%    20%     1%     0% |   -0.2 /  -15.9 |   -0.1 /  -15.8
vocals    -33.9    -18.8 |     0%     2%    38%    50%     2%     8% |   -0.0 /  -15.9 |   -0.0 /  -15.8
Read it from right to left. Muting the vocal leaves the true peak at 0.0, so turning the vocal down buys no headroom at all. Muting the chords frees 0.2 dB. Muting the 808 frees 1.9 dB and muting the drums frees 8. But look at the middle columns: the drums alone peak at −2.1 dBTP and the 808 alone at −10.4. Neither one is over the ceiling by itself. Together they hit 0.0. That’s two parts landing on the same moments in the same low band (the drum stem is 91% sub and bass energy, the 808 is 94% sub). The kick and the 808 are stacking.
Also notice that turning the 808 down 3 dB only gets you to −0.5. A plain level change isn’t enough. The real fix is a mix move: duck the 808 under the kick with a short sidechain, shorten the 808’s attack so it doesn’t start on the kick’s transient, or choose which one owns the very bottom. Then limit the mix bus. You can only do that properly in the session, where the kick and the 808 are still separate tracks.

### What happens when the stems come from a separator?
Known stems are the best case. Usually you only have the stereo file. So we ran the same synthetic mix through Demucs (the htdemucs model described in the Hybrid Transformer Demucs paper), on an ordinary CPU with no GPU. It took about 14 seconds for 30 seconds of audio.
$ pip install demucs
$ demucs -n htdemucs --float32 -o sep stems/mix.wav
# writes sep/htdemucs/mix/drums.wav, bass.wav, vocals.wav, other.wav
Then we compared each separated stem with the real one. SDR (signal-to-distortion ratio) is the standard score from the BSS Eval / museval tools and from benchmarks like MUSDB18 and the Music Demixing Challenge. Higher is better. At 10 dB, the error has about a tenth of the stem’s power, and at 6 dB about a quarter. We also split each error into bleed (bits of the other stems) and artifacts (sound that wasn’t in any stem).
$ python3 sep_compare.py stems sep/htdemucs/mix
stem     SDR dB   own  bleed  artif.  biggest leak from
drums       6.1   85%   7.6%      8%  bass (7.6%)
bass       10.7   93%   0.0%      7%  drums (0.0%)
vocals      6.2   76%   0.3%     24%  other (0.3%)
other      10.9   92%   0.3%      8%  vocals (0.2%)

separated stems summed back: residual vs mix -25.7 dB
mix.wav           -15.8 LUFS, true peak -0.0 dBTP
sum of separated  -15.9 LUFS, true peak -0.7 dBTP
