That’s a good separation. It’s also clearly not the original. The drum stem carries 7.6% of the 808, so the two parts that were colliding are now mixed into each other’s stems. The synth “voice” came out with 24% artifacts, which makes sense because the model learned singing from real recordings and our lead isn’t one. Put all four separated stems back together and they don’t rebuild the mix: the leftover is only 25.7 dB down, and the true peak of the sum is −0.7 dBTP where the real mix was 0.0. Just splitting and re-summing changed the master’s peak by 0.7 dB.
Don’t read our numbers as a benchmark. One generated beat says nothing about how Demucs does on your genre. What it does show is the shape of the problem, and that shape holds for every separator.

### Is the diagnosis still right with separated stems?
Yes, and that’s the good news. Here’s the same leave-one-out check on the Demucs stems:
$ python3 stem_check.py sep/htdemucs/mix
summed mix: -15.9 LUFS, true peak -0.7 dBTP

stem       LUFS  TP dBTP |    sub   bass lowmid    mid   pres   high | mute: TP / LUFS   | -3 dB: TP / LUFS
bass      -19.1    -12.4 |    98%     2%     0%     0%     0%     0% |   -2.0 /  -19.1 |   -1.0 /  -17.1
drums     -19.3     -2.2 |    40%    53%     5%     0%     0%     2% |  -10.6 /  -18.9 |   -3.1 /  -17.1
other     -35.0    -25.7 |     1%     1%    76%    22%     1%     0% |   -0.8 /  -15.9 |   -0.7 /  -15.9
vocals    -36.0    -22.6 |     0%     2%    38%    58%     2%     0% |   -0.7 /  -15.9 |   -0.7 /  -15.9
Compare each row with the −0.7 baseline of the re-summed stems. Muting the vocal or the chords changes nothing (−0.7, −0.8). Muting the 808 frees 1.3 dB and muting the drums frees about 10. It’s the same answer as the known stems: kick and 808 together. The exact dBs moved a little and the verdict didn’t. That’s why stems are good for diagnosing a mix: you need the right suspect, not perfect numbers.

### Can I master or remix from separated stems instead?
You can, and sometimes it’s the only option, like a two-track beat with no session. Just know what you’re working with. Turn the separated 808 down and the 7.6% of it that leaked into the drum stem stays exactly where it was. Push a stem up and its artifacts come up too. Every move you make is a move on the separator’s guess.
That’s different from stem mastering, where a mix engineer prints real stems out of the session so the master can be balanced a little. Printed stems add back up to the mix exactly. Separated stems don’t, as you saw above.
So here’s the workflow we’d suggest:
1. Separate the bounce and listen to each stem soloed. Solo is a flashlight.
2. Measure with the leave-one-out test. Write down which part moves the true peak and which parts share a band.
3. Fix in the session if you have one. If you don’t, ask the producer for the session or for printed stems.
4. Re-measure the new bounce, not the stems. The mix you release is the one that has to pass.

### Does separating my song mean uploading it?
It doesn’t have to. Demucs runs offline on an ordinary computer, as the timing above shows. NoDAW StemSplit also separates on your own machine, so an unreleased song never leaves it. You can hear what separated stems sound like on this page, and the mix panel on the CoProducer page shows what a finished bounce is doing.
Note: Try the stem player in StemSplit, or drop a bounce on the live mix panel in See what the mix is doing. Both stay on your machine.
Q: Can stem separation fix a bad mix?
A: Not on its own. A separator guesses which sound belongs to which part, and every guess leaves some bleed and artifacts behind. It’s great for finding out what’s wrong, like which part is eating the headroom or hiding the vocal. The fix belongs in the original session, where the parts are still clean.
Q: Can I master from separated stems?
A: You can, but you’re mastering the separator’s guesses as well as the song. In our test, adding the four separated stems back together didn’t even rebuild the original: the leftover difference was only 25.7 dB down and the true peak moved by 0.7 dB. Stem mastering works well when the mix engineer prints real stems from the session. Separated stems are a diagnostic copy.
Q: Do stems fix true peak?
A: No. Stems help you find which parts are stacking up and using the ceiling. Then you fix that in the mix, for example by shortening the 808 under the kick, and limit the mix bus afterwards.
Q: How do I find what’s using up the headroom in my mix?
A: Mute one stem at a time and re-measure the true peak of what’s left. When muting a stem barely changes the peak, that stem isn’t the cause. When muting it, or turning it down 3 dB, frees up a dB or more, you’ve found your suspect. Two stems that peak together are the usual answer.

---

## Does a slowed or screwed version need its own master? Measure the peak again
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/screw-tempo-still-needs-a-legal-peak.html
Section: ScrewAI · 21 August 2026 · 7 min
Summary: Slowing a song doesn’t make its peaks safe. Varispeed can turn hidden overs into real ones and reverb adds new peaks, so measure the slowed file before upload.

Yes, a slowed or screwed version needs its own peak check, and often a light re-master. Slowing a song changes its length, pitch and tone, and it can turn peaks that were hiding between samples into real ones. Adding reverb or echo stacks new peaks on top. Measure the slowed render, and keep its true peak under −1 dBTP before it goes to a store or a streaming service.
Slowed versions are everywhere now: the official “slowed + reverb” cut next to the original, the screwed tape a DJ makes for the car, the half-speed edit for a video. They feel like a creative bonus, so they tend to skip the checks the main master got. That’s where the trouble starts. The slowed file is a new render, and the meter doesn’t care how good it sounds.

### What actually changes when you slow a song down?
The classic screw sound comes from slowing the whole record, the way a turntable or tape machine does when you drop the speed. Tempo and pitch go down together. The Houston style that DJ Screw pioneered pulled songs down to roughly 60 to 70 BPM and then chopped, skipped and repeated parts on top. Digital tools call this varispeed: play the samples back at a lower rate, then resample to a normal rate like 44.1 or 48 kHz.
Three things move when you do that:
- Length. At 80% speed a three-minute song runs three minutes and 45 seconds.
- Pitch and tone. Everything drops, by about four semitones at 80%. Energy moves toward the low end, so the song feels heavier.
- Measured loudness. Loudness meters built on ITU-R BS.1770 weight the upper mids more than the deep lows. When the song’s energy slides down, the reading usually drops a little, about a LU in our test below, even though nobody turned anything down.
What doesn’t change is the rulebook at the other end. A store or streaming service measures the slowed file exactly as it measures any other master.

### Why can a slowed version clip when the original didn’t?
There are two common reasons, and they stack.
The first is peaks between samples. A loud master often has a sample peak of −0.1 dBFS but a true peak over 0 dBTP, because the smooth wave the samples describe rises higher between them. Those are the overs that codecs and converters run into. When you slow the song and resample it, the new samples land in new places on that same wave, and some land right on top of those hidden peaks. The over that only a true-peak meter could see becomes a real sample value over full scale. If anything downstream works in fixed point, that’s hard clipping.
The second is what you add. Slowed versions almost always get extra processing: reverb, echo, a bass boost, a bit of saturation. Reverb and echo are delayed copies of the song mixed back in. On a sustained pad they mostly add a wash. On a kick, a snare or a hard vocal consonant, the delayed copy can land on the next hit and the two add together. A master with a perfectly legal peak can come out of a reverb plugin a dB or two over.
There’s also a quieter third reason: people slow the loud master, the one that was already squeezed to the ceiling, because it’s the file they have. That master had no headroom to begin with.

### How do you check a slowed render?
Measure it like any other master: integrated loudness plus true peak. Here’s a small script that does the slowdown and the before/after check in one go. It uses FFmpeg’s asetrate, aresample and ebur128 filters, so the only things you need are Python and FFmpeg. It writes a 32-bit float file, so nothing is clipped on disk while you look at the numbers.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""screw_check.py: slow a finished master the way a screw/varispeed render does, then check it again.
Usage: python3 screw_check.py MASTER [SPEED] [--reverb]
SPEED 0.8 = 80% speed (pitch drops with tempo, like slowing a record). --reverb adds a simple echo tail
like the "slowed + reverb" style. Prints integrated loudness and true peak (FFmpeg ebur128, ITU-R BS.1770)
before and after, and the gain that puts the slowed render back under -1.0 dBTP.
Writes slowed.wav (32-bit float, so nothing is clipped on disk). Your master is only read.
Needs: Python 3, FFmpeg on PATH."""
import re, subprocess, sys

def meter(path):
    err = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-hide_banner", "-nostats", "-i", path, "-af", "ebur128=peak=true+sample",
                          "-f", "null", "-"], capture_output=True, text=True).stderr
    peaks = re.findall(r"Peak:\s+(-?[\d.inf]+) dBFS", err)
    return dict(I=float(re.findall(r"I:\s+(-?[\d.]+) LUFS", err)[-1]),
                SP=float(peaks[-2]), TP=float(peaks[-1]))

def render(src, dst, speed, reverb):
    rate = int(re.search(r"(\d+) Hz", subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-hide_banner", "-i", src],
               capture_output=True, text=True).stderr).group(1))
    chain = f"asetrate={rate * speed:.0f},aresample={rate}"      # varispeed: tempo and pitch together
    if reverb:
        chain += ",volume=-12dB,aecho=1.0:1.0:60|130|210:0.35|0.25|0.15,volume=12dB"  # echo tail added to dry (run 12 dB down: aecho clips at full scale)
    subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-y", "-i", src, "-af", chain, "-c:a", "pcm_f32le", dst], check=True)

def main(src, speed=0.8, reverb=False):
    a = meter(src); render(src, "slowed.wav", speed, reverb); b = meter("slowed.wav")
    label = f"slowed {speed:.0%}" + (" + reverb" if reverb else "")
    print(f"{'':20}{'LUFS':>8}{'sample pk':>11}{'true pk':>9}")
    for name, d in (("original", a), (label, b)):
        ok = "ok" if d["TP"] <= -1.0 else "OVER -1 dBTP"
        print(f"{name:20}{d['I']:8.1f}{d['SP']:+11.1f}{d['TP']:+9.1f}  {ok}")
    if b["TP"] > -1.0:
        g = -1.0 - b["TP"] - 0.1
        print(f"\nturn the slowed render down {-g:.1f} dB (or re-limit it with true-peak mode) before upload")
    else:
        print("\nslowed render is under -1.0 dBTP")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    args = [x for x in sys.argv[1:] if not x.startswith("--")]
    main(args[0], float(args[1]) if len(args) > 1 else 0.8, "--reverb" in sys.argv)
We ran it on synthetic test material, not a real song: a 30-second generated beat with a kick, a snare, hats, bass and chords. One copy is a typical loud bounce, pushed 6 dB into a sample-peak limiter at −0.1 dBFS. The other is the same master turned down so its true peak sits at a legal −1.2 dBTP.
$ python3 screw_check.py master.wav 0.8
                        LUFS  sample pk  true pk
original                -7.6       -0.1     +1.2  OVER -1 dBTP
slowed 80%              -8.7       +1.1     +1.1  OVER -1 dBTP

turn the slowed render down 2.2 dB (or re-limit it with true-peak mode) before upload

$ python3 screw_check.py master_legal.wav 0.8
                        LUFS  sample pk  true pk
original               -10.0       -2.5     -1.2  ok
slowed 80%             -11.1       -1.3     -1.3  ok

slowed render is under -1.0 dBTP

$ python3 screw_check.py master_legal.wav 0.8 --reverb
                        LUFS  sample pk  true pk
original               -10.0       -2.5     -1.2  ok
slowed 80% + reverb    -10.5       +0.9     +0.9  OVER -1 dBTP

turn the slowed render down 2.0 dB (or re-limit it with true-peak mode) before upload
Here’s what those three runs show, still on synthetic audio:
- The loud master was already illegal (+1.2 dBTP) even though its sample peak read −0.1 dBFS. Slowing it barely moved the true peak, but the sample peak jumped from −0.1 to +1.1 dBFS. The hidden over became a real one.
- The legal master stayed legal when we only slowed it (−1.3 dBTP). Slowing on its own is not the villain.
- Add a simple three-tap echo tail and the same legal master came out at +0.9 dBTP, about 2 dB over the line.
Your song will give different numbers. That’s the point: you can’t predict them, so you measure them.

### What should you do when the slowed version is over?
You have three fixes. Pick the highest one you can.
1. Slow the mix, then master it. If you have the session or a pre-limiter bounce, slow that and add your reverb, then put the limiter last. The limiter then sees the peaks it actually has to catch. This sounds best, because the limiter isn’t fighting a file that was already limited once.
2. Run a true-peak limiter on the slowed render. Set its ceiling to −1 dBTP (or −2 dBTP for a loud master) and turn on its true-peak or oversampling mode. Keep the gain reduction small. If it’s working hard, go back to fix 1.
3. Turn it down. Plain gain is the cleanest fix of all. The script prints how much it takes. A slowed version a couple of dB quieter is usually fine, for the reason in the next section.
Then measure again. Every fix is a new render, and the only number that counts is the one from the file you upload.

### Should a slowed version be as loud as the original?
It doesn’t have to be. Most streaming services turn tracks up or down to a common level when people play them. Spotify’s loudness normalization page says it adjusts tracks to −14 LUFS by ITU 1770, asks for true peak below −1 dBTP, and asks for below −2 dBTP when a master is louder than −14 LUFS, because loud tracks pick up more distortion when they’re encoded. It also says it only turns a quiet track up as far as its true peak allows, leaving 1 dB of headroom for lossy formats.
So a slowed version that lands at −11 LUFS instead of −9 doesn’t lose anything on a normalized playlist. It just gets turned down less. Chasing the original’s loudness by pushing the limiter harder buys you nothing there and costs you punch. The essay on why streaming turns loud masters down walks through that trade.
The exception is a slowed version that will sit in a DJ set or a mixtape next to other tracks with no normalization. There, match it by ear against its neighbours at the same level, and still keep the true peak legal.

### A quick checklist for slowed and screwed releases
- Start from the mix, or the quietest master you have, not the loudest.
- Slow it, add the reverb or chops, then limit last with true-peak mode on.
- Measure the exact file you’ll upload: integrated LUFS and true peak.
- Keep true peak under −1 dBTP, or under −2 dBTP if it’s louder than −14 LUFS.
- Listen to the low end on small speakers. Dropping the pitch moves bass notes down, and a sub that worked at full speed can turn into a rumble you can’t hear on a phone.
- If you also make an MP3 or AAC for socials, check that too. Why does my master clip after MP3 or AAC? on its own.
Note: If you make slowed versions often, the ScrewAI page and the syrup lab demo let you preview the sound locally. Whatever renders the file, the final step is the same: measure it. CoProducer’s analyzer reads true peak and loudness on your own machine, without uploading the song.
Slowed doesn’t mean exempt. Treat the slowed version as its own master and it’ll survive the trip to the store just as well as the original.
Q: Does slowing a song down fix clipping?
A: No. Slowing it moves the peaks around and can lower them a little, but a master that was over the ceiling usually stays over. In our synthetic test, a master at +1.2 dBTP was still at +1.1 dBTP after slowing to 80%. Measure the slowed file, not the original.
Q: Why does my slowed and reverb version clip when the original didn’t?
A: Usually because of what you added. Reverb and echo add delayed copies of the song on top of itself, and when those copies line up with a kick or a vocal hit the peaks add up. Slowing can also turn peaks that sat between samples into real sample values. Either way the file needs a fresh peak check.
Q: What LUFS should a slowed version be?
A: The same delivery rules apply as for any master. Spotify normalizes to about −14 LUFS and asks for true peak under −1 dBTP, or under −2 dBTP if the master is louder than −14 LUFS. A slowed version can be a bit quieter than the original without anyone noticing, because playback normalization evens it out.
Q: Should I slow the master or the mix?
A: If you have the session, slow the mix before the limiter and master the slowed version, so the limiter sees the final peaks. If you only have the finished master, slow it, then turn it down or run a true-peak limiter on the slowed render, and measure the result.

---

## What LUFS for Reels, TikTok and Shorts? Why vertical video is a loudness trap
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/vertical-video-is-a-loudness-trap.html
Section: Social · 21 August 2026 · 8 min
Summary: Reels, TikTok and Shorts don’t publish a LUFS target. Check the exported clip instead: true peak under −1 dBTP, a strong first 3 seconds, a mono check.

There isn’t an official number to hit. TikTok, Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts don’t publish a LUFS target the way Spotify publishes −14, so mastering to “the TikTok LUFS” means chasing a rumour. Master the clip you actually export instead: true peak at or below −1 dBTP after the editing app has encoded it, an opening three seconds that isn’t buried, the voice clearly on top of the beat, and a quick check in mono on a phone.
You know the move. The beat video sounds huge in the session, you cut 15 seconds of the hook, drop it into the editor, export, post. Then you watch it on your phone between two other clips and it’s either a whisper or it crunches on the snare. Nothing about the music changed. The trip from the timeline to the feed did.
It looks like delivery is done when you hit export. It isn’t. Your audio gets encoded by the editor, encoded again by the platform, levelled by a player you don’t control, and played through a tiny speaker. Here’s what you can control, with a test you can run on your own clips.

### What LUFS should a Reel, TikTok or Short be?
Here’s what is actually documented, as far as we can find:
- Spotify publishes its number: tracks are adjusted to −14 LUFS, and it asks for true peak below −1 dBTP, or below −2 dBTP if the master is louder than −14 LUFS (Spotify for Artists). That’s music streaming, but it’s the clearest public reference there is.
- Instagram and Facebook: Meta’s engineers have written that Reels and Stories use xHE-AAC loudness management, which brings the average loudness of every clip to the same target level and manages dynamic range for the playback environment, in the player (Meta Engineering). They don’t give the number.
- YouTube doesn’t publish a figure either, but you can watch it work. Stats for nerds shows a “content loudness” value, and as the Production Advice write-up explains, a positive value means the video is being turned down, while quieter videos aren’t turned up, at least when it was written (Production Advice).
- TikTok doesn’t publish a loudness target that we could find.
If you want a starting point, around −14 LUFS integrated is a sane habit: nothing has to lift you much, and no normaliser has to turn you down hard. It isn’t a rule, and it’s rarely why a clip fails on a phone.

### Why does my Reel sound quieter (or more crushed) than everyone else’s?
A few usual suspects:
- It was mastered hot and got turned down. A clip cut from a loud master can easily sit 6 LU or more above −14 (our synthetic one below measured −7.6 LUFS). Turned down to match its neighbours, all that limiting just sounds flat and small.
- The opening is quiet. Levelling is decided by the loud part, so a soft talking intro plays under everything else.
- The voice is fighting the beat in the midrange, which is most of what a phone speaker plays.
- Something cancels in mono, which plenty of small speakers effectively are.
- The export clipped it. That one surprises people.

### Does the editing app change my audio when I export?
Almost always, yes. A typical MP4 export carries lossy AAC audio, so pick the highest audio bitrate your editor offers. Lossy encoders rebuild the waveform rather than copying it, and the rebuilt peaks can come out higher than the ones you limited. Then the platform encodes it again.
We measured it on synthetic test material (no real songs; trust the shape more than the decimals). The “chorus clip” is 15 seconds cut from a dense synthetic beat that was pushed 6 dB into a plain sample-peak limiter set to −0.1 dBFS, the way a lot of loud masters get made. We exported it the way an editor might, AAC at 128 kbps, using FFmpeg’s built-in encoder.
Synthetic clip | Integrated | True peak before export | True peak after AAC 128k
Chorus clip, as limited | −7.6 LUFS | +0.7 dBTP | +2.3 dBTP
Same clip, trimmed to −2.0 dBTP first | −10.3 LUFS | −2.0 dBTP | −1.6 dBTP
Talking intro, beat drops at 9 s | −10.5 LUFS | +0.7 dBTP | +1.7 dBTP
Voice over a beat, balanced | −15.5 LUFS | −1.1 dBTP | −1.3 dBTP
The limiter promised −0.1 dBFS, yet the clip measured +0.7 dBTP before export, because a sample-peak limiter doesn’t see the peaks between samples. After the AAC export it was +2.3 dBTP, with decoded samples above full scale that will clip anywhere the playback chain is fixed-point. Trimming 2.7 dB first left it at −1.6 dBTP. Encoders differ, so measure the exported file, not the timeline.
On any platform that levels loudness, that trim costs you nothing. The player was going to turn a −7.6 LUFS clip down anyway.

### How do I check a clip before I post it?
You don’t need a special plugin. If you have FFmpeg installed, this reads the audio straight out of a video file and gives you the numbers that matter for a short clip. It uses FFmpeg’s ebur128 filter, which follows the ITU-R BS.1770 loudness and true-peak method.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""clip_check.py: a loudness check for short vertical clips (Reels, Shorts, TikTok).
    python3 clip_check.py my_reel.mp4 [more files...]
Works on video or audio files (anything ffmpeg can read). Prints integrated loudness,
the loudest 3-second stretch (max short-term), how far that jumps above the average,
the opening 3 seconds (where people decide to keep watching), true peak, and how much
level the clip loses when it is played in mono (0 = nothing lost)."""
import re, subprocess, sys

def ebur128(path, mono=False):
    af = ("pan=stereo|c0=0.5*c0+0.5*c1|c1=0.5*c0+0.5*c1," if mono else "") + "ebur128=peak=true"
    err = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-hide_banner", "-nostats", "-i", path, "-vn", "-af", af,
                          "-f", "null", "-"], capture_output=True, text=True).stderr
    I = float(re.findall(r"I:\s+(-?[\d.]+) LUFS", err)[-1])
    tp = float(re.findall(r"Peak:\s+(-?[\d.]+|-inf) dBFS", err)[-1])
    # per-100 ms lines: "t: 3.1  ... M: -14.2 S: -15.0 ..."; skip the first 3 s (window not full yet)
    S = [(float(t), float(s)) for t, s in re.findall(r"t:\s*([\d.]+).*?S:\s*(-?[\d.]+)", err)]
    full = [s for t, s in S if t >= 3.0]
    opening = min(full[0:1] or [-70.0])  # the first full 3 s window
    return I, max(full), opening, tp

for path in sys.argv[1:]:
    I, smax, opening, tp = ebur128(path)
    Im = ebur128(path, mono=True)[0]
    notes = []
    if tp > -1.0: notes.append("true peak above -1 dBTP")
    if smax - I > 5.0: notes.append("loudest 3 s jumps more than 5 LU over the average")
    if opening - I < -4.0: notes.append("opening 3 s is much quieter than the rest")
    if Im - I < -3.0: notes.append("loses a lot in mono: check wideners/polarity")
    print(f"{path}\n  integrated {I:6.1f} LUFS | loudest 3 s {smax - I:+5.1f} LU | opening 3 s {opening - I:+5.1f} LU"
          f" | true peak {tp:+5.1f} dBTP | mono {Im - I:+5.1f} LU")
    print("  " + ("; ".join(notes) if notes else "nothing flagged"))
Run on the synthetic clips above (example data, not real songs):
$ python3 clip_check.py clip_chorus.wav clip_chorus_export.m4a clip_chorus_trim2_export.m4a clip_dropintro.wav clip_widebed.wav
clip_chorus.wav
  integrated   -7.6 LUFS | loudest 3 s  +0.3 LU | opening 3 s  -0.1 LU | true peak  +0.7 dBTP | mono  -0.2 LU
  true peak above -1 dBTP
clip_chorus_export.m4a
  integrated   -7.7 LUFS | loudest 3 s  +0.2 LU | opening 3 s  -0.2 LU | true peak  +2.3 dBTP | mono  -0.2 LU
  true peak above -1 dBTP
clip_chorus_trim2_export.m4a
  integrated  -10.4 LUFS | loudest 3 s  +0.3 LU | opening 3 s  -0.1 LU | true peak  -1.6 dBTP | mono  -0.2 LU
  nothing flagged
clip_dropintro.wav
  integrated  -10.5 LUFS | loudest 3 s  +3.2 LU | opening 3 s  -5.6 LU | true peak  +0.7 dBTP | mono  -0.2 LU
  true peak above -1 dBTP; opening 3 s is much quieter than the rest
clip_widebed.wav
  integrated  -14.1 LUFS | loudest 3 s  +0.2 LU | opening 3 s  -0.2 LU | true peak  +0.3 dBTP | mono  -5.1 LU
  true peak above -1 dBTP; loses a lot in mono: check wideners/polarity
How to read it: loudest 3 s and opening 3 s are short-term loudness relative to the whole clip. Mono is how much level the clip loses when left and right are summed and played on both sides; 0 means nothing lost. The flag thresholds are our rules of thumb, not a standard. Measure the file you’re about to upload, after export, not the session.

### Why do the first three seconds matter so much?
Because that’s when someone decides whether to keep watching, and it’s often the quietest part. Take the talking-intro clip: nine seconds of speech over a soft bed, then the beat drops. Its integrated loudness (−10.5 LUFS) is set mostly by the drop. The opening three seconds sit 5.6 LU under that, and the loudest three seconds sit 3.2 LU over it, so there’s close to 9 LU between what people hear first and the loudest moment.
When a player levels that clip to a shared target, it levels the average. The talking gets turned down along with the drop, and the opener ends up playing well under the clip before it in the feed.
Broadcast has a rule for the opposite problem. For adverts and promos, EBU R 128 s1 keeps the loudest 3-second short-term reading within +5 LU of the programme’s loudness target, so a short spot can’t sneak in one massive moment (EBU R 128 s1). It’s a useful ceiling for clips too. For a scroll feed, also watch the floor: bring the talking up, tuck the bed under it, or open on the hook and talk after.

### How loud should my voice be over the beat?
There’s no official ratio. What helps is measuring the voice and the bed separately instead of guessing from the mix: solo each, export, and run the same script on both.
In our balanced example the voice measured −16.0 LUFS and the bed −24.0 LUFS, so the bed sat 8 LU under the voice. Treat that as a starting point, not a rule, and judge it the only way that counts: on a phone, at normal volume, next to a clip you like. For a beat showcase with a spoken intro, automate the bed down under the talking and back up after.
For sung vocals over a beat, see how loud the vocal should sit.

### Why does my clip sound thin or hollow on a phone?
Two reasons. First, phone speakers don’t reproduce much real bass, so an 808 that carries the track on headphones can vanish (see why your 808 disappears on phone speakers). Give the low end some harmonics higher up.
Second, mono. Our wide-bed clip has a pad through a careless “widener” that flips one side’s polarity. Summed to mono it lost 5.1 LU, because the pad cancels itself and only the voice survives. If your mono number drops more than a few LU, find the plugin doing it. Wide mixes fail in mono walks through the mid/side check.

### What should I check before I batch-export?
1. Pick the hero clip: the loudest moment or the most talking.
2. Cut from a loud master? Trim it to about −2 dBTP true peak.
3. Check the opening isn’t more than a few LU under the clip.
4. Export, then measure the exported file: true peak at or below −1 dBTP, little mono loss.
5. Listen once on a phone speaker, next to a clip you like.
6. Only then batch-resize the visuals with the same audio settings.
If you’d rather not run scripts, export the clip’s audio as a WAV and drop it into CoProducer’s analyzer. It reads integrated LUFS, true peak and clipped samples on your machine, so you can see the problem before your followers hear it.
Note: No platform gives you a short-form LUFS number, so control what survives the trip instead. The music side of the same problem: why streaming turns loud masters down and why masters clip after MP3 or AAC.
Q: What LUFS should I use for TikTok, Reels and Shorts?
A: None of them publishes a LUFS target the way Spotify publishes −14, so there is no official number to hit. Around −14 LUFS integrated is a common working habit. What matters more is the exported file: true peak at or below −1 dBTP, a strong opening and a clear voice.
Q: Do TikTok and Spotify use the same loudness target?
A: Don’t assume it. Spotify documents −14 LUFS for music playback. TikTok doesn’t publish a target, and Meta says Reels and Stories bring clips to a common target level in the player but doesn’t publish the number. Treat each platform as its own lane, and still keep true peak under −1 dBTP everywhere.
Q: Why does my video sound quieter after I upload it?
A: Usually because it was louder than the platform’s reference, so the player turned it down. Meta describes this kind of loudness management for Reels and Stories, and YouTube shows it as content loudness in Stats for nerds. A crushed clip that gets turned down just sounds small next to the clip before it.
Q: Can I resize and master a clip in one step?
A: Keep them separate. Fix the sound first, export one hero clip, measure the exported file, then batch-resize the visuals with the same audio settings. Re-check the audio any time the export preset changes.

---

## Can mastering fix a bad mix? When a mastering pass is enough and when to reopen the session
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/mastering-bat-vs-opening-the-session.html
Section: Mastering · 21 August 2026 · 6 min
Summary: Mastering fixes whole-file problems like loudness, ceiling and broad tone. Clipped vocals, bad edits and mono cancellation live in the mix. Here’s how to tell.

Mastering can fix problems that affect the whole song the same way: overall loudness, the peak ceiling, and broad tone. It can’t fix problems that live inside the mix, like a vocal that clipped, a bad edit, a buried snare or a widener that cancels in mono. If the mix is honest, a quick mastering pass, even an automatic one, is a real time saver. If it isn’t, reopen the session first.
There’s a reason this question keeps coming up. One-click mastering is cheap and fast, and the mix is the part that takes forever. It’s tempting to bounce, drop the file on a mastering tool and hope it smooths everything out. Sometimes that works fine. Sometimes it makes a bad mix louder, which mostly makes its problems easier to hear.

### What can a mastering pass actually fix?
Think of mastering as processing that treats the stereo file as one thing. It works on everything at once, so it’s good at problems that are everywhere at once:
- Overall loudness. A mix sitting at −19 LUFS can be brought up toward a delivery level with gain and a limiter.
- The ceiling. A true-peak limiter keeps the loudest moments under −1 dBTP so encoders and converters don’t clip them.
- Broad tone. A mix that’s a little dull or a touch heavy in the low mids can take a gentle EQ tilt.
- Consistency. Several songs that need to sit together can be lined up in loudness and tone.
Notice what those have in common: if you turn the whole song up 2 dB, every instrument goes up 2 dB. That’s fine when the balance inside the mix is already right.

### What can’t mastering fix?
Anything that happens to one part and not the others. A mastering EQ that tames a harsh vocal also dulls the cymbals sitting at the same frequencies. A limiter that catches a clipped snare also squashes the kick. The usual suspects:
- Clipping that happened before the bounce. If a channel, a bus or a fixed-point bounce clipped, the tops of the wave are gone. Turning the file down afterwards doesn’t bring them back.
- Balance. A vocal that’s too quiet in the chorus, a bass that disappears on one note. Those are fader and automation moves.
- Edits and timing. Clicks at comp joins, a late double, a breath cut in half.
- Mono cancellation. A widener or a flipped polarity on one side can make a part vanish when the song plays in mono, on a phone speaker or a club system. The phase correlation essay covers how to hear it.
- DC offset. A constant offset from a faulty plugin or a bad recording chain eats headroom. You can high-pass it out at mastering, but the plugin that caused it is still in the session waiting to do it again.

### How do you tell which problem you have?
Ears first, but numbers help, especially for the problems you can’t hear on your monitors. Here’s a small triage script. It reads a bounce and sorts what it finds into two piles: things a mastering pass can handle, and things that send you back to the session. Loudness and true peak come from FFmpeg’s ebur128 filter, which follows ITU-R BS.1770. The rest is a few lines of NumPy.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""mix_triage.py: should this mix go through a mastering pass, or back into the session?
Usage: python3 mix_triage.py MIX.wav [MIX2.wav ...]
Reads each file and sorts what it finds into two piles:
  MASTER CAN FIX   whole-file gain and ceiling: integrated loudness, true peak
  OPEN THE SESSION problems baked into the mix: flat-topped (clipped) runs, a big DC offset,
                   left/right that cancel in mono (more than 4.5 dB lost when folded to mono;
                   identical channels lose 0 dB, unrelated ones about 3 dB)
Loudness and true peak come from FFmpeg ebur128 (ITU-R BS.1770). The clip check counts runs of 4+
consecutive samples within 0.01 dB of the file's own peak, which catches audio that was clipped
upstream and turned down afterwards. Your files are only read. Needs: Python 3, NumPy, FFmpeg."""
import re, subprocess, sys
import numpy as np

def meter(path):
    err = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-hide_banner", "-nostats", "-i", path, "-af", "ebur128=peak=true",
                          "-f", "null", "-"], capture_output=True, text=True).stderr
    return float(re.findall(r"I:\s+(-?[\d.]+) LUFS", err)[-1]), float(re.findall(r"Peak:\s+(-?[\d.]+) dBFS", err)[-1])

def samples(path):
    raw = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", path, "-f", "f32le", "-ac", "2", "-"], capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
    return np.frombuffer(raw, np.float32).reshape(-1, 2).astype(np.float64)

def clip_runs(ch, min_run=4):
    top = np.abs(ch).max() * 10 ** (-0.01 / 20)
    hot = np.abs(ch) >= top
    edges = np.diff(np.concatenate([[0], hot.astype(int), [0]]))
    starts, ends = np.where(edges == 1)[0], np.where(edges == -1)[0]
    return int(np.sum(ends - starts >= min_run))

def triage(path, target=-14.0):
    I, TP = meter(path); x = samples(path)
    runs = sum(clip_runs(x[:, c]) for c in range(2))
    dc = 20 * np.log10(np.abs(x.mean(0)).max() + 1e-12)
    mono = 10 * np.log10(np.mean(((x[:, 0] + x[:, 1]) / 2) ** 2) / np.mean((x ** 2).mean(1)) + 1e-12)
    fix, session = [], []
    gain = min(target - I, -1.0 - TP)          # loudest it can go by gain alone without breaking -1 dBTP
    if target - I <= -1.0 - TP:
        fix.append(f"{I:.1f} LUFS, true peak {TP:+.1f} dBTP: {target - I:+.1f} dB of plain gain reaches {target:.0f} LUFS"
                   f" with true peak at {TP + target - I:+.1f} dBTP")
    elif gain >= 0:
        fix.append(f"{I:.1f} LUFS, true peak {TP:+.1f} dBTP: gain can add {gain:.1f} dB before -1 dBTP;"
                   f" {target:.0f} LUFS needs a true-peak limiter")
    else:
        fix.append(f"{I:.1f} LUFS, true peak {TP:+.1f} dBTP: needs {-gain:.1f} dB less, or a true-peak limiter")
    if runs >= 3: session.append(f"{runs} flat-topped runs: something clipped before the bounce. Find it and fix it there")
    if dc > -40: session.append(f"DC offset {dc:.0f} dBFS: find the track or plugin causing it")
    if mono < -4.5: session.append(f"mono fold-down loses {-mono:.1f} dB: parts cancel in mono. Check wideners and polarity")
    print(f"== {path}")
    for s in fix: print("  MASTER CAN FIX   " + s)
    for s in session: print("  OPEN THE SESSION " + s)
    print("  verdict: " + ("open the session first" if session else "honest mix, a mastering pass is fine") + "\n")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for p in sys.argv[1:]: triage(p)
We ran it on three synthetic files, made from a generated beat and a speech-like test voice, not a real song. The first is an honest mix that’s simply quiet. The second is the same mix where a 6-second chorus flat-topped in a fixed-point bounce and then the whole file was turned down 3 dB. The third adds a pad whose left and right channels are opposite polarity, the kind of thing a careless stereo widener does.
$ python3 mix_triage.py mix_quiet.wav mix_clipped.wav mix_wide.wav
== mix_quiet.wav
  MASTER CAN FIX   -19.0 LUFS, true peak -3.3 dBTP: gain can add 2.3 dB before -1 dBTP; -14 LUFS needs a true-peak limiter
  verdict: honest mix, a mastering pass is fine

== mix_clipped.wav
  MASTER CAN FIX   -13.8 LUFS, true peak -0.1 dBTP: needs 0.9 dB less, or a true-peak limiter
  OPEN THE SESSION 547 flat-topped runs: something clipped before the bounce. Find it and fix it there
  verdict: open the session first

== mix_wide.wav
  MASTER CAN FIX   -19.0 LUFS, true peak -6.7 dBTP: +5.0 dB of plain gain reaches -14 LUFS with true peak at -1.7 dBTP
  OPEN THE SESSION mono fold-down loses 4.9 dB: parts cancel in mono. Check wideners and polarity
  verdict: open the session first
Reading those, still on synthetic audio:
- The quiet mix is a mastering job. Plain gain gets it 2.3 dB louder before true peak hits −1 dBTP. Going further toward −14 LUFS needs a true-peak limiter, which is exactly what a mastering pass does.
- The clipped mix is louder than the quiet one and its peak reads below full scale, so a quick look says it’s fine. It has 547 flat-topped runs. No limiter can put those tops back.
- The wide mix measures well: −19 LUFS, lots of peak headroom. But it loses 4.9 dB when folded to mono, where an ordinary stereo mix loses well under 3 dB. A mastering pass would make it louder and leave the pad vanishing on phones.
Treat the thresholds as starting points, not rules. Some genres clip on purpose, and some wide ambient music is meant to be wide. The script only tells you where to look.

### Why does a clipped mix look fine on a peak meter?
Because a peak meter only tells you the highest value in the file, not how it got there. If a bounce clips at full scale and someone later turns the file down 3 dB, the peak reads −3 dBFS and looks like a sensible, careful mix. The flat tops are still there, just 3 dB lower. That’s why the script looks for runs of several identical samples at the file’s own maximum, instead of checking for 0 dBFS.
You can see it by eye, too. Zoom into the loudest moment of the waveform. A healthy wave is rounded at its peaks. A clipped one has a flat lid on it, often for several samples in a row.

### When is a one-click mastering pass the right call?
More often than purists admit. If the triage comes back clean and the mix sounds right on two or three systems, an automatic pass that brings it to a sensible level with a legal peak is a perfectly good master for a lot of releases: demos, beat tapes, socials, a single you need out by Friday. The reason to use a local tool for that is speed and privacy. Your unreleased song stays on your machine, and you can rerun it as often as you like.
It’s the wrong call when you’re hoping it will fix something you already suspect is wrong. If you’re reaching for the mastering tool because the vocal feels buried, the vocal fader is the faster fix. The essay on when not to reach for the limiter makes the same point from the other side, and splitting stems can help you find which part is causing trouble when you only have the bounce.

### What should you check after the master?
A master is a new render, so check it like one:
1. Measure the file you’ll upload. Integrated LUFS and true peak. Under −1 dBTP for most services; Spotify’s own guidance asks for under −2 dBTP when a master is louder than −14 LUFS.
2. Compare at matched loudness. Turn the master down to the mix’s level and switch between them. If the master only sounds better when it’s louder, it isn’t better.
3. Listen in mono and on a small speaker. That’s where widener problems and lost bass show up.
4. Keep the mix file. If you need a different master later, start from the mix, not from the master.
Note: If you do want a quick local pass for honest mixes, the Audio Mix & Mastering .bat runs on your own machine. Pair it with CoProducer’s analyzer before and after, so you know whether the mix was ready and whether the render is legal.
The short version: master the mix you have when it’s honest, and reopen the session when it isn’t. Ten minutes of fixing a clipped bus beats an hour of trying to hide it.
Q: Can mastering fix a bad mix?
A: Only the parts of it that affect the whole file the same way: overall loudness, the peak ceiling, and broad tone like a mix that’s a little dark. Anything inside one part of the mix, like a clipped vocal, a buried snare, a bad edit or a widener that cancels in mono, has to be fixed in the session.
Q: Will an automatic mastering tool replace a mastering engineer?
A: It replaces waiting on simple jobs: turning an honest mix up to a sensible level with a legal peak. It doesn’t replace judgment on a mix with real problems, and it can’t tell you that the problem is in the mix. That’s still your call, or an engineer’s.
Q: How can I tell if my mix clipped before I bounced it?
A: Look for flat tops: runs of several samples in a row sitting at the file’s highest level. A peak meter won’t show it if the file was turned down afterwards, because the peak then reads below 0 dBFS. A clip detector, or zooming in on the loudest part of the waveform, will.
Q: Should I check the file again after mastering?
A: Yes. Measure the exact file you’ll upload: integrated loudness, true peak, and a quick mono listen. Any processing, including a one-click master, is a new render with new peaks.

---

## What does a mix score mean? How to read a CoProducer score
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/how-to-read-a-coproducer-score.html
Section: Scoring · 21 August 2026 · 7 min
Summary: A CoProducer score is 100 minus points lost for loudness, true peak, clipping, phase and sample rate. 90+ means release ready. Here’s how to read the findings.

A CoProducer score is 100 minus the points a file loses for specific technical findings: loudness far from −14 LUFS, true peak over −1 dBTP, clipped samples, squashed dynamics, weak mono compatibility, and a sample rate under 44.1 kHz. 90 or more rates as Release ready, which means it passes those checks. It doesn’t mean the song is good. The number is a headline. The findings underneath tell you what to fix, and two files with nearly the same score can need completely different fixes.
It’s natural to stare at the number. You bounce, you get a 77, you want an 85. But a 77 is a sum, and sums hide things. One big problem and three small ones can add up to the same score. So it helps to know how the number is built, then mostly ignore it.

### Where does a CoProducer score come from?
The desktop engine’s scoring is in plain sight in the CoProducer source on GitHub. It measures the file, checks each result against a target, and charges points on a ramp. A tiny miss costs nearly nothing, and a big miss costs up to a fixed maximum for that check. The main ones:
- Loudness, measured to ITU-R BS.1770, against −14 LUFS. That’s where Spotify normalizes playback. Too loud costs more than too quiet, because a loud master gets turned down anyway and keeps its distortion.
- True peak against −1 dBTP, with a small tolerance. This is the ceiling Spotify recommends so lossy encoding doesn’t add distortion.
- Clipped samples. A handful costs a few points. Around 500 or more cost the maximum.
- Dynamics, as peak-to-RMS. Under about 6 dB starts to cost.
- Phase correlation and stereo width. Negative correlation costs the most, because parts cancel when the song plays in mono.
- Sample rate, lossy source and noise floor. Smaller, fixed costs.
Two rules sit on top. Automatic scores stop at 97, because 100 is kept for a human check. And a repair never lowers the score: if the engine’s plan wouldn’t help, you keep the original number.

### What do the rating bands mean?
- 90 and up: Release ready. Nothing serious left on the technical checks.
- 75–89: Good with minor corrections. Usually one fix away, often a trim or a true-peak limiter.
- 60–74: Usable after technical corrections. Real problems, but fixable.
- 40–59: Major corrections required. Usually several problems at once, and often a trip back to the mix.
- Under 40: Not release ready.

### Why is a 70 with 831 clips different from a 77?
The three before-and-after pairs on the CoProducer page are a good example of why you read the findings and not the integer.
- Crazy Stacy, 70 to 90. The before had 831 clipped samples, a true peak of +0.33 dBTP and −12.61 LUFS. Clipping is the emergency there, because flat-topped samples are already damaged. After the repair: 0 clips, −13.63 LUFS, true peak +0.04 dBTP.
- BeatGoHard, 77 to 95. No clips at all. The headline problem was a true peak of −0.3 dBTP, just over the ceiling, on a mix at −15.11 LUFS. That’s a small, clean fix, and the after landed at −1.0 dBTP.
- Drippin, 66 to 93. 231,310 clipped samples, −11.92 LUFS and +1.06 dBTP. That’s a file being driven far too hard. The after sits at −14.12 LUFS with 0 clips.
A 70 and a 77 are seven points apart, but one is “stop, the file is damaged” and the other is “trim it a little”. The integer can’t tell you that. The findings can.

### Can I see how the points add up on my own files?
Yes. To show the shape without using anybody’s real song, we wrote a small open script. It’s a simplified re-creation of the engine’s penalty table, not the engine itself, so its numbers can differ from CoProducer’s. It needs Python 3, NumPy and FFmpeg, and it only reads your files.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""score_explain.py: show where a 0-100 'release readiness' score loses its points.
Usage: python3 score_explain.py FILE [FILE ...]
This is a SIMPLIFIED, OPEN RE-CREATION of the kind of graduated penalty table CoProducer's desktop
engine uses (target -14 LUFS, ceiling -1.0 dBTP, 0 clips, phase, 44.1 kHz minimum). It is not the
engine itself, so its numbers can differ from CoProducer's. The point is the shape: each finding
costs points on a ramp, the total is just 100 minus the costs, and the findings tell you what to fix.
Needs: Python 3, NumPy, FFmpeg/ffprobe on PATH."""
import json, re, subprocess, sys
import numpy as np

TARGET, CEILING, MIN_RATE, TP_TOL, MAX_AUTO = -14.0, -1.0, 44100, 0.15, 97

def ramp(x, start, full, most):
    """0 below start, `most` above full, a straight line in between."""
    if x <= start: return 0.0
    return most if x >= full else most * (x - start) / (full - start)

def measure(path):
    err = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-hide_banner", "-nostats", "-i", path, "-af",
                          "ebur128=peak=true+sample", "-f", "null", "-"], capture_output=True, text=True).stderr
    summ = err[err.rindex("Summary:"):]
    I = float(re.search(r"I:\s+(-?[\d.]+) LUFS", summ).group(1))
    peaks = re.findall(r"Peak:\s+(-?[\d.]+|-inf) dBFS", summ)       # [sample peak, true peak]
    sp, tp = float(peaks[0]), float(peaks[1])
    rate = int(json.loads(subprocess.run(["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-show_streams", "-of", "json", path],
                                         capture_output=True, text=True).stdout)["streams"][0]["sample_rate"])
    raw = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", path, "-f", "f32le", "-ac", "2", "-"], capture_output=True).stdout
    x = np.frombuffer(raw, np.float32).reshape(-1, 2).astype(np.float64)
    pk = np.max(np.abs(x)); rms = np.sqrt(np.mean(x ** 2))
    clips = int(np.sum(np.abs(x) >= 10 ** (-0.01 / 20))) if pk >= 10 ** (-0.01 / 20) else 0
    phase = float(np.sum(x[:, 0] * x[:, 1]) / np.sqrt(np.sum(x[:, 0] ** 2) * np.sum(x[:, 1] ** 2)))
    return dict(lufs=I, tp=tp, sp=sp, rate=rate, clips=clips, phase=phase, dyn=20 * np.log10(pk / rms))

def score(m):
    f = []  # (points lost, finding, what to do)
    d = m["lufs"] - TARGET
    if d > 1: f.append((ramp(d, 1, 6, 14), f"Loud for streaming: {m['lufs']:.1f} LUFS ({d:+.1f} LU)", "turn the master down; platforms will anyway"))
    elif d < -2: f.append((ramp(-d, 2, 10, 8), f"Quiet: {m['lufs']:.1f} LUFS ({d:+.1f} LU)", "optional: raise level, or accept a quieter release"))
    over = max(m["tp"], m["sp"]) - CEILING
    if over > TP_TOL: f.append((ramp(over, TP_TOL, 2.5, 16), f"True peak {m['tp']:+.1f} dBTP over the {CEILING:.0f} dBTP ceiling", "true-peak limiter or a small gain trim"))
    if m["clips"]:
        p = ramp(m["clips"], 1, 500, 18); p = min(p, 4) if m["clips"] < 8 else p
        f.append((p, f"{m['clips']} samples at full scale (clipping)", "go back to the unclipped mix; limiting can't rebuild flat tops"))
    if m["dyn"] < 6: f.append((ramp(6 - m["dyn"], 0, 4, 10), f"Peak-to-RMS only {m['dyn']:.1f} dB", "ease off compression/limiting"))
    if m["phase"] < 0: f.append((ramp(-m["phase"], 0, 0.5, 18), f"Phase correlation {m['phase']:.2f} (negative)", "fix polarity/widening; check in mono"))
    elif m["phase"] < 0.25: f.append((ramp(0.25 - m["phase"], 0, 0.25, 9), f"Phase correlation {m['phase']:.2f} (weak mono)", "check in mono; narrow the widest part"))
    if m["rate"] < MIN_RATE: f.append((8, f"Sample rate {m['rate']} Hz", "export at 44.1 kHz or higher"))
    f = [(int(round(p)), a, b) for p, a, b in f]
    s = max(0, 100 - sum(p for p, _, _ in f))
    capped = s > MAX_AUTO; s = min(s, MAX_AUTO)
    band = "Release ready" if s >= 90 else "Good with minor corrections" if s >= 75 else \
           "Usable after technical corrections" if s >= 60 else "Major corrections required" if s >= 40 else "Not release ready"
    return s, band, f, capped

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for p in sys.argv[1:]:
        m = measure(p); s, band, f, capped = score(m)
        print(f"{p.split('/')[-1]}: {s}  {band}")
        print(f"  measured: {m['lufs']:.1f} LUFS | TP {m['tp']:+.1f} dBTP | sample peak {m['sp']:+.1f} dBFS | clips {m['clips']} | phase {m['phase']:.2f} | {m['rate']} Hz")
        for pts, what, todo in f: print(f"  -{pts:<3} {what}  ->  {todo}")
        if not f: print("  no findings" + (f" (automatic scores stop at {MAX_AUTO}; a listen is still yours to do)" if capped else ""))
        print()
We ran it on five synthetic bounces of one generated 30-second beat (no real song): one pushed into a hard clip, one with its sample peaks limited to −0.2 dBFS, one left quiet at −21 LUFS, one limited and trimmed so its true peak lands at −1.3 dBTP, and the same clean one with a polarity-flipped noise layer added, the kind of thing a careless widener does.
$ python3 score_explain.py bounces/*.wav
a_clipped.wav: 51  Major corrections required
  measured: -6.1 LUFS | TP +2.9 dBTP | sample peak +0.0 dBFS | clips 144802 | phase 0.96 | 48000 Hz
  -14  Loud for streaming: -6.1 LUFS (+7.9 LU)  ->  turn the master down; platforms will anyway
  -16  True peak +2.9 dBTP over the -1 dBTP ceiling  ->  true-peak limiter or a small gain trim
  -18  144802 samples at full scale (clipping)  ->  go back to the unclipped mix; limiting can't rebuild flat tops
  -1   Peak-to-RMS only 5.4 dB  ->  ease off compression/limiting

b_hot_peak.wav: 85  Good with minor corrections
  measured: -13.4 LUFS | TP +1.3 dBTP | sample peak -0.2 dBFS | clips 0 | phase 0.96 | 48000 Hz
  -15  True peak +1.3 dBTP over the -1 dBTP ceiling  ->  true-peak limiter or a small gain trim

c_quiet.wav: 95  Release ready
  measured: -21.0 LUFS | TP -5.8 dBTP | sample peak -6.4 dBFS | clips 0 | phase 0.96 | 48000 Hz
  -5   Quiet: -21.0 LUFS (-7.0 LU)  ->  optional: raise level, or accept a quieter release

d_clean.wav: 97  Release ready
  measured: -14.6 LUFS | TP -1.3 dBTP | sample peak -2.8 dBFS | clips 0 | phase 0.96 | 48000 Hz
  no findings (automatic scores stop at 97; a listen is still yours to do)

e_phasey.wav: 95  Release ready
  measured: -13.3 LUFS | TP -1.3 dBTP | sample peak -1.8 dBFS | clips 0 | phase -0.14 | 48000 Hz
  -5   Phase correlation -0.14 (negative)  ->  fix polarity/widening; check in mono
$ ffmpeg -i d_clean.wav -af "pan=mono|c0=0.5*c0+0.5*c1,ebur128" -f null - 2>&1 | grep "I:" | tail -1
    I:         -17.8 LUFS
$ ffmpeg -i e_phasey.wav -af "pan=mono|c0=0.5*c0+0.5*c1,ebur128" -f null - 2>&1 | grep "I:" | tail -1
    I:         -20.7 LUFS
Each one teaches something:
- The clipped bounce (51) loses points on four separate findings. A low score is usually several problems, not one huge one. The fix list starts with “go back to the unclipped mix”, because no limiter can rebuild flat tops.
- The hot-peak bounce (85) has a single finding. Its highest sample is −0.2 dBFS, which looks fine on a sample meter, but the true peak between samples is +1.3 dBTP. One true-peak limiter pass fixes it.
- The quiet bounce (95) is 7 LU under target and still rates as Release ready, because quiet isn’t damage. Spotify does turn quiet tracks up, but only as far as their headroom allows. Using Spotify’s rule, this one (true peak −5.8 dBTP) would come up to about −16.2 LUFS, so it would still play a couple of dB quieter than its neighbours. Whether that matters is your call.
- The clean bounce (97) has no findings, so it stops at the cap.
- The phasey bounce (95) is the one to remember. It rates as Release ready with a negative correlation of −0.14. Folded to mono with FFmpeg, it fell from −13.3 to −20.7 LUFS, a 7.4 LU drop, against 3.2 LU for the clean bounce, because the flipped layer cancels itself out. On a phone speaker or a club’s mono sub, that layer is gone. A 95 can hide a real problem, so read the findings.

### Why can a repaired file score 90 with a red cell?
Because the score is graded, and the table isn’t. Crazy Stacy’s repaired file has a true peak of +0.04 dBTP. That’s still over −1, so the cell stays red even though the overall total cleared 90. That’s on purpose. Painting the cell green would be a nicer story and a worse report.
On the web analyzer there’s also an “If repaired” column. It’s a forecast of what the desktop repair plan would likely do, not a master you’ve downloaded. If the forecast still misses a target, what’s left is a mix decision, or a risk you choose to accept.

### Why does the browser show a different number from the desktop app?
The analyzer on the CoProducer page sends your file to an engine on your own computer when one is running. When it isn’t, the page estimates in the browser instead. That estimate is honest but simpler: its loudness meter is approximate and it uses its own gates (−14 LUFS within 1.5 LU, true peak at −1 dBTP or lower, 0 clips, phase at 0.2 or more, 44.1 kHz or more). A file that misses any gate is held under 90 there, while the desktop engine grades each miss on a ramp. So the same bounce can read a few points apart. Treat the desktop report as the reference and the browser number as a quick read. Either way, the file stays on your machine.

### What should I fix first?
1. Clipping. Go back to a bounce that isn’t clipped. Every other fix sits on top of this one.
2. True peak. A true-peak limiter at about −1 dBTP, or a small trim.
3. Loudness. If you’re far over −14 LUFS, turn it down rather than limit harder. Platforms will turn it down anyway.
4. Phase. Listen in mono. Find the widener or flipped layer that disappears.
5. Stop. Once the findings are clear, the last few points aren’t worth another week. The song is.
Note: Want to see your own findings? Drop a bounce on Analyze. It runs on your machine, and the table shows what each red cell is costing you.
Q: What does a CoProducer score of 90 mean?
A: It means the file passed the technical checks well enough to rate as Release ready: loudness near −14 LUFS, true peak near or under −1 dBTP, no clipping, healthy mono compatibility and a sample rate of at least 44.1 kHz. It says nothing about whether the song is good. That part is still yours.
Q: Is a score of 100 possible?
A: Not automatically. The desktop engine stops at 97, and keeps 100 for a human check. A file with no findings at all reads 97. Don’t chase the last few points. Clear the findings and trust your ears.
Q: Why can the true peak stay red after a repair?
A: Because the table shows the measurement, not a nicer story. Crazy Stacy’s repaired file reached 90 with a true peak of +0.04 dBTP. That’s still over the −1 dBTP ceiling, so the cell stays red, and the remaining fix is a gentler limiter or a small trim.
Q: Why does the browser give a different score from the desktop app?
A: When no local engine is running, the analyzer page estimates in your browser. That estimate uses a simpler meter and its own gate rules, so it can land a few points away. Use the desktop engine’s report as the reference and the browser number as a quick read.

---

## Why does my master clip after MP3 or AAC? Re-encoding eats true-peak headroom
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/reencoding-eats-true-peak-headroom.html
Section: Codecs · 21 August 2026 · 7 min
Summary: A WAV peaking at −0.1 dBFS can clip once it’s encoded to AAC or MP3. Why it happens, how much true-peak headroom to leave, and a script to test it.

Your master clips after MP3 or AAC because a lossy encoder doesn’t copy your waveform, it rebuilds it. AAC, MP3, Opus and Ogg Vorbis keep a reduced description of the sound and reconstruct it on playback, and the rebuilt peaks can land higher than the ones you limited, even above 0 dBFS. A master whose sample peaks sit at −0.1 dBFS is the classic victim. Keep true peak at or below −1.0 dBTP on the file you hand off (−2.0 if it’s louder than −14 LUFS, as Spotify asks), then encode a test and measure the result.
This one catches careful people. Your limiter is set to −0.1, the meter never goes red, the WAV has zero clipped samples. You upload it, and the streamed version has a crunch on the loudest snare hits that you can’t find anywhere in the session. You didn’t imagine it. The file the listener hears isn’t the file you bounced.

### What’s the difference between sample peak and true peak?
A sample-peak meter reports the biggest number stored in the file. But a digital file is a set of dots, and what comes out of a converter is the smooth line through them. That line can swing higher between two dots than either dot is. Those are inter-sample peaks.
The cleanest example is a bit of arithmetic. Take a 12 kHz sine at a 48 kHz sample rate. That’s exactly four samples per cycle. If the samples happen to land at 45°, 135°, 225° and 315° of the wave, every single one sits at 0.707 of the real crest. A sample-peak meter reads 3 dB low, and the wave between the samples is 3 dB hotter than anything in the file.
A true-peak meter estimates that line by oversampling the signal, following the method in ITU-R BS.1770 (the same standard that defines LUFS). Its unit is dBTP. That’s why delivery specs talk in dBTP, not dBFS.

### Why does converting to MP3 or AAC make peaks louder?
Two things happen inside a lossy encoder, and both can push peaks up:
- Rounding. The encoder cuts the audio into short blocks, turns each block into frequency components and stores them with less precision than the original. On playback the components are added back together, plus a small error. That error goes up and down at random, and wherever it adds to a peak, the peak gets taller.
- Missing top end. Lower bitrates throw away the highest frequencies. Take the sharp corners off a heavily limited waveform and it rings, overshooting where the corners used to be. That’s the same physics as the Gibbs phenomenon.
Apple says it plainly in its Apple Digital Masters guide: checking the encoded file matters, because levels that don’t show overs in PCM can still clip once encoded. The same guide recommends leaving at least 1 dB of headroom.

### What happens to a −0.1 dBFS master after five different encodes?
To put numbers on it we built a 30-second synthetic beat (kick, snare, hats, saturated bass, detuned chords; no real songs) and pushed it 6 dB into a plain sample-peak limiter set to −0.1 dBFS, the way plenty of loud masters get made. Then we encoded it with FFmpeg’s built-in AAC encoder, LAME MP3 and libopus, decoded each one to 32-bit float so overs above 0 dBFS are kept, and measured true peak. We ran it three times: as limited, trimmed so the WAV sat at −1.0 dBTP, and trimmed to −2.0 dBTP.
Decoded true peak | As limited | Trimmed to −1.0 dBTP | Trimmed to −2.0 dBTP
Source WAV | +1.2 dBTP | −1.0 dBTP | −2.0 dBTP
AAC 256 kbps | +2.6 | −0.4 | −1.3
AAC 128 kbps | +2.6 | +0.3 | −1.4
MP3 320 kbps | +1.2 | −1.2 | −2.0
MP3 128 kbps | +1.7 | −1.2 | −2.0
Opus 128 kbps | +1.2 | −1.0 | −2.0
Integrated loudness was −7.6 LUFS as limited, −9.8 and −10.8 LUFS trimmed. Synthetic material and one encoder of each kind, so trust the shape more than the decimals. What we take from it:
- The “−0.1 dBFS” master was already over before any codec touched it. The sample-peak limiter held every sample at −0.1 dBFS, and the true peak was still +1.2 dBTP. Every encode of it decoded with samples above full scale.
- −1.0 dBTP was enough for MP3 and Opus, not for AAC. MP3 and Opus stayed at or under −1.0. FFmpeg’s AAC rose 0.6 dB at 256 kbps and 1.3 dB at 128 kbps, which put the 128k file over 0 dBFS.
- −2.0 dBTP cleared everything. The worst encode came out at −1.3 dBTP.
We also ran a less-limited version of the same beat. It didn’t fare better at 128 kbps AAC: trimmed to −1.0 dBTP, it decoded at +1.9. So the encoder and bitrate decide a lot, and −1 dBTP is a floor, not a guarantee. (One method note: FFmpeg’s AAC encoder threw a spurious spike in its first few milliseconds when audio started on sample one, so each test file has half a second of silence at both ends.)
The BeatGoHard A/B above is the real-world version of the same lesson: zero clipped samples, and the true peak still had to come down from −0.3 to −1.0 dBTP before it was safe to ship.

### How much true-peak headroom do I need for streaming?
The published numbers line up:
- Spotify asks for true peak below −1 dBTP, and below −2 dBTP if the master is louder than −14 LUFS integrated, because louder tracks are more susceptible to extra distortion when encoded.
- Apple’s mastering guide recommends at least 1 dB of headroom.
So: −1.0 dBTP is the minimum. Go to −2.0 if the master is loud, or if you know it’s heading somewhere that encodes at low bitrates. If one master goes to every store, the strictest ceiling wins. And if you do any processing after the limiter (normalising, dithering, sample-rate conversion), measure after the last step you control, not on the DAW meter.

### Does a higher bitrate fix it?
It helps, but it won’t rescue a master that’s already over. In our test, AAC at 256 kbps rose 0.6 dB from a −1.0 dBTP start where 128 kbps rose 1.3 dB. But from the as-limited master, both bitrates decoded at +2.6 dBTP. Bitrate is the platform’s choice anyway. Headroom is yours.

### Why does re-encoding an already encoded file make it worse?
Because every generation starts from the last one’s overshoot. We took the −1.0 dBTP master, encoded it to AAC at 256 kbps (think: the MP4 your video editor exports), then encoded that to Opus at 128 kbps (think: what a platform makes of your upload). Straight from the WAV, Opus came out at −1.0 dBTP. Via the AAC file it came out at −0.7, and the AAC file itself was −0.4.
That 0.3 dB isn’t dramatic on its own, but it stacks with everything else. The practical rules: send stores WAV or FLAC, never an MP3 you made; give your video editor the WAV, not a streaming rip; and export video audio at the highest bitrate your editor offers.

### How do I test my own master before upload?
You don’t have to guess what an encoder will do. Encode it yourself and measure. This script runs a master through five encodes with FFmpeg and prints the true peak of each decoded file:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""codec_overshoot.py: how much does a lossy encode push your peaks up?
    python3 codec_overshoot.py master.wav            # as delivered
    python3 codec_overshoot.py master.wav -1.0       # first trim so true peak sits at -1.0 dBTP
Needs ffmpeg (with libmp3lame and libopus). Encodes to AAC, MP3 and Opus, decodes to
32-bit float (so overs above 0 dBFS are kept, not clipped) and measures each file with
ffmpeg's ebur128 filter (true peak is BS.1770 style, oversampled)."""
import re, subprocess, sys, tempfile, os

def measure(path):
    err = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-hide_banner", "-nostats", "-i", path, "-af",
                          "ebur128=peak=true+sample", "-f", "null", "-"],
                         capture_output=True, text=True).stderr
    tp = float(re.findall(r"True peak:\s+Peak:\s+(-?[\d.]+|-inf)", err)[-1])
    sp = float(re.findall(r"Sample peak:\s+Peak:\s+(-?[\d.]+|-inf)", err)[-1])
    lufs = float(re.findall(r"I:\s+(-?[\d.]+) LUFS", err)[-1])
    return lufs, sp, tp

def run(*args):
    subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-y", *args], check=True)

src = sys.argv[1]
tmp = tempfile.mkdtemp()
if len(sys.argv) > 2:                      # trim to a true-peak ceiling first
    ceiling = float(sys.argv[2])
    gain = ceiling - measure(src)[2]
    trimmed = os.path.join(tmp, "trimmed.wav")
    run("-i", src, "-af", f"volume={gain:.2f}dB", "-c:a", "pcm_f32le", trimmed)
    src = trimmed

codecs = [("AAC 256k", "m4a", ["-c:a", "aac", "-b:a", "256k"]),
          ("AAC 128k", "m4a", ["-c:a", "aac", "-b:a", "128k"]),
          ("MP3 320k", "mp3", ["-c:a", "libmp3lame", "-b:a", "320k"]),
          ("MP3 128k", "mp3", ["-c:a", "libmp3lame", "-b:a", "128k"]),
          ("Opus 128k", "opus", ["-c:a", "libopus", "-b:a", "128k"])]
I, sp, tp = measure(src)
print(f"{'file':10s} {'LUFS':>6s} {'sample pk':>10s} {'true pk':>8s} {'rise':>6s}")
print(f"{'source':10s} {I:6.1f} {sp:+9.2f}  {tp:+7.2f}")
for name, ext, opts in codecs:
    enc = os.path.join(tmp, f"enc.{ext}"); dec = os.path.join(tmp, "dec.wav")
    run("-i", src, *opts, enc)
    run("-i", enc, "-ar", "48000", "-c:a", "pcm_f32le", dec)
    _, sp2, tp2 = measure(dec)
    flag = "  <- over 0 dBFS" if sp2 > 0 else ""
    print(f"{name:10s} {'':6s} {sp2:+9.2f}  {tp2:+7.2f} {tp2 - tp:+6.2f}{flag}")
Our run on the synthetic master, trimmed to −1.0 dBTP:
$ python3 codec_overshoot.py loud_master.wav -1.0
file         LUFS  sample pk  true pk   rise
source       -9.8     -2.30    -1.00
AAC 256k              -0.70    -0.40  +0.60
AAC 128k              +0.10    +0.30  +1.30  <- over 0 dBFS
MP3 320k              -1.50    -1.20  -0.20
MP3 128k              -1.20    -1.20  -0.20
Opus 128k             -1.30    -1.00  +0.00
If anything prints over 0 dBFS, or comes out much above −1.0, trim the master and run it again. On a Mac, Apple’s own afclip tool (described in the same Apple guide) checks a file for clipping, encoded files included.
If you’d rather not run scripts at all, CoProducer’s analyzer reads true peak, integrated LUFS and clipped samples on your bounce locally. It’s a quick way to catch the −0.1 dBFS master before an encoder does.

### Do slowed, sped-up or retuned versions need a new check?
Yes, every time. Changing speed or pitch resamples the audio, which rebuilds the waveform between samples just like an encoder does, so the true peak moves even when the sample peak looks the same. A screwed render, a sped-up TikTok version and a 432 Hz retune are each a new master. Measure them as one. We’ve covered it for screwed tempos and 432 Hz retunes.
Note: Short version: limit to true peak, not sample peak, leave at least 1 dB (2 if it’s loud), and measure the encoded file once before you trust it. More on the meter itself in true peak is what codecs clip, and on doing it at the limiter in clipper vs limiter for hip-hop delivery.
Q: Why does my song clip after converting to MP3 or AAC?
A: Lossy encoders rebuild your waveform from a reduced description of it, and the rebuilt peaks can land higher than the originals, even above 0 dBFS. A master limited to −0.1 dBFS sample peak has no room for that. Leave true-peak headroom and measure the encoded file.
Q: Does MP3 need more headroom than AAC?
A: It depends on the encoder and bitrate more than the format name. In our synthetic test, FFmpeg’s AAC encoder overshot the most (a −1.0 dBTP master rose 1.3 dB at 128 kbps), while MP3 and Opus barely moved. Your distributor uses its own encoders, so measure an encode rather than trusting folklore.
Q: Is −1 dBTP enough headroom for streaming?
A: It’s the usual floor. Spotify asks for true peak below −1 dBTP, or below −2 dBTP if the master is louder than −14 LUFS, and Apple recommends at least 1 dB of headroom. In our test, −1 dBTP was enough for MP3 and Opus but not for FFmpeg’s AAC (−0.4 dBTP at 256 kbps, +0.3 at 128 kbps); −2 dBTP kept every encode at or below −1.3 dBTP.
Q: Do slowed, sped-up or retuned versions need a new true-peak check?
A: Yes. Changing speed or pitch resamples the audio, which rebuilds the waveform and moves the peaks between samples. Re-measure every screwed, sped-up or retuned render before it ships, even if the original master passed.
